aliases.value: Santa Cruz black salamander (A. f. niger)
Red-lipped plateau lizard (former subspecies S. undulatus erythrocheilus in Wyoming)
Northern plateau lizard (former subspecies S. undulatus elongatus in Wyoming)
western lyre snake (former subspecies T. biscutatus lambda)
Mississippi mud turtle (subspecies K. s. hippocrepis)
Western slender glass lizard (O. a. longicaudus)
Eastern slender glass lizard (O. a. attenuatus)
Black ratsnake (former name Elaphe o. obsoleta)

resources.title: American alligator
resources.description: Identify the american alligator (Alligator mississippiensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis): Blackish or olive-drab above; young have bold yellowish crossbands that may persist faintly in adults. Broadly rounded snout; no conspicuous upward-protruding lower teeth when the mouth is closed. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal North Carolina to the Florida Keys, west to southern Texas, north to southeastern Oklahoma and Arkansas. Not native to Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web lists the family as Crocodylidae; NatureServe gives Alligatoridae, used here.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal North Carolina to the Florida Keys, west to southern Texas, north to southeastern Oklahoma and Arkansas. Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Blackish or olive-drab above; young have bold yellowish crossbands that may persist faintly in adults.
Broadly rounded snout; no conspicuous upward-protruding lower teeth when the mouth is closed.
Adults generally 4 m or less (maximum about 5.8 m); males much larger than females.
Hatchlings about 21-23 cm.
Compared with the american crocodile: Narrower snout and a fourth lower tooth that protrudes upward near the snout tip.
Compared with the spectacled caiman: Has a curved bony crosswise ridge in front of the eyes, which the alligator lacks.

habitat.text: Fresh and brackish marshes, ponds, lakes, rivers, swamps, bayous and canals; basks on logs or banks.

behavior.text: Spring courtship includes loud bellowing and head slaps on the water
Inactive or less active from about late November to March in the northern range
Digs dens in banks and 'gator holes' used in cold spells and drought
Opportunistic feeder: invertebrates and small fish when young; birds, reptiles and mammals as large adults

resources.title: Burmese python
resources.description: Identify the burmese python (Python bivittatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Burmese python (Python bivittatus): Large reddish-brown blotches outlined in cream or gold over a pale tan, yellowish-brown or grey base. Arrow-shaped marking on top of the head pointing toward the nose. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to northeastern India east through southern China and Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. Established in the Florida Everglades (first nest found in 2006). Not native to Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Crother (2008) treated it as a subspecies of the Indian python (P. molurus); Nicholson (2025) recognizes P. bivittatus. Animal Diversity Web also uses the subspecies treatment.

rangeSummary.value: Native to northeastern India east through southern China and Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. Established in the Florida Everglades (first nest found in 2006). Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Large reddish-brown blotches outlined in cream or gold over a pale tan, yellowish-brown or grey base.
Arrow-shaped marking on top of the head pointing toward the nose.
Heavy-bodied; can exceed 5 m, females larger than males.
Every life stage larger than any native snake in its Florida range.
Compared with the northern african python: Less vivid back pattern and black-and-white belly scales; Burmese python belly scales are white.

habitat.text: Grasslands, swamps, marshes, rocky foothills, open woodland and river valleys.

behavior.text: Excellent swimmers, often partly or fully submerged; tied to permanent fresh water
Generalist ambush predator of mammals, birds and reptiles
Everglades mating season is December-April, eggs laid May-June; breeding aggregations of several males with one female

resources.title: Argentine black and white tegu
resources.description: Identify the argentine black and white tegu (Salvator merianae), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Argentine black and white tegu (Salvator merianae): Large lizard reaching nearly 5 ft. Mottled black and white, often arranged in bands across the back and tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, Uruguay and Argentina. Breeding populations in Florida (Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Charlotte counties per FWC); NatureServe lists Florida and Georgia as established and possibly South Carolina. Not native to Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Native to Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, Uruguay and Argentina. Breeding populations in Florida (Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Charlotte counties per FWC); NatureServe lists Florida and Georgia as established and possibly South Carolina. Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Large lizard reaching nearly 5 ft.
Mottled black and white, often arranged in bands across the back and tail.
Hatchlings have similar markings and bright green heads; the green fades after about one month.

habitat.text: Savannas and disturbed habitats such as forest clearings, roadsides and fence rows; tolerates flooded marshes.

behavior.text: Terrestrial, rarely climbs more than a few feet, strong swimmer
Retreats into burrows for winter brumation; in south Florida emerges from about February
Omnivore and efficient egg predator of ground-nesting birds and reptiles

resources.title: Green iguana
resources.description: Identify the green iguana (Iguana iguana), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green iguana (Iguana iguana): Typically green, but can be brown or nearly black; some adults turn orange or pink seasonally. Row of spikes down the centre of neck, back and upper tail; dark black rings on the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Central America through tropical South America and some Caribbean islands. Introduced in southern Florida (mostly the southern half of the peninsula, commonest near the coast), Puerto Rico and Hawaii. Not native to Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Native from Central America through tropical South America and some Caribbean islands. Introduced in southern Florida (mostly the southern half of the peninsula, commonest near the coast), Puerto Rico and Hawaii. Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Typically green, but can be brown or nearly black; some adults turn orange or pink seasonally.
Row of spikes down the centre of neck, back and upper tail; dark black rings on the tail.
Mature males have heavy jowls and a much larger dewlap (throat fan) than females.
Males reach over 5 ft and 17 lb; females usually stay under 7 lb.

habitat.text: Trees, shrubs and ground in forest, urban, suburban and agricultural settings; lives in burrows and culverts in cleared areas of Florida.

behavior.text: Mostly arboreal; excellent swimmer that can submerge up to four hours
Mainly herbivorous: leaves, flowers and fruit; adults also take bird eggs and carrion
Males signal with head-bobbing and dewlap extension
Not cold-hardy, which limits establishment northward

resources.title: Common snapping turtle
resources.description: Identify the common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina): Upper shell saw-toothed at the rear, usually under 36 cm (max nearly 50 cm). Tail as long as or longer than the shell, with a crest of large bony scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: East of the Rockies from the Canadian border to the Gulf and Atlantic; in Canada mainland Nova Scotia, southern New Brunswick, southern and central Québec and Ontario, southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan. Introduced in the western US and Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses Snapping Turtle and notes the 'common' adjective was dropped (Crother et al. 2008); some authors have proposed splitting the Florida population (C. osceola).

rangeSummary.value: East of the Rockies from the Canadian border to the Gulf and Atlantic; in Canada mainland Nova Scotia, southern New Brunswick, southern and central Québec and Ontario, southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan. Introduced in the western US and Canada.

identification.text: Upper shell saw-toothed at the rear, usually under 36 cm (max nearly 50 cm).
Tail as long as or longer than the shell, with a crest of large bony scales.
Large head with hooked jaws; small lower shell (plastron) leaves limbs exposed.
Hatchlings rough-shelled with conspicuous ridges, looking like a dead leaf.

habitat.text: All freshwater habitats, especially soft mud bottoms with abundant vegetation or submerged brush and logs; also brackish water.

behavior.text: Mostly on the bottom; younger animals and far-northern turtles sometimes bask
Decreases activity in late summer, relatively inactive in winter, resumes about April
Females may travel up to several km to nest, often in open soft soil far from water
Eats many vertebrates, invertebrates and plants

resources.title: Spiny softshell
resources.description: Identify the spiny softshell (Apalone spinifera), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spiny softshell (Apalone spinifera): Soft, flat, leathery shell without scutes, olive to tan with black speckles; flexible edge bears small spines. Narrow head ending in a tubular nose. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Montana to southern Québec, south to northern Mexico and the Florida panhandle, with introductions elsewhere. In Québec it is concentrated around Lake Champlain and its tributaries.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe recognizes six subspecies and notes Apalone was split from Trionyx; Animal Diversity Web still lists the older name Trionyx spiniferus.

rangeSummary.value: Montana to southern Québec, south to northern Mexico and the Florida panhandle, with introductions elsewhere. In Québec it is concentrated around Lake Champlain and its tributaries.

identification.text: Soft, flat, leathery shell without scutes, olive to tan with black speckles; flexible edge bears small spines.
Narrow head ending in a tubular nose.
Two light black-bordered bands on each side of the head.
Males 12.7-24 cm, females larger at 24-48 cm and mottled grey.

habitat.text: Large rivers, impoundments, lakes and pools with open sandy or mud banks and soft bottoms.

behavior.text: Basks on shores or partly submerged logs; buries in bottom sediment when inactive
Activity mainly April/May to October in the north; some nocturnal activity in summer
In Vermont-Québec waters moved about 3 km between wintering and nesting sites
Eats crayfish, insects, mollusks, fish and amphibians

resources.title: Red-eared slider
resources.description: Identify the red-eared slider (Trachemys scripta), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red-eared slider (Trachemys scripta): Bright red horizontal streak behind each eye. Shell 10-29 cm, greenish-yellow to gray, brown or black, rough and indented; plastron usually yellow with dark spots. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Michigan to Argentina, east of New Mexico. Established outside its range in many areas including Florida, New York and New Mexico; Animal Diversity Web also lists Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the species as Pond Slider; the red-eared slider is one subspecies (T. s. elegans) of Trachemys scripta.
Native in the south-central US; introduced elsewhere

rangeSummary.value: Native from Michigan to Argentina, east of New Mexico. Established outside its range in many areas including Florida, New York and New Mexico; Animal Diversity Web also lists Canada.

identification.text: Bright red horizontal streak behind each eye.
Shell 10-29 cm, greenish-yellow to gray, brown or black, rough and indented; plastron usually yellow with dark spots.
Females larger than males.
Older males may turn melanistic (darker).
Compared with the painted turtle: Two yellow patches behind each eye instead of the slider's single red streak (per Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Quiet water with abundant aquatic vegetation, soft bottom and basking sites; tolerant of pollution.

behavior.text: Primarily diurnal; basks on sunny days and is gregarious
Juveniles mostly carnivorous; adults omnivorous
Generally inactive in winter in the north

resources.title: Timber rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Timber rattlesnake (Crotalus horridus): Horny rattle on the tail tip; broad head and vertical pupil in bright light. Heat-sensing pit on each side of the face between eye and nostril. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central New England to northern Florida, west to eastern Texas, central Oklahoma, eastern Kansas, southeastern Nebraska, Iowa and southeastern Minnesota; spotty at the western and northern edges. NatureServe ranks it NX (presumed extirpated) in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Central New England to northern Florida, west to eastern Texas, central Oklahoma, eastern Kansas, southeastern Nebraska, Iowa and southeastern Minnesota; spotty at the western and northern edges. NatureServe ranks it NX (presumed extirpated) in Canada.

identification.text: Horny rattle on the tail tip; broad head and vertical pupil in bright light.
Heat-sensing pit on each side of the face between eye and nostril.
Almost always dark crossbands on a yellow, black or gray background, sometimes a reddish mid-back stripe.
Heavy-bodied with keeled scales and a coarse, dull skin; usually under 150 cm.
Compared with the milk snake: Slender with smooth glossy skin, no rattle and no facial pit.
Compared with the northern water snake: Lacks the rattle and the facial pit.
Compared with the eastern hognose snake: Lacks the rattle and the facial pit.

habitat.text: Northeast: hilly forest with rocky outcrops and ledges; Midwest: rocky bluffs; South: hardwood forest, river bottoms and swampy areas.

behavior.text: Emerges from dens about mid-April to May and returns about mid-September to October
Northern and upland snakes hibernate communally; males typically stay within 3.6 km of the den
Eats mainly small mammals; lizards in the south
Ambushes prey along fallen logs

resources.title: Eastern copperhead
resources.description: Identify the eastern copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern copperhead (Agkistrodon contortrix): Reddish-brown body with tan, copper and rich brown crossbands. Solid brown head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern New England to northern Florida, west through the southern Great Lakes states and southern Iowa to southeastern Nebraska, eastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas. Not a Canadian species.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses Eastern Copperhead and recognizes no subspecies; Animal Diversity Web names it Southern Copperhead.

rangeSummary.value: Southern New England to northern Florida, west through the southern Great Lakes states and southern Iowa to southeastern Nebraska, eastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas. Not a Canadian species.

identification.text: Reddish-brown body with tan, copper and rich brown crossbands.
Solid brown head.
Adults average about 76 cm.
Juveniles greyer with a yellow-tinted tail tip until about age 3-4.
Compared with the water snakes and cottonmouth: Animal Diversity Web notes they resemble copperheads but differ in pattern and behaviour.

habitat.text: Deciduous forest with rock outcrops, floodplains and swamp edges; often with rocks, logs, stumps or leaf litter as cover.

behavior.text: Diurnal in spring and fall, mostly nocturnal in summer
Active about April to October/November in the north; hibernates communally in rocky dens or burrows
Sit-and-wait feeder on small mammals, snakes, lizards, amphibians, insects and small birds
May migrate several hundred metres between winter den and summer range

resources.title: Prairie rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the prairie rattlesnake (Crotalus viridis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Prairie rattlesnake (Crotalus viridis): 45-165 cm; light brown to black with a yellow head stripe (per Animal Diversity Web). Horny rattle on the tail tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan south to northern Mexico, west to Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and extreme eastern Arizona, east to the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (following Crother 2017) restricts C. viridis to the prairie forms; the western forms are C. oreganus. Animal Diversity Web still treats oreganus as a C. viridis subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan south to northern Mexico, west to Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and extreme eastern Arizona, east to the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

identification.text: 45-165 cm; light brown to black with a yellow head stripe (per Animal Diversity Web).
Horny rattle on the tail tip.
Cryptic belly pattern in tan, yellow and gray.
Compared with the western rattlesnake: Formerly grouped with C. viridis; ranges from southern British Columbia to Baja California and east to the Rockies.

habitat.text: Prairies, arid basins and wooded mountains; uses mammal burrows, crevices and caves when inactive.

behavior.text: Mostly diurnal in cool weather, active in the evening and at night in hot weather
Active about late March/April to October/November
Migrates up to about 11 km between winter den and summer range and shows den fidelity
Eats mainly small mammals; juveniles in some regions mostly lizards

resources.title: Western rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the western rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus): Horny rattle on the tail tip; head much broader than the neck. Heat-sensing pit on each side of the face; vertical pupil in bright light. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia south to central Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains.

taxonomicNotes.text: Recently split from C. viridis (Pook 2000; Ashton & de Queiroz 2001; Douglas 2002); some older sources treat it as a subspecies of C. viridis. NatureServe notes the boundary in the Four Corners region needs clarification.

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia south to central Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains.

identification.text: Horny rattle on the tail tip; head much broader than the neck.
Heat-sensing pit on each side of the face; vertical pupil in bright light.
Colour from light tan or pink to black with large blotches on back and sides, banded tail.
Light stripe from behind the eye to the mouth corner; rarely exceeds 3.3 ft.
Compared with the prairie rattlesnake: Former parent species; occupies the plains east of the Rockies from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Compared with the gopher snake: Makes a hiss that can sound like rattling but has no rattle.

habitat.text: Shrubby coastal dunes to timberline, basins, canyons and open mountain forest; uses mammal burrows and crevices.

behavior.text: Rattle can sound for minutes; burrowing owls and gopher snakes make hissing that resembles it
Diet mainly small mammals, also birds, lizards and rarely amphibians
In British Columbia gravid females generally did not feed
Pregnant females may congregate near winter dens

resources.title: American bullfrog
resources.description: Identify the american bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus): Green or brown, usually with dark spots or mottling, not large rounded spots. No ridges along each side of the back; large eardrum with a skin fold curving around it. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and southern Québec west to the Great Lakes and south through most of the central and eastern US to northeastern Mexico; widely introduced in the west.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes American ranid genus arrangements are contested (Lithobates vs Rana); the batch name follows NatureServe's Lithobates. NatureServe's English name is North American Bullfrog.
Introduced and invasive in the west

rangeSummary.value: Native from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and southern Québec west to the Great Lakes and south through most of the central and eastern US to northeastern Mexico; widely introduced in the west.

identification.text: Green or brown, usually with dark spots or mottling, not large rounded spots.
No ridges along each side of the back; large eardrum with a skin fold curving around it.
Males: eardrum distinctly larger than the eye, yellow throat in breeding season, swollen thumb base.
Up to about 20 cm snout-vent; 4th hind toe extends past the webbing.
Compared with the green frog: Has a ridge along each side of the back and a banjo-string call; bullfrogs have no such ridges.

habitat.text: Ponds, swamps, lakes, marshes and ditches with floating or emergent vegetation.

behavior.text: Breeding call is a deep bellowing 'um-rum'
Movements and breeding mostly at dusk and at night, though it calls by day too
Larvae usually overwinter at least once in the north
Eats any animal it can swallow

resources.title: Green frog
resources.description: Identify the green frog (Lithobates clamitans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green frog (Lithobates clamitans): Green, brownish or bronze (nearly black when cold) with dark spots. A straight ridge along each side of the back from behind the eye that does not reach the groin. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States and adjacent southeastern Canada. Introduced in Newfoundland, British Columbia, Washington and Utah.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes American ranid genus arrangements are contested (Lithobates vs Rana); the batch name follows NatureServe's Lithobates. NatureServe does not recognize subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States and adjacent southeastern Canada. Introduced in Newfoundland, British Columbia, Washington and Utah.

identification.text: Green, brownish or bronze (nearly black when cold) with dark spots.
A straight ridge along each side of the back from behind the eye that does not reach the groin.
Hind legs crossbanded; toe webbing does not reach the tip of the 5th toe.
Male eardrum much larger than the eye, throat may be yellow; up to 10.8 cm.
Compared with the american bullfrog: Lacks the dorsolateral ridges.
Compared with the mink frog: Animal Diversity Web says the dorsolateral folds separate green frogs from mink frogs.

habitat.text: Almost any permanent or semi-permanent water and vernal pools.

behavior.text: Call is a single croak or series, like a plucked loose banjo string
Males call mainly May-August in the north
Often leaps into water with a 'squeenk' when approached
Inactive in cold weather; many overwinter in small streams

resources.title: Northern leopard frog
resources.description: Identify the northern leopard frog (Lithobates pipiens), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern leopard frog (Lithobates pipiens): Slim, long-legged, green or brownish. Well-defined round or oval dark spots with pale borders. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Great Slave Lake, Hudson Bay and Labrador south to southern New England, Kentucky, Nebraska, New Mexico and Arizona, west to southeastern British Columbia and eastern Washington/Oregon; spotty and partly introduced in the west.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes American ranid genus arrangements are contested (Lithobates vs Rana); the batch name follows NatureServe's Lithobates.

rangeSummary.value: Great Slave Lake, Hudson Bay and Labrador south to southern New England, Kentucky, Nebraska, New Mexico and Arizona, west to southeastern British Columbia and eastern Washington/Oregon; spotty and partly introduced in the west.

identification.text: Slim, long-legged, green or brownish.
Well-defined round or oval dark spots with pale borders.
Pale dorsolateral ridges not inset at the rear; white stripe on the upper jaw.
Adults 5-9 cm, occasionally to 11 cm.
Compared with the pickerel frog: Squarish spots and yellow or orange on the hidden hind-limb and groin surfaces.
Compared with the plains leopard frog: Never green, usually a pale spot on the eardrum, ridge rear ends inset.

habitat.text: Near springs, slow streams, marshes, bogs, ponds and lakes with rooted aquatic vegetation; wet meadows in summer.

behavior.text: Egg laying about April in southern Québec and the Great Lakes, later farther north
Summer use of wet meadows and fields
Eats small invertebrates at the water's edge or in fields

resources.title: Plains leopard frog
resources.description: Identify the plains leopard frog (Lithobates blairi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plains leopard frog (Lithobates blairi): Never green; usually a distinct pale spot on the eardrum. Posterior end of the dorsolateral ridges inset or angled inward. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern South Dakota to central Texas, west to eastern Colorado and eastern New Mexico, east to Indiana and southeastern Missouri; disjunct in southeastern Arizona. Hybridizes with northern leopard frog in eastern Colorado and Nebraska. Not a Canadian species.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes American ranid genus arrangements are contested (Lithobates vs Rana); the batch name follows NatureServe's Lithobates. Older literature refers to it as Rana pipiens.

rangeSummary.value: Southern South Dakota to central Texas, west to eastern Colorado and eastern New Mexico, east to Indiana and southeastern Missouri; disjunct in southeastern Arizona. Hybridizes with northern leopard frog in eastern Colorado and Nebraska. Not a Canadian species.

identification.text: Never green; usually a distinct pale spot on the eardrum.
Posterior end of the dorsolateral ridges inset or angled inward.
Light line along the upper jaw and a dark snout spot (per Animal Diversity Web).
Yellow on the groin and underside of the thigh (per Animal Diversity Web).
Compared with the northern leopard frog: Can be green, usually lacks the pale eardrum spot, ridges not inset at the rear.

habitat.text: Streams, ponds, ditches and marshes in prairie, desert grassland and farmland; may range into surrounding land in wet weather.

behavior.text: Males call from the water surface; call of 2-3 distinct 'chucks' (Animal Diversity Web)
Lays eggs in spring, summer or early fall, often after heavy rain
Burrows into mud in winter; some move up to 8 km between ponds

resources.title: Northwestern salamander
resources.description: Identify the northwestern salamander (Ambystoma gracile), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northwestern salamander (Ambystoma gracile): Smooth olive-green to brown or dark brown back, often with blotches and sometimes yellow flecks along the sides. Swollen parotoid glands behind each eye, unusual among ambystomatids. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Pacific coast from extreme southeastern Alaska through coastal British Columbia, Washington and Oregon to northern California (Mendocino area), from sea level to about 3,110 m.

rangeSummary.value: Pacific coast from extreme southeastern Alaska through coastal British Columbia, Washington and Oregon to northern California (Mendocino area), from sea level to about 3,110 m.

identification.text: Smooth olive-green to brown or dark brown back, often with blotches and sometimes yellow flecks along the sides.
Swollen parotoid glands behind each eye, unusual among ambystomatids.
Glandular ridge along the top of the tail, which tapers sharply toward the tip.
Terrestrial adults about 14-22 cm total length; aquatic adults reach about 26 cm.
Breeding males are darker than females; unmetamorphosed males have enlarged hind limbs and feet.

habitat.text: Humid forest, woodland and open grassland near breeding ponds; adults shelter under rotting logs, leaf litter and debris along stream banks or in animal burrows.
Eggs are laid attached to vegetation in ponds, lakes and slow streams; montane populations are often paedomorphic (remain gilled).

behavior.text: Non-paedomorphic adults live underground most of the year and are seen mainly at breeding time and on fall rains.
Adults migrate on rainy nights between nonbreeding habitat and breeding ponds; breeding runs from January in the south to July in the north or at elevation.
Nocturnal on land; aquatic forms are strictly nocturnal where fish are present. When alarmed it assumes a defensive posture and secretes a milky toxic substance.
Feeds on soft-bodied invertebrates such as worms, snails and insect larvae; introduced trout reduce larval survival.

resources.title: Western tiger salamander
resources.description: Identify the western tiger salamander (Ambystoma mavortium), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western tiger salamander (Ambystoma mavortium): Large, stout terrestrial salamander (average about 20 cm, up to about 36 cm) with broad flat head, blunt snout and small eyes. Light grey to grey-black back with scattered black or yellow spots, and yellow bars or lines along the body. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Canada south through much of the western and central United States to central Mexico; absent from most of the Great Basin and the far western US west of the Rockies, where it has been introduced in many localities. Meets the eastern tiger salamander's range in the Great Plains.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats A. mavortium as a species, recognising five subspecies, but notes Lannoo (2005) and Johnson et al. (2011) included it in A. tigrinum; Animal Diversity Web calls it Barred tiger salamander.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Canada south through much of the western and central United States to central Mexico; absent from most of the Great Basin and the far western US west of the Rockies, where it has been introduced in many localities. Meets the eastern tiger salamander's range in the Great Plains.

identification.text: Large, stout terrestrial salamander (average about 20 cm, up to about 36 cm) with broad flat head, blunt snout and small eyes.
Light grey to grey-black back with scattered black or yellow spots, and yellow bars or lines along the body.
Long, thick tail; four toes on front feet and five on hind feet, none webbed; no colour difference between the sexes.
Larvae are yellow-green with brown spots and black lateral stripes and carry external gills and a tail fin; some become large cannibal morphs in drying ponds.
Compared with the eastern tiger salamander: Ranges meet and meld in the Great Plains, so the two cannot be separated by appearance alone; locality is the practical guide.

habitat.text: Almost any terrestrial habitat (forest, woodland, open fields, meadows) provided there is soil to burrow in and a lake, pond or slow stream pool for breeding.
Ponds used for breeding are usually fishless.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and fossorial; adults hibernate in burrows about 60 cm deep near breeding ponds and return to the same pond.
Most surface activity is during and after rain; most populations migrate up to several hundred metres between uplands and breeding water.
Eats beetles, earthworms and crickets, and occasionally frogs or other salamanders.
Males are aggressive during the breeding season.

conservationStatus.text: Sonoran tiger salamander (Ambystoma mavortium stebbinsi): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1997-01-06.

resources.title: Eastern tiger salamander
resources.description: Identify the eastern tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum): Thick-bodied salamander 17-33 cm long with a large head and broad rounded snout. Black background with yellow (occasionally tan or olive) blotches or spots of no fixed shape, size or position. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central North America; Animal Diversity Web describes the broadly defined tiger salamander as ranging from southeastern Alaska to southern Labrador and south across the US to the Mexican Plateau, a range that includes forms NatureServe now assigns to other species.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe restricts A. tigrinum to the eastern tiger salamander and treats A. mavortium as a separate species; Lannoo (2005) and Animal Diversity Web use A. tigrinum in the broad sense, so the ADW range is wider than the NatureServe concept.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central North America; Animal Diversity Web describes the broadly defined tiger salamander as ranging from southeastern Alaska to southern Labrador and south across the US to the Mexican Plateau, a range that includes forms NatureServe now assigns to other species.

identification.text: Thick-bodied salamander 17-33 cm long with a large head and broad rounded snout.
Black background with yellow (occasionally tan or olive) blotches or spots of no fixed shape, size or position.
Belly usually yellowish or olive with invading dark pigment; about 12-13 costal grooves.
Males are proportionally longer with a more compressed tail and longer hind legs, and have a swollen vent in breeding season.
Larvae are yellow-green or olive with dark blotches, a stripe on each side and a whitish belly.
Compared with the western tiger salamander: Ranges meld in the Great Plains; distribution is the practical guide.

habitat.text: Found in virtually any habitat with soil suitable for burrowing and a body of water nearby for breeding; less tied to forest than other mole salamanders.
Breeds in fishless ponds, from clear mountain ponds to temporary lowland pools.

behavior.text: Adults live underground most of the year in self-dug burrows, found below 60 cm; surface activity is mainly during and after rain.
Migrates up to a few hundred metres between burrows and fishless breeding ponds, often on rainy nights; breeding is in spring in the north.
Eats worms, snails, insects and slugs; larvae eat aquatic invertebrates and amphibian larvae.

resources.title: Western toad
resources.description: Identify the western toad (Anaxyrus boreas), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western toad (Anaxyrus boreas): Medium to large stocky toad, 2-5 in (females larger), blunt head, broad waist, short legs, warty skin. Thin light stripe down the middle of the back from head to rear end. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Pacific coast from southern Alaska to Baja California and east through the Rocky Mountains to west-central Alberta, Montana, Wyoming, Utah and Colorado; absent from most of the desert Southwest.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the English name Boreal Toad is sometimes used for this taxon (and older references use the genus Bufo); the A. boreas group is taxonomically unsettled, with several former populations now separate species.

rangeSummary.value: Pacific coast from southern Alaska to Baja California and east through the Rocky Mountains to west-central Alberta, Montana, Wyoming, Utah and Colorado; absent from most of the desert Southwest.

identification.text: Medium to large stocky toad, 2-5 in (females larger), blunt head, broad waist, short legs, warty skin.
Thin light stripe down the middle of the back from head to rear end.
Prominent oval parotoid glands behind the eyes; no L-shaped cranial crests (Woodhouse's toad has elongate parotoids and L-shaped crests).
Back brown, green, olive, grey or reddish-brown with warts ringed by dark blotches; underside light with irregular dark marks.
Breeding males have smoother skin than females; newly metamorphosed toads lack obvious parotoids and the dorsal stripe may be faint or absent.
Compared with the woodhouse's toad: Woodhouse's toad has L-shaped cranial crests and parotoid glands longer than the eye; the western toad has neither.

habitat.text: Wide range from desert springs to mountain wetlands, using prairies, forests, canyon grasslands and pine-oak habitat.
Breeds in ponds, lakes, reservoir coves, wetlands and river backwaters.

behavior.text: Call is a soft chirruping, plinking peep like a chick, heard day or night and audible only within about 100 ft; a rapid chirp is given as a release call.
Breeds in still or slow water from mid-April at low elevation in western Washington, later at higher elevation; egg strings are laid in shallow water.
Transformed toads are mostly terrestrial but stay near water in drier areas; they dig burrows or use small-mammal burrows, logs or rocks, and overwinter in cold climates.
Feeds on insects and other small invertebrates; at lower elevations active in daylight in cool weather and mostly at night in warm weather.

resources.title: Great Plains toad
resources.description: Identify the great plains toad (Anaxyrus cognatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great Plains toad (Anaxyrus cognatus): Olive to pale grey-brown toad, 47-115 mm, with large dark green blotches edged in white covering the back. Cranial ridges between the eyes diverge in a V and meet at the snout in a raised knob or shield (Woodhouse's toad has an L-shaped crest). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Great Plains, southwestern US and northern Mexico: from southern Manitoba and southeastern Alberta south to central Mexico; east to western Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Oklahoma, west to central Montana, Colorado and southeastern California.

rangeSummary.value: Great Plains, southwestern US and northern Mexico: from southern Manitoba and southeastern Alberta south to central Mexico; east to western Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Oklahoma, west to central Montana, Colorado and southeastern California.

identification.text: Olive to pale grey-brown toad, 47-115 mm, with large dark green blotches edged in white covering the back.
Cranial ridges between the eyes diverge in a V and meet at the snout in a raised knob or shield (Woodhouse's toad has an L-shaped crest).
Faint pale stripe down the rear back; belly mostly white and rarely spotted.
Spades on the heels of the hind feet for digging.
Compared with the woodhouse's toad: Woodhouse's toad has an L-shaped cranial crest and a white back stripe rather than a raised snout shield with V-shaped ridges and large white-edged blotches.

habitat.text: Short-grass prairie, desert, semidesert shrubland, open floodplains and irrigated farmland, typically in stream valleys, on heavier soils than Woodhouse's toad.
Breeds in temporary rain pools, flooded areas and fluctuating ponds.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and solitary; spends most of the year dormant in burrows 15-55 cm deep, emerging after heavy rain or at breeding.
Males call with a loud continuous trill of 20-50 seconds from shallow rain pools and flooded areas.
Sit-and-wait feeder on beetles, ants, moth larvae and other insects, mostly at night.

resources.title: Red-spotted toad
resources.description: Identify the red-spotted toad (Anaxyrus punctatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red-spotted toad (Anaxyrus punctatus): Small toad, typically 38-64 mm snout-vent (maximum about 76 mm), females larger than males. Dry skin, round snout and a round enlarged gland behind each eye; no bony crests between or behind the eyes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: California, Nevada, central Utah, Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to southern Baja California and Querétaro, Mexico, at elevations up to about 1,980 m. Not reported from Canada in the sources read.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the genus Anaxyrus was split from Bufo (Frost et al. 2006) and many references still use Bufo punctatus.

rangeSummary.value: California, Nevada, central Utah, Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to southern Baja California and Querétaro, Mexico, at elevations up to about 1,980 m. Not reported from Canada in the sources read.

identification.text: Small toad, typically 38-64 mm snout-vent (maximum about 76 mm), females larger than males.
Dry skin, round snout and a round enlarged gland behind each eye; no bony crests between or behind the eyes.
Head, limbs and body uniform brown or grey with small warts that may or may not be tipped red.
Belly yellowish with small blackish spots; males have a dark throat.

habitat.text: Rocky canyons, gullies and gypsum or limestone outcrops in deserts, dry prairies, grasslands and dry woodlands.
Eggs laid singly on plants in shallow rain pools, spring-fed pools and pools along intermittent streams.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; hides under moist rocks or underground by day and is active after heavy rain, including mornings and late afternoon.
Opportunistic breeder: gathers in small numbers at canyon pools and intermittent streams after spring or summer rain; males chorus in the evening.
Eats beetles, ants, bees and other small arthropods; generally inactive November-March in the north.

resources.title: Woodhouse's toad
resources.description: Identify the woodhouse's toad (Anaxyrus woodhousii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Woodhouse's toad (Anaxyrus woodhousii): Medium to large stocky toad, about 2-5 in, with warty skin, round head and short snout. L-shaped cranial crests between and behind the eyes; the post-orbital crest typically touches the long parotoid gland behind the eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central and southwestern United States from southern Texas to northern Montana and North Dakota and west across the desert Southwest to Utah, with isolated populations in Idaho, Washington, Oregon and California; adjacent northern Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the specific epithet is widely misspelled 'woodhousei' and that Fowler's toad (A. fowleri) was formerly included in this species.

rangeSummary.value: Central and southwestern United States from southern Texas to northern Montana and North Dakota and west across the desert Southwest to Utah, with isolated populations in Idaho, Washington, Oregon and California; adjacent northern Mexico.

identification.text: Medium to large stocky toad, about 2-5 in, with warty skin, round head and short snout.
L-shaped cranial crests between and behind the eyes; the post-orbital crest typically touches the long parotoid gland behind the eye.
Gray, light brown or olive with dark blotches and spots, a white stripe down the centre of the back, and a speckled light underside.
Males have a dark throat; each hind foot has two dark digging spades.
Young toads often lack the back stripe and have reddish warts.
Compared with the western toad: Western toad lacks cranial crests and has short oval parotoid glands; Woodhouse's has L-shaped crests and elongate glands longer than the eye.
Compared with the great plains toad: Great Plains toad has a raised snout knob with V-shaped ridges and large white-bordered dark blotches.

habitat.text: Floodplains, river valleys, grassland, shrubsteppe and agricultural areas with loose sandy or friable soil near permanent or temporary water.
Burrows or hides under cover when inactive.

behavior.text: Call is a loud nasal, bleating 'waaaah' lasting about 1-10 seconds, carrying up to about 800 m.
Mostly nocturnal (adult activity at twilight into night in Washington), spending the day burrowed or hidden under debris or in rodent burrows; diurnal activity is not uncommon in other regions.
Active from late April-May into October in Washington; inactive in cold months. Eats small terrestrial arthropods.
Breeds in shallow still water from May into July; egg strings are wrapped around vegetation.

resources.title: Clouded salamander
resources.description: Identify the clouded salamander (Aneides ferreus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Clouded salamander (Aneides ferreus): Brown back overlain with greenish grey, pale gold or reddish hues and sprinkled with brassy specks, mostly on snout, shoulders and upper tail base. Dusky grey belly; expanded toes with squared tips; rounded prehensile tail; 16-17 costal grooves. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal forests of Oregon and northern California, from the Columbia River south, plus a separate group on Vancouver Island and adjacent islands in British Columbia; sea level to about 1,500-1,700 m.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal forests of Oregon and northern California, from the Columbia River south, plus a separate group on Vancouver Island and adjacent islands in British Columbia; sea level to about 1,500-1,700 m.

identification.text: Brown back overlain with greenish grey, pale gold or reddish hues and sprinkled with brassy specks, mostly on snout, shoulders and upper tail base.
Dusky grey belly; expanded toes with squared tips; rounded prehensile tail; 16-17 costal grooves.
Adult males have triangular heads from strong jaw muscles; females are slightly longer (max about 65 mm snout-vent).
Young are dark brown with a brassy stripe from neck to tail tip and a brassy triangle on the head.

habitat.text: Mesic coniferous forest (Douglas-fir, redwood, hemlock, Port Orford cedar), especially forest edges, clearings and burned areas.
Uses large, mid-decay logs with sloughing bark.

behavior.text: Usually found singly under bark, in decaying stumps and logs, and in cliff cracks; partly arboreal.
Inactive in cold and hot, dry weather; may gather in moist decayed logs in dry summers.
Carnivorous on invertebrates; males often bear fight scars.

resources.title: Black salamander
resources.description: Identify the black salamander (Aneides flavipunctatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black salamander (Aneides flavipunctatus): Adults slate to black above and below, often with small white spots or a wash of bronze or olive. Up to about 94 mm snout-vent and 160 mm total length; 15-16 costal grooves; short limbs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Oregon south through the California coastal mountains to the Russian River (Sonoma County), with isolated populations near Santa Cruz and around Shasta Lake; sea level to about 1,700 m. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: The Oregon assessment notes the A. flavipunctatus complex may comprise several species (e.g. the Santa Cruz form A. f. niger and the Shasta lineage); NatureServe treats it as one species, Speckled Black Salamander.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Oregon south through the California coastal mountains to the Russian River (Sonoma County), with isolated populations near Santa Cruz and around Shasta Lake; sea level to about 1,700 m. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Adults slate to black above and below, often with small white spots or a wash of bronze or olive.
Up to about 94 mm snout-vent and 160 mm total length; 15-16 costal grooves; short limbs.
Larger adults have a triangular head from large jaw muscles; toe tips are not squared, unlike its congeners.
Juveniles are green-grey or brassy with yellow limb bases and small white or blue spots; in the far north adults keep the juvenile greenish-grey or brassy look.

Compared with the clouded salamander: Clouded salamander has squared toe tips and brassy specks on a brown, often lighter back; black salamander toe tips are not squared and adults are slate to black.

habitat.text: Forest, woodland and grassland; southern populations prefer moist woodland along streams and seepages, northern populations grassy areas, and far-north populations moss-covered rockslides.
Found under surface cover such as rocks, logs and talus near creeks or seeps.

behavior.text: Terrestrial and needs no standing water for any life stage; eggs are laid underground in July-August and hatch as miniature adults.
Active on the surface year-round in moist places and the south, but retreats underground in dry summers in drier northern sites; active mainly October-April in the north.
Aggressive, with bite-hold behaviour; 35% of field-caught animals were scarred. Good jumper using its tail.
Eats terrestrial arthropods, snails and worms.

resources.title: Arboreal salamander
resources.description: Identify the arboreal salamander (Aneides lugubris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Arboreal salamander (Aneides lugubris): 4 to 7 1/4 in long, dark brown to grey back with yellowish or white spotting (spotting varies or may be absent). Solid cream underside; large head relative to body; 15-16 costal grooves. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: California Coast Ranges from Humboldt County into Baja California, the central Sierra Nevada foothills, and offshore islands (South Farallon, Santa Catalina, Los Coronados); sea level to about 5,000 ft.

rangeSummary.value: California Coast Ranges from Humboldt County into Baja California, the central Sierra Nevada foothills, and offshore islands (South Farallon, Santa Catalina, Los Coronados); sea level to about 5,000 ft.

identification.text: 4 to 7 1/4 in long, dark brown to grey back with yellowish or white spotting (spotting varies or may be absent).
Solid cream underside; large head relative to body; 15-16 costal grooves.
Expanded toe tips, elongated digits and a moderately prehensile tail for climbing.

habitat.text: Coastal live-oak woodland, and yellow pine and black oak forest in the Sierra Nevada foothills; on ground under leaf litter, rocks and logs, and in trees.
A direct developer, not dependent on water for breeding.

behavior.text: Excellent climber, found up to about 60 ft above ground; nocturnal, hiding by day in leaf litter and retreats.
Surfaces with the first heavy fall rains and stays out until early to mid spring; retreats to tree cavities, rodent burrows and caves in summer.
May share a retreat with up to about eleven others; bites and squeaks when handled. Eats crickets, termites and other invertebrates.

resources.title: Wandering salamander
resources.description: Identify the wandering salamander (Aneides vagrans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Wandering salamander (Aneides vagrans): Slender salamander with light grey or bronze mottling over a brown to greyish-black head, back and tail. Adults 75-130 mm total length (50-76 mm snout-vent), weighing 1.5-5.6 g. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Humid coastal forests of northern California (Del Norte to Sonoma County) and, in Canada, Vancouver Island, adjacent small islands and one Sunshine Coast location in British Columbia; absent from Oregon and Washington.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes A. vagrans was formerly included in A. ferreus (clouded salamander); some of the Vancouver Island populations are believed by some authors to derive from human-mediated introductions, though the Canadian management plan considers a natural origin better supported.

rangeSummary.value: Humid coastal forests of northern California (Del Norte to Sonoma County) and, in Canada, Vancouver Island, adjacent small islands and one Sunshine Coast location in British Columbia; absent from Oregon and Washington.

identification.text: Slender salamander with light grey or bronze mottling over a brown to greyish-black head, back and tail.
Adults 75-130 mm total length (50-76 mm snout-vent), weighing 1.5-5.6 g.
Squared-off toes and no constriction at the base of the tail separate it from other lungless salamanders in British Columbia.
Juveniles have a bronze dorsal stripe and a bronze patch on the head and snout that fade with age; adult colour is reached at about 45 mm snout-vent.
Compared with the clouded salamander: Formerly treated as the same species (A. ferreus); the sources read give no simple field mark, so locality and expert identification are the guides.

habitat.text: Moist forest (Douglas-fir, redwood, hardwood-conifer) in humid coastal areas, using logs, bark, talus and rock crevices for refuge and breeding.
Needs large, mid-decay down logs with sloughing bark.

behavior.text: Terrestrial and probably nocturnal; moves short distances (94% of recaptures within 10 m) and estivates deep in logs and moist crevices in dry periods.
Lives in and on large decaying logs and bark, and in old-growth forest canopy; on seabird islands it uses drift logs and burrows.
Eggs (3-28) are laid in a gelatinous cluster under bark or in a rotting log; females guard nests and young hatch as miniature adults.
Feeds on small arthropods such as ants, beetles, spiders, isopods and mites.

resources.title: Glossy snake
resources.description: Identify the glossy snake (Arizona elegans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Glossy snake (Arizona elegans): Medium non-venomous snake, 75-130 cm typical (up to 178 cm), with smooth glossy scales. Light beige or grey ground colour with dark-edged blotches filled with gold, brown or olive-grey. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central and southern California, southern Nevada, southern Utah, Colorado, southern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, south into Baja California and Mexico; not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Central and southern California, southern Nevada, southern Utah, Colorado, southern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, south into Baja California and Mexico; not in Canada.

identification.text: Medium non-venomous snake, 75-130 cm typical (up to 178 cm), with smooth glossy scales.
Light beige or grey ground colour with dark-edged blotches filled with gold, brown or olive-grey.
Prominent eye stripe, lidless eyes with slightly vertical pupils, single anal scale, countersunk lower jaw.
Juveniles similar but darker marked, lightening with age; sexes alike.

habitat.text: Semi-arid grassland, sandy desert and scrub, sagebrush flats, chaparral and rocky washes, preferring open areas with sandy or loamy soil.
Shelters and lays eggs underground; from below sea level to about 2,200 m.

behavior.text: Crepuscular and nocturnal, mostly active April-September; primarily nocturnal, sometimes by day.
Excellent burrower; uses crevices and rodent burrows as daytime retreats. Constrictor; about half its diet is other reptiles, especially lizards.
Gentle and calm; moves by lateral undulation.

resources.title: Tiger whiptail
resources.description: Identify the tiger whiptail (Aspidoscelis tigris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Tiger whiptail (Aspidoscelis tigris): Slender lizard 127-330 mm total length with a triangular head, slim body and long tail. Light brown or orange ground colour with eight light or dark longitudinal stripes from head base to tail, plus small black or white spots on the back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Oregon and Idaho south through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado and western Texas to Baja California and northern Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web files this species as Cnemidophorus tigris/western whiptail; NatureServe uses Aspidoscelis tigris, Tiger Whiptail, and notes that some authorities treat the marbled whiptail (A. t. marmorata) as a separate species.

rangeSummary.value: Oregon and Idaho south through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado and western Texas to Baja California and northern Mexico.

identification.text: Slender lizard 127-330 mm total length with a triangular head, slim body and long tail.
Light brown or orange ground colour with eight light or dark longitudinal stripes from head base to tail, plus small black or white spots on the back.
Males slightly larger than females; juveniles are light orange with dark spots or stripes.
Similar to sympatric whiptails; the all-female New Mexico whiptail is smaller with a blue tint on the belly and tail end.
Compared with the new mexico whiptail: Female-only species, smaller than the western whiptail, with a blue tint on the underbelly and tail end.

habitat.text: Deserts and semiarid shrublands with sparse vegetation, plus open woodland, dry forest, canyons and riparian areas on firm, sandy or rocky soil.
Shelters in burrows or under surface objects; eggs are laid underground.

behavior.text: Diurnal, active forager that digs for prey and uses chemical senses; active mainly April-September in the north, with juveniles active longer.
Uses rodent burrows or digs its own, and shelters in burrows overnight and in inclement weather.
Insectivore; grasshoppers, beetles and termites are frequent prey in New Mexico.

resources.title: Plateau striped whiptail
resources.description: Identify the plateau striped whiptail (Aspidoscelis velox), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plateau striped whiptail (Aspidoscelis velox): Long, slender lizard with dark and light stripes running the length of the body. Adults reach about 8.7 cm snout-vent (28 cm total length). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Colorado Plateau and vicinity in southern Utah, western Colorado, northern Arizona and northern New Mexico at about 1,200-2,440 m; introduced and established at Cove Palisades State Park, Oregon.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the name A. velox was applied to triploid parthenogens by Wright (1993) while the diploid A. innotata is treated as a separate species; older references use Cnemidophorus velox.

rangeSummary.value: Colorado Plateau and vicinity in southern Utah, western Colorado, northern Arizona and northern New Mexico at about 1,200-2,440 m; introduced and established at Cove Palisades State Park, Oregon.

identification.text: Long, slender lizard with dark and light stripes running the length of the body.
Adults reach about 8.7 cm snout-vent (28 cm total length).
Hatchlings (33-37 mm snout-vent) have a bright blue tail.
All individuals are female; the species reproduces by parthenogenesis.

habitat.text: Pinyon-juniper woodland, mountain shrubland, sagebrush, open chaparral, oak woodland and riparian areas, and lower elevations of ponderosa pine and Douglas-fir forest.

behavior.text: Diurnal; usually active from May to September (hatchlings may be active into mid-October).
Reproduces without males: clutches of 3-5 eggs are laid late June to early July and hatchlings emerge from mid-August.
Eats any available arthropod.

resources.title: California slender salamander
resources.description: Identify the california slender salamander (Batrachoseps attenuatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California slender salamander (Batrachoseps attenuatus): Extremely elongated, worm-like body with short limbs and very small digits; only four toes on each hind foot. Dark brown to black ground colour with a reddish-brown, buff or yellowish dorsal stripe that may fade or vanish in older adults. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal southwestern Oregon south through coastal northern California and the Coast Ranges to the Monterey Bay lowlands and Tres Pinos Creek area (Santa Cruz and San Benito counties), plus parts of the inner Coast Ranges; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes B. attenuatus is highly differentiated genetically and Highton (2014) suggested it may comprise many species; range has changed with taxonomic revisions.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal southwestern Oregon south through coastal northern California and the Coast Ranges to the Monterey Bay lowlands and Tres Pinos Creek area (Santa Cruz and San Benito counties), plus parts of the inner Coast Ranges; not in Canada.

identification.text: Extremely elongated, worm-like body with short limbs and very small digits; only four toes on each hind foot.
Dark brown to black ground colour with a reddish-brown, buff or yellowish dorsal stripe that may fade or vanish in older adults.
Slate-grey underside with fine white stippling; tail makes up 55-65% of total length.
18-22 costal grooves (20-21 most common); adult snout-vent length 45-55 mm.

habitat.text: Humid low-elevation coastal areas: redwood and conifer forest, oak woodland, chaparral, coastal scrub and grassland with scattered trees.
Found under leaf litter, rotten logs and surface debris, including in garden stones and debris.

behavior.text: Surfaces from under logs, rocks and bark when topsoil is wet; most active from first fall rains through late spring.
Retreats into burrows and soil cavities in hot, dry weather, and is inactive in cold.
Sit-and-wait feeder on snails, springtails, mites, flies and small spiders; spends much of its time within a very small area.

resources.title: Southern California slender salamander
resources.description: Identify the southern california slender salamander (Batrachoseps major), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern California slender salamander (Batrachoseps major): Slender, worm-like salamander of the genus Batrachoseps. Slightly wider body and a lighter grey belly than the black-bellied slender salamander; body colour varies widely. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California from the base of the San Gabriel and San Bernardino mountains south to El Rosario, Baja California, plus Catalina and offshore islands; up to about 1,500 m. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe calls this species Southern California Slender Salamander but lists Garden Slender Salamander as an alternate name; the desert slender salamander B. aridus is now treated as the subspecies B. m. aridus.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California from the base of the San Gabriel and San Bernardino mountains south to El Rosario, Baja California, plus Catalina and offshore islands; up to about 1,500 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Slender, worm-like salamander of the genus Batrachoseps.
Slightly wider body and a lighter grey belly than the black-bellied slender salamander; body colour varies widely.

Compared with the black-bellied slender salamander: Black-bellied has a thinner body and may have a lighter dorsal stripe; the garden slender salamander has a slightly wider body and lighter grey belly.

habitat.text: Oak woodland, chaparral and grassy slopes in canyons and washes, and rural gardens and urban edges next to natural areas.
Prefers moist areas with rocky cover and is tied to seepages.

behavior.text: Nocturnal on the surface, mostly active November-April in cool, wet or humid weather; found under rocks, bark and logs, and formerly common in gardens under stones, boards and potted plants.
Retreats to burrows or underground crevices in sandy or gravelly soil in cold or dry weather.
Terrestrial breeder with no aquatic larval stage; eggs are laid in fall and winter. Feeds on small invertebrates such as insects, spiders, snails and sowbugs.

resources.title: Zebra-tailed lizard
resources.description: Identify the zebra-tailed lizard (Callisaurus draconoides), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Zebra-tailed lizard (Callisaurus draconoides): Relatively large, long-legged lizard (snout-vent 65-93 mm) with a flattened tail and long hind limbs. Grey to brown back with yellow blotches and dark spots on both sides of the mid-dorsal line. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico: northwestern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through southeastern California, Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico to Baja California and Sinaloa; sea level to about 1,520 m. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico: northwestern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through southeastern California, Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico to Baja California and Sinaloa; sea level to about 1,520 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Relatively large, long-legged lizard (snout-vent 65-93 mm) with a flattened tail and long hind limbs.
Grey to brown back with yellow blotches and dark spots on both sides of the mid-dorsal line.
Tail and limbs have 4-8 dark cross bands, and the tail underside is boldly black and white striped.
Both sexes have a dark throat with radiating black lines; males also have sky to navy blue patches on each side of the belly, which females lack.
Males show metallic green-blue (sometimes orange and yellow) on the sides in breeding season.

habitat.text: Open, sparsely vegetated desert with loose sandy soil: washes, dunes, floodplains and desert pavement, often among shrubs.
Uses boulders as basking perches and, at higher elevation, sometimes rocky shaded leaf-litter areas.

behavior.text: Diurnal and heat-tolerant: often basks and is active in midday heat when other lizards shelter; most active about 0900-1300 in Nevada.
Wags and curls the black-and-white tail as a display to other lizards and when a predator is near.
Active in warm months and hibernates roughly October to April; digs burrows, usually under shrubs, for shelter and night retreats.
Eats mostly small invertebrates (ants, flies, spiders, scorpions), plus some plant material.

resources.title: Northern rubber boa
resources.description: Identify the northern rubber boa (Charina bottae), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern rubber boa (Charina bottae): Usually 38-64 cm (range 35-84 cm); thick, smooth-scaled body with loose, wrinkled skin that looks and feels like rubber. Uniform brown to olive-green above and yellow to cream below; occasional dark spots or mottling (more often in northern populations). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia and Alberta south to west-central California, central Nevada and southern Utah; Pacific coast east to north-central Wyoming and western Montana. Distribution is patchy, especially at southern and eastern edges.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and the SSAR list (Nicholson 2025) recognise a single species, the Rubber Boa, with northern (C. b. bottae) and southern (C. b. umbratica) subspecies; earlier authors (Crother 2017) treated the southern form as a separate species.

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia and Alberta south to west-central California, central Nevada and southern Utah; Pacific coast east to north-central Wyoming and western Montana. Distribution is patchy, especially at southern and eastern edges.

identification.text: Usually 38-64 cm (range 35-84 cm); thick, smooth-scaled body with loose, wrinkled skin that looks and feels like rubber.
Uniform brown to olive-green above and yellow to cream below; occasional dark spots or mottling (more often in northern populations).
Small dark eyes with vertical pupils.
Blunt, head-like tail tip with a bulb of bone, usually scarred; the snake curls up and presents the tail when threatened.
Northern subspecies has sub-triangular frontal scales and 42 or more mid-dorsal scale rows; the southern subspecies has fewer.

habitat.text: Moist coniferous forest, woodlands, forest clearings, meadows and grassy streamsides, generally not far from water, from sea level to about 3,050 m.
Uses rodent burrows, rock outcrops, fallen logs and deep duff for cover.

behavior.text: Solitary, burrowing and slow-moving; mostly nocturnal or at dusk, but also active by day in mild cloudy weather, and sometimes basks.
Active mostly March-November; docile, does not strike, and deters predators with the tail or a strong odour.
Eats nestling mice, voles and shrews found in nests, and occasionally lizard or snake eggs; found under rotting logs, stumps, rocks and bark.
Prehensile tail allows it to climb shrubs and small trees.

resources.title: Western shovel-nosed snake
resources.description: Identify the western shovel-nosed snake (Chionactis occipitalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western shovel-nosed snake (Chionactis occipitalis): Small snake with a shovel-shaped snout and an inset lower jaw; smooth scales in 15 rows and a divided anal plate (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies). Coral-snake-like banding: pale yellow to cream body with 21 or more black or brown saddle-like bands across the back, with orange-red saddles between (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies; bands vary among forms). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mojave, Sonoran and Colorado deserts of southern California, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona, Baja California and northwestern Sonora, below about 1,400 m in California.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists this as Sonora occipitalis (Mohave Shovel-nosed Snake) following Cox et al. (2018), who proposed merging Chionactis into Sonora; Wood et al. (2014) split C. annulata from C. occipitalis, and the USFWS assessment treats the Tucson form as a subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Mojave, Sonoran and Colorado deserts of southern California, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona, Baja California and northwestern Sonora, below about 1,400 m in California.

identification.text: Small snake with a shovel-shaped snout and an inset lower jaw; smooth scales in 15 rows and a divided anal plate (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies).

Coral-snake-like banding: pale yellow to cream body with 21 or more black or brown saddle-like bands across the back, with orange-red saddles between (USFWS description of the Tucson subspecies; bands vary among forms).

habitat.text: Sparsely vegetated desert with fine, wind-blown sand: sandy flats, washes, dunes and scrub bases; less often rocky slopes.
Uses sand and other animals' burrows for cover.

behavior.text: Burrows or 'swims' through fine sand; nocturnal and rarely seen on the surface by day, when it may lie coiled under a bush.
Active most of the year in the south and in the warmer months in the north; inactive in cold and extreme heat.
Eats insects, spiders, scorpions and centipedes; lays eggs underground in spring.

resources.title: Painted turtle
resources.description: Identify the painted turtle (Chrysemys picta), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Painted turtle (Chrysemys picta): Smooth, relatively flat, unkeeled shell, 4-8 in (about 9-25 cm), with a non-serrated rear edge; olive-green to brown or black with thin red or orange lines and red edges on the marginals. Skin olive to black with yellow stripes on the head, neck, limbs and tail; yellow eyes with a dark bar through the pupil. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Only turtle spanning North America coast to coast: from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick across southern Canada to Vancouver Island, and through most of the eastern and central US to the Gulf Coast in Louisiana; a few isolated populations occur in the southwest US and Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Starkey et al. (2003) recognised C. dorsalis (southern painted turtle) as a separate species, while some herpetologists keep it in C. picta; NatureServe lists three subspecies (bellii, marginata, picta).

rangeSummary.value: Only turtle spanning North America coast to coast: from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick across southern Canada to Vancouver Island, and through most of the eastern and central US to the Gulf Coast in Louisiana; a few isolated populations occur in the southwest US and Mexico.

identification.text: Smooth, relatively flat, unkeeled shell, 4-8 in (about 9-25 cm), with a non-serrated rear edge; olive-green to brown or black with thin red or orange lines and red edges on the marginals.
Skin olive to black with yellow stripes on the head, neck, limbs and tail; yellow eyes with a dark bar through the pupil.
Plastron is red or orange with dark markings that fade with age (a large grey 'oak leaf' blotch in the western form).
Males are smaller than females, with thicker tails and elongated foreclaws.

habitat.text: Slow-moving, shallow fresh water with soft bottoms and dense aquatic vegetation: marshes, ponds, shallow lake bays, slow rivers and backwaters.
Needs basking sites; nests in soft soil up to several hundred metres from water.

behavior.text: Diurnal; basks in large groups on logs and rocks (sometimes 50 stacked on one log) and dives quickly at danger.
Active about March (late April-May in the far north) to October; overwinters buried in mud at the bottom of wetlands.
Omnivore eating plants, algae, aquatic insects, fish and crustaceans, feeding only in water.

resources.title: Western banded gecko
resources.description: Identify the western banded gecko (Coleonyx variegatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western banded gecko (Coleonyx variegatus): Small, fragile-looking lizard, 2-3 in, cream coloured with dark crossbands. Large eyes with vertical pupils. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico, and throughout Baja California and western Sonora; from below sea level to about 2,000 m. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico, and throughout Baja California and western Sonora; from below sea level to about 2,000 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, fragile-looking lizard, 2-3 in, cream coloured with dark crossbands.
Large eyes with vertical pupils.
Sexes are not dimorphic in appearance (per CWHR); two forms occur in California: the desert banded gecko and the San Diego banded gecko.

habitat.text: Wide range of desert and semi-arid habitats from creosote and sagebrush desert to pinyon-juniper and chaparral, on rocky areas and sandy flats or dunes; most abundant in sandy flats and washes.
The San Diego form favours coastal scrub and chaparral granite or rocky outcrops.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; peak activity about two hours after sunset, sometimes emerging in late afternoon to warm up; active April-October with a peak in May.
Spends the day under rocks, boards, fallen yucca stems and other litter or in mammal burrows; hibernates in burrows.
Eats beetles, termites, spiders and other arthropods; females lay a clutch of two eggs, buried in soil or under rocks.

resources.title: North American racer
resources.description: Identify the north american racer (Coluber constrictor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: North American racer (Coluber constrictor): Slender, smooth-scaled snake 90-190 cm long with a narrow head wider than the neck and distinct brow ridges. Adults are uniformly dark above (black, bluish, grey or olive-brown) with a white to yellow chin and throat and a varied belly; 17 scale rows at midbody. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia, southern Saskatchewan, southern Ontario and southern Maine south through most of the United States (to southern California, Arizona, Texas and Florida) and into Mexico, Guatemala and Belize.

taxonomicNotes.text: Nicholson (2025) via NatureServe retains North American Racer in Coluber while placing the striped, whip and coachwhip snakes in Masticophis; some sources give 'Eastern Racer'.
