rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia, southern Saskatchewan, southern Ontario and southern Maine south through most of the United States (to southern California, Arizona, Texas and Florida) and into Mexico, Guatemala and Belize.

identification.text: Slender, smooth-scaled snake 90-190 cm long with a narrow head wider than the neck and distinct brow ridges.
Adults are uniformly dark above (black, bluish, grey or olive-brown) with a white to yellow chin and throat and a varied belly; 17 scale rows at midbody.
Divided anal plate; male tail is longer with a wide base, female tail tapers abruptly.
Juveniles are strongly patterned in grey, brown and red, fading at about 30 in.

habitat.text: Dry sunny areas with cover: old fields, open woodland, hedgerows, thickets and woodland edges; also deserts, prairies, sandhills, canyons and streamsides.
Climbs shrubs and small trees; absent from the driest deserts and subalpine zones.

behavior.text: Diurnal and fast; flees to burrows, thick vegetation or low branches, but if cornered coils, strikes and vibrates its tail.
Inactive in cold weather and dormant roughly October-March over much of its range; adults often hibernate communally.
Broad carnivorous diet: insects, frogs, lizards, small rodents and nestling birds; does not constrict prey.

resources.title: Coachwhip
resources.description: Identify the coachwhip (Coluber flagellum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Coachwhip (Coluber flagellum): One of the largest North American snakes, 91-259 cm snout-vent, with smooth scales and a slender, whip-like tail. Colour varies widely by region: dark brown front half with a red or pink belly midline (eastern), black bands broken by red bands (Sonoran), or pink, red, yellow and grey to black phases in the west. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern United States from North Carolina and Florida west through Kansas and southern Nebraska to Arizona and California (to San Francisco Bay), and north-central Mexico; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Sources place this species in Masticophis (NatureServe, Nicholson 2025) rather than Coluber; NatureServe also notes O'Connell and Smith (2018) split populations west of the Cochise Filter Barrier as M. piceus, and renamed the English name Common Coachwhip.

rangeSummary.value: Southern United States from North Carolina and Florida west through Kansas and southern Nebraska to Arizona and California (to San Francisco Bay), and north-central Mexico; not in Canada.

identification.text: One of the largest North American snakes, 91-259 cm snout-vent, with smooth scales and a slender, whip-like tail.
Colour varies widely by region: dark brown front half with a red or pink belly midline (eastern), black bands broken by red bands (Sonoran), or pink, red, yellow and grey to black phases in the west.

habitat.text: Dry, open terrain: desert, prairie, scrubland, juniper grassland, woodland, farmland, creek valleys and chaparral; terrestrial but climbs into vegetation.
Takes cover in burrows, under rocks or in vegetation.

behavior.text: Diurnal and solitary; active mid-morning and late afternoon but, unlike most snakes, stays active at the hottest time of day (ambient about 33 C).
Active hunter of lizards, other snakes, insects and birds and their eggs; hibernates in winter.
Active April-October in the north and mid-March to late October in Texas.

resources.title: Striped racer
resources.description: Identify the striped racer (Coluber lateralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Striped racer (Coluber lateralis): Slender, diurnal snake; a yellow stripe runs along each side (1 and 2 half scales wide in the Alameda form), hence 'striped racer' (NPS, Alameda subspecies). Underside of the head may carry sparse speckled spots, or none; underside shades from cream to pink toward the tail; these features separate the Alameda form from other California whipsnakes (NPS). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: California from the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges through southwestern California to northwestern Baja California; up to about 1,835 m in California. The Alameda striped racer subspecies is restricted to the Coast Ranges east of San Francisco Bay. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Sources place this species in Masticophis (Nicholson 2025 via NatureServe) rather than Coluber; CWHR uses Coluber lateralis and notes it was formerly called California whipsnake.

rangeSummary.value: California from the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges through southwestern California to northwestern Baja California; up to about 1,835 m in California. The Alameda striped racer subspecies is restricted to the Coast Ranges east of San Francisco Bay. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Slender, diurnal snake; a yellow stripe runs along each side (1 and 2 half scales wide in the Alameda form), hence 'striped racer' (NPS, Alameda subspecies).
Underside of the head may carry sparse speckled spots, or none; underside shades from cream to pink toward the tail; these features separate the Alameda form from other California whipsnakes (NPS).

habitat.text: Chaparral, coastal scrub, shrubland with grassy patches, rocky canyons and watercourses, and woodland; prefers open-canopy stands with woody debris and rock outcrops on south-facing slopes.

behavior.text: Strictly diurnal and actively foraging on the surface, occasionally climbing shrubs or small trees; active March-November in California and non-migratory.
Preys mainly on lizards, also frogs, snakes, nestling birds, rodents and insects, hunting by sight and scent; shelters under objects, in crevices and rodent burrows.
Males are trapped more than females in spring because they roam widely for mates.

resources.title: Striped whipsnake
resources.description: Identify the striped whipsnake (Coluber taeniatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Striped whipsnake (Coluber taeniatus): Slender snake 36-72 in (90-183 cm) with smooth scales in 15 rows at midbody and a divided anal plate. Dark brown, grey or blue above with three light grey-to-white stripes on each side; the side stripe is split by a broken or continuous dark band. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Washington and southern Idaho south through Oregon, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and western and central Texas into northern Mexico; up to about 3,077 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: Sources place this species in Masticophis (Nicholson 2025 via NatureServe), not Coluber.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Washington and southern Idaho south through Oregon, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and western and central Texas into northern Mexico; up to about 3,077 m.

identification.text: Slender snake 36-72 in (90-183 cm) with smooth scales in 15 rows at midbody and a divided anal plate.
Dark brown, grey or blue above with three light grey-to-white stripes on each side; the side stripe is split by a broken or continuous dark band.

habitat.text: Shrublands, arid grassland, sagebrush flats, canyons, pinyon-juniper and pine-oak woodland, and rocky stream courses; often near ponds and rivers.
Eggs are laid in abandoned small-mammal burrows.

behavior.text: Fast, alert and diurnal; flees to rocks, rodent burrows or shrubs, but cornered individuals often stand their ground and strike.
Active hunter using vision and scent, taking lizards, other snakes, amphibians, nestling birds and rodents; juveniles take insects.
Active mainly April-October in Colorado and Utah; retreats underground or into crevices in cold weather; climbs (terrestrial and arboreal).

resources.title: Forest sharp-tailed snake
resources.description: Identify the forest sharp-tailed snake (Contia longicauda), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Forest sharp-tailed snake (Contia longicauda): Longer tail than the common sharp-tailed snake, with 43-58 subcaudal scales (C. tenuis has 24-42). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Outer Coast Ranges of northern California and southwestern Oregon, the Klamath Mountains, and parts of the southern Oregon Cascades; parapatric with C. tenuis in places. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly included in Contia tenuis; recognised as a distinct species by Feldman and Hoyer (2010), originally spelled longicaudae; NatureServe gives the corrected spelling longicauda.

rangeSummary.value: Outer Coast Ranges of northern California and southwestern Oregon, the Klamath Mountains, and parts of the southern Oregon Cascades; parapatric with C. tenuis in places. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Longer tail than the common sharp-tailed snake, with 43-58 subcaudal scales (C. tenuis has 24-42).
Compared with the common sharp-tailed snake: Shorter tail with fewer subcaudal scales (24-42 versus 43-58).

habitat.text: Fairly mesic, well-shaded areas, typically mixed evergreen forest dominated by Douglas-fir and redwood, and woodland with mixed conifer and oak canopy.

behavior.text: Active mostly in the rainy season; retreats underground in the dry season and is sometimes found alive on roads at night.
Diet is apparently restricted mainly to slugs; females lay a clutch of up to 9 eggs, probably in June or July.

resources.title: Common sharp-tailed snake
resources.description: Identify the common sharp-tailed snake (Contia tenuis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common sharp-tailed snake (Contia tenuis): Diminutive snake, usually under 12 in (most about 30 cm), rarely over 16 in; shiny reddish-brown or grey above with indistinct reddish stripes. Belly has alternating black and cream or pale bars (in Washington the only snake with such bands). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Vancouver Island and Gulf Islands (British Columbia) south through Washington, Oregon and northern California, including the Sierra foothills; in Washington it occurs in about thirteen disjunct areas.

taxonomicNotes.text: Feldman and Hoyer (2010) split C. tenuis into two species, C. tenuis and C. longicauda, so older sources (including Animal Diversity Web) describe both as 'sharp-tailed snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Vancouver Island and Gulf Islands (British Columbia) south through Washington, Oregon and northern California, including the Sierra foothills; in Washington it occurs in about thirteen disjunct areas.

identification.text: Diminutive snake, usually under 12 in (most about 30 cm), rarely over 16 in; shiny reddish-brown or grey above with indistinct reddish stripes.
Belly has alternating black and cream or pale bars (in Washington the only snake with such bands).
Short tail ends in a small spike-like scale, occasionally lost to injury; smooth scales in 15 rows.
Young snakes are redder with more distinct side lines.
Compared with the forest sharp-tailed snake: Forest sharp-tailed snake has a longer tail with more subcaudal scales (43-58 versus 24-42 in this species).

habitat.text: Edges of coniferous or open hardwood forest, oak woodland, meadows, pasture and broken chaparral; in Washington also riparian floodplains and shrub-steppe with woody debris and rocks.

behavior.text: Small and secretive; under cover in moist rotting logs, stumps, talus and rocks, often near streams, and sometimes several share one cover object.
Surface activity is mostly in cool, moist spring and fall and the rainy season (October-April), with retreat underground in dry summers.
Feeds mainly on slugs, using long re-curved teeth; breeds April-May, lays eggs late June-July and they hatch in fall.

resources.title: Western diamond-backed rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the western diamond-backed rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western diamond-backed rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox): Light-coloured body with diamond-shaped spots along the back, outlined in white and black (NDOW). Alternating black and white bands on the tail (NDOW); band widths are fairly uniform, unlike the Mohave rattlesnake's broad white and narrow black tail bands (NPS Saguaro). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern California, central and southern Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas south into Mexico; in Nevada only the far southern tip (NDOW) and rare in far southeastern California (CDFW). Kansas records may be translocated animals (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern California, central and southern Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas south into Mexico; in Nevada only the far southern tip (NDOW) and rare in far southeastern California (CDFW). Kansas records may be translocated animals (NatureServe).

identification.text: Light-coloured body with diamond-shaped spots along the back, outlined in white and black (NDOW).
Alternating black and white bands on the tail (NDOW); band widths are fairly uniform, unlike the Mohave rattlesnake's broad white and narrow black tail bands (NPS Saguaro).
Arrow-shaped head and a rattle at the tail tip (NDOW).
Largest rattlesnake in Nevada and in the western U.S.; total length 30-90 in (76-230 cm) (NDOW; NPS Saguaro).
Compared with the mohave rattlesnake: Often slightly greenish, with thick white and narrower black tail bands, where the diamondback's tail bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro).

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid country from plains to mountains and from sandy flats to rocky uplands, including desert, grassland, shrubland, woodland and open pine forest (NatureServe).
Hibernates in rock crevices or cavities, sometimes in animal burrows; southeastern Arizona populations used creosotebush flats but moved to rocky slopes in winter (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Mostly crepuscular and nocturnal in summer but also active by day, especially in cooler months; in the north active mainly April to late September or early October (NatureServe).
May congregate at winter dens; migrates up to 3.5 km between winter den and summer range (NatureServe).
Eats mainly rabbits, squirrels, mice and rats, also lizards and birds; forages actively or ambushes prey (NatureServe).
Often holds its ground rather than retreating when approached (NPS Saguaro).

resources.title: Sidewinder
resources.description: Identify the sidewinder (Crotalus cerastes), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sidewinder (Crotalus cerastes): Raised scales over the eyes look like horns (NDOW; NPS Death Valley). Heavy-bodied pit viper, tan to lighter cream with dark dorsal blotches; large triangular head (NDOW; NPS Death Valley). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern California, southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through southwestern Arizona into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora; from below sea level to about 1,830 m (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern California, southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through southwestern Arizona into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora; from below sea level to about 1,830 m (NatureServe).

identification.text: Raised scales over the eyes look like horns (NDOW; NPS Death Valley).
Heavy-bodied pit viper, tan to lighter cream with dark dorsal blotches; large triangular head (NDOW; NPS Death Valley).
Usually 1.5 ft or less, up to about 3 ft; 17-33 in (NPS Death Valley; NDOW).
Moves by throwing the body sideways in an S-shaped curve; tracks in sand are J-shaped and may end in a small depression where it has buried itself (NPS Death Valley).

habitat.text: Open desert with fine windblown sand, sandy washes, or sparsely vegetated dunes with creosotebush or mesquite; sometimes rocky or gravelly sites (NatureServe).
Overwinters in rodent or tortoise burrows (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Crepuscular, and nocturnal in warm periods; by day it hides in rodent burrows or shifts side to side until nearly buried in sand, then waits for prey (NPS Death Valley).

Active mainly February-November in extreme southern California; in the eastern Mojave Desert activity starts March or April and ends October or November, peaking May-June and late September-October (NatureServe).
Eats mainly lizards, pocket mice, kangaroo rats and other small mammals; occasionally small birds and snakes (NatureServe).
Seasonal moves of up to several hundred metres between hibernation burrows and sandy summer habitat were recorded in the eastern Mojave (NatureServe).

resources.title: Southwestern speckled rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the southwestern speckled rattlesnake (Crotalus pyrrhus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southwestern speckled rattlesnake (Crotalus pyrrhus): Colour ranges from pale sandy gray to dark brown; the speckled pattern makes the diamond markings less distinct than on other rattlesnakes (NDOW). Alternating light and dark tail rings are prominent (NDOW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern half of the Baja California Peninsula north into southern California, southern Nevada, western Arizona and southwestern Utah (NatureServe); in Nevada a small range in the southeast, overlapping the Panamint rattlesnake near Las Vegas (NDOW).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats C. pyrrhus as distinct from C. mitchellii of Baja California (Meik et al. 2015); other agency pages (CDFW) still use C. mitchellii for the same desert snakes, so this slug and speckled-rattlesnake may describe one U.S. population.

rangeSummary.value: Northern half of the Baja California Peninsula north into southern California, southern Nevada, western Arizona and southwestern Utah (NatureServe); in Nevada a small range in the southeast, overlapping the Panamint rattlesnake near Las Vegas (NDOW).

identification.text: Colour ranges from pale sandy gray to dark brown; the speckled pattern makes the diamond markings less distinct than on other rattlesnakes (NDOW).
Alternating light and dark tail rings are prominent (NDOW).
Medium-sized pit viper; NatureServe gives about 92-130 cm (NatureServe).

habitat.text: Rugged, rocky terrain in the Mojave and Sonoran desert mountains; rarely on adjacent desert flats; primary habitat is rocky lower slopes and canyons, also seeps, springs and riparian areas (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Ambush predator of small mammals, lizards and birds (NatureServe).
Inactive through cold winter months in sheltered crevices; females give birth to live young in late summer, typically 3-11 per litter (NDOW).
When inactive it shelters under rocks or bushes, in crevices, caves, abandoned mines, rodent burrows or woodrat nests (NatureServe).

resources.title: Mohave rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the mohave rattlesnake (Crotalus scutulatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mohave rattlesnake (Crotalus scutulatus): Slightly greenish tinge to the body, which gives 'Mojave green'; the western rattlesnake lacks the greenish tinge (NPS Parashant). Tail bands have thick white bands and narrower black bands; the western diamondback's bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas into central Mexico; sea level to about 2,530 m (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (following Crother 2017) spells the name Mohave; others spell it Mojave.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas into central Mexico; sea level to about 2,530 m (NatureServe).

identification.text: Slightly greenish tinge to the body, which gives 'Mojave green'; the western rattlesnake lacks the greenish tinge (NPS Parashant).
Tail bands have thick white bands and narrower black bands; the western diamondback's bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro).
Averages 2-4 ft in length (NPS Parashant).
Newborns have a single silent button rather than a full rattle (NPS Parashant).
Compared with the western diamond-backed rattlesnake: Tail bands are more uniform in width and the body lacks the Mohave's greenish tinge (NPS Saguaro; NPS Parashant).
Compared with the western rattlesnake: Lacks the Mohave's greenish tinge (NPS Parashant).

habitat.text: Mostly upland desert and lower mountain slopes: barren desert, grassland, open woodland and scrub with creosotebush, palo verde, mesquite or cacti; usually not in broken rocky terrain or dense vegetation (NatureServe).
In spring it commonly coils under a small tree or shrub in early morning (NatureServe).

behavior.text: At lower elevations mainly nocturnal in summer and commonly active in morning and late afternoon in spring and fall; may be active by day in summer at higher elevations (NatureServe).
Above ground March-November, probably most active late April or May through September (NatureServe).
Eats kangaroo rats, ground squirrels, mice, rabbits and other small mammals; lizards are eaten especially by the young (NatureServe).
Uses rodent burrows to overwinter; hibernates alone or in groups of two or three (NPS Parashant; NPS Saguaro).

resources.title: Panamint rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the panamint rattlesnake (Crotalus stephensi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Panamint rattlesnake (Crotalus stephensi). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Part of southern California (not the southernmost part) and adjacent southwestern Nevada (NatureServe); overlaps the southwestern speckled rattlesnake in parts of the Las Vegas Valley (NDOW).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: elevated to species by Douglas et al. (2007).

rangeSummary.value: Part of southern California (not the southernmost part) and adjacent southwestern Nevada (NatureServe); overlaps the southwestern speckled rattlesnake in parts of the Las Vegas Valley (NDOW).

habitat.text: Canyons, foothills, buttes and erosion gullies of rocky desert; sometimes sandy arroyos or desert flats with shrubs and burrows for cover; vegetation may include pinyon-juniper (NatureServe).
When inactive it occurs under rocks or bushes or in crevices, caves, abandoned mines or animal burrows (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Generally solitary in summer; may congregate at favourable hibernation dens (NatureServe).
Diurnal in spring and fall, active mainly at dusk and at night in summer; in the north most activity is April-October (NatureServe).
Eats lizards, birds and mammals up to the size of woodrats and ground squirrels; lizards seem most important for juveniles (NatureServe).

resources.title: Great Basin collared lizard
resources.description: Identify the great basin collared lizard (Crotaphytus bicinctores), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great Basin collared lizard (Crotaphytus bicinctores): Two black collars around the neck enclosing a lighter collar; olive-brown to gray body with many lighter spots that continue onto the tail in a reticulated pattern; white or light belly (NDOW). No black pigment lining the mouth, unlike C. collaris (NatureServe). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Oregon and southern Idaho south through northeastern California, Nevada, and western and central Utah to southeastern California and western Arizona (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Oregon and southern Idaho south through northeastern California, Nevada, and western and central Utah to southeastern California and western Arizona (NatureServe).

identification.text: Two black collars around the neck enclosing a lighter collar; olive-brown to gray body with many lighter spots that continue onto the tail in a reticulated pattern; white or light belly (NDOW).
No black pigment lining the mouth, unlike C. collaris (NatureServe).
Adult males: strongly laterally compressed tail with a pale white dorsal stripe, enlarged dark inguinal patches, and a pale, patternless top of the head (NatureServe).
Gravid females have orange spots on the sides (NDOW).
Compared with the eastern collared lizard: Eastern collared lizard has a black-lined mouth; Great Basin lacks oral melanin (NatureServe; CPW).
Compared with the baja california collared lizard: Baja California collared lizard has widely separated posterior collars and slender white transverse dorsal bars (NatureServe).

habitat.text: Xeric, sparsely vegetated rocky areas: hillsides, rocky plains and canyons; sometimes adjacent areas with little rock (NDOW; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Perches on rocks; when startled hides under rocks or in rodent burrows; very fast and can run on hind legs alone (NDOW).
Breeding males are territorial, bobbing from a rock and extending a blue and black throat dewlap (NDOW).
Eats insects, spiders, other lizards and some plant material (NDOW; NatureServe).
Inactive in cold winter weather; activity begins as early as March in Arizona (NatureServe).

resources.title: Eastern collared lizard
resources.description: Identify the eastern collared lizard (Crotaphytus collaris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern collared lizard (Crotaphytus collaris): Two incomplete black or dark brown collars across a narrow neck; large head, sometimes bright yellow; long tail (CPW; MDC). Turquoise to green or brown back with many small light spots and dark bands; to about 36 cm (14 in) (CPW; MDC). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado, Kansas and central and southern Missouri south through Arizona, New Mexico, western and central Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas into northern Mexico; Louisiana records may not be natural (NatureServe). Missouri populations north of the Missouri River appear introduced (MDC).

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado, Kansas and central and southern Missouri south through Arizona, New Mexico, western and central Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas into northern Mexico; Louisiana records may not be natural (NatureServe). Missouri populations north of the Missouri River appear introduced (MDC).

identification.text: Two incomplete black or dark brown collars across a narrow neck; large head, sometimes bright yellow; long tail (CPW; MDC).
Turquoise to green or brown back with many small light spots and dark bands; to about 36 cm (14 in) (CPW; MDC).
Breeding males most colourful, with turquoise and yellow scales; throat dark-spotted or yellow to orange (CPW).
Breeding females have orange-red bars or spots on the sides of the body and neck; juveniles have wide dark bands or large dark spots (CPW).
Adult males lack dark pigment in the gular fold, and the mouth lining is usually black (NatureServe; CPW).
Compared with the great basin collared lizard: Great Basin lacks the black mouth lining and males have a compressed tail with a pale dorsal stripe (NatureServe).

habitat.text: Rocky areas with sparse vegetation: canyons, gullies, slopes, mesa tops and dry glades; often basks on boulders (CPW; MDC; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Diurnal; basks on boulders, hides under large rocks or in crevices when approached, and may run on its hind limbs (MDC).
Males defend territories; in Oklahoma about 6.4 dominant males per hectare (MDC; NatureServe).
Eats insects, spiders, other lizards and small snakes, occasionally plant material (MDC; NatureServe).
Active about March or April to October in the north; overwinters in burrows under large rocks (NatureServe; MDC).

resources.title: Baja California collared lizard
resources.description: Identify the baja california collared lizard (Crotaphytus vestigium), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Baja California collared lizard (Crotaphytus vestigium): Slender white transverse bars across the back (NatureServe). Widely separated posterior collars; no black pigment lining the mouth (NatureServe). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Desert slopes of the Peninsular Ranges in southern California north to the San Jacinto Mountains near Palm Springs, and much of Baja California; an isolated Tecate Mountain (San Diego County) population needs confirmation (NatureServe; theNAT).

rangeSummary.value: Desert slopes of the Peninsular Ranges in southern California north to the San Jacinto Mountains near Palm Springs, and much of Baja California; an isolated Tecate Mountain (San Diego County) population needs confirmation (NatureServe; theNAT).

identification.text: Slender white transverse bars across the back (NatureServe).
Widely separated posterior collars; no black pigment lining the mouth (NatureServe).
Adult males: strongly laterally compressed tail with a white or off-white dorsal stripe, pale patternless head, and enlarged dark inguinal patches (NatureServe).
Up to about 5 in (127 mm) snout-vent length (theNAT).
Compared with the great basin collared lizard: Great Basin lacks the widely separated posterior collars and slender white dorsal bars (NatureServe); listed as similar species by theNAT.

habitat.text: Rocky areas in arid and semiarid country, usually with scant vegetation: hillsides, alluvial fans, canyons and lava flows (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Eats arthropods, small lizards and sometimes plant material (NatureServe).
Seasonal activity begins in March-April; members of the genus can lay two clutches a year (NatureServe).

resources.title: Ring-necked snake
resources.description: Identify the ring-necked snake (Diadophis punctatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ring-necked snake (Diadophis punctatus): Smooth, unkeeled scales, gray to olive above (CPW). Orange or yellow ring around the neck, usually bordered in black (CPW; NPS Jewel Cave). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coast to coast across North America; northern limit of the continuous range reaches Nova Scotia, southern Quebec and southern Ontario, and it occurs disjunctly in the West (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Coast to coast across North America; northern limit of the continuous range reaches Nova Scotia, southern Quebec and southern Ontario, and it occurs disjunctly in the West (NatureServe).

identification.text: Smooth, unkeeled scales, gray to olive above (CPW).
Orange or yellow ring around the neck, usually bordered in black (CPW; NPS Jewel Cave).
Belly orange with black spots and red underside of the tail; when threatened it coils the tail to show the red underside (CPW; NPS Jewel Cave).
Small and slender: rarely over about 42 cm (16.5 in), average about 14 in (CPW; NPS Jewel Cave).

habitat.text: Forests, woodlands, grassland, chaparral and riparian corridors; moist at least seasonally; often near abandoned buildings and junk piles in wooded areas (NatureServe; CPW).

behavior.text: Hides by day under flat rocks, logs or other cover and is rarely seen in the open; several of mixed age may share one rock, especially in spring (CPW; NatureServe).
Eats earthworms, slugs, small salamanders, frogs, lizards and snakes (NatureServe).
Releases a foul musk when caught (NPS Jewel Cave).
Inactive in winter in most areas; eggs are often laid communally (NatureServe).

conservationStatus.text: Key ring-necked snake (Diadophis punctatus acricus): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2026-08-20.

resources.title: Coastal giant salamander
resources.description: Identify the coastal giant salamander (Dicamptodon tenebrosus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Coastal giant salamander (Dicamptodon tenebrosus): Large, stocky, marbled gold and brown salamander with a rounded, wide wedge-shaped head, fleshy legs and a laterally compressed tail (WDFW; BC). Largest terrestrial salamander in North America: to about 6.7 in snout-vent and 13.4 in total length; marbling may persist only on the head of very old animals (WDFW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Extreme southwestern British Columbia (Chilliwack River drainage) south through western Washington and Oregon to northwestern California (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Extreme southwestern British Columbia (Chilliwack River drainage) south through western Washington and Oregon to northwestern California (NatureServe).

identification.text: Large, stocky, marbled gold and brown salamander with a rounded, wide wedge-shaped head, fleshy legs and a laterally compressed tail (WDFW; BC).
Largest terrestrial salamander in North America: to about 6.7 in snout-vent and 13.4 in total length; marbling may persist only on the head of very old animals (WDFW).
12-13 costal grooves, indistinct; underside white to light gray, unmarked (WDFW).
Larvae are stream-type: short gills, low tail fin ending near the hind limbs, hard black digit tips (WDFW).
Compared with the cope's giant salamander: Pacific giant is larger with a wider head and longer legs; when legs are pressed against the body the toes touch or cross (WDFW).
Compared with the torrent salamanders (rhyacotriton): Stream larvae have orange undersides and tiny gills barely visible out of water (WDFW).

habitat.text: Small to medium mountain streams in moist coniferous forest; larvae in clear, cold, well-oxygenated streams under stones; transformed adults in humid forest under rocks and logs near streams (WDFW; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Larvae are active on the streambed at night and under cover by day (NatureServe).
Adults eat terrestrial invertebrates, small snakes, shrews, mice and other salamanders; larvae eat aquatic invertebrates and some small vertebrates (NatureServe).
Migrates between aquatic breeding and terrestrial non-breeding habitat; larvae usually metamorphose in 18-24 months, some become sexually mature as larvae (NatureServe).
Female attends eggs laid in water-filled chambers under rocks or logs in or beside streams (NatureServe; BC).

resources.title: Desert iguana
resources.description: Identify the desert iguana (Dipsosaurus dorsalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert iguana (Dipsosaurus dorsalis): Medium-sized, pale lizard with a blunt head and a tail usually longer than the body (NDOW). Darker lines and stripes run the length of the body and through the tail (NDOW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Nevada, southern California east of the Sierra Nevada and Coast ranges, and western and central Arizona south through Baja California and Sonora; United States range closely matches that of creosote bush; below sea level to about 1,520 m (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Southern Nevada, southern California east of the Sierra Nevada and Coast ranges, and western and central Arizona south through Baja California and Sonora; United States range closely matches that of creosote bush; below sea level to about 1,520 m (NatureServe).

identification.text: Medium-sized, pale lizard with a blunt head and a tail usually longer than the body (NDOW).
Darker lines and stripes run the length of the body and through the tail (NDOW).

habitat.text: Sandy arroyos and open areas with loose soil, typically creosote bush desert with sand hummocks and firm patches with scattered rocks; sometimes nearby rocky hillsides (NatureServe; NDOW).

behavior.text: Often one of the only lizards active in the hottest part of the day; among the most heat-tolerant reptiles in North America (NDOW).
Mostly eats leaves, buds and flowers, especially creosote bush, plus occasional insects and carrion (NDOW; NatureServe).
Shelters in rodent burrows, rock crevices or under creosote; when cornered wedges into a tight space and inflates its body (NDOW; NatureServe).
Mates April-May and lays 3-8 eggs June-August; inactive in cold weather (NatureServe).

resources.title: Northern alligator lizard
resources.description: Identify the northern alligator lizard (Elgaria coerulea), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern alligator lizard (Elgaria coerulea): Small, slim, gray-brown lizard with keeled scales, short legs, a long tail and a fold of small scales along each side; up to about 3.9 in snout-vent (WDFW). Brown back with black spots forming transverse bands; white spots on the edges of side scales (WDFW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia including Vancouver Island, south through western Washington and Oregon to west-central coastal California and the central Sierra Nevada, and in the Rockies to northern Idaho and western Montana, with disjunct populations in south-central Oregon, northeastern California and northwestern Nevada (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia including Vancouver Island, south through western Washington and Oregon to west-central coastal California and the central Sierra Nevada, and in the Rockies to northern Idaho and western Montana, with disjunct populations in south-central Oregon, northeastern California and northwestern Nevada (NatureServe).

identification.text: Small, slim, gray-brown lizard with keeled scales, short legs, a long tail and a fold of small scales along each side; up to about 3.9 in snout-vent (WDFW).
Brown back with black spots forming transverse bands; white spots on the edges of side scales (WDFW).
Brown eyes; underside light with dark pigment on the lateral edges of each scale (WDFW).
Males have a broader, more triangular head; hatchlings are plain brown or have one line of dark spots down the midline (WDFW).
Compared with the southern alligator lizard: Larger (up to 5.5 in snout-vent), yellow or gold eyes, and no dark pigment on the lateral edges of the belly scales (WDFW).

habitat.text: Grassy, brushy or rocky openings in forest, clearcuts and stream margins; rock walls, rock piles and woody debris in lightly developed areas (WDFW; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Active by day but secretive; usually found by turning rocks or woody debris (WDFW).
Tail is easily shed when threatened (WDFW).
Eats insects, ticks, spiders, millipedes and snails; litters average 4-6 (NatureServe).
Hibernates in winter; in British Columbia individuals did not make long moves between summer habitat and hibernation sites (NatureServe).

resources.title: Southern alligator lizard
resources.description: Identify the southern alligator lizard (Elgaria multicarinata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern alligator lizard (Elgaria multicarinata): Large, slim, gray-brown lizard with keeled scales, short legs and a tail about twice the body length; up to 5.6 in snout-vent (WDFW). Brown back with black spots in transverse bands; fold of small scales along each side (WDFW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mainly west of the Cascade-Sierra Nevada crest from south-central Washington through western Oregon and California to northern Baja California; introduced at Las Vegas, Nevada (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Mainly west of the Cascade-Sierra Nevada crest from south-central Washington through western Oregon and California to northern Baja California; introduced at Las Vegas, Nevada (NatureServe).

identification.text: Large, slim, gray-brown lizard with keeled scales, short legs and a tail about twice the body length; up to 5.6 in snout-vent (WDFW).
Brown back with black spots in transverse bands; fold of small scales along each side (WDFW).
Yellow or gold eyes; underside light with no dark pigment on the lateral edges of the scales (WDFW).
Juveniles have a plain brownish to reddish back and scales lighter than the body folds (WDFW).
Compared with the northern alligator lizard: Smaller (under 3.9 in snout-vent), brown eyes, dark pigment on the lateral edges of the belly scales (WDFW).

habitat.text: Grassland, chaparral, oak woodland and open pine forest; in drier regions along streams and other moist, vegetated areas; also logs, thickets, rocks and old woodpiles around houses (NatureServe; WDFW).

behavior.text: Active by day and much less secretive than the northern alligator lizard; climbs shrubs and lower trunks with its prehensile tail and swims and basks on creek rocks (WDFW).
Bites when captured; tail is easily shed (WDFW).
Eats slugs, insects, centipedes, scorpions and spiders, plus lizards, small mammals and occasionally bird eggs and nestlings (NatureServe).
Lays 1-3 clutches of usually 5-20 eggs May-July; inactive in the coldest weather but active over a wide temperature range (NatureServe).

resources.title: Ensatina
resources.description: Identify the ensatina (Ensatina eschscholtzii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ensatina (Ensatina eschscholtzii): Slender, small salamander: total length up to about 120 mm (BC). Uniform pinkish brown, often with a yellow tinge at the base of the legs and digits; yellow or brown flecks sometimes on the sides (BC). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern British Columbia south along the Coast Ranges to northwestern Baja California, and on the western slopes of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada; absent from the Sacramento-San Joaquin valley; sea level to about 8,000 ft (NatureServe). North of the Sunshine Coast it is known from only a few isolated sites in British Columbia (BC).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the taxonomy of this complex is controversial: some authors recognize from two to eleven or more species, others treat it as one.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern British Columbia south along the Coast Ranges to northwestern Baja California, and on the western slopes of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada; absent from the Sacramento-San Joaquin valley; sea level to about 8,000 ft (NatureServe). North of the Sunshine Coast it is known from only a few isolated sites in British Columbia (BC).

identification.text: Slender, small salamander: total length up to about 120 mm (BC).
Uniform pinkish brown, often with a yellow tinge at the base of the legs and digits; yellow or brown flecks sometimes on the sides (BC).
Large head and eyes, relatively long limbs, and a narrow constriction at the tail base that can be hard to see in small animals (BC).
Hatchlings are black or dark gray mottled with lighter flecks, with bright yellow leg bases (BC).

habitat.text: Douglas-fir and maple forest and clearings in the north; redwood forest, chaparral, oak woodland and canyons on the coast; pine-oak-incense cedar forest in the Sierra Nevada (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Lives entirely on the forest floor from egg to adult; no aquatic larval stage, young hatch as miniature adults (BC; NatureServe).
Sheltering under or inside rotting logs, stumps, bark piles, rodent burrows or moist crevices (BC).
Eats insects, spiders and millipedes; inactive in cold or hot dry weather, emerging with fall rains and active until about May or June in the north and at high elevations (NatureServe).
Female broods a cluster of 7-25 eggs, which hatch in fall or early winter (NatureServe).

resources.title: Long-nosed leopard lizard
resources.description: Identify the long-nosed leopard lizard (Gambelia wislizenii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Long-nosed leopard lizard (Gambelia wislizenii): Moderate-sized lizard with a tail more than twice the length of the rest of the body and a relatively large head (NDOW). Small scales over the whole body; white, gray or cream with darker spots on the back and legs (NDOW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Oregon, southern Idaho, Utah and western Colorado south through eastern and southern California, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to northeastern Baja California and north-central mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Oregon, southern Idaho, Utah and western Colorado south through eastern and southern California, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to northeastern Baja California and north-central mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

identification.text: Moderate-sized lizard with a tail more than twice the length of the rest of the body and a relatively large head (NDOW).
Small scales over the whole body; white, gray or cream with darker spots on the back and legs (NDOW).
Breeding females develop bright orange spots along the sides (NDOW).

habitat.text: Sandy and rocky desert and semidesert with scattered low shrubs (creosotebush, sagebrush), especially areas with many rodent burrows; avoids dense vegetation (NDOW; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Mostly ground-dwelling; when threatened runs to the base of a shrub and freezes (NDOW; NatureServe).
Not territorial; adults largely ignore each other except when mating (NDOW).
Eats insects, spiders, lizards, snakes, small rodents and some plant material, and can eat a lizard nearly its own size (NDOW).
Active about May-August in the north and late March or April to late summer or fall in the south; animals active in late summer are mostly hatchlings (NatureServe).

resources.title: Mediterranean gecko
resources.description: Identify the mediterranean gecko (Hemidactylus turcicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mediterranean gecko (Hemidactylus turcicus): Soft, see-through skin; pale pink to white with dark markings on the back and tail (NDOW). Large lidless eyes with vertical pupils and sticky toe pads (NDOW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Introduced in North America. Native to the Mediterranean region and nearby (NatureServe; NDOW); established from Florida to Texas and north into southeastern states, in Arizona and southern California, and in southern Nevada urban areas (NatureServe; NDOW).

rangeSummary.value: Introduced in North America. Native to the Mediterranean region and nearby (NatureServe; NDOW); established from Florida to Texas and north into southeastern states, in Arizona and southern California, and in southern Nevada urban areas (NatureServe; NDOW).

identification.text: Soft, see-through skin; pale pink to white with dark markings on the back and tail (NDOW).
Large lidless eyes with vertical pupils and sticky toe pads (NDOW).
Bumpy skin covered with small raised tubercles, which separates it from the native western banded gecko (NDOW).
Compared with the western banded gecko: Native western banded gecko lacks the Mediterranean gecko's raised tubercles on bumpy skin (NDOW).

habitat.text: In North America usually on or in occupied buildings, on walls and ceilings; also under palm leaves, in bark crevices and rocky outcrops (NatureServe; NDOW).

behavior.text: Nocturnal; often seen on buildings, window screens and walls near lights hunting moths, crickets, cockroaches and spiders, hiding in cracks and crevices or under bark by day (NDOW; NatureServe).
Can vocalize with chirps and clicks and can drop its tail (NDOW).
Females lay two eggs per clutch, several clutches a year, often in communal nests (NDOW); in Texas eggs are laid May to early September (NatureServe).

resources.title: Common lesser earless lizard
resources.description: Identify the common lesser earless lizard (Holbrookia maculata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common lesser earless lizard (Holbrookia maculata): No external ear openings (CPW). Striped or speckled back; two black bars on each side of the belly, sometimes described as bars near the armpits; up to about 13 cm total length (CPW; TPWD). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern South Dakota to central Texas, southwest to southeastern Utah and Arizona, and south to Jalisco and Guanajuato, Mexico (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (Nicholson 2025) recognizes subspecies campi, flavilenta and maculata; TPWD's page covers the subspecies H. m. maculata (northern earless lizard).

rangeSummary.value: Southern South Dakota to central Texas, southwest to southeastern Utah and Arizona, and south to Jalisco and Guanajuato, Mexico (NatureServe).

identification.text: No external ear openings (CPW).
Striped or speckled back; two black bars on each side of the belly, sometimes described as bars near the armpits; up to about 13 cm total length (CPW; TPWD).
Mature male: two enlarged scales under the tail behind the vent, black blue-edged belly bars, possible yellowish wash on the sides (CPW).
Mature female: belly bars lack blue edging; breeding females show yellow-orange on the throat, head and neck and orange on the sides (CPW).

habitat.text: Sparsely vegetated sandy or gravelly ground: sandhills, prairie-dog towns, washes, streambanks, dunes, sagebrush flats and open prairie (CPW; NatureServe).

behavior.text: Mainly diurnal, but may be active in the evening and at night in hot weather (NatureServe).
Takes cover in rodent burrows or burrows into sand (CPW).
Eats mainly insects and spiders (NatureServe).
Active March-October in the north; lays 1-2 clutches between April and September (NatureServe).

resources.title: Canyon treefrog
resources.description: Identify the canyon treefrog (Hyla arenicolor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Canyon treefrog (Hyla arenicolor): Head and body up to about 57 mm (2.2 in) (CPW). Light brown or gray, often matching the rock, turning chalky in full midday sun (CPW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western and southeastern Colorado and southern Utah south through Arizona and western New Mexico into Mexico, with isolated populations in northeastern New Mexico and the Big Bend area of Texas (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses Dryophytes arenicolor (Duellman et al. 2016 restricted Hyla to Eurasia and North Africa).

rangeSummary.value: Western and southeastern Colorado and southern Utah south through Arizona and western New Mexico into Mexico, with isolated populations in northeastern New Mexico and the Big Bend area of Texas (NatureServe).

identification.text: Head and body up to about 57 mm (2.2 in) (CPW).
Light brown or gray, often matching the rock, turning chalky in full midday sun (CPW).
Paddle-shaped toe tips, extensive webbing on the hind toes, and orange-yellow rear thighs and groin (CPW).
Call is a loud, nasal, rapid stuttering 'ah-ah-ah-ah-ah' lasting 0.75-2 seconds; breeding males have loose dusky throat skin and a two-lobed vocal sac (CPW).

habitat.text: Only along rocky stream courses in canyons, in pools of temporary or permanent streams; also arroyos in semiarid grassland and streams in pinyon-juniper and pine-oak woodland, about 300-3,000 m (NatureServe; CPW).

behavior.text: Basks on rocks and hides in rock crevices; most active at night but can be seen on rocks along streams by day (CPW; NatureServe).
Inactive in cold temperatures and hot dry weather, when it retreats to crevices (NatureServe).
Breeds mainly April-July in pools along intermittent streams; adults eat ants, beetles, centipedes and spiders (NatureServe; CPW).

resources.title: Desert nightsnake
resources.description: Identify the desert nightsnake (Hypsiglena chlorophaea), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert nightsnake (Hypsiglena chlorophaea): Smooth scales and many dark blotches above, the largest and most conspicuous on the neck (CPW). Pupil vertically elongate, like a cat's; 19-21 scale rows at midbody; divided anal scale (CPW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah and western Colorado to Arizona, northeastern Baja California and northwestern mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats Hypsiglena chlorophaea and H. ochrorhyncha as separate species following Mulcahy (2008), who split the former H. torquata; Colorado Parks and Wildlife lists the Colorado animals as H. jani and H. chlorophaea, and Idaho Fish and Game lists several H. torquata names under chlorophaea.

rangeSummary.value: South-central British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah and western Colorado to Arizona, northeastern Baja California and northwestern mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

identification.text: Smooth scales and many dark blotches above, the largest and most conspicuous on the neck (CPW).
Pupil vertically elongate, like a cat's; 19-21 scale rows at midbody; divided anal scale (CPW).
Extra scale in front of the eye behind the nostril separates it from the Chihuahuan nightsnake (CPW).
Maximum about 62 cm (24 in) total length (CPW).
Compared with the chihuahuan nightsnake: Lacks the extra scale in front of the eye, behind the nostril (CPW).

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid plains, canyons and hillsides, usually rocky, dissected terrain with sandy or gravelly soil, including desert, grassland, shrubland and woodland (NatureServe; CPW).

behavior.text: Exclusively nocturnal and rarely seen; mildly venomous but not dangerous to humans (CPW).
Spends most of its time under rocks, in crevices or in rodent burrows; found under rocks mainly in mild weather of spring, late summer and fall (CPW).
Eats mainly lizards and lizard eggs, sometimes small snakes, frogs, insects and salamanders (NatureServe; CPW).

resources.title: Coast nightsnake
resources.description: Identify the coast nightsnake (Hypsiglena ochrorhyncha), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Coast nightsnake (Hypsiglena ochrorhyncha): 12-26 in (300-660 mm) snout-vent length (theNAT). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern California south through western California to southern Baja California (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats Hypsiglena chlorophaea and H. ochrorhyncha as separate species following Mulcahy (2008), who split the former H. torquata; Colorado Parks and Wildlife lists the Colorado animals as H. jani and H. chlorophaea, and Idaho Fish and Game lists several H. torquata names under chlorophaea.

rangeSummary.value: Northern California south through western California to southern Baja California (NatureServe).

identification.text: 12-26 in (300-660 mm) snout-vent length (theNAT).
Compared with the desert nightsnake: Listed by theNAT as a similar species; no distinguishing marks were published on the pages read.

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid plains, canyons and hillsides, usually rocky, dissected terrain with sandy or gravelly soil, including desert, grassland, shrubland, savanna and woodland (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Eats mainly lizards and lizard eggs (NatureServe).
Spends inactive periods under rocks or other surface cover, in crevices or underground (NatureServe).

resources.title: California kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the california kingsnake (Lampropeltis californiae), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California kingsnake (Lampropeltis californiae): Smooth, glossy scales (NPS Cabrillo). Highly variable pattern: black and white or brown and cream, with bands or longitudinal stripes; aberrant animals may show dots, zippers or bars (NPS Cabrillo). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Oregon, western and southern Nevada, southern Utah and extreme southwestern Colorado south through California and Arizona to southern Baja California and northern Sinaloa (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses a narrow sense of L. californiae that excludes L. nigrita (Krysko et al. 2017); NPS Death Valley lists it as Lampropeltis getula californiae.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Oregon, western and southern Nevada, southern Utah and extreme southwestern Colorado south through California and Arizona to southern Baja California and northern Sinaloa (NatureServe).

identification.text: Smooth, glossy scales (NPS Cabrillo).
Highly variable pattern: black and white or brown and cream, with bands or longitudinal stripes; aberrant animals may show dots, zippers or bars (NPS Cabrillo).
Usually 2.5-3.5 ft, up to about 4 ft (NPS Cabrillo); NatureServe gives typically 76-107 cm.
Compared with the california mountain kingsnake: Red, black and white ringed pattern with red bands bordered by black (WDFW); listed as a similar species by theNAT.
Compared with the long-nosed snake: Listed by theNAT as a similar species; no distinguishing marks were published on the page read.

habitat.text: Primarily terrestrial; forest, woodland, shrubland, swamps, marshes, river bottoms, grassland, semidesert, desert and farmland (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Constrictor that eats small mammals, lizards, amphibians, birds, large invertebrates and other snakes (NPS Cabrillo).
Resistant to rattlesnake venom and known to eat rattlesnakes (CDFW).
Inactive periods are spent in crevices or burrows, or under rocks, logs, stumps or other cover (NatureServe).

resources.title: Western milk snake
resources.description: Identify the western milk snake (Lampropeltis gentilis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western milk snake (Lampropeltis gentilis): Black, white and red bands in the order red-black-white-black-red, with red the widest and black and white similar or black thinner (CPW). Smooth scales; to about 85 cm in eastern Colorado and 72 cm in western Colorado (CPW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Utah, eastern Montana, South Dakota and Nebraska south through parts of Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas and Oklahoma to southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico, southern Texas, southern Arkansas and Louisiana west of the Mississippi; to about 2,740 m (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe recognizes L. gentilis as a species (Ruane et al. 2014) and notes alternate views (Chambers and Hillis 2020) that it is not distinct; Colorado Parks and Wildlife treats the animals as Lampropeltis triangulum (milksnake). The CPW facts below are for that Colorado milksnake.

rangeSummary.value: Utah, eastern Montana, South Dakota and Nebraska south through parts of Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas and Oklahoma to southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico, southern Texas, southern Arkansas and Louisiana west of the Mississippi; to about 2,740 m (NatureServe).

identification.text: Black, white and red bands in the order red-black-white-black-red, with red the widest and black and white similar or black thinner (CPW).
Smooth scales; to about 85 cm in eastern Colorado and 72 cm in western Colorado (CPW).
US coral snakes instead run red-yellow or white-black-yellow or white-red, with red and black bands about equal and the pale band thin; coral snakes do not occur in Colorado (CPW).
Compared with the coral snakes: Coral snakes have red and black bands of about equal width separated by thin yellow or white bands; the milksnake's red is widest (CPW).

habitat.text: Varies widely: semiarid to wet, lowland valleys to mountains, grassland and shrubland to forest edges, dunes to rocky areas, and semiagricultural and suburban areas (NatureServe); in Colorado prairie, sandhills, canyons, river valleys, ponderosa pine and pinyon-juniper (CPW).

behavior.text: Secretive; hides in or under logs, stumps and other surface cover by day but may be found in the open (NatureServe; CPW).
Opportunistic feeder on eggs and small vertebrates; diet dominated by lizards and mammals (CPW; NatureServe).
Hibernates underground or in deep crevices; eggs laid in soil or under cover (NatureServe).

resources.title: Arizona mountain kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the arizona mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis pyromelana), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Arizona mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis pyromelana): Medium-sized snake with red, white and black bands and a flat, wide head (NDOW). Non-venomous; its red, white and black coloration mimics a coral snake (NDOW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Discontinuous from east-central Nevada and central and western Utah south to near (mostly north of) the Mogollon Rim in Arizona and New Mexico (NatureServe); in Nevada limited to east-central mountains (NDOW).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's English name is Sonoran mountain kingsnake; per Burbrink et al. (2011) L. pyromelana (as circumscribed by Stebbins 2003) comprises northern L. pyromelana and southern L. knoblochi.

rangeSummary.value: Discontinuous from east-central Nevada and central and western Utah south to near (mostly north of) the Mogollon Rim in Arizona and New Mexico (NatureServe); in Nevada limited to east-central mountains (NDOW).

identification.text: Medium-sized snake with red, white and black bands and a flat, wide head (NDOW).
Non-venomous; its red, white and black coloration mimics a coral snake (NDOW).
Compared with the coral snakes: US coral snakes have the pattern red-yellow or white-black-yellow or white-red with thin pale bands, with red and black about equal in width (CPW).

habitat.text: Rocky, montane country often near streams or springs, also mesic lower canyons; pinyon-juniper, oak-juniper, pine-oak or pine-Douglas-fir woodland or chaparral (NatureServe; NDOW).

behavior.text: Mostly active by day; hides among rocks, logs and vegetation to avoid heat and predators (NDOW).
Constrictor that eats lizards, frogs, snakes, small mammals and even rattlesnakes (NDOW; NatureServe).
In Arizona adults and hatchlings were most often encountered in July and August (NatureServe).
Females lay 3-6 eggs; inactive in cold and extreme heat (NDOW; NatureServe).

resources.title: California mountain kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the california mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis zonata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis zonata): Slender, cylindrical snake 1.5-3 ft long with red, black and white bands; red bands always bordered by black on both sides (WDFW; ADW). Top of the head black, chin and throat often white, and the first band behind the head is white (ADW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western United States: around the Central Valley of California along the Sierra Nevada and Northern Coast Ranges, north into the Klamath Mountains in Oregon, with a disjunct population in the Columbia Gorge in Washington; populations south of Monterey Bay are treated as L. multifasciata by NatureServe (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Western United States: around the Central Valley of California along the Sierra Nevada and Northern Coast Ranges, north into the Klamath Mountains in Oregon, with a disjunct population in the Columbia Gorge in Washington; populations south of Monterey Bay are treated as L. multifasciata by NatureServe (NatureServe).

identification.text: Slender, cylindrical snake 1.5-3 ft long with red, black and white bands; red bands always bordered by black on both sides (WDFW; ADW).
Top of the head black, chin and throat often white, and the first band behind the head is white (ADW).
Red bands may be broken into wedges or reduced or absent, especially in Sierra Nevada populations (ADW).
Smooth, unkeeled scales (ADW).
Compared with the coral snakes: Harmless and superficially resembles a coral snake; its red bands are bordered by black (WDFW).

Compared with the california kingsnake: Mountain kingsnake has red, black and white bands with red bordered by black (WDFW, ADW); California kingsnake is black and white or brown and cream, banded or striped (NPS Cabrillo).

habitat.text: Moist open coniferous forest, oak woodland, riparian woodland, chaparral, coastal sage scrub and open woodland with rocks or rotting logs, often near streams; sea level to about 2,750 m (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Mainly diurnal, but may be nocturnal in hot weather (NatureServe; WDFW).
Searches under surface objects for lizards, small snakes and bird eggs; also eats mammals, and juveniles mainly eat lizards (NatureServe).
Mating April-May, eggs laid June-July, 2-9 per clutch (NatureServe).
Found under woody debris and rocks; inactive in cold and extreme heat (WDFW; NatureServe).

resources.title: Northern three-lined boa
resources.description: Identify the northern three-lined boa (Lichanura orcutti), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern three-lined boa (Lichanura orcutti): Cream to light pink skin with three distinct stripes from head to tail, usually black but sometimes lighter brown (NPS Organ Pipe). Relatively heavy-bodied, 15-36 in (38-90 cm), with a blunt tail tip (NPS Organ Pipe). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: San Diego County, California, along the coastal Peninsular Ranges, north into the Mohave Desert and east in the Sonoran Desert of California and western Arizona (north of the Gila River), plus the Newberry Mountains in southern Nevada (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe splits Lichanura orcutti (primary name Northern Rosy Boa / Desert Rosy Boa) from L. trivirgata (Wood et al. 2008), and notes an unpublished reanalysis would replace orcutti with L. roseofusca. NPS Organ Pipe and Arizona pages use L. trivirgata for the rosy boa; the NPS field marks below are for that rosy boa.

rangeSummary.value: San Diego County, California, along the coastal Peninsular Ranges, north into the Mohave Desert and east in the Sonoran Desert of California and western Arizona (north of the Gila River), plus the Newberry Mountains in southern Nevada (NatureServe).

identification.text: Cream to light pink skin with three distinct stripes from head to tail, usually black but sometimes lighter brown (NPS Organ Pipe).
Relatively heavy-bodied, 15-36 in (38-90 cm), with a blunt tail tip (NPS Organ Pipe).

habitat.text: Desert, arid scrub, brushland, sandy plains, rocky slopes and chaparral foothills, particularly near springs, streams and canyon floors, though not dependent on permanent water; mainly terrestrial, sometimes climbs shrubs (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Spends most time in rocky crevices or abandoned burrows, emerging at night to hunt and warm itself; usually most active at night (NPS Organ Pipe; NatureServe).
Constricts small mammals and birds; docile, but releases musk from glands when threatened (NPS Organ Pipe; NatureServe).
Inactive in cold temperatures and extreme heat; live-bearing (NatureServe).

resources.title: Rio Grande leopard frog
resources.description: Identify the rio grande leopard frog (Lithobates berlandieri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rio Grande leopard frog (Lithobates berlandieri): Adults 5.7-11.4 cm snout-vent, a rather large leopard frog with an angular nose and long powerful legs (ADW; CDFW). Gray, green or brown back with many irregular dark brown spots edged olive-green or light tan (ADW). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to extreme southern New Mexico and central and western Texas south through eastern and southern Mexico to Nicaragua; introduced and well established in the Imperial Valley and along the lower Colorado and Gila rivers in California and Arizona, replacing native lowland leopard frogs (NatureServe).

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web and NAS list the older name Rana berlandieri; NatureServe notes three competing generic arrangements for American ranids and follows Nicholson (2025) in keeping Lithobates.

rangeSummary.value: Native to extreme southern New Mexico and central and western Texas south through eastern and southern Mexico to Nicaragua; introduced and well established in the Imperial Valley and along the lower Colorado and Gila rivers in California and Arizona, replacing native lowland leopard frogs (NatureServe).

identification.text: Adults 5.7-11.4 cm snout-vent, a rather large leopard frog with an angular nose and long powerful legs (ADW; CDFW).
Gray, green or brown back with many irregular dark brown spots edged olive-green or light tan (ADW).
Prominent dorsolateral folds, usually pale yellow, that turn inward in front of the groin (ADW).
Cream belly fading to pale yellow on the upper thighs; females lighter and smaller than males (ADW).

habitat.text: Streams, rivers, springs, stock ponds, backwaters, canals, ditches and arroyo pools in grassland, shrubland, savanna, desert and woodland; where introduced, mainly ditches, canals, irrigation sumps and modified rivers (NatureServe).

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal; chiefly a stream dweller that uses temporary and permanent water and is rarely far from it (NatureServe; CDFW; ADW).
Lays eggs after rains at almost any time of year, mostly March-May and August-November in Texas (NatureServe).
Males give mating trills, release calls and chuckle calls (ADW).
Disperses along canals, ditches and rivers (CDFW).

resources.title: Southern leopard frog
resources.description: Identify the southern leopard frog (Lithobates sphenocephalus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern leopard frog (Lithobates sphenocephalus): Green or brown with irregularly spaced, rounded dark spots on the back and a few on the sides. A continuous, usually yellowish ridge runs along each side of the back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Lowlands of the southeastern United States from southern New York to the Florida Keys, west to eastern Kansas, central Oklahoma and eastern Texas; introduced on Little Bahama Bank. Not reported for Canada in the source.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the generic placement of American ranids is unsettled (Rana, Lithobates or other genera depending on the arrangement) and follows Nicholson (2025) in using Lithobates; older names are Rana sphenocephala / Rana utricularia.

rangeSummary.value: Lowlands of the southeastern United States from southern New York to the Florida Keys, west to eastern Kansas, central Oklahoma and eastern Texas; introduced on Little Bahama Bank. Not reported for Canada in the source.

identification.text: Green or brown with irregularly spaced, rounded dark spots on the back and a few on the sides.
A continuous, usually yellowish ridge runs along each side of the back.
Head is pointed; usually a light spot in the centre of the eardrum.
Hind toes are extensively webbed; adults reach about 13 cm snout-vent length.
Breeding call is a short chuckling or ratchet-like trill; breeding males have spherical vocal sacs at the angles of the jaw.

habitat.text: Occurs near virtually any freshwater habitat and in some places slightly brackish marshes.
Breeds in still, shallow, permanent or temporary water.

behavior.text: Males call from shallow or deep water, floating or submerged, sometimes from crayfish burrows.
Breeds usually March-June in the north of the range and in any month in the far south.
In summer may disperse from water into moist upland vegetation; migrates between breeding pools and adjacent terrestrial habitat; inactive in cold winter weather in the north.
Adults eat small terrestrial invertebrates; egg masses are baseball-sized and hold roughly 1,000-1,500 eggs.

resources.title: Smooth green snake
resources.description: Identify the smooth green snake (Opheodrys vernalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Smooth green snake (Opheodrys vernalis): Slender, bright green above with smooth dorsal scales (15 rows at midbody) and a white or yellowish belly. Adults usually 30-51 cm, up to about 61 cm; the tail is nearly half of total length. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Nova Scotia west across southern Canada (Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba) to southeastern Saskatchewan, south through the northeastern and Midwestern US to Virginia, Missouri, Nebraska, New Mexico and Utah; western populations are highly disjunct.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe spells the common name 'Smooth Greensnake' and notes some authors placed the species in genus Liochlorophis; Animal Diversity Web uses 'Smooth Green Snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Nova Scotia west across southern Canada (Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba) to southeastern Saskatchewan, south through the northeastern and Midwestern US to Virginia, Missouri, Nebraska, New Mexico and Utah; western populations are highly disjunct.

identification.text: Slender, bright green above with smooth dorsal scales (15 rows at midbody) and a white or yellowish belly.
Adults usually 30-51 cm, up to about 61 cm; the tail is nearly half of total length.
Young are dull olive-gray to bluish-gray or grayish brown; adults turn blue or gray after death.
Smooth scales separate it from the rough green snake (keeled scales); single nostril scale and smaller size separate it from racers.
Compared with the rough green snake: Has keeled rather than smooth dorsal scales.
Compared with the racer: Larger; nostril sits between two scales rather than centred in one scale.

habitat.text: Grassy, open areas: meadows, grassy marshes, moist fields at forest edges, bogs, stream borders and open moist woodland.
Often near wetlands or open water.

behavior.text: Diurnal; basks on boulders or logs and may hang in low branches; inactive roughly November-March.
Eats small terrestrial invertebrates such as caterpillars, crickets, grasshoppers and spiders.
Can aggregate in hibernacula (groups of 100-150 found in Manitoba and Minnesota) and sometimes uses abandoned ant mounds.
Eggs are laid under rotting wood, underground or under rocks; some individuals cross roads at night during warm rains.

resources.title: Great Plains ratsnake
resources.description: Identify the great plains ratsnake (Pantherophis emoryi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great Plains ratsnake (Pantherophis emoryi): Gray to light-brown ground colour with large brown blotches down the midline of the back, flanked by two rows of smaller blotches. A V- or spear-point mark on the head leading toward the neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Illinois, Missouri, southern South Dakota and southeastern Colorado south to San Luis Potosi and Veracruz, through most of Texas, with a disjunct population in eastern Utah and western Colorado. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes recent genomic work and that P. slowinskii may be treated as a separate species or a subspecies of P. emoryi, and that P. emoryi itself may comprise two subspecies; Animal Diversity Web uses 'Great Plains rat snake' and the older Elaphe/Pantherophis placement.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Illinois, Missouri, southern South Dakota and southeastern Colorado south to San Luis Potosi and Veracruz, through most of Texas, with a disjunct population in eastern Utah and western Colorado. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Gray to light-brown ground colour with large brown blotches down the midline of the back, flanked by two rows of smaller blotches.
A V- or spear-point mark on the head leading toward the neck.
Belly is a black-and-white checkerboard with stripes under the tail; scales slightly keeled; anal plate divided.
Adults 61-153 cm snout-vent length.
Compared with the bullsnake: Scales have more distinct keels (Animal Diversity Web).
Compared with the black ratsnake: Lacks the spear-point mark on the head.
Compared with the glossy snake: Smooth scales and a single anal plate.

habitat.text: Fields, hill prairie, brushy areas, woodlands, riparian areas, canyons, barnyards and abandoned buildings; avoids heavily forested regions.
Also rocky hillsides and areas near springs and cave entrances.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal forager; hides by day under rocks, logs, boards, in crevices and small mammal burrows.
Semi-arboreal; climbs high in trees to hunt birds; also swims.
Eats mainly rodents plus birds and eggs, and occasionally snakes, lizards and frogs; kills by constriction.
When agitated shakes the tail (audible in dry leaf litter, often mistaken for a rattlesnake), strikes and releases musk; hibernates alone.

resources.title: Mearns' rock lizard
resources.description: Identify the mearns' rock lizard (Petrosaurus mearnsi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mearns' rock lizard (Petrosaurus mearnsi). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
