keyFacts.value: From San Gorgonio Pass (Riverside County, California) south through the Peninsular Ranges to at least Bahia de los Angeles in Baja California, plus some Gulf of California islands; in the US limited to eastern San Diego and central Riverside counties, to about 1,200 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe spells it 'Mearns's Rock Lizard' (alt. 'Banded Rock Lizard'); the California agency account spells 'Mearn's'. NatureServe notes Grismer (1999) treated P. mearnsi and P. slevini as separate species and that northern and southern clades exist within P. mearnsi.

rangeSummary.value: From San Gorgonio Pass (Riverside County, California) south through the Peninsular Ranges to at least Bahia de los Angeles in Baja California, plus some Gulf of California islands; in the US limited to eastern San Diego and central Riverside counties, to about 1,200 m.

habitat.text: Most abundant among massive rocks: cliffs, boulder piles and canyon walls in shaded, narrow parts of desert-slope canyons, and desert washes and palm oases.
Rarely found on open ground; shelters in rock cracks and crevices.

behavior.text: Diurnal; shuttles between sun and shade, active all day even in hot weather, from about mid-March to late summer.
Forages on vertical and under-rock surfaces; eats beetles, ants, bees, flies, spiders and some buds and blossoms.
Males defend territories (tolerating subadult males); females defend against other females; home ranges about 85 m2 (males) and 40 m2 (females) in one study.
Lays 2-6 eggs, June-August.

resources.title: Pygmy short-horned lizard
resources.description: Identify the pygmy short-horned lizard (Phrynosoma douglasii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pygmy short-horned lizard (Phrynosoma douglasii): Toad-shaped: blunt snout, squat flattened body, short legs and a short triangular tail. Spines project from the back of the head, with fringe-like spines along the sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern Washington south to northeastern California and east to northern Nevada and eastern Idaho; an old record exists from extreme southwestern Montana. Historical records near Osoyoos Lake, British Columbia, but considered extirpated from Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly treated as one species ('Short-horned Lizard') with P. hernandesi; Montana Field Guide and NatureServe treat them as separate species. WDFW lists the family as Iguanidae; NatureServe uses Phrynosomatidae.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern Washington south to northeastern California and east to northern Nevada and eastern Idaho; an old record exists from extreme southwestern Montana. Historical records near Osoyoos Lake, British Columbia, but considered extirpated from Canada.

identification.text: Toad-shaped: blunt snout, squat flattened body, short legs and a short triangular tail.
Spines project from the back of the head, with fringe-like spines along the sides.
Back is mottled white, gray, beige, tan, brown or black, sometimes yellow or orange, with dark blotches in transverse rows; underside white, sometimes with a yellow or gray wash.
Small: about 2.5 inches (without tail) as an adult; females larger than males; males have enlarged femoral pores.
Head horns are small and project nearly vertically, and lack the wide notch that gives the greater short-horned lizard a heart-shaped head (Montana Field Guide).
Compared with the greater short-horned lizard: Larger; wide notch between the head horns gives a heart-shaped head, horns project horizontally.

habitat.text: Semiarid plains to high mountains in open, sparsely vegetated shrubby or openly wooded areas: sagebrush, bunchgrass, pinyon-juniper, open pine.
Soil varies from rocky to sandy; in Washington occupies shrubsteppe.

behavior.text: Live-bearing; gives birth to 3-15 young, mainly August to mid-September.
Surface active roughly March-early November in Washington; mid-day active in spring and fall, inactive at mid-day in summer.
Diet is primarily ants (about three-quarters in adults) plus other insects; newborns feed almost exclusively on ants.
Colour tracks the substrate, which makes it cryptic; burrows into soil or uses rodent burrows when inactive.

resources.title: Greater short-horned lizard
resources.description: Identify the greater short-horned lizard (Phrynosoma hernandesi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Greater short-horned lizard (Phrynosoma hernandesi): Broad, flattened body with a spiny back, especially a single row of scales fringing each side of the body. Short, stubby head spines about as long as wide at the base, separated by a wide, deep notch that gives a heart-shaped head from above. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan south through eastern Montana, the western Dakotas, Wyoming, western Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, eastern Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona and western Texas to northern Mexico; limits around southeastern Idaho, northern Utah and Nevada are not precisely known.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (citing Nicholson 2025) treats P. ornatissimum as a separate species, removing some New Mexico, Texas and Chihuahua populations previously placed in P. hernandesi; Montana Field Guide notes the former 'Short-horned Lizard' was split into P. douglasii and P. hernandesi.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan south through eastern Montana, the western Dakotas, Wyoming, western Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, eastern Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona and western Texas to northern Mexico; limits around southeastern Idaho, northern Utah and Nevada are not precisely known.

identification.text: Broad, flattened body with a spiny back, especially a single row of scales fringing each side of the body.
Short, stubby head spines about as long as wide at the base, separated by a wide, deep notch that gives a heart-shaped head from above.
Back is gray, brown or pink blending with soil, usually with two paired rows of dark brown blotches often edged in white.
Total length up to about 15 cm; females larger than males; males have a swelling at the tail base.
Compared with the pygmy short-horned lizard: Much smaller as an adult, lacks the wide notch between head horns, horns project almost vertically.
Compared with the common sagebrush lizard: Not broad and flattened; no head horns.

habitat.text: Semiarid plains to high mountains in open, shrubby or openly wooded areas with sparse ground vegetation; soil rocky to sandy.
In Montana occurs in sagebrush and grassland.

behavior.text: Viviparous: broods of 5-36 (3-15 in the Pacific Northwest), July-September.
Eats ants and other insects, spiders, snails and sowbugs; inactive in cold weather (active April-October in Colorado).
Burrows into soil or uses rodent burrows when inactive.

resources.title: Desert horned lizard
resources.description: Identify the desert horned lizard (Phrynosoma platyrhinos), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert horned lizard (Phrynosoma platyrhinos): Flat, round body with horns and bumps; colour beige, tan, brown or slightly reddish to match the local soil. Long head spines; 2.5-3.75 inches total (NPS Zion key); similar to the short-horned lizards but found at low elevations. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho and northern Utah south through eastern and southern California, Nevada and western Arizona to northeastern Baja California; from below sea level to about 1,980 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes populations south of the Gila River in southwestern Arizona and northwestern Sonora are now recognized as a separate species, P. goodei, and discusses possible cryptic diversity within P. platyrhinos.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho and northern Utah south through eastern and southern California, Nevada and western Arizona to northeastern Baja California; from below sea level to about 1,980 m.

identification.text: Flat, round body with horns and bumps; colour beige, tan, brown or slightly reddish to match the local soil.
Long head spines; 2.5-3.75 inches total (NPS Zion key); similar to the short-horned lizards but found at low elevations.
Compared with the greater short-horned lizard: Short head spines and high-elevation habitat, versus long head spines at low elevation.
Compared with the pygmy short-horned lizard: Short head spines and high-elevation habitat, versus long head spines at low elevation.

habitat.text: Desert shrublands (sagebrush, shadscale, hopsage, creosotebush, greasewood) on sandy flats, alluvial fans, washes and dune edges.
Most consistently where bare ground lies among open shrubs; found in sandy or gravelly valleys in Nevada.

behavior.text: Ant specialist: bulk of the diet is large harvester ants; also other insects, spiders and some plant material.
Active mostly by day from about March, scarce above ground after mid-July in southern Nevada; buries itself in soil or uses burrows when inactive or too hot.
Not fast; relies on camouflage, and can inflate its body when pursued.
Egg layer: females bury eggs in soil; average clutch about 7; one or two clutches a year.

resources.title: Spotted leaf-nosed snake
resources.description: Identify the spotted leaf-nosed snake (Phyllorhynchus decurtatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spotted leaf-nosed snake (Phyllorhynchus decurtatus): Small snake with pale ground colour and dark blotches. A greatly enlarged, upturned scale on the tip of the snout gives the 'leaf-nosed' look. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California (north to Inyo County), southern Nevada, extreme southwestern Utah and central Arizona south to southern Baja California and southern Sonora, Mexico; in Nevada only the south of the state; below sea level to about 1,220 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes named subspecies are questionable; a BLM Red Rock Canyon checklist labels the species 'western leaf-nosed snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California (north to Inyo County), southern Nevada, extreme southwestern Utah and central Arizona south to southern Baja California and southern Sonora, Mexico; in Nevada only the south of the state; below sea level to about 1,220 m.

identification.text: Small snake with pale ground colour and dark blotches.
A greatly enlarged, upturned scale on the tip of the snout gives the 'leaf-nosed' look.

habitat.text: Rocky, gravelly or sandy desert plains or dunes with creosote bush.
Burrows into loose soil or sand and hides under rocks, surface debris or abandoned rodent burrows.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; active in the early evening in mild to warm weather, most on the surface on June nights (Nevada); spends most of its time under the soil.
Eats lizard eggs and small lizards such as banded geckos.
Hibernates in late fall and winter; peak surface activity in June in Arizona and May-June in southern California.
Lays 2-4 eggs, apparently in June-July.

resources.title: Gophersnake
resources.description: Identify the gophersnake (Pituophis catenifer), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gophersnake (Pituophis catenifer): Yellowish or cream dorsum with numerous dark brown to black blotches; a dark stripe across the head between the eyes and another from each eye to the jaw angle. Dorsal scales keeled, anal scale single, usually four prefrontal scales; belly cream or yellowish, often with dark spots. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia, southern Alberta, southern Saskatchewan, Minnesota and Indiana south through most of western and central North America to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Zacatecas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes mitochondrial data suggest P. catenifer may hide additional species but retains the current subspecies; NatureServe spells 'Gophersnake', others 'gopher snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia, southern Alberta, southern Saskatchewan, Minnesota and Indiana south through most of western and central North America to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Zacatecas.

identification.text: Yellowish or cream dorsum with numerous dark brown to black blotches; a dark stripe across the head between the eyes and another from each eye to the jaw angle.
Dorsal scales keeled, anal scale single, usually four prefrontal scales; belly cream or yellowish, often with dark spots.
Large: usually up to 180 cm, rarely to about 280 cm; relatively large head and narrow neck.
Non-venomous and often mistaken for a rattlesnake; has no rattle.
Compared with the rattlesnakes (crotalus spp.): Have a rattle; the gophersnake lacks one (Animal Diversity Web).
Compared with the great plains ratsnake: Has a divided anal plate and only two prefrontal scales in Elaphe; gophersnake has keeled scales, four prefrontals and an undivided anal scale (NatureServe).

habitat.text: Wide range from lowlands to mountains: desert, prairie, shrubland, woodland, open conifer forest, farmland and marshes.
Terrestrial, fossorial and sometimes arboreal.

behavior.text: Mostly diurnal but may be nocturnal or bimodal in hot weather; active roughly April-October in the north.
Feeds mainly on small mammals, also ground birds and eggs, lizards and insects; forages underground and climbs trees for nests.
When alarmed may hiss loudly, flatten and widen the head, and vibrate the tail, which sounds like a rattle in dry vegetation.
Uses mammal burrows or digs its own; winters underground, sometimes migrating several hundred metres between den and summer range.

resources.title: Gilbert's skink
resources.description: Identify the gilbert's skink (Plestiodon gilberti), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gilbert's skink (Plestiodon gilberti): Smooth, shiny scales; olive to brown above, sometimes with dark patterning; up to about 4.5 inches. Young have a brilliant blue or pink tail contrasting with the body. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges of California south to northern Baja California, with isolated populations in southeastern California, southern Nevada and west-central Arizona; sea level to about 2,200 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (citing Nicholson 2025) recognizes three subspecies (Sierran, Western Red-tailed, and an unnamed Inyo skink); formerly in genus Eumeces.

rangeSummary.value: Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges of California south to northern Baja California, with isolated populations in southeastern California, southern Nevada and west-central Arizona; sea level to about 2,200 m.

identification.text: Smooth, shiny scales; olive to brown above, sometimes with dark patterning; up to about 4.5 inches.
Young have a brilliant blue or pink tail contrasting with the body.
Compared with the western skink: Western skink has a conspicuous white or beige stripe down each side; confirm against a field guide.

habitat.text: Varied: grassland, salt flats, high desert, open chaparral, pinyon-juniper and open pine forest, often rocky areas near streams and springs.
In California foothills up to about 1,980 m, favouring chaparral, black oak woodland and riparian deciduous habitat.

behavior.text: Eats insects and spiders, searching under leaves and surface objects.
Lays 3-9 eggs in summer, in chambers in loose soil (peak activity around 1 July in one California account); not territorial.
Inactive in cold temperatures and extreme heat.

resources.title: Many-lined skink
resources.description: Identify the many-lined skink (Plestiodon multivirgatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Many-lined skink (Plestiodon multivirgatus): Smooth, glossy scales and short fore and hind limbs; total length 10.2-19.4 cm. Multiple stripes down the body alternating light and dark on a dark brown to olive-green base. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern South Dakota, Nebraska, southeastern Wyoming and northeastern Colorado (northern segment); southern Colorado, southeastern Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (southern segment); roughly 910-2,620 m. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly in genus Eumeces; NatureServe notes disagreement over whether the southern subspecies is E. m. epipleurotus or E. m. gaigeae.

rangeSummary.value: Southern South Dakota, Nebraska, southeastern Wyoming and northeastern Colorado (northern segment); southern Colorado, southeastern Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (southern segment); roughly 910-2,620 m. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Smooth, glossy scales and short fore and hind limbs; total length 10.2-19.4 cm.
Multiple stripes down the body alternating light and dark on a dark brown to olive-green base.
A pair of white stripes on the third scale row from the middle of the back.

habitat.text: Northern populations: short- and mixed-grass prairie and sandhills on sandy or loose soil.
Southern populations: desert, streamside thickets, pinyon-juniper and pine-oak woodland, fir forest and shrublands.

behavior.text: Diurnal; active about April to early October (March-October in the north of the range), with crepuscular activity in hot weather.
Secretive; usually found under ground cover such as rocks, logs and cow dung; overwinters underground.
Eats mainly terrestrial arthropods.
Lays 2-9 eggs in spring; the female attends the eggs.

resources.title: Western skink
resources.description: Identify the western skink (Plestiodon skiltonianus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western skink (Plestiodon skiltonianus): Slender, long-bodied lizard with smooth, shiny scales and a tail about as long as the body; adults about 5-8 cm snout-vent, up to 19 cm total. Brown, black and cream/golden-yellow longitudinal stripes from the nose onto the tail; belly light gray to cream. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Western North America from south-central British Columbia to northwestern Baja California, from the Pacific coast east to western Montana, Idaho, eastern Utah and north-central Arizona, to about 2,530 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly Eumeces skiltonianus (still used in some sources, including the Montana Field Guide text and the Zion NPS key); Montana notes the southern Baja form is sometimes treated as a separate species.

rangeSummary.value: Western North America from south-central British Columbia to northwestern Baja California, from the Pacific coast east to western Montana, Idaho, eastern Utah and north-central Arizona, to about 2,530 m.

identification.text: Slender, long-bodied lizard with smooth, shiny scales and a tail about as long as the body; adults about 5-8 cm snout-vent, up to 19 cm total.
Brown, black and cream/golden-yellow longitudinal stripes from the nose onto the tail; belly light gray to cream.
Young and young adults have a brilliant blue tail that fades with age.
Males develop reddish-orange on the chin and sides of the head in the breeding season; tail may be stumpy after loss.
Compared with the western fence lizard: Keeled, prickly scales and never a blue tail.
Compared with the northern alligator lizard: Has a skin fold on the side of the body and short legs.

habitat.text: Grassland, chaparral, open juniper-sage shrubland, pinyon-juniper, pine-oak and mixed conifer forest.
Favours grassy openings and rocky areas near streams and dry shaded hillsides.

behavior.text: Secretive; shelters under rocks, leaves and logs and digs burrows; inactive in cold winter weather.
Eats crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, flies, spiders and earthworms.
In Utah mates May-June and lays eggs in July (clutch 2-6, up to 10); the female guards eggs and stays with hatchlings.
Non-migratory.

resources.title: Dunn's salamander
resources.description: Identify the dunn's salamander (Plethodon dunni), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Dunn's salamander (Plethodon dunni): Washington's largest woodland salamander: about 2.5-3 inches snout-vent, 5.5-6 inches total. Tan, yellow or green dorsal stripe over a dark black or brown body; juveniles have a brighter stripe. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Washington (Willapa Hills) south through western Oregon to extreme northwestern California (Smith River watershed), from sea level to about 1,000 m.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Washington (Willapa Hills) south through western Oregon to extreme northwestern California (Smith River watershed), from sea level to about 1,000 m.

identification.text: Washington's largest woodland salamander: about 2.5-3 inches snout-vent, 5.5-6 inches total.
Tan, yellow or green dorsal stripe over a dark black or brown body; juveniles have a brighter stripe.
Stripe does not reach the tail tip and has an uneven 'eroding' edge invaded by blotches of the side colour.
Sides have patchy blotches and flecks the colour of the stripe; usually 15 costal grooves.
Nasolabial grooves separate it from non-plethodontid salamanders such as the long-toed salamander.
Compared with the western red-backed salamander: Lacks blotches and flecks of the stripe colour on the sides of the body.
Compared with the long-toed salamander: No nasolabial grooves, rounded snout, noticeably longer fourth hind toe.

habitat.text: Shaded, rocky edges of humid forested streams, stream seepages and moist talus slopes; moss-covered outcrops.
Needs cool, permanently moist conditions but not flowing water.

behavior.text: Active above ground mostly at night during or after rain, mainly spring and fall in Washington; hard to find in the dry summer.
Eats small invertebrates including mites, springtails, snails and flies.
Eggs are laid on land in clusters of roughly 4-18 in moist crevices, rotted logs or cavities; no free-living larval stage.
Hides under rocks, logs, moss and leaf litter; may enter water to escape predators.

resources.title: California treefrog
resources.description: Identify the california treefrog (Pseudacris cadaverina), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California treefrog (Pseudacris cadaverina): Gray or light brown with small dark brown spots; rough skin; white belly with yellowish limbs and groin. Adults 2.5-5.1 cm snout-vent length; toe pads are large and wide, with webbing. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern California south into northern Baja California, Mexico, from near sea level to about 2,290 m. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Some authors (Duellman et al. 2016) place it in Hyliola; NatureServe notes Banker et al. (2020) argued against that and that Hyliola has not been widely adopted. The USGS fact sheet calls it the 'California chorus frog'.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern California south into northern Baja California, Mexico, from near sea level to about 2,290 m. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Gray or light brown with small dark brown spots; rough skin; white belly with yellowish limbs and groin.
Adults 2.5-5.1 cm snout-vent length; toe pads are large and wide, with webbing.
Baja California treefrog more often has a dark eye stripe, is more often green and has smaller toe pads; males of this species have a dusky yellow throat.
Call is a repeated pattern of fast, loud, low-pitched quacks; tadpoles have eyes inside the outline of the head.
Compared with the baja california treefrog: Usually has a dark eye stripe, more often green, smaller toe pads; tadpoles have eyes at the margin of the head.

habitat.text: Rocky canyons near streams and washes with permanent pools, from desert and coastal stream courses to mountain pine belt.
Requires some shade; breeds in quiet water of rocky streams.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal except in the breeding season, when it may call day and night; breeds about February-early October.
By day retreats to shaded rock crevices near the waterline; most movements are under 25 m.
Eats insects, spiders and centipedes as adults; lays eggs singly, attached to twigs or loose on the bottom.
Aestivates in extreme heat or cold; inactive in cold or hot, dry weather.

resources.title: Baja California treefrog
resources.description: Identify the baja california treefrog (Pseudacris hypochondriaca), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Baja California treefrog (Pseudacris hypochondriaca): Small treefrog, 19-50 mm snout-vent length, with small toe pads. Dorsal colour varies (green, reddish, tan, gray, brown or black) but typically green or brown; usually a dark eye stripe that rarely extends beyond the shoulder. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Under the Recuero et al. (2006) arrangement, from southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah (possibly extirpated) and western Arizona south to southern Baja California; Recuero et al. did not give distributional details.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe: Recuero et al. (2006) split P. regilla into P. regilla, P. sierra and P. hypochondriaca, but nuclear DNA data (Barrow et al. 2014) did not support it and Holycross (2022) awaits further analysis, whereas Jadin et al. (2021) supported the three species (as Hyliola); the genus Hyliola is also disputed.

rangeSummary.value: Under the Recuero et al. (2006) arrangement, from southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah (possibly extirpated) and western Arizona south to southern Baja California; Recuero et al. did not give distributional details.

identification.text: Small treefrog, 19-50 mm snout-vent length, with small toe pads.
Dorsal colour varies (green, reddish, tan, gray, brown or black) but typically green or brown; usually a dark eye stripe that rarely extends beyond the shoulder.
Versus the California treefrog: dark eye stripe more often present, green more common, toe pads smaller and less conspicuous.
Call is a loud two-part 'kreck-ek'; shorter, lower and less musical than the California treefrog's call.
No distinct morphological criteria separate it from the Pacific treefrog.
Compared with the california treefrog: Larger toe pads and usually no dark eye stripe.
Compared with the pacific treefrog: Not separable by morphology; range and genetics are used.

resources.title: Boreal chorus frog
resources.description: Identify the boreal chorus frog (Pseudacris maculata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Boreal chorus frog (Pseudacris maculata): Small: maximum snout-vent length about 37 mm; a dark stripe or mask runs from the snout through the eye to the groin. Back is cream, gray, brown, reddish or green, typically with three green, brown or gray stripes or rows of spots down the back and one row on each side. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Large parts of Canada and the western and north-central US, from Great Bear Lake (Northwest Territories) and northern Ontario south to Arizona, New Mexico, northern Oklahoma, Missouri, Arkansas and Illinois, with disjunct populations in southern Ontario, southern Quebec, northern New York and northwestern Vermont; to about 3,670 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: Montana Field Guide notes it is treated by some as the subspecies Pseudacris triseriata maculata of the Western Chorus Frog; NatureServe treats it as a full species.

rangeSummary.value: Large parts of Canada and the western and north-central US, from Great Bear Lake (Northwest Territories) and northern Ontario south to Arizona, New Mexico, northern Oklahoma, Missouri, Arkansas and Illinois, with disjunct populations in southern Ontario, southern Quebec, northern New York and northwestern Vermont; to about 3,670 m.

identification.text: Small: maximum snout-vent length about 37 mm; a dark stripe or mask runs from the snout through the eye to the groin.
Back is cream, gray, brown, reddish or green, typically with three green, brown or gray stripes or rows of spots down the back and one row on each side.
Toes have minute disks and little webbing; belly cream, possibly with a few small black spots.
Call is a stuttering 'preeep' rising in pitch, likened to running a finger over the teeth of a comb; audible up to about 400 m.
Compared with the sierran treefrog: Adults of other Montana frogs and toads are much larger with webbed hind feet; only the Sierran treefrog is similarly small, and its range does not overlap.

habitat.text: Near quiet, permanent or temporary water: marshes, rain pools, snowmelt pools, bog and beaver ponds, marshy lake edges, in grassland, shrubland and forest parkland.
Occurs from lowlands to alpine.

behavior.text: Males begin calling late March or April in lowlands (typically when air temperature is above 10 C) and chorus through spring and early summer; calling may resume after heavy rain.
Emerges from winter sites typically in March in lowlands (later in mountains); freeze-tolerant and overwinters under vegetation, in rodent burrows or rock and log crevices.
Adults are in water mainly during breeding; otherwise found in damp grassy or marshy areas, usually within 100 m (up to about 500 m) of water; seasonal movements around 250 m.
Eggs are laid in loose clusters of 7-190 attached to submerged vegetation.

resources.title: Pacific treefrog
resources.description: Identify the pacific treefrog (Pseudacris regilla), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pacific treefrog (Pseudacris regilla): Small, up to about 5 cm snout-vent length; colour highly variable (usually green or brown; also gray, tan, bronze, blackish or reddish) with irregular dark spots. Dark stripe from the snout to the shoulder; toe tips expanded. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia south through the western United States to southern Baja California, east to Montana, Idaho and Nevada; introduced populations on Haida Gwaii (Queen Charlotte Islands) and Revillagigedo Island, Alaska, and probably in desert California and Arizona. Montana populations are now attributed to the Sierran treefrog.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Recuero et al. (2006) split P. regilla into three species (regilla, sierra, hypochondriaca) that other nuclear data did not support; NatureServe records list the synonym Hyliola regilla, and Montana Field Guide says Montana animals once called Pacific treefrog are the Sierran treefrog.

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia south through the western United States to southern Baja California, east to Montana, Idaho and Nevada; introduced populations on Haida Gwaii (Queen Charlotte Islands) and Revillagigedo Island, Alaska, and probably in desert California and Arizona. Montana populations are now attributed to the Sierran treefrog.

identification.text: Small, up to about 5 cm snout-vent length; colour highly variable (usually green or brown; also gray, tan, bronze, blackish or reddish) with irregular dark spots.
Dark stripe from the snout to the shoulder; toe tips expanded.
Mature males have a dark throat; breeding call is a loud repeated 'kreck-ek'.
Tadpoles brown or olive, eyes widely spaced at the margin of the head when seen from above, up to about 44 mm.
Compared with the sierran treefrog: Not separable by appearance; genetics and range distinguish them (Montana Field Guide).
Compared with the baja california treefrog: No distinct morphological criteria known.

habitat.text: Grassland, shrubland, woodland, forest and farmland; on land except in the breeding season.
Breeds in shallow marshes, lakes, ponds, ditches, reservoirs and slow streams.

behavior.text: Breeding mostly winter or spring, sometimes summer; calling often happens outside the breeding season and far from breeding sites.
Eggs in soft loose clumps of about 10-80, in shallow water; larvae metamorphose in about 2-3 months.
After breeding they bask on leaves of broad-leaved shrubs far from water and sometimes climb into trees; migrate up to several hundred metres between breeding and upland sites.
Eats beetles, flies, spiders, ants and isopods; inactive in freezing weather and extreme drought.

resources.title: Sierran treefrog
resources.description: Identify the sierran treefrog (Pseudacris sierra), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sierran treefrog (Pseudacris sierra): Toes are long with large disks and very little webbing. Nearly all have a black stripe from the snout through the nostril, eye and eardrum to just above the front leg. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central California, Nevada, eastern Oregon, Idaho and western Montana, possibly extreme northwestern Utah; genetic work (Jadin et al. 2021) found it, not the Pacific treefrog, in Idaho and Montana.

taxonomicNotes.text: Often lumped in Pseudacris regilla in older literature (Montana Field Guide: material before 2022 calls it Pacific treefrog); NatureServe notes nuclear DNA (Barrow et al. 2014) did not support the three-species split and Hyliola is a disputed genus.

rangeSummary.value: Central California, Nevada, eastern Oregon, Idaho and western Montana, possibly extreme northwestern Utah; genetic work (Jadin et al. 2021) found it, not the Pacific treefrog, in Idaho and Montana.

identification.text: Toes are long with large disks and very little webbing.
Nearly all have a black stripe from the snout through the nostril, eye and eardrum to just above the front leg.
Back commonly tan mottled with dark brown spots; can be solid green or other colours.
Often heard but not seen; tadpoles have eyes outside the outline of the body from above.
Compared with the pacific treefrog: Distinguishable only by genetics (Montana Field Guide).

habitat.text: Grassland, chaparral, woodland, forest and farmland; on land except when breeding.
Eggs are laid in shallow marshes, lakes, ponds, ditches, reservoirs and slow streams.

behavior.text: Females can lay 500-750 eggs in total; clutches of a few cm hold 18-119 eggs (mean 68 in northwest Montana).
Breeds in shallow water of marshes, lakes, ponds and ditches; spends most of its time on the ground and may bask on woody plants far from water or climb into trees.
Can be quite abundant locally.

resources.title: Western threadsnake
resources.description: Identify the western threadsnake (Rena humilis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western threadsnake (Rena humilis): Very small, thin, earthworm-like snake; light purple, pink or brown. Tail ends in a small spine; eyes are non-functional (often called a blind snake). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas to southern Baja California and Colima, Mexico; from below sea level to about 1,520 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly Leptotyphlops humilis; NatureServe notes Adalsteinsson et al. (2009) moved North American threadsnakes to Rena.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas to southern Baja California and Colima, Mexico; from below sea level to about 1,520 m.

identification.text: Very small, thin, earthworm-like snake; light purple, pink or brown.
Tail ends in a small spine; eyes are non-functional (often called a blind snake).

habitat.text: Deserts and desert grasslands to brush-covered slopes: sand dunes, washes, rocky hillsides, canyon bottoms, riparian zones and areas near springs, sometimes gardens.
Prefers loose soils for burrowing.

behavior.text: Secretive and fossorial; found under rocks, wood or debris, among roots or in crevices, often in loose damp soil.
Appears on the surface at night, especially after warm-season rains.
Eats ants and termites (following ant pheromone trails to nests), other small insects and their larvae and eggs, spiders, centipedes and millipedes.
Lays 2-6 eggs in July-August; females may stay with eggs and may nest communally.

resources.title: Long-nosed snake
resources.description: Identify the long-nosed snake (Rhinocheilus lecontei), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Long-nosed snake (Rhinocheilus lecontei): Smooth scales, a single anal scale and a generally white, unpatterned belly; at least half of the underside tail scales are not divided. Yellowish or cream ground colour with 18-35 black blotches separated by pink or reddish interspaces; tail has 6-17 blotches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern California, southern Idaho, Utah, southeastern Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to central Baja California, Jalisco, San Luis Potosi and Tamaulipas; below sea level to about 1,900 m. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Manier (2004) concluded no subspecies should be recognized.

rangeSummary.value: Northern California, southern Idaho, Utah, southeastern Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to central Baja California, Jalisco, San Luis Potosi and Tamaulipas; below sea level to about 1,900 m. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Smooth scales, a single anal scale and a generally white, unpatterned belly; at least half of the underside tail scales are not divided.
Yellowish or cream ground colour with 18-35 black blotches separated by pink or reddish interspaces; tail has 6-17 blotches.
Adults usually 56-76 cm, maximum about 104 cm; rostrum protrudes (used for burrowing).

habitat.text: Deserts, dry prairies, arid river valleys, thornbrush and shrubland; sometimes oak-hackberry woodland.
Rocky and sandy areas.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; retreats to underground burrows or under rocks by day and burrows deep in winter; active about April-September.
Eats lizards and their eggs, small snakes, small mammals and sometimes birds.
Mates in spring; lays 4-11 eggs June-August, hatching in 2-3 months.

resources.title: Western patch-nosed snake
resources.description: Identify the western patch-nosed snake (Salvadora hexalepis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western patch-nosed snake (Salvadora hexalepis): Light tan ground colour with a wide brown-black stripe running the length of each side; 20-46 inches (Zion NPS key). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern and eastern California, western and southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and southwestern Texas to the tip of Baja California, southern Sinaloa and Chihuahua; below sea level to about 2,135 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes the desert form S. h. deserticola is sometimes treated as a separate species (S. deserticola) but is retained as a subspecies by Crother (2017).

rangeSummary.value: Southern and eastern California, western and southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and southwestern Texas to the tip of Baja California, southern Sinaloa and Chihuahua; below sea level to about 2,135 m.

identification.text: Light tan ground colour with a wide brown-black stripe running the length of each side; 20-46 inches (Zion NPS key).
Compared with the striped whipsnake: Slender, black to brown back with four narrow stripes (Zion NPS key).
Compared with the coachwhip: Pinkish or tan with faint crossbands, more distinct on the neck (Zion NPS key).

habitat.text: Sandy and rocky plains and lower slopes: creosote desert, washes, sagebrush semidesert, chaparral, pinyon-juniper and coastal scrub.
Mainly terrestrial; uses whatever cover is available.

behavior.text: Active, diurnal snake; all day in mild spring weather, restricted to morning and late afternoon in summer; greatest activity May-June.
Opportunistic feeder on lizards, small mammals and eggs of lizards and snakes.
Takes refuge in bushes, rock crevices and other animals' burrows; lays 4-10 eggs in summer.

resources.title: Common chuckwalla
resources.description: Identify the common chuckwalla (Sauromalus ater), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common chuckwalla (Sauromalus ater): Large, flattened, dark-bodied lizard with loose skin folds on the neck and sides, small granular scales, and a blunt, broad-based tail. Adult males mainly dark (marked gray, red or yellow) with a pale yellow tail; females retain juvenile crossbands. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Nevada, southern Utah, southeastern California and western Arizona south to southern Baja California and west-central Sonora, Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the synonym S. obesus and notes Sumarli et al. (2024) suggest most Baja California peninsula populations may be a different species.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Nevada, southern Utah, southeastern California and western Arizona south to southern Baja California and west-central Sonora, Mexico.

identification.text: Large, flattened, dark-bodied lizard with loose skin folds on the neck and sides, small granular scales, and a blunt, broad-based tail.
Adult males mainly dark (marked gray, red or yellow) with a pale yellow tail; females retain juvenile crossbands.
Young are crossbanded brown and gray-brown on body and tail.
Largest native iguanid in the US: adult snout-vent length usually 14-20 cm; lacks head horns and expanded toe tips.
Compared with the gila monster: Dorsal scales are large and beadlike and lack femoral pores; chuckwalla has small granular scales and femoral pores.

habitat.text: Rocky desert: lava flows, hillsides and outcrops, typically with creosote bush.
Shelters in rock crevices.

behavior.text: Basks on rocks by day; inactive in cold or extreme heat, but can be active most of the year in mild winters.
Herbivore: browses leaves, buds, flowers and fruit; occasionally insects.
Retreats into rock crevices, puffing up with air to wedge in (BLM Red Rock Canyon leaflet).
Lays 5-16 eggs underground, about June-August; life expectancy about 15 years.

resources.title: Prairie lizard
resources.description: Identify the prairie lizard (Sceloporus consobrinus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Prairie lizard (Sceloporus consobrinus): Small, rough-scaled gray to brown lizard with no head horns; scales raised and keeled. Males: dark gray or brown above with little pattern; belly strongly marked with deep iridescent blue bordered by black, throat also blue. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central North America from southwestern Wyoming, Nebraska, southern South Dakota and Missouri south through eastern Colorado, eastern New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas to Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and southwestern Alabama. Not found in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly included in Sceloporus undulatus (eastern fence lizard); Missouri Department of Conservation still lists 'Northern Fence Lizard' as an other common name.

rangeSummary.value: Central North America from southwestern Wyoming, Nebraska, southern South Dakota and Missouri south through eastern Colorado, eastern New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas to Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and southwestern Alabama. Not found in Canada.

identification.text: Small, rough-scaled gray to brown lizard with no head horns; scales raised and keeled.
Males: dark gray or brown above with little pattern; belly strongly marked with deep iridescent blue bordered by black, throat also blue.
Females: distinct wavy lines across the back, some orange or red at the tail base, belly white with faint dark spots and possibly pale blue along the sides.
Total length 3.5-5.5 inches; females grow larger than males.
Compared with the eastern fence lizard: Can be impossible to tell apart by pattern in Missouri; DNA testing needed (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Open woodlands, woodland and field edges and rocky glades; grassland, prairie, desert and dunes in parts of range.
Usually sunny, open situations; some populations are rock-dwelling.

behavior.text: Diurnal and often escapes capture by running up trees; inactive in cold and in the hottest part of a summer day.
Eats insects, spiders and other arthropods.
Lays eggs in soil; retreats underground or to crevices when inactive.

resources.title: Common sagebrush lizard
resources.description: Identify the common sagebrush lizard (Sceloporus graciosus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common sagebrush lizard (Sceloporus graciosus): Small (up to about 15 cm total length), gray to brown, usually with blotches or crossbars and a pale dorsolateral stripe on each side. Scales small, slightly rough with short spines; no distinct blue patches on the throat sides (throat may be blue-mottled). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Washington, Idaho, Montana and North Dakota south to northern Baja California, northern Arizona and northwestern New Mexico, east into western Nebraska; about 150-3,200 m. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes disjunct southern California and Sierra San Pedro Martir populations were treated as a distinct species by Grismer (2002).

rangeSummary.value: Washington, Idaho, Montana and North Dakota south to northern Baja California, northern Arizona and northwestern New Mexico, east into western Nebraska; about 150-3,200 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small (up to about 15 cm total length), gray to brown, usually with blotches or crossbars and a pale dorsolateral stripe on each side.
Scales small, slightly rough with short spines; no distinct blue patches on the throat sides (throat may be blue-mottled).
Males: dark blue patch on each side of the belly and blue-mottled or streaked throat; females whitish below with faint or absent blue.
Versus western fence lizard: smaller, less prickly scales, no yellow on the back of the thighs, and pale stripes rather than a checkered pattern.
Compared with the western fence lizard: Larger, prickly scales with longer spines, yellow or orange on the rear of the thighs, and a checkered or V-shaped pattern.

habitat.text: Sagebrush and other shrublands (manzanita, ceanothus), pinyon-juniper and open ponderosa pine or Douglas-fir woodland.
Needs open ground with some low bushes.

behavior.text: Ground dweller that perches on rocks, logs and snags; uses rodent burrows, shrubs and logs for cover.
Active about March-April to September-October; inactive in cold winter weather.
Eats beetles, flies, ants, caterpillars, spiders, ticks and mites.
Eggs laid May-July; most adult females in Colorado and Utah produce two clutches a year.

resources.title: Desert spiny lizard
resources.description: Identify the desert spiny lizard (Sceloporus magister), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert spiny lizard (Sceloporus magister): Stout, strong-looking lizard 3.25-5.5 inches (Zion key; 3.25-6 in per Saguaro NPS). Gray to brown mottled with yellow, green, brown and metallic blue; black shoulder markings. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Nevada and southwestern Colorado south to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Coahuila; west of the Central Valley in California and east to western Texas; near sea level to about 1,520 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes S. magister is treated as a full species with ongoing gene flow to S. bimaculosus and S. uniformis, which some treat as subspecies; a BLM Red Rock Canyon leaflet lists the yellow-backed spiny lizard as S. uniformis.

rangeSummary.value: Nevada and southwestern Colorado south to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Coahuila; west of the Central Valley in California and east to western Texas; near sea level to about 1,520 m.

identification.text: Stout, strong-looking lizard 3.25-5.5 inches (Zion key; 3.25-6 in per Saguaro NPS).
Gray to brown mottled with yellow, green, brown and metallic blue; black shoulder markings.
Males have iridescent blue along the sides and belly and more orange and yellow than Clark's spiny lizard; large overlapping scales.
Underside of the tail has black bars (Zion key).
Compared with the clark's spiny lizard: Found at higher elevation, often in trees; black and white stripes on the forelimbs (Tuzigoot NPS page).

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid plains and lower slopes: desert shrubland and woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, juniper-mesquite woodland, arroyos, playa edges and cottonwood-willow river zones.
Occurs on trees, rocks and the ground near cover.

behavior.text: Active about April-May to September-October in the north; more comfortable on ground and rocks than on trees.
Shelters under rocks or in rodent burrows; eggs laid in soil.
Eats mainly insects and spiders, sometimes centipedes, lizards and plant material.
Two clutches a year in Utah; hatchlings appear from July in Texas.

resources.title: Western fence lizard
resources.description: Identify the western fence lizard (Sceloporus occidentalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western fence lizard (Sceloporus occidentalis): Back scales fairly large, keeled and pointed (prickly look); gray, brown or black with wavy dark and light bands or V-shaped blotches, often 5-10 dark rows. Rear of the thighs yellow or orange; solid blue belly patches and throat in males, faint or absent in females and young. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Washington and southeastern Idaho south through Oregon, California, Nevada and western Utah to northwestern Baja California; sea level to about 3,350 m. Non-native in Montana.

rangeSummary.value: Washington and southeastern Idaho south through Oregon, California, Nevada and western Utah to northwestern Baja California; sea level to about 3,350 m. Non-native in Montana.

identification.text: Back scales fairly large, keeled and pointed (prickly look); gray, brown or black with wavy dark and light bands or V-shaped blotches, often 5-10 dark rows.
Rear of the thighs yellow or orange; solid blue belly patches and throat in males, faint or absent in females and young.
Breeding males may have blue or greenish dorsal scales and enlarged postanal scales; never a blue tail.
Up to about 9.5-9.9 cm snout-vent length.
Compared with the common sagebrush lizard: Smaller scales with shorter spines and pale dorsolateral stripes; no yellow on the thighs.
Compared with the western skink: Smooth, shiny scales and a blue tail in young.

habitat.text: Grassland, sagebrush, woodland, open conifer forest, rocky canyons, talus slopes and fence rows.
Not in severe desert but reaches mountain slopes near it.

behavior.text: Usually on the ground or low perches (logs, fences) but sometimes climbs bushes or trees; moves to the far side of a trunk when approached.
Adult males defend home ranges during the breeding season; seasonal home range under 0.01 ha in central California.
Eats mainly insects and spiders; eggs buried in loose soil, clutch 3-17, hatching mostly August-September.
Inactive in cold weather; emerges in late winter or early spring.

resources.title: Granite spiny lizard
resources.description: Identify the granite spiny lizard (Sceloporus orcutti), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Granite spiny lizard (Sceloporus orcutti). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: From the north side of San Gorgonio Pass (Peninsular Ranges, southern California) south to near La Paz in southern Baja California, including several Gulf of California islands; sea level to about 2,130 m.

rangeSummary.value: From the north side of San Gorgonio Pass (Peninsular Ranges, southern California) south to near La Paz in southern Baja California, including several Gulf of California islands; sea level to about 2,130 m.

identification.text: Compared with the desert spiny lizard: Listed as a similar species by the San Diego Natural History Museum atlas (no distinguishing marks given).
Compared with the western fence lizard: Listed as a similar species by the San Diego Natural History Museum atlas (no distinguishing marks given).

habitat.text: Granite outcrops in chaparral and oak-covered slopes on the coastal side of southern California mountains, also yellow pine habitat.
On the desert side, rocky canyons and upper alluvial slopes with chaparral, palms or mesquite.

behavior.text: Generally associated with rocks, but sometimes climbs into vegetation (agaves, palms, willows) or occurs on the ground among shrubs.
Eats insects, lizards and occasionally buds and fleshy fruits.
Lays 6-15 eggs May-July; probably buries eggs in the soil; inactive in cold and extreme heat.

resources.title: Plateau fence lizard
resources.description: Identify the plateau fence lizard (Sceloporus tristichus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plateau fence lizard (Sceloporus tristichus): Spiny lizard: keeled, pointed scales on the upper side and keeled, overlapping scales on the rear of the thigh. Colour extremely variable, usually striped or crossbanded. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Wyoming, eastern and southern Utah, western and south-central Colorado, northern and central Arizona and northern New Mexico; not in Canada. In Wyoming it is confined to the lower Green River valley and a narrow strip at the east edge of the Laramie Mountains.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes S. tristichus was formerly lumped in S. undulatus and that precise boundaries with S. consobrinus and S. cowlesi remain unresolved; Colorado Parks and Wildlife still presents prairie lizard and plateau fence lizard on one page.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Wyoming, eastern and southern Utah, western and south-central Colorado, northern and central Arizona and northern New Mexico; not in Canada. In Wyoming it is confined to the lower Green River valley and a narrow strip at the east edge of the Laramie Mountains.

identification.text: Spiny lizard: keeled, pointed scales on the upper side and keeled, overlapping scales on the rear of the thigh.
Colour extremely variable, usually striped or crossbanded.
Adult males have blue patches on the sides of the throat and belly, in Colorado mountain populations with a wide black margin.
Adult males show two enlarged scales on the underside of the tail base behind the vent and two bulges from the hemipenes.
Total length up to about 19 cm (7.5 in); Colorado Parks and Wildlife describes it as slightly spinier than the prairie lizard.

Compared with the prairie lizard (sceloporus consobrinus): Near-identical in the hand; Colorado Parks and Wildlife says the plateau fence lizard looks slightly spinier, and they are separated mainly by range.
Compared with the southwestern fence lizard (sceloporus cowlesi): Separated by range (eastern Arizona and central New Mexico southward); the two hybridize in an ecotone in eastern Arizona.

habitat.text: Open, rocky or shrubby ground: sunny rock outcrops, boulders, sandstone cliffs, hogbacks and canyon walls in sagebrush and shrubland, sometimes near abandoned buildings.
NatureServe lists openly wooded, shrubby or rocky areas.

behavior.text: Diurnal basker: inactive in cold spells and in the hottest part of a summer day, using sunny open spots in cool weather and shade when hot.
Active roughly May to early October in Wyoming; females lay one to three clutches of 4-17 eggs in June or July and hatchlings appear in August.
Insectivore: flies, grasshoppers, crickets, leafhoppers, ants, moths, plus spiders, ticks, millipedes and snails.
Perches on rocks but also uses trees, logs, debris piles, buildings and dirt banks.

resources.title: Yellow-backed spiny lizard
resources.description: Identify the yellow-backed spiny lizard (Sceloporus uniformis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Yellow-backed spiny lizard (Sceloporus uniformis): Large, robust spiny lizard: adults to about 5.5 in (14 cm) snout-to-vent, tail slightly longer than the body. Brown or tan with yellow and black dorsal stripes or mottling and a black collar on each side of the neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah (Mojave, Great Basin and San Joaquin deserts); endemic to the United States, not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes S. uniformis was elevated to a full species (Schulte et al. 2006), returned to synonymy with S. magister (Leache and Mulcahy 2007), and is currently recognized as a full species by Crother (2017); Wikipedia says it was a subspecies of S. magister until recently.

rangeSummary.value: California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah (Mojave, Great Basin and San Joaquin deserts); endemic to the United States, not in Canada.

identification.text: Large, robust spiny lizard: adults to about 5.5 in (14 cm) snout-to-vent, tail slightly longer than the body.
Brown or tan with yellow and black dorsal stripes or mottling and a black collar on each side of the neck.
Males are larger, with a swollen tail base, enlarged postanal scales and femoral pores, and bluish markings on the throat and belly.
Females have a pale throat and belly with faint or no blue; a female's head may turn orange or reddish in the breeding season.

Compared with the desert spiny lizard (sceloporus magister): Treated as a subspecies of S. magister until recently; the sources read give no field character, so separate mainly by range and the black neck collar with yellow dorsal pattern described here.

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid country from plains to lower mountain slopes: desert shrubland and woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, juniper and mesquite woodland, shrubby arroyos and cottonwood-willow along rivers.

behavior.text: Mainly an ambush predator that sometimes forages actively; eats ants, beetles, grasshoppers, spiders, centipedes and caterpillars, and occasionally small lizards, nestling birds and plant material.
Basks in the morning on rocks or other sunlit hard surfaces and shelters, usually underground, during the hottest part of a summer day.
Hibernates from late fall through winter and emerges in spring.
Uses trees, rocks and the ground near cover; eggs are laid in soil.

resources.title: Western groundsnake
resources.description: Identify the western groundsnake (Sonora semiannulata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western groundsnake (Sonora semiannulata): Small snake, total length about 8-19 in (20-48 cm), with smooth dorsal scales, a small head and a round pupil. Colour and pattern vary widely even within one area: brown, red or orange with black banding, orange or brown striping, or solid-coloured. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho, eastern California, western Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and extreme western Texas. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the primary name 'Variable Groundsnake' and follows Cox et al. (2018), which split the former S. semiannulata into S. semiannulata, S. episcopa, S. taylori and S. mosaueri; Wikipedia's wider range (including Colorado, Kansas, Missouri and Oklahoma) reflects the older, broader concept.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho, eastern California, western Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and extreme western Texas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small snake, total length about 8-19 in (20-48 cm), with smooth dorsal scales, a small head and a round pupil.
Colour and pattern vary widely even within one area: brown, red or orange with black banding, orange or brown striping, or solid-coloured.
Underside is typically white or gray.
The head marking is said to suggest a bishop's miter, the origin of the name 'miter snake'.

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid country: river bottoms, desert flats, sand hummocks and rocky hillsides with pockets of loose soil, from prairie and desert lowlands to pinyon-juniper and oak-pine zones; in California it favours areas with fine wind-blown sand, up to about 1,400 m.

behavior.text: Secretive and mostly nocturnal, sometimes abroad at dusk; often found on roadsides or in dry drainage ditches at night.
Active from spring to late summer; active as early as mid-March in west Texas.
Eats spiders, scorpions, centipedes, crickets, grasshoppers and insect larvae.
Shelters under rocks and other cover or burrows in fine windblown sand at the base of bushes or grass hummocks; lays 3-6 eggs, usually June-July.

resources.title: Plains spadefoot
resources.description: Identify the plains spadefoot (Spea bombifrons), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plains spadefoot (Spea bombifrons): Vertical (catlike) pupil in bright light and a single hard, wedge-shaped black 'spade' on each hind foot. Hard raised boss (bony lump) between the eyes, set slightly forward of a line across the middle of both eyes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central Canada (southern Alberta and Saskatchewan, north to near Outlook, SK) south to north-central Mexico, west to western Montana, eastern Colorado and eastern Arizona and east to western Iowa, eastern Missouri and central Arkansas, with disjunct populations in southern Texas and Arkansas.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web places it in Pelobatidae, whereas NatureServe (citing Garcia-Paris et al. 2003) uses Scaphiopodidae for North American spadefoots.

rangeSummary.value: South-central Canada (southern Alberta and Saskatchewan, north to near Outlook, SK) south to north-central Mexico, west to western Montana, eastern Colorado and eastern Arizona and east to western Iowa, eastern Missouri and central Arkansas, with disjunct populations in southern Texas and Arkansas.

identification.text: Vertical (catlike) pupil in bright light and a single hard, wedge-shaped black 'spade' on each hind foot.
Hard raised boss (bony lump) between the eyes, set slightly forward of a line across the middle of both eyes.

Brown or gray, sometimes greenish, with dark splotches and small warts; often an hourglass-like marking formed by four light lines, which can be faint or absent in small animals; some have red or orange spots.
Snout-vent length to about 6 cm (2.5 in); spadefoots are not true toads (Bufonidae).
Breeding males have dark pads on the inner 2-3 fingers; call is a brief, loud, harsh snore audible up to about 3 km.

Compared with the mexican spadefoot (spea multiplicata): Lacks the hard boss between the eyes, has red-tipped tubercles, and reportedly smells of peanuts when handled; its call is a longer, stuttering snore.

Compared with the great basin spadefoot (spea intermontana): Separated mainly by range: Great Basin spadefoot lies between the Cascade-Sierra axis and the Rockies, plains spadefoot on the Great Plains.

habitat.text: Shrublands, grasslands and semi-desert with loose soil for burrowing, plus nearby ephemeral pools such as cattle ponds, vernal pools, playas and flooded fields for breeding.

behavior.text: Nocturnal: stays in a burrow by day (to about 1 m deep) and emerges on humid nights to forage; burrows deeper in drought, summer heat and winter.
Explosive breeder: 2.5-10.4 cm of rain brings adults to temporary pools, mainly May-August, with choruses lasting about 2 days.
Adults eat small invertebrates; tadpoles may develop a carnivorous morph that eats other tadpoles and fairy shrimp.
Migrates up to several hundred metres between breeding pools and non-breeding ground.

resources.title: Great Basin spadefoot
resources.description: Identify the great basin spadefoot (Spea intermontana), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Great Basin spadefoot (Spea intermontana): Gray, olive or brown back mottled with darker spots that have light centres, with gray streaks outlining an hourglass-shaped mark; underside light gray to cream and unmarked. Large, catlike golden-yellow eyes with vertical pupils; a dark brown or orange spot on each upper eyelid; nose slightly upturned with a raised callus between the eyes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern British Columbia south through central and eastern Washington and Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, Wyoming and northwestern Colorado to northwestern Arizona, from the Cascade-Sierra axis east to the Rockies.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes inconsistency in older literature among S. hammondii, S. intermontana and S. multiplicata (hammondii and multiplicata were once treated as conspecific).

rangeSummary.value: Southern British Columbia south through central and eastern Washington and Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, Wyoming and northwestern Colorado to northwestern Arizona, from the Cascade-Sierra axis east to the Rockies.

identification.text: Gray, olive or brown back mottled with darker spots that have light centres, with gray streaks outlining an hourglass-shaped mark; underside light gray to cream and unmarked.
Large, catlike golden-yellow eyes with vertical pupils; a dark brown or orange spot on each upper eyelid; nose slightly upturned with a raised callus between the eyes.
Black keratinized spade on the underside of each hind foot; body short and fat with stubby limbs, 32-67 mm long.
Skin is relatively smooth with small bumps and no parotoid glands, unlike true toads (Bufo).
Male call: monotonous duck-like snoring of 1-3 notes, carrying over long distances.
Compared with the plains spadefoot (spea bombifrons): Separated mainly by range; plains spadefoot has a hard boss between the eyes, a four-line hourglass marking and a brief snore call.

habitat.text: Arid regions: sagebrush flats, semi-desert shrubland, alkali flats and pinyon-juniper, up to ponderosa pine and spruce-fir near 2,800 m, wherever soils are loose enough to burrow.
Breeds in temporary or permanent still water such as seasonal pools, springs, irrigation ditches and ponds.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal but also active early morning and late afternoon; more active after rain and in humid periods.
Survives dry country by burrowing with its hind-foot spades or using rodent burrows; daytime burrows are shallow, typically 35-45 cm deep, deeper when drier.
Explosive breeder, May-August, at still or slow water; adults migrate 1-5 km at night; pools must hold water about 40 days for tadpoles to transform.
Generalist insectivore; ants and darkling beetles are the commonest prey.

resources.title: Mexican spadefoot
resources.description: Identify the mexican spadefoot (Spea multiplicata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mexican spadefoot (Spea multiplicata): Gray, brown, tan or greenish with dark spots or small blotches on the back and upper legs; faint light stripes occasionally on the back and sides. Red-tipped tubercles scattered over the back, head and upper surfaces of the legs; large eyes; short spade-shaped tubercle on the underside of each hind foot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado and northern Oklahoma south through Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to Mexico (Guerrero and Oaxaca); up to about 2,470 m. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes older literature treated it as conspecific with S. hammondii and that northern and southern populations of the western spadefoot are genetically distinct.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado and northern Oklahoma south through Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to Mexico (Guerrero and Oaxaca); up to about 2,470 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Gray, brown, tan or greenish with dark spots or small blotches on the back and upper legs; faint light stripes occasionally on the back and sides.
Red-tipped tubercles scattered over the back, head and upper surfaces of the legs; large eyes; short spade-shaped tubercle on the underside of each hind foot.
About 2.5 in (6 cm) snout-vent length.
Unlike the plains spadefoot, it has no bony boss between the eyes; it is reported to smell like peanuts when handled.

Compared with the plains spadefoot (spea bombifrons): Has a hard bony boss between the eyes and does not smell of peanuts; its call is a brief snore, faster than the Mexican spadefoot's long stuttering snore.

habitat.text: Desert grassland, shortgrass plains, creosote bush, sagebrush and semi-desert shrubland, mixed grassland-chaparral, pinyon-juniper and pine-oak woodland and open pine forest; breeds in temporary pools formed by heavy rain.

behavior.text: Active at night, usually during humid or wet periods of spring and summer (late March-September in northern Texas).
Emerges after heavy rain; breeding choruses last 1-2 days and eggs hatch in about 2 days; ponds often dry before metamorphosis.
Burrows underground or uses rodent burrows when inactive; migrates between breeding pools and non-breeding terrestrial habitat.
Tadpoles occur as a carnivorous morph (mainly fairy shrimp) and an omnivorous morph that eats more detritus and algae.

resources.title: Smith's black-headed snake
resources.description: Identify the smith's black-headed snake (Tantilla hobartsmithi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Smith's black-headed snake (Tantilla hobartsmithi): Small, slender snake, uniformly brown above with a black head and a cream or white collar. Belly has a broad reddish stripe down the centre of the ventral scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Discontinuous from southern California, southern Nevada, Utah and west-central Colorado south to Arizona, southern New Mexico and Texas, and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes certain populations were formerly called Tantilla planiceps or T. utahensis (Cole and Hardy 1981 revision); Animal Diversity Web and BLM list it as 'southwestern blackhead snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Discontinuous from southern California, southern Nevada, Utah and west-central Colorado south to Arizona, southern New Mexico and Texas, and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, slender snake, uniformly brown above with a black head and a cream or white collar.
Belly has a broad reddish stripe down the centre of the ventral scales.
Secretive, semi-fossorial: usually seen only under cover or moving at night.

Compared with the western black-headed snake (tantilla planiceps): Visually similar; separated mainly by range, as T. planiceps is now the California and Baja California species while populations east of California belong to T. hobartsmithi.

habitat.text: Pinyon-juniper, chaparral-woodland, riparian woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, sagebrush-greasewood and other arid scrub with friable sandy or organic soil and surface debris; prefers moist niches in arid country.

behavior.text: Secretive and difficult to detect except under specific temperature, moisture and time conditions; found under loose boards, logs, wood, rocks and fallen shrubs.
Probably nocturnal; active about April to October in the north and from early March in Texas.
Eats insect larvae (beetles, caterpillars), centipedes and millipedes.
Known clutches have held a single large egg, laid June-August.

resources.title: Western black-headed snake
resources.description: Identify the western black-headed snake (Tantilla planiceps), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western black-headed snake (Tantilla planiceps): Small, slender snake 7-15 in (18-38 cm), brown to olive-gray above. Black head bordered behind by a white collar; head noticeably flattened. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: California Coast Ranges from east of Livermore and south of San Francisco Bay, through the Transverse Ranges, south to the tip of Baja California, reaching the desert side of mountains in southern California; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe says Cole and Hardy (1981) narrowed T. planiceps so that populations east of California now belong to T. hobartsmithi, T. atriceps or T. yaquia, and that T. eiseni is now included; Wikipedia's wider range (to Utah and Texas) reflects the older circumscription.

rangeSummary.value: California Coast Ranges from east of Livermore and south of San Francisco Bay, through the Transverse Ranges, south to the tip of Baja California, reaching the desert side of mountains in southern California; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, slender snake 7-15 in (18-38 cm), brown to olive-gray above.
Black head bordered behind by a white collar; head noticeably flattened.
Semi-fossorial and crevice-dwelling, so usually seen under flat rocks or other surface objects.

Compared with the smith's black-headed snake (tantilla hobartsmithi): Visually similar; Smith's has a cream collar and a reddish belly stripe and occurs east of California, whereas the western black-headed snake is the California/Baja species.

habitat.text: Grassland, coastal scrub, chaparral, oak and oak-pine woodland, desert-edge and thornscrub, often rocky areas and along streams, sea level to about 1,220-1,830 m; moist niches within otherwise arid or semiarid country.

behavior.text: Nocturnal: most active on warm nights from spring to early fall, with a winter period of inactivity; underground or under cover by day.
Eats millipedes, centipedes, spiders and beetle larvae.
Clutch of 1-3 eggs laid May-June; several snakes are occasionally found together under one rock or log.

resources.title: Rough-skinned newt
resources.description: Identify the rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa): Rough, grainy skin, dark brown to light brown above and yellow to orange or reddish-orange below. Small eyes that do not extend beyond the outline of the head seen from above; yellow irises. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Pacific coast from Santa Cruz County, California, north to Juneau, Alaska, including Vancouver Island and other coastal islands, from sea level to about 2,740 m. Isolated populations in Latah County, Idaho and Saunders County, Montana; the Idaho population is probably introduced.

rangeSummary.value: Pacific coast from Santa Cruz County, California, north to Juneau, Alaska, including Vancouver Island and other coastal islands, from sea level to about 2,740 m. Isolated populations in Latah County, Idaho and Saunders County, Montana; the Idaho population is probably introduced.

identification.text: Rough, grainy skin, dark brown to light brown above and yellow to orange or reddish-orange below.
Small eyes that do not extend beyond the outline of the head seen from above; yellow irises.
Adults 12.7-21.6 cm total length (to about 9 cm snout-vent length).
Breeding males turn temporarily aquatic with smooth, spongy, lighter skin, a swollen vent, a flattened tail crest and dark toe pads; breeding females keep rough skin with a cone-shaped vent.
When threatened it arches its head back and curls the tail up to show the bright belly (unken reflex).

habitat.text: Forested hills and mountains on land, under rotting logs, and in ponds, lakes, slow streams and sometimes ditches; occasionally open fields.

behavior.text: Produces the potent skin toxin tetrodotoxin, in varying amounts geographically; common garter snakes are a known predator that tolerates it.
Mostly terrestrial and found under rotting wood on forested slopes, but returns to still or slow water to breed; some become aquatic in dry summers and some high-elevation adults stay aquatic.
Migrates to and from breeding sites, navigating by celestial cues and smell; activity timing varies by population (diurnal or nocturnal).
Adults are opportunistic carnivores taking insects, snails and other amphibians; larvae eat small aquatic invertebrates.

resources.title: Aquatic gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the aquatic gartersnake (Thamnophis atratus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Aquatic gartersnake (Thamnophis atratus): Slender garter snake 46-102 cm long whose colour varies: pale gray with alternating rows of darker side blotches, dark brown with less distinct borders, or nearly all black.
