Yellow dorsal stripe may be present, confined to the neck, very indistinct or absent; throat and belly whitish to yellow. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Oregon and western California north of Point Conception (Coast Ranges from the Oregon border to central Santa Barbara County), from sea level to about 1,920 m; absent from the Salinas Valley. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: CWHR places Thamnophis in Natricidae while NatureServe uses Colubridae; NatureServe notes atratus, hydrophilus and aquaticus were formerly treated as subspecies of T. couchii, and Wikipedia recognizes three subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Oregon and western California north of Point Conception (Coast Ranges from the Oregon border to central Santa Barbara County), from sea level to about 1,920 m; absent from the Salinas Valley. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Slender garter snake 46-102 cm long whose colour varies: pale gray with alternating rows of darker side blotches, dark brown with less distinct borders, or nearly all black.
Yellow dorsal stripe may be present, confined to the neck, very indistinct or absent; throat and belly whitish to yellow.
One morph is blue-gray with a faint olive dorsal stripe and white dots along the sides; another has a yellow stripe and black side spots.
Closely tied to streams: basks on streamside rocks and banks and retreats into the water.

Compared with the sierra gartersnake (thamnophis couchii): Distinguished mainly by range: Sierra gartersnake is the Sierra Nevada species, aquatic gartersnake the Coast Ranges species; both were once lumped as T. couchii.

Compared with the terrestrial gartersnake (thamnophis elegans): Formally distinct species (Rossman and Stewart 1987); aquatic gartersnake forages almost entirely in and along streams, terrestrial also occurs in deserts, meadows and forests.

habitat.text: Rocky fast-flowing streams, sluggish soft-bottomed streams, ponds, small lakes and adjacent riparian zone, within woodlands, woodland-grass edges or chaparral; usually tied closely to water but sometimes travels on land.

behavior.text: Active diurnal snake that basks on streamside rocks or vegetation and flees rapidly into the water when disturbed.
Forages in and along streams for fish (especially trout and sculpins), tadpoles, frogs, salamanders and their larvae; also leeches and earthworms.
May be active in any month but is most often found April-July; mates in spring and gives birth to live young, August-October, in secluded sites such as under bark.
Seeks cover under water beneath rocks or among exposed tree roots.

resources.title: Sierra gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the sierra gartersnake (Thamnophis couchii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sierra gartersnake (Thamnophis couchii): Medium-sized, slender, highly aquatic garter snake with a somewhat pointed head. Found in or right beside water, basking in streamside vegetation and fleeing into water when disturbed. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Sierra Nevada of California from the Pit and Sacramento rivers south to the Tehachapi Mountains, east along major rivers to the Owens Valley and west-central Nevada, about 90-2,440 m. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes T. hammondii, T. gigas and T. atratus (with hydrophilus and aquaticus) were formerly included in T. couchii; CWHR places Thamnophis in Natricidae while NatureServe uses Colubridae.

rangeSummary.value: Sierra Nevada of California from the Pit and Sacramento rivers south to the Tehachapi Mountains, east along major rivers to the Owens Valley and west-central Nevada, about 90-2,440 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Medium-sized, slender, highly aquatic garter snake with a somewhat pointed head.
Found in or right beside water, basking in streamside vegetation and fleeing into water when disturbed.
Compared with the aquatic gartersnake (thamnophis atratus): Distinguished mainly by range; aquatic gartersnake occupies the Coast Ranges west of the Central Valley.
Compared with the terrestrial gartersnake (thamnophis elegans): Sierra gartersnake is much more tightly tied to water; terrestrial gartersnake also ranges into drier habitats.

habitat.text: Pools of permanent or seasonal streams (often rocky), meadow ponds, lakes, reservoirs and riparian zones, in oak woodland, chaparral, montane conifer forest, or pine-juniper-sagebrush east of the Sierra crest.

behavior.text: Active diurnal snake: low-elevation animals can be active about 10 months a year, high-elevation ones less than 4 months.
Forages in and along water: larval and newly transformed amphibians in ephemeral water; fish (trout, Sacramento suckers, mosquitofish) in permanent streams.
Retreats at night to holes, crevices and surface objects and rapidly to water when disturbed; young are born July-September in secluded sites such as under bark.

resources.title: Black-necked gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the black-necked gartersnake (Thamnophis cyrtopsis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black-necked gartersnake (Thamnophis cyrtopsis): Olive-gray to brown back, gray or bluish-gray head, whitish to greenish or brownish belly; adults 41-71 cm (rarely to 109 cm). Yellow to white mid-dorsal stripe, shading to orange toward the head, separating two black blotches, one on each side of the neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Colorado, southwestern Utah, central and eastern Arizona, New Mexico (except the far east) and western and central Texas, south through Mexico to Guatemala. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes T. cyrtopsis was for many years called T. eques; Animal Diversity Web lists it as 'Blackneck Garter Snake'.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Colorado, southwestern Utah, central and eastern Arizona, New Mexico (except the far east) and western and central Texas, south through Mexico to Guatemala. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Olive-gray to brown back, gray or bluish-gray head, whitish to greenish or brownish belly; adults 41-71 cm (rarely to 109 cm).
Yellow to white mid-dorsal stripe, shading to orange toward the head, separating two black blotches, one on each side of the neck.
Two rows of alternating dark spots between the stripes give a checkerboard look; lateral stripes (cream, tan or yellow) on scale rows 2 and 3.
19 rows of keeled dorsal scales; juveniles are brighter and more contrasting than adults.

Compared with the checkered gartersnake (thamnophis marcianus): Checkered gartersnake has 21 rows of keeled dorsal scales, a pale-yellow crescent behind the head and a single thick black neck line, versus 19 rows and two black neck blotches in the black-necked.

habitat.text: Streams in valleys and canyons and shallow rocky pools, also riparian woodland, pine-oak forest, scrub, desert flats and dry grassland; may use cattle tanks as water recedes.

behavior.text: Semi-aquatic and most active by day, though night activity is not unusual; if threatened it flees into cover or water, flattens and broadens its head, and releases foul-smelling musk.
Eats mainly frogs, toads and tadpoles, plus small fish, skinks, crustaceans and earthworms; forages actively in spring when water and prey are abundant and uses sit-and-wait ambush in summer.
At night shelters in exposed roots along stream banks, crevices, rodent holes and debris; hibernates in winter dens.

resources.title: Terrestrial gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the terrestrial gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Terrestrial gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans): Generally grayish-green back and yellow belly; pale (not white) stripes on the sides on the 2nd and 3rd scale rows above the belly scales. Mid-dorsal stripe is bright and runs the full body length in some areas, dull and fading at midbody in others; dark spots sometimes on the back; melanistic forms occur. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Mexico (Baja California) through the western United States, from New Mexico to western Oklahoma and Nebraska, the Dakotas and the Canadian border west to the Pacific Coast; in Canada, central and southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes mitochondrial clades do not follow subspecies boundaries and Crother (2017) tentatively retains three subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Northern Mexico (Baja California) through the western United States, from New Mexico to western Oklahoma and Nebraska, the Dakotas and the Canadian border west to the Pacific Coast; in Canada, central and southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba.

identification.text: Generally grayish-green back and yellow belly; pale (not white) stripes on the sides on the 2nd and 3rd scale rows above the belly scales.
Mid-dorsal stripe is bright and runs the full body length in some areas, dull and fading at midbody in others; dark spots sometimes on the back; melanistic forms occur.
Often two large blackish marks on the neck and irregular black marks on the belly.
Usually 8 upper labials on each side, keeled dorsal scales and usually 21 scale rows at midbody.
Total length to 109 cm, but few exceed 76 cm.

Compared with the common gartersnake (thamnophis sirtalis): Common gartersnake has 7 upper labials, 19 scale rows at midbody and a uniformly dark head; terrestrial usually has 8 upper labials and 21 rows.
Compared with the aquatic gartersnake (thamnophis atratus): Separate species (Rossman and Stewart 1987); the aquatic gartersnake is the stream-bound Pacific Coast snake.

habitat.text: Often near lakes and slow streams but also in deserts, plains, mountains, meadows and forests, from sea level to about 3,990 m; hibernates in rocky areas.

behavior.text: Diurnal: warms in the morning sun on heat-retaining surfaces, hunts through the day, and returns to shelter in the evening or in summer heat.
Solitary while active but dens communally in winter, usually returning to the same rocky hibernation site each year.

Coastal snakes mainly eat land prey (slugs, salamanders, small mammals, lizards); inland snakes hunt in and around water for frog and toad larvae, leeches and fish; hunts by movement and chemical cues.
When threatened it secretes a foul-smelling chemical from the cloaca and musk glands.

resources.title: Checkered gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the checkered gartersnake (Thamnophis marcianus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Checkered gartersnake (Thamnophis marcianus): Checkered pattern of black and light-gray spots along the body, with pale-yellow stripes on the spine and sides and a cream belly. Olive-green head with a single thick black line on the neck and a pale-yellow crescent just behind the head; red tongue with a black tip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern California, southwestern Arizona and southern New Mexico in the United States (abundant along the Gila and Colorado rivers), plus Mexico and Central America per Animal Diversity Web. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern California, southwestern Arizona and southern New Mexico in the United States (abundant along the Gila and Colorado rivers), plus Mexico and Central America per Animal Diversity Web. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Checkered pattern of black and light-gray spots along the body, with pale-yellow stripes on the spine and sides and a cream belly.
Olive-green head with a single thick black line on the neck and a pale-yellow crescent just behind the head; red tongue with a black tip.
21 rows of keeled dorsal scales; adults 45-106 cm, average about 55 cm; females bulkier and longer than males.
Juveniles show the same checkerboard as adults.

Compared with the black-necked gartersnake (thamnophis cyrtopsis): Black-necked has 19 dorsal scale rows and two black blotches on the neck sides, versus 21 rows and a single black neck line in the checkered.

habitat.text: Sea level to about 2,200 m, from wetlands to drylands, always at or near water (rivers, ponds, springs, irrigation ditches, lakes); also backyards and gardens, and it is spreading west along irrigation canals.

behavior.text: Mainly diurnal, but active at night in southern habitats; solitary, hibernating in groups of around 100 from October to March and basking on warm winter days.

Hunts small prey in irrigation ditches and streams using smell and sight; eats earthworms, tadpoles, frogs, salamanders, fish, lizards, mice, slugs and eggs (juveniles favour earthworms, adults tadpoles).
Uses species-specific pheromone trails to find mates; males follow females more than females follow males.

resources.title: Northwestern gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the northwestern gartersnake (Thamnophis ordinoides), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northwestern gartersnake (Thamnophis ordinoides): Highly variable: brown, gray or black back, sometimes with a green or bluish tint, with a red tongue. Vertebral stripe usually yellow or orange (also red, white or blue) and may fade or be absent; lateral stripe indistinct or absent. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern half of Humboldt County, California north through Oregon and Washington, east to the Cascades and west to the Pacific, and in Canada in southwestern British Columbia (Vancouver Island, Vancouver, north to Bella Coola).

rangeSummary.value: Northern half of Humboldt County, California north through Oregon and Washington, east to the Cascades and west to the Pacific, and in Canada in southwestern British Columbia (Vancouver Island, Vancouver, north to Bella Coola).

identification.text: Highly variable: brown, gray or black back, sometimes with a green or bluish tint, with a red tongue.
Vertebral stripe usually yellow or orange (also red, white or blue) and may fade or be absent; lateral stripe indistinct or absent.
Small dark marks on the scales either side of the vertebral stripe are common.
Adults 22.5-95 cm, most averaging 40 cm; females larger, males with slightly longer tails.

habitat.text: Grasslands, meadows, shrublands, wetlands and forest, most often along the wood line or forest-edge thickets; unlike most garter snakes not commonly tied to open water; 0-1,800 m.

behavior.text: Diurnal and solitary, constantly moving in search of food; a slug specialist (especially banana slugs) that also takes earthworms, and occasionally small frogs and salamanders.
Finds prey largely by chemical cues; uses the sun to orient to den sites.
Hibernates in winter and breeds on emerging in spring; females store sperm.

resources.title: Plains gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the plains gartersnake (Thamnophis radix), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plains gartersnake (Thamnophis radix): Long striped garter snake, usually 40-70 cm (occasionally to 109 cm), dark brown to dark greenish with a dorsal and two lateral yellow or orange stripes. Lateral stripes lie on scale rows 3 and 4; some red pigment may show on the sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Great Plains from the Oklahoma panhandle, northern Texas and northeastern New Mexico north to southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and east through Minnesota, Wisconsin and Indiana.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes no subspecies are recognized.

rangeSummary.value: Great Plains from the Oklahoma panhandle, northern Texas and northeastern New Mexico north to southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and east through Minnesota, Wisconsin and Indiana.

identification.text: Long striped garter snake, usually 40-70 cm (occasionally to 109 cm), dark brown to dark greenish with a dorsal and two lateral yellow or orange stripes.
Lateral stripes lie on scale rows 3 and 4; some red pigment may show on the sides.
A row of black spots runs between each lateral stripe and the belly scales.
Keeled scales in 19-21 rows and an undivided anal plate; males have tubercles on the chin shields and slightly longer tails.
Compared with the common gartersnake (thamnophis sirtalis): Plains gartersnake's lateral stripe sits on scale rows 3 and 4; the common gartersnake's is on rows 2 and 3.

habitat.text: Meadows, prairies and other grasslands near ponds, streams, marshes and sloughs, also swampy areas, rivers and suburban vacant lots; where it overlaps the common gartersnake it uses drier habitat.

behavior.text: Active March-November depending on region; hibernates in rodent or ant burrows, rock crevices and human-made crevices and may emerge on warm winter days.
Diurnal at 21-29 C, switching to night activity above 31 C and becoming inactive in much colder weather.
Follows odour trails to prey, mates and hibernacula; eats frogs, toads, salamanders, fish, earthworms, small rodents and birds.

resources.title: Common gartersnake
resources.description: Identify the common gartersnake (Thamnophis sirtalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common gartersnake (Thamnophis sirtalis): Typically three light stripes (one down the back, one on each side) on a black, brown, gray or olive ground; stripes may be white, yellow, blue, greenish or brown, sometimes absent or checkerboarded by dark spots. Head wider than neck and uniformly dark; red tongue tipped in black; keeled scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Across much of North America from Florida to coastal Quebec and west to British Columbia, south into southern California east of the Sierras and through the less arid Southwest (largely absent from the arid southwestern United States).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes recent genome-scale work does not support the traditional subspecies but found four geographic lineages, and Nicholson (2025) retains subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Across much of North America from Florida to coastal Quebec and west to British Columbia, south into southern California east of the Sierras and through the less arid Southwest (largely absent from the arid southwestern United States).

identification.text: Typically three light stripes (one down the back, one on each side) on a black, brown, gray or olive ground; stripes may be white, yellow, blue, greenish or brown, sometimes absent or checkerboarded by dark spots.
Head wider than neck and uniformly dark; red tongue tipped in black; keeled scales.
19 dorsal scale rows at midbody, lateral stripe on rows 2 and 3, 7 upper labials, undivided anal scale.
Adults usually 41-66 cm (to about 131 cm); some populations are entirely black; newborns 12-23 cm.
Compared with the ribbon snakes (thamnophis sauritus, t. butleri): Close relatives of similar appearance; Animal Diversity Web lists them as the species commonly confused with the common gartersnake.
Compared with the plains gartersnake (thamnophis radix): Plains gartersnake has its lateral stripe on scale rows 3 and 4 rather than 2 and 3.
Compared with the terrestrial gartersnake (thamnophis elegans): Usually 8 upper labials and 21 scale rows at midbody, versus 7 and 19.

habitat.text: Very adaptable: meadows, marshes, woodland and hillsides, preferring moist grassy areas near ponds, lakes, ditches and streams, and common in suburbs with cover such as debris, boards or rocks.

behavior.text: Active mainly by day across a wider range of temperatures than most snakes; hibernates from late October to March or early April, often communally in rodent or crayfish burrows, rock piles and stumps, and may bask on mild winter days.
Eats earthworms, amphibians (immune to toad secretions), leeches, slugs, snails, insects, crayfish and small fish, and occasionally small mammals and nestlings; hunts by smell and sight.
Mostly solitary outside the breeding and hibernation seasons; follows pheromone trails.

conservationStatus.text: San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Sonoran lyresnake
resources.description: Identify the sonoran lyresnake (Trimorphodon lambda), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sonoran lyresnake (Trimorphodon lambda): Medium to large slender snake (23-88 cm snout-vent, sometimes over 1 m total) with a broad, flat head distinct from a slim neck and large eyes with vertical pupils. Pale gray, tan or light brown with 18-31 dark brown saddles or blotches edged pale and with light, divided centres, widest at the midline; 8-17 more on the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Nevada (Nye County) and extreme southwestern Utah south through most of Arizona (except the northeast), southwestern New Mexico and southeastern California east of the Salton Trough to Sonora, western Chihuahua and northern Sinaloa. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly treated as a subspecies of Trimorphodon biscutatus (and lumped with T. lyrophanes); NatureServe follows Devitt et al. (2008) in recognizing it as a full species.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Nevada (Nye County) and extreme southwestern Utah south through most of Arizona (except the northeast), southwestern New Mexico and southeastern California east of the Salton Trough to Sonora, western Chihuahua and northern Sinaloa. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Medium to large slender snake (23-88 cm snout-vent, sometimes over 1 m total) with a broad, flat head distinct from a slim neck and large eyes with vertical pupils.
Pale gray, tan or light brown with 18-31 dark brown saddles or blotches edged pale and with light, divided centres, widest at the midline; 8-17 more on the tail.
Dark V- or lambda-shaped (lyre) mark on top of the head and a dark bar across the snout between the eyes.
Underside tan, pale yellow or light gray with scattered dark flecks near the edges.

Compared with the california lyresnake (trimorphodon lyrophanes): Occurs west of the Salton Trough in southern California and Baja California; specimens from contact zones in southeastern California or southern Nevada may be hard to identify.
Compared with the texas lyresnake (trimorphodon vilkinsonii): Hybridizes with the Sonoran lyresnake in extreme southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico; identify by locality.

habitat.text: Chiefly rocky areas of lowlands, canyons, mesas and lower mountain slopes: desert grassland, desert scrub, chaparral, pinyon-juniper and oak woodland, open conifer forest and thornscrub; rarely far from rock, to about 910 m in California.

behavior.text: Nocturnal: forages at night and occasionally early morning; reported active in every month but November, with a peak in April and May; hides in rock crevices by day.

Eats bats, small rodents and lizards (such as side-blotched and granite night lizards) and probably ground-nesting birds; rear-fanged, with a hemolytic venom that CWHR calls presumably not dangerous to people.
Secretive and never found in great numbers; lays eggs deep under rock cover.

resources.title: California lyresnake
resources.description: Identify the california lyresnake (Trimorphodon lyrophanes), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: California lyresnake (Trimorphodon lyrophanes): Brown snake with irregular blotches that camouflage it against rocky desert ground; adults reach about 47 in (1,200 mm) snout-vent length per the San Diego atlas. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern California generally west of the Salton Trough (north to near Los Angeles on the coast and in the Mojave Desert to the Argus and Amargosa mountains) south through most of the Baja California peninsula and several Gulf of California islands.

taxonomicNotes.text: Older sources, including the UC Irvine Orange County natural history site, list it as Trimorphodon biscutatus lyrophanes; NatureServe follows Devitt et al. (2008) in recognizing six species in the complex.

rangeSummary.value: Southern California generally west of the Salton Trough (north to near Los Angeles on the coast and in the Mojave Desert to the Argus and Amargosa mountains) south through most of the Baja California peninsula and several Gulf of California islands.

identification.text: Brown snake with irregular blotches that camouflage it against rocky desert ground; adults reach about 47 in (1,200 mm) snout-vent length per the San Diego atlas.

Compared with the sonoran lyresnake (trimorphodon lambda): Sonoran lyresnake occurs east of the Salton Trough; specimens from contact zones in southeastern California or southern Nevada may be difficult to identify.

habitat.text: Chiefly rocky areas of lowlands, canyons, mesas and lower mountain slopes: desert grassland, desert scrub, chaparral, pinyon-juniper and oak woodland, open conifer forest, thornscrub and thornforest; usually rocky uplands, much less often rockless lowland desert.

behavior.text: Rock-dwelling: in daytime sits in crevices or similar refuges.
Ambush predator of geckos and granite night lizards, but eats other available prey.

resources.title: Long-tailed brush lizard
resources.description: Identify the long-tailed brush lizard (Urosaurus graciosus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Long-tailed brush lizard (Urosaurus graciosus): Small gray or tan lizard almost always seen on a tree or shrub, well camouflaged against branches. Tail more than twice the snout-vent length. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Nevada south into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora, and from southeastern California east to northwestern and south-central Arizona. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes two subspecies (graciosus, shannoni) are recognized but Wiens (1993) did not, and a reassessment is needed; Animal Diversity Web lists it as 'Brush Lizard'.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Nevada south into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora, and from southeastern California east to northwestern and south-central Arizona. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small gray or tan lizard almost always seen on a tree or shrub, well camouflaged against branches.
Tail more than twice the snout-vent length.
Relatively large dorsal scales that change abruptly to granular side scales, with no row of smaller scales down the middle of the band of enlarged dorsal scales (unlike the tree lizard).
Distinguishable from the other brush lizards (Urosaurus) by geography as well.
Compared with the ornate tree lizard (urosaurus ornatus): Tail under twice the body length and a series of smaller scales down the middle of the enlarged dorsal band.
Compared with the baja california brush lizard (urosaurus nigricaudus): Tail under twice the body length and only slightly enlarged dorsal scales that grade gradually into the granular side scales.

habitat.text: Desert flats, washes and riparian strips with loose sand and scattered shrubs or trees such as creosote bush, catclaw, mesquite, ironwood, paloverde and saltbush, up to about 1,070 m.

behavior.text: Sit-and-wait feeder: waits on bush or grass-clump perches for beetles, ants, bees, termites and spiders, moving fast within the vegetation; seldom comes to the ground.
Not very active; relies on crypsis and spends days and nights in bushes and grass clumps, sleeping on branch tips.
Becomes active mid-April and stays out until mid-summer or early fall; lays clutches of 1-6 (average 4) eggs May-July.

resources.title: Baja California brush lizard
resources.description: Identify the baja california brush lizard (Urosaurus nigricaudus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Baja California brush lizard (Urosaurus nigricaudus): Small, small-scaled brush lizard: dorsal scales only slightly enlarged and grading gradually into the granular side scales, and tail under twice the body length (unlike the long-tailed brush lizard). Good climber, most often seen on rock piles, rock outcrops or canyon walls and sheltering in cracks and crevices. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Extreme southern California (mountains of San Diego County north nearly to the Riverside County line) into Baja California, per the California account that treats U. microscutatus as part of this species.

taxonomicNotes.text: Sources disagree on what this name covers: CWHR and Aguirre et al. (1999) lumped U. microscutatus into U. nigricaudus, which CWHR says is otherwise restricted to southern Baja California, whereas NatureServe (citing Gottscho 2015 and Crother 2017) treats them as separate species and holds no record for U. nigricaudus; the NatureServe facts used here (family, order, habitat, clutch size) are from its U. microscutatus record (the southern California/northern Baja population), and Wikipedia spells the name U. nigricauda.

rangeSummary.value: Extreme southern California (mountains of San Diego County north nearly to the Riverside County line) into Baja California, per the California account that treats U. microscutatus as part of this species.

identification.text: Small, small-scaled brush lizard: dorsal scales only slightly enlarged and grading gradually into the granular side scales, and tail under twice the body length (unlike the long-tailed brush lizard).
Good climber, most often seen on rock piles, rock outcrops or canyon walls and sheltering in cracks and crevices.
Compared with the long-tailed brush lizard (urosaurus graciosus): Tail more than twice the body length and relatively large dorsal scales that change abruptly to granular side scales.
Compared with the ornate tree lizard (urosaurus ornatus): Has a series of smaller scales down the middle of the band of enlarged dorsal scales.

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid country with a good mix of rocks, outcrops, canyons and boulder piles: woodland, chaparral and desert habitats, particularly desert wash; nowhere common in California.

behavior.text: Diurnal: out all day in spring, restricted to morning and late afternoon in summer; emerges in early spring (mid-March near Poway and Julian, California) and stays active until about September.
Eats beetles, ants, flies, thrips, aphids, termites, hemipterans and spiders.
Complex social system with territorial males; clutches average 6 eggs (4-8), up to four clutches a season, hatching about 2 months after laying.

resources.title: Ornate tree lizard
resources.description: Identify the ornate tree lizard (Urosaurus ornatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ornate tree lizard (Urosaurus ornatus): Small, slim lizard (about 3.8-5.9 cm) with a body and tail patterned with blotches or irregular crossbars in black, dark brown, tan or gray to match the local substrate. Two bands of enlarged scales run down the back with a series of smaller scales between them; base of the tail is usually rusty. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern California, southern Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and southwest/central Texas, south to Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Coahuila. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes deep mtDNA structure within U. ornatus and that its phylogeography deserves further study (Crother 2017); ADW lists it as 'Tree Lizard'.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern California, southern Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and southwest/central Texas, south to Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Coahuila. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, slim lizard (about 3.8-5.9 cm) with a body and tail patterned with blotches or irregular crossbars in black, dark brown, tan or gray to match the local substrate.
Two bands of enlarged scales run down the back with a series of smaller scales between them; base of the tail is usually rusty.
Adult males have blue to blue-green belly patches with a metallic sheen and a green, blue-green, orange or yellow throat patch (dewlap).
Females have a white belly, with a white, orange or yellow throat.
Compared with the long-tailed brush lizard (urosaurus graciosus): Tail more than twice the body length and no row of smaller scales down the middle of the enlarged dorsal band.

habitat.text: Riparian forest (mesquite, oaks, cottonwoods), rocky terrain, and the sides of buildings and fence posts near streams and rivers; also desert with or without trees, sheltering in shrubs, up to about 2,770 m.

behavior.text: Perches on trees, rocks and fence posts and ambushes spiders, beetles, ants, termites and other insects from an elevated, motionless position.
Hunts from dawn into the late afternoon; males hold small overlapping territories with a dominance hierarchy in which the heaviest male dominates.
Aggregates in winter hibernacula from mid-November to late February; climbs high into trees for protection.

resources.title: Common side-blotched lizard
resources.description: Identify the common side-blotched lizard (Uta stansburiana), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common side-blotched lizard (Uta stansburiana): Dark blotch on each side of the chest just behind the forearm (less obvious in females); gular fold. Males lack stripes and have blue or orange patches (densest on the tail) and a blue, gray, red or orange throat; females are drab gray or brown with dorsolateral stripes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Arid western North America: central Washington and eastern Oregon south through the Great Basin, Nevada, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico to western Texas, plus central and southern California (north to San Francisco), Baja California and islands off the Pacific and Gulf of California coasts. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes some authors treat Durango populations as U. stejnegeri but Crother (2017) does not recognize that split.

rangeSummary.value: Arid western North America: central Washington and eastern Oregon south through the Great Basin, Nevada, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico to western Texas, plus central and southern California (north to San Francisco), Baja California and islands off the Pacific and Gulf of California coasts. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Dark blotch on each side of the chest just behind the forearm (less obvious in females); gular fold.
Males lack stripes and have blue or orange patches (densest on the tail) and a blue, gray, red or orange throat; females are drab gray or brown with dorsolateral stripes.
Scales along the middle of the back are uniform in size, and at least one scale on the top of the head behind the eyes is obviously larger than them.
Maximum snout-vent length about 6.3 cm (2.5 in); juveniles are brown-gray like females.

habitat.text: Arid and semi-arid desert, often sagebrush or other scrub on sandy to gravelly soil, needing low-hanging shrub cover and bare ground; also roadsides, desert canyons and dunes.

behavior.text: Solitary, diurnal and crepuscular, most active in the morning and late afternoon; shelters in burrows or under shrubs and rocks in extreme heat, cold or rain.
Sit-and-wait generalist predator eating ants, termites, beetles, grasshoppers, flies, spiders and scorpions, with large males also taking smaller lizards.
Basks on rocks or low shrubs; breeding females stay near cover such as packrat nests.

resources.title: Desert night lizard
resources.description: Identify the desert night lizard (Xantusia vigilis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Desert night lizard (Xantusia vigilis): Very small lizard (average adult total length about 8 cm, about 1.3 g) with soft granular scales on the back. Grey, yellow-brownish or olive, often uniform but sometimes dark-spotted; can shift from light olive in the evening to dark brown by day. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Utah, western Arizona, southern Nevada and southern California south to southwestern Sonora and Baja California. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Crother (2017) recognizes X. sierrae and X. wigginsi as separate species and that Papenfuss et al. (2001) split Arizona populations into X. vigilis, X. arizonae and X. bezyi, a change Stebbins (2003) did not adopt.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Utah, western Arizona, southern Nevada and southern California south to southwestern Sonora and Baja California. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Very small lizard (average adult total length about 8 cm, about 1.3 g) with soft granular scales on the back.
Grey, yellow-brownish or olive, often uniform but sometimes dark-spotted; can shift from light olive in the evening to dark brown by day.
Usually 12 longitudinal rows of rectangular ventral scales; males are lighter and shorter with a stouter tail and enlarged femoral pores.
Usually found under fallen yucca and Joshua tree logs or in rock-outcrop crevices rather than in the open.

Compared with the arizona night lizard (xantusia arizonae): Granite-adapted rather than yucca-dwelling; Arizona populations formerly called X. vigilis are now split among X. arizonae, X. bezyi and X. wigginsi.

habitat.text: Arid and semiarid habitats among fallen yucca, agave and Joshua tree logs, in rock crevices and under foothill pine bark, into pinyon-juniper, sagebrush-blackbrush and chaparral-oak; 300-2,070 m in California.

behavior.text: Secretive: lives most of its life under cover, typically yucca logs, and is diurnal despite the name, sometimes active at night in summer.
Waits for termites, small beetles, ants, flies, spiders and other arthropods to wander by rather than actively searching.
Active from early April (low elevations) or May (higher) to late summer; gives live birth, about 2 young (1-3) in September-October.
Adult and young stay in family groups; groups of a few individuals aggregate under logs in winter.

resources.title: Northern cricket frog
resources.description: Identify the northern cricket frog (Acris crepitans), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern cricket frog (Acris crepitans): Small frog, 22-29 mm; eastern animals are smaller (22-26 mm) than western ones (24-29 mm). Polymorphic dorsal stripe that can be green, red or grey (green most common); stripe is absent on tadpoles and appears after metamorphosis. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the eastern US from New York and Pennsylvania south to Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; it is not recorded for Canada in that source.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe names it Eastern Cricket Frog and treats A. blanchardi as a separate species (Gamble et al. 2008); ADW's Northern Cricket Frog account gives a wider range extending to Texas, Mexico and Ontario, consistent with the older combined concept.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the eastern US from New York and Pennsylvania south to Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; it is not recorded for Canada in that source.

identification.text: Small frog, 22-29 mm; eastern animals are smaller (22-26 mm) than western ones (24-29 mm).
Polymorphic dorsal stripe that can be green, red or grey (green most common); stripe is absent on tadpoles and appears after metamorphosis.
Compared with the southern cricket frog it is larger and stockier, with a blunter snout, shorter legs, more toe webbing and more prominent warts.
Compared with the southern cricket frog: Southern is smaller and more slender, with a more pointed snout, longer legs, less toe webbing, and a dark longitudinal stripe on the rear of the thigh.

habitat.text: Edges of sunny marshes, marshy ponds and small slow-moving streams in open country; eggs and larvae develop in shallow water.
Hibernates underground on land near water, sometimes communally.

behavior.text: Call is a series of short clicks given in rapid bouts; males lower call pitch to assert dominance.
Diet is mostly small terrestrial insects plus some spiders, taken opportunistically.
Diurnal in cool weather and active day and night in warm months; inactive in the coldest months in the north, brumating in bank crevices, under logs or vegetation; moves after heavy rain.

resources.title: Southern cricket frog
resources.description: Identify the southern cricket frog (Acris gryllus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern cricket frog (Acris gryllus): Small frog, 15-33 mm (females slightly larger); colour ranges from black, brown or reddish brown to bright green or grey. Contrasting stripe from the top of the snout along the back, and a triangular marking between the eyes joined to that stripe. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

identification.text: Small frog, 15-33 mm (females slightly larger); colour ranges from black, brown or reddish brown to bright green or grey.
Contrasting stripe from the top of the snout along the back, and a triangular marking between the eyes joined to that stripe.
Darker longitudinal stripe on the rear of the thigh; markedly pointed snout; more slender than the northern cricket frog with longer legs and less toe webbing.
Males have darker throats and a single subgular sac; females have white throats.
Compared with the northern cricket frog: Northern is larger and stockier with a blunter snout, shorter legs, more webbing and more prominent warts.

habitat.text: Grassy margins of swamps, marshes, lakes, ponds, streams, ditches, bogs and nearby temporary pools, including open woodland that is not heavily shaded; eggs and larvae develop in shallow water.

behavior.text: Call is a steady, rapid 'click-click-click' at about one per second, given in choruses in most weather and at any time of day.
Sit-and-wait insectivore; mosquitoes are a large part of the diet; tadpoles are herbivorous.
Active throughout the year; day or night in warm months, probably mostly diurnal in cold months. Good jumper.

resources.title: Cottonmouth
resources.description: Identify the cottonmouth (Agkistrodon piscivorus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Cottonmouth (Agkistrodon piscivorus): Heavy-bodied venomous snake, to about 1.8 m; adults olive, brown or black with dark, dumbbell-shaped crossbands that are darker at the edges and lighter in the centre, blackening toward the tail. Large spade-shaped head, brown, black or olive on top, with brown patches on the chin; inside of the mouth is bright white. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists the species in Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas; Florida populations are assigned to A. conanti in that source.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats A. piscivorus as a species without subspecies and elevates A. conanti (Florida cottonmouth) to a separate species, calling the present one Northern Cottonmouth; ADW's account is titled A. piscivorus (conanti) and includes Florida within its range.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists the species in Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas; Florida populations are assigned to A. conanti in that source.

identification.text: Heavy-bodied venomous snake, to about 1.8 m; adults olive, brown or black with dark, dumbbell-shaped crossbands that are darker at the edges and lighter in the centre, blackening toward the tail.
Large spade-shaped head, brown, black or olive on top, with brown patches on the chin; inside of the mouth is bright white.
Juveniles are brighter with more distinct crossbands and a yellow tail tip.
Males are longer and heavier than females.

habitat.text: Wide range of aquatic and wetland habitats: swamps, sloughs, bayous, ponds and streams in pine flatwoods, marshes, river bottoms, floodplains, tidal stream courses and sometimes brackish water.
Winters in rocky hillsides, crayfish burrows, stumps or mammal burrows.

behavior.text: Threat display: shakes the tail, raises the head a few inches, coils and gapes to show the white mouth; also emits a foul musk.
Mostly nocturnal but may bask by day; adults stay within about 500 m of water; most active roughly March-November in the Carolinas and inactive in cold weather.
Eats fishes, amphibians, reptiles, small mammals, birds and carrion; gives live birth to 1-16 young, mainly August-September.

resources.title: Spotted salamander
resources.description: Identify the spotted salamander (Ambystoma maculatum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spotted salamander (Ambystoma maculatum): Stout salamander, 15-25 cm total length (females larger), with a broadly rounded snout and a head often swollen behind the jaw. Black, dark brown or dark grey above with two irregular rows of large round yellow or orange spots (24-45) from head to tail; unspotted individuals are rare. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Québec, and in the eastern and central US from New England and Minnesota south to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Québec, and in the eastern and central US from New England and Minnesota south to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas.

identification.text: Stout salamander, 15-25 cm total length (females larger), with a broadly rounded snout and a head often swollen behind the jaw.
Black, dark brown or dark grey above with two irregular rows of large round yellow or orange spots (24-45) from head to tail; unspotted individuals are rare.
Pale slate-grey underside; skin glands release a sticky white toxic fluid when threatened.
Larvae are dull olive green with a nearly white belly; egg masses are compact, attached to submerged objects and covered in clear or milky-white jelly.

habitat.text: Hardwood and mixed forests near swamps and vernal pools; breeds in vernal pools and semipermanent ponds, mostly fishless, in or beside forest.

behavior.text: Spends most of the year underground or under logs, stumps and mammal burrows; adults surface mainly on rainy nights during the breeding migration.
Migrates to breeding pools March-April in the north and mainly December-February in the south; eggs may be laid under ice if adults are already in the pond.
Adults eat forest-floor invertebrates (worms, snails, slugs, millipedes, insects); larvae eat small aquatic animals and can turn cannibalistic when pools dry.

resources.title: Marbled salamander
resources.description: Identify the marbled salamander (Ambystoma opacum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Marbled salamander (Ambystoma opacum): Small, stout salamander about 9-10.7 cm long with white or light-grey crossbands across head, back and tail, hence 'banded salamander'. Males are smaller with silvery-white bands that turn very white in the breeding season, and swollen cloacal glands; females are larger with silvery-grey bands. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it across the eastern US from New Hampshire and Massachusetts west to Wisconsin, Missouri and Texas and south to Florida; it is not recorded for Canada in that source.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it across the eastern US from New Hampshire and Massachusetts west to Wisconsin, Missouri and Texas and south to Florida; it is not recorded for Canada in that source.

identification.text: Small, stout salamander about 9-10.7 cm long with white or light-grey crossbands across head, back and tail, hence 'banded salamander'.
Males are smaller with silvery-white bands that turn very white in the breeding season, and swollen cloacal glands; females are larger with silvery-grey bands.

habitat.text: Wooded habitats near swamps and vernal pools, including rocky bluffs, slopes and wooded sand dunes; more tolerant of dry conditions than most salamanders; adults entirely terrestrial.

behavior.text: Solitary and mostly nocturnal; lives under leaf litter or underground (to about 1 m) and may defend its burrow.

Breeds in late summer to fall (August-November), earlier in the north; females lay a single clutch of up to about 250 eggs in dry pond basins or depressions under cover and attend them until autumn rains flood the nest.
Larvae hatch in fall or as late as spring depending on flooding and metamorphose in spring or early summer; adults are inactive through most of winter.

resources.title: Mole salamander
resources.description: Identify the mole salamander (Ambystoma talpoideum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mole salamander (Ambystoma talpoideum): Short, stout body with a broad, disproportionately large head; 8-12 cm long. Terrestrial adults are grey to black, sometimes with clusters of small bluish-white flecks on the back and tail and often a white edge along the top of the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US (Virginia and the Carolinas to Florida, west to Texas and north to Illinois, Indiana, Missouri and Kentucky); not recorded for Canada.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US (Virginia and the Carolinas to Florida, west to Texas and north to Illinois, Indiana, Missouri and Kentucky); not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Short, stout body with a broad, disproportionately large head; 8-12 cm long.
Terrestrial adults are grey to black, sometimes with clusters of small bluish-white flecks on the back and tail and often a white edge along the top of the tail.
Paedomorphic (gilled, aquatic) adults keep larval form, with light and dark belly stripes and distinctive yellow ventral stripes that remain as remnants for a time after metamorphosis.
Facultatively paedomorphic: both terrestrial and aquatic adult forms occur.

habitat.text: Usually near breeding ponds in pine flatwoods, floodplains and bottomland hardwood forest; terrestrial adults live in burrows or under logs in damp places; breeds in shallow fishless ponds with abundant vegetation; paedomorphs occur in permanent ponds.

behavior.text: Active at any hour but mostly at night; moves on moist, cool nights; relatively sedentary near its natal pond or the forest around it (adults average about 170 m to breeding ponds).
Breeds in winter in the south and fall in the north; adults leave breeding ponds by mid-May (March in South Carolina).
Adults eat earthworms, arthropods, aquatic insects and tadpoles; larvae eat zooplankton and sometimes other Ambystoma larvae.

resources.title: Smallmouth salamander
resources.description: Identify the smallmouth salamander (Ambystoma texanum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Smallmouth salamander (Ambystoma texanum): Relatively small head with a blunt, short snout, swollen behind the eyes, with the lower jaw barely protruding past the upper. Pale grey to black above with irregular light blotches that darken toward the sides; dark belly; 14-16 costal grooves; adults 11-17.8 cm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the central US (Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee and the states south to Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, and west to Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma) and in Ontario.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the central US (Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee and the states south to Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, and west to Nebraska, Kansas and Oklahoma) and in Ontario.

identification.text: Relatively small head with a blunt, short snout, swollen behind the eyes, with the lower jaw barely protruding past the upper.
Pale grey to black above with irregular light blotches that darken toward the sides; dark belly; 14-16 costal grooves; adults 11-17.8 cm.
Males are smaller with longer, more compressed tails; breeding animals look paler with more conspicuous light markings.
Larvae have light bars on an olive-green or dark-brown background.

habitat.text: Tolerates a wide range: tall-grass prairie, moist pine woodland, floodplain and oak forest and heavily farmed land; breeds in forest ponds, temporary pools, ditches and slow stream pools.

behavior.text: Secretive; hides under rotting logs, rocks or leaf litter or in crayfish and small-mammal burrows; an evening rain may bring it above ground.
Adults eat earthworms, insects, slugs and other invertebrates; larvae are generalist aquatic predators.
Inactive during the coldest and driest months.

resources.title: Two-toed amphiuma
resources.description: Identify the two-toed amphiuma (Amphiuma means), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Two-toed amphiuma (Amphiuma means): Eel-like, cylindrical salamander, 36.8-117 cm long, with four tiny vestigial legs each bearing two toes. Smooth skin, dark brown or black above and dark grey below; sexes alike. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US coastal plain: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US coastal plain: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

identification.text: Eel-like, cylindrical salamander, 36.8-117 cm long, with four tiny vestigial legs each bearing two toes.
Smooth skin, dark brown or black above and dark grey below; sexes alike.
Tiny eyes covered by skin with no lids; oily, slippery skin makes it hard to hold.
Compared with the three-toed amphiuma: Three-toed has three toes on each foot (two-toed has two), and the two species overlap in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.

habitat.text: Swamps, bayous, muddy sloughs, cypress heads, ditches, sluggish streams, wet meadows and muddy lakes with soft substrate or thick vegetation, usually near shore; often uses crayfish burrows.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal sit-and-wait ambush predator; finds prey by smell and touch; eats aquatic insects, crayfish, amphibians and water snakes.
Digs or takes over burrows in muddy bottoms; primarily aquatic but may cross land, especially on rainy nights.
Some populations may brumate in moss and mud in winter; Florida populations appear active year-round.

resources.title: Three-toed amphiuma
resources.description: Identify the three-toed amphiuma (Amphiuma tridactylum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Three-toed amphiuma (Amphiuma tridactylum): One of the largest salamanders: long cylindrical body to about 117 cm with four vestigial legs, each foot with three toes; hind legs shorter than front. Dark brown to black above with a markedly lighter belly and a dark underside to the neck. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the central and lower Mississippi valley region: Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the central and lower Mississippi valley region: Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.

identification.text: One of the largest salamanders: long cylindrical body to about 117 cm with four vestigial legs, each foot with three toes; hind legs shorter than front.
Dark brown to black above with a markedly lighter belly and a dark underside to the neck.
Lidless, reduced eyes; retains a laterally compressed tail and lateral-line system as an adult; copious mucus makes it hard to grip; males have wider, heavier heads.
Compared with the two-toed amphiuma: Two-toed has two toes on each foot (three-toed has three); both occur in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.

habitat.text: Wooded alluvial swamps, calcareous streams, floodland marshes and lakes, seepy pools and bayou or cypress-slough banks with extensive crayfish burrow networks.

behavior.text: Nocturnal, most active around midnight; ambush predator that eats mainly crayfish, plus fish, insects, snails and amphibians.
Non-migratory with a small home range around a burrow; aestivates in burrows in dry seasons; individuals often show bite marks.
Active throughout the year along the Gulf Coast.

resources.title: American toad
resources.description: Identify the american toad (Anaxyrus americanus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: American toad (Anaxyrus americanus): Stout toad 50-100 mm (usually about 75 mm) with thick, warty skin; brown, olive, grey or reddish, changing with temperature, humidity and stress. Dark spots on the back each contain only one or two warts, sometimes ringed with white or yellow; oval pupils with a gold ring. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it across eastern and central North America: Labrador, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Nunavut, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Québec, and most of the eastern and central US; Newfoundland is listed as introduced.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it across eastern and central North America: Labrador, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Nunavut, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Québec, and most of the eastern and central US; Newfoundland is listed as introduced.

identification.text: Stout toad 50-100 mm (usually about 75 mm) with thick, warty skin; brown, olive, grey or reddish, changing with temperature, humidity and stress.
Dark spots on the back each contain only one or two warts, sometimes ringed with white or yellow; oval pupils with a gold ring.
Males have dark (black or brown) throats; females are larger with white throats; belly white or yellow.
Toxic milky skin secretions irritate eyes and mouths.
Compared with the southern toad: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which American lacks.
Compared with the fowler's toad: Fowler's has three or more warts in each dark back spot and a mostly unspotted belly with a single dark chest spot; American has one or two warts per spot.

habitat.text: Terrestrial apart from a short breeding season; occupies forests to prairies wherever moisture, food and a breeding site are available; breeds in shallow, slow or still water, often with few fish.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal and most active in warm humid weather; by day hides under rocks and logs or digs into leaf litter and soil, backing in; digs deeper to hibernate.
Call is a long trill lasting 4-20 seconds, given by males at breeding ponds in late spring and early summer.
Eats a wide range of invertebrates (beetles, slugs, snails, earthworms), up to about 1,000 insects a day; tadpoles graze algae.

resources.title: Fowler's toad
resources.description: Identify the fowler's toad (Anaxyrus fowleri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Fowler's toad (Anaxyrus fowleri): Toad 5-9.5 cm, brown, grey or olive-green, with black-edged dark back spots that each contain three or more warts and a light mid-dorsal stripe. Belly usually whitish and almost unspotted apart from a single dark spot on the chest. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in southern Ontario and across the eastern US from New England and Michigan south to Florida and west to Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

taxonomicNotes.text: ADW's account uses the older genus name Bufo (Bufo fowleri); NatureServe uses Anaxyrus fowleri, noting Anaxyrus was split from Bufo by Frost et al. (2006) and that some references still use Bufo.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in southern Ontario and across the eastern US from New England and Michigan south to Florida and west to Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

identification.text: Toad 5-9.5 cm, brown, grey or olive-green, with black-edged dark back spots that each contain three or more warts and a light mid-dorsal stripe.
Belly usually whitish and almost unspotted apart from a single dark spot on the chest.
Males tend to be darker, females lighter; enlarged parotoid glands behind the eyes release a noxious secretion.
Tadpoles are short-bodied with a long tail and upper and lower fins.
Compared with the american toad: American has only one or two warts per dark back spot.

habitat.text: Wooded areas, river valleys and floodplains including farmland and residential areas, usually with deep friable soils; breeds in shallow marshes, rain pools, ponds and reservoirs with little current. Beach and dune habitat is also used.

behavior.text: Sources disagree on timing: described as completely nocturnal in one account and mostly diurnal in another; burrows during very hot or cold spells.
Adults eat insects and small terrestrial invertebrates and avoid earthworms, unlike the American toad; tadpoles scrape algae.
Inactive in fall, winter and early spring; hybridizes with the American toad in some areas.

resources.title: Oak toad
resources.description: Identify the oak toad (Anaxyrus quercicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Oak toad (Anaxyrus quercicus): Smallest toad in North America, 1.9-3.3 cm, with a short head, pointed nose and flat body. Black or brown with a long pale dorsal stripe (white, cream, yellow or orange) and 4-5 pairs of dark blotches; fine reddish bumps give a rough texture. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern coastal plain: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

taxonomicNotes.text: ADW's account uses the older genus name Bufo (Bufo quercicus); NatureServe uses Anaxyrus quercicus.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern coastal plain: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

identification.text: Smallest toad in North America, 1.9-3.3 cm, with a short head, pointed nose and flat body.
Black or brown with a long pale dorsal stripe (white, cream, yellow or orange) and 4-5 pairs of dark blotches; fine reddish bumps give a rough texture.
Elongated teardrop-shaped parotoid glands; grey-white, unblotched underside; males have dusky throats.
Adults can be mistaken for half-grown southern toads.
Compared with the southern toad: Adult oak toads are often mistaken for half-grown southern toads; the oak toad is only 1.9-3.3 cm with a long pale dorsal stripe and teardrop-shaped parotoid glands.

habitat.text: Sandy pine flatwoods, oak scrub, open pine and pine-oak woods, savannas with sandy soil and maritime forest, favouring open-canopy pine flatwoods with grassy cover; eggs and larvae develop in rain pools, ditches and flatwoods ponds.

behavior.text: More diurnal than most toads, sheltering by day buried in sand or under leaves or rocks; solitary outside breeding, when it may call at night.
Male call is a high-pitched, bird-like chirp.
Eats small terrestrial insects and arthropods such as ants and beetles; most active during the breeding period.

resources.title: Southern toad
resources.description: Identify the southern toad (Anaxyrus terrestris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern toad (Anaxyrus terrestris): Toad 40-113 mm, brown, grey or reddish with several dorsal spots and warts; belly greyish with a spotted chest. High cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the large, protruding eyes distinguish it from the American and Fowler's toads. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US: Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana.

identification.text: Toad 40-113 mm, brown, grey or reddish with several dorsal spots and warts; belly greyish with a spotted chest.
High cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the large, protruding eyes distinguish it from the American and Fowler's toads.
Males smaller with darker throats; tadpoles are solid black with a diagonal gold line behind the eye.
Compared with the american toad: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which helps separate it from the American toad.
Compared with the fowler's toad: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which helps separate it from Fowler's toad.

habitat.text: Wide variety of wooded and unwooded habitats, usually on sandy soil; burrows when inactive; breeds in permanent ponds, woodland pools and flooded depressions.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal; hides in self-made burrows by day and often feeds under lights near buildings.
Terrestrial until breeding, when it migrates to nearby wetlands; males call during breeding and sometimes in heavy rain at other times.
Eats spiders, beetles, ants and other invertebrates; inactive in the coldest months.

resources.title: Green anole
resources.description: Identify the green anole (Anolis carolinensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green anole (Anolis carolinensis): Slender lizard 4-8 cm (body) with a tail over half the total length; 2-6 g. Colour changes between green, brown and grey with temperature and excitement; dark brown or black typically signals cold or stress. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US (North Carolina to Florida, west to Oklahoma and Texas, north to Tennessee and Arkansas); Hawaii is listed as introduced.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and ADW place it in Polychrotidae; NatureServe notes a revised anole taxonomy (Poe et al. 2017) followed by Nicholson (2025) that treats anoles differently.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern US (North Carolina to Florida, west to Oklahoma and Texas, north to Tennessee and Arkansas); Hawaii is listed as introduced.

identification.text: Slender lizard 4-8 cm (body) with a tail over half the total length; 2-6 g.
Colour changes between green, brown and grey with temperature and excitement; dark brown or black typically signals cold or stress.
Males usually have a pinkish dewlap under the throat that is extended in displays, rarely seen in females; females often have a pale dorsal line from neck to tail base.

habitat.text: Wide range of edge habitats: upland forest, pine-palmetto scrub, rocky escarpments, swamps, wooded parks, fields, maritime scrub and residential lots.

behavior.text: Diurnal, sitting on a perch and watching for prey; usually stays within a small territory (about 50-100 m2) and bobs its head in displays.
Eats insects, spiders and other small arthropods; does not hibernate and can be active on sunny winter days.
Mostly arboreal; climbs trunks, shrubs, fence posts and building walls and sleeps in vegetation at night.

resources.title: Smooth softshell turtle
resources.description: Identify the smooth softshell turtle (Apalone mutica), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Smooth softshell turtle (Apalone mutica): Medium-large softshell; female carapace 16.5-35.6 cm, males 11.5-26.6 cm; leathery, skin-covered oval carapace without spines on the front edge. Olive to orange carapace with dark spots, streaks or blotches (females blotchier); plastron plain white or grey. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native across the central and south-central US (NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, the Midwest and Great Plains south to Texas, New Mexico and Florida); introduced in France (ADW). Not recorded for Canada in NatureServe.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe includes two subspecies (A. m. mutica, A. m. calvata) and notes some field guides treat calvata as a full species; ADW titles the species 'Smooth Softshelled Turtle'.

rangeSummary.value: Native across the central and south-central US (NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, the Midwest and Great Plains south to Texas, New Mexico and Florida); introduced in France (ADW). Not recorded for Canada in NatureServe.

identification.text: Medium-large softshell; female carapace 16.5-35.6 cm, males 11.5-26.6 cm; leathery, skin-covered oval carapace without spines on the front edge.
Olive to orange carapace with dark spots, streaks or blotches (females blotchier); plastron plain white or grey.
Cream or orange line bordered in black runs from behind each eye to the neck; tubular snout with round nostrils and no septal ridge.
Males have thicker tails than females.

habitat.text: Large rivers and streams, sometimes lakes, impoundments and shallow bogs, usually with sand or mud bottoms and little vegetation; nests on open sandbars and banks near water.

behavior.text: Most aquatic of the North American softshells; buries in bottom sediment so only the snout reaches the surface, and overwinters buried underwater.
Emerges from hibernation in March or early April in Kansas; basks on sandbars and mudflats.
Carnivorous generalist eating insects, crayfish, snails, fish and amphibians.

resources.title: Six-lined racerunner
resources.description: Identify the six-lined racerunner (Aspidoscelis sexlineatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Six-lined racerunner (Aspidoscelis sexlineatus): Long, slender, fast lizard 6-9.5 in with six light stripes (yellow, white, grey or pale blue) running from head onto the tail on a dark brown, black or dark grey ground colour. Tail is grey or brown, rougher in feel and often shows only one or two light stripes on its side; skinks, which look similar, have smooth shiny scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it across the central and southeastern US, from Maryland, Michigan, Wisconsin and Wyoming south to Florida, Texas and New Mexico; it is not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Tennessee WRA spells the epithet 'sexlineata' and SREL uses Cnemidophorus [Aspidoscelis]; NatureServe uses Aspidoscelis sexlineatus (older literature places racerunners in Cnemidophorus).

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it across the central and southeastern US, from Maryland, Michigan, Wisconsin and Wyoming south to Florida, Texas and New Mexico; it is not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Long, slender, fast lizard 6-9.5 in with six light stripes (yellow, white, grey or pale blue) running from head onto the tail on a dark brown, black or dark grey ground colour.
Tail is grey or brown, rougher in feel and often shows only one or two light stripes on its side; skinks, which look similar, have smooth shiny scales.
Belly is white to salmon-pink in females and bluish in males; males become bluer in the breeding season and have a broader head, females a heavier body.
Hatchlings resemble adults but have pale blue tails and distinct yellow stripes.

habitat.text: Open, dry, sunny habitats with loose sandy or gravelly soil and sparse vegetation: grassland, sandhills, stream floodplains, rocky slopes at mountain bases, woodland edges, dunes, glades, rock quarries and roadsides.

behavior.text: Active only in warm daylight and seeks shelter during the hottest midday period in summer; often active at body temperatures near 100 F.
Emerges later from winter burrows than many lizards; activity runs May-September in the north and longer in the south.
Eats insects, spiders and snails; shelters underground or under rocks and other objects, and sometimes escapes by submerging in water.
Eggs are laid in nests dug in soft soil or sawdust or under logs, 1-3 clutches of 1-6 eggs May-August.

resources.title: Worm snake
resources.description: Identify the worm snake (Carphophis amoenus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Worm snake (Carphophis amoenus): Small, slender, glossy snake 7-14 in (up to about 15 in) that looks like an earthworm; uniform chocolate brown to grey-brown above. Pink to white belly that extends partly up the sides; small, narrow head barely distinct from the neck with tiny eyes; smooth shiny scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern US from southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, through Connecticut and southeastern New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, to northwestern Georgia and Alabama and west to the Mississippi River; not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's primary name is Common Wormsnake (Carphophis amoenus) and it notes Crother (2017) treats the western C. vermis as a separate species; state sources call it Eastern Wormsnake (C. a. amoenus).

rangeSummary.value: Eastern US from southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, through Connecticut and southeastern New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, to northwestern Georgia and Alabama and west to the Mississippi River; not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Small, slender, glossy snake 7-14 in (up to about 15 in) that looks like an earthworm; uniform chocolate brown to grey-brown above.
Pink to white belly that extends partly up the sides; small, narrow head barely distinct from the neck with tiny eyes; smooth shiny scales.
Short tail ending in a sharp spine-like tip that it presses against fingers instead of biting; may release musk.
Hatchlings are 3-4 in, patterned like adults but darker with a brighter pink belly.

Compared with the northern red-bellied snake: Connecticut DEEP notes the worm snake is sometimes confused with it; the worm snake is uniform brown above with a pink belly, a tiny head and a spined tail tip.

habitat.text: Moist deciduous, mixed or pine woodland with loose, damp, well-drained soil, deep leaf litter and decaying wood, often along woodland edges or near wetlands and farm-field margins; occasionally gardens.

behavior.text: Secretive and mostly underground; found under leaf litter, rotting logs, flat rocks or debris; surface activity peaks in spring and early summer, often after rain, and it may be active day or night.
Active roughly March-October in the north (May-September in southern New England); goes deep underground in cold or dry weather.
Specialist earthworm predator that also takes soft-bodied insects; females lay 2-8 eggs in rotting wood or under rocks in June-July.

resources.title: Scarlet snake
resources.description: Identify the scarlet snake (Cemophora coccinea), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Scarlet snake (Cemophora coccinea): Slender, small to medium snake, 14-20 in (rarely to 32 in), with wide red bands bordered in black, separated by cream, white or light-yellow bands from head to tail. Red, pointed snout and head; plain white or cream belly; smooth glossy scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US, from New Jersey and Indiana south to Florida and west to Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; Texas populations in SREL's account are a separate species (C. lineri). Not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and SREL recognize two subspecies (C. c. coccinea and C. c. copei) and treat the Texas scarletsnake as a separate species, C. lineri.

rangeSummary.value: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US, from New Jersey and Indiana south to Florida and west to Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; Texas populations in SREL's account are a separate species (C. lineri). Not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Slender, small to medium snake, 14-20 in (rarely to 32 in), with wide red bands bordered in black, separated by cream, white or light-yellow bands from head to tail.
Red, pointed snout and head; plain white or cream belly; smooth glossy scales.
