Black bands separate the red bands from the yellow ones, which tells it from a coral snake; the plain white or cream belly separates it from scarlet kingsnakes and milksnakes, whose pattern extends onto the belly.
Compared with the scarlet kingsnake: Its bands encircle the whole body including the belly; scarlet snake has a plain white belly.
Compared with the eastern coral snake: North Carolina WRC: scarlet snakes have black bands separating the wide red bands from the yellow bands, unlike coral snakes.

habitat.text: Pine or hardwood forest and woodland and adjacent open areas with sandy or loamy well-drained soil; also fields, grassy edges and roadsides near woods; found under logs, rocks, leaf litter or boards.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and secretive; spends most time underground or under cover and is seen mostly crossing roads on warm summer nights, especially after rain; surface activity mostly May-September, peaking June-July.
Eats mainly reptile eggs, pierced with enlarged rear teeth, plus small lizards, snakes, frogs and mice.
Lays 2-9 elongated white eggs underground in summer.

resources.title: Ocellated skink
resources.description: Identify the ocellated skink (Chalcides ocellatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ocellated skink (Chalcides ocellatus): Typical skink with smooth, glossy overlapping scales, a cone-shaped head, cylindrical body and relatively small limbs; maximum snout-vent length 149 mm (Mesa, Arizona animals 68-118 mm, 160-230 mm total). Usually light-centred dark spots (ocelli) on a light brown, bronze, yellowish-green or grey background; ocelli may merge into dark bands, some animals have dark lateral stripes and others lack ocelli. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Italy across the Mediterranean and Middle East to Pakistan and North Africa; introduced and established in Mesa, Arizona (first confirmed 2007) and reported established in Florida, Britain and France. NatureServe lists only Arizona as exotic for the US.

rangeSummary.value: Native from Italy across the Mediterranean and Middle East to Pakistan and North Africa; introduced and established in Mesa, Arizona (first confirmed 2007) and reported established in Florida, Britain and France. NatureServe lists only Arizona as exotic for the US.

identification.text: Typical skink with smooth, glossy overlapping scales, a cone-shaped head, cylindrical body and relatively small limbs; maximum snout-vent length 149 mm (Mesa, Arizona animals 68-118 mm, 160-230 mm total).

Usually light-centred dark spots (ocelli) on a light brown, bronze, yellowish-green or grey background; ocelli may merge into dark bands, some animals have dark lateral stripes and others lack ocelli.
Belly usually white; juveniles have a greenish tail.

habitat.text: In Arizona found in and around potted plants, block walls, planters and shrubbery and inside garages and storerooms; in the native range it occupies open forest, Mediterranean and coastal scrub, palm oases, farms and gardens.

behavior.text: Basks on open ground and uses dense vegetation, rocks or woody debris for cover.
Live-bearing (eggs retained until hatching); one or two litters of 2-20 in summer; mating likely in spring.
Eats insects, arachnids and small lizards, including its own young.

resources.title: Southern painted turtle
resources.description: Identify the southern painted turtle (Chrysemys dorsalis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern painted turtle (Chrysemys dorsalis): Small aquatic turtle, 4-6 in, with a smooth olive-brown to nearly black carapace lacking a keel and a prominent yellow, orange or red stripe down the centre of the back. Marginal scutes have prominent red or orange; plastron plain yellow or tan, sometimes with a faint brown central blotch. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central Mississippi valley to the Gulf: NatureServe lists Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama; not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and state agencies treat it as a full species, C. dorsalis; it was formerly a subspecies of the painted turtle (C. picta dorsalis) and some herpetologists still treat it that way, citing intergrades.

rangeSummary.value: Central Mississippi valley to the Gulf: NatureServe lists Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama; not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Small aquatic turtle, 4-6 in, with a smooth olive-brown to nearly black carapace lacking a keel and a prominent yellow, orange or red stripe down the centre of the back.
Marginal scutes have prominent red or orange; plastron plain yellow or tan, sometimes with a faint brown central blotch.
Yellow lines on the head and chin, a yellow spot behind each eye, and red or orange lines on the neck and forelimbs; young are brighter with a slight keel.

Compared with the painted turtle: The painted turtle (western painted in Missouri) usually lacks the broad lengthwise stripe on the carapace; Tennessee WRA notes genetics are required to separate them with certainty.

habitat.text: Shallow swamps, slow streams, sloughs, oxbows, ditches, lakes and reservoirs with soft mud bottoms, aquatic vegetation and basking sites; in Missouri, wetlands within bottomland forest.

behavior.text: Usually active from late March into early November; basks on logs, rocks and banks, often many on one log, and slips into water at slight disturbance.
Eats plants and animals including algae, duckweed, snails, crayfish, frogs and fish.
Often lays more than one clutch per year (4-20 eggs); hatchlings usually winter in the nest and emerge in spring.

resources.title: Barking frog
resources.description: Identify the barking frog (Craugastor augusti), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Barking frog (Craugastor augusti): Toad-shaped frog 64.5-75 mm with a large head and small truncated toe pads. Greenish to tan, smooth skin with scattered dark spots; dorsolateral skin folds on the back, one fold across the back of the head, and a disk-shaped fold on the belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central Texas to southeastern New Mexico and south into Mexico; NatureServe lists Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. Not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly placed in the genus Eleutherodactylus (NatureServe); NatureServe notes subspecies latrans and cactorum have been proposed as separate species but it currently recognizes no subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Central Texas to southeastern New Mexico and south into Mexico; NatureServe lists Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. Not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Toad-shaped frog 64.5-75 mm with a large head and small truncated toe pads.
Greenish to tan, smooth skin with scattered dark spots; dorsolateral skin folds on the back, one fold across the back of the head, and a disk-shaped fold on the belly.
Young are often greenish with a fawn band across the middle of the back.

habitat.text: Low-elevation rocky shrubland, desert and woodland, often on limestone or rhyolite outcrops, in caves or crevices or rodent burrows; under rocks or logs, including oak and juniper woodland in Texas.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; call carries like a dog's bark at a distance and sounds like a throaty 'whurr' close up.
Breeds with rain: February-May in Texas, late June-July in Arizona; eggs are laid on land under rocks, logs or in crevices and there is no free-living tadpole stage.
Walks with the body held high and inflates to several times normal size when threatened; most active at night during rains.

resources.title: Eastern diamondback rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus): Largest rattlesnake, heavy-bodied, usually 1.0-1.5 m and sometimes over 2.4 m; males larger than females. Olive, brown or near-black with diamond-shaped outlines of tan-yellow scales around blackish-brown centres down the back; keeled scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern coastal plain: NatureServe lists North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; not recorded for Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern coastal plain: NatureServe lists North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Largest rattlesnake, heavy-bodied, usually 1.0-1.5 m and sometimes over 2.4 m; males larger than females.
Olive, brown or near-black with diamond-shaped outlines of tan-yellow scales around blackish-brown centres down the back; keeled scales.
Large spade-shaped head, vertical pupils, pits between eye and nostril, and two light lines running from behind the eye to the back of the jaw.
Rattle at the tail tip; hatchlings (about 0.3 m) closely resemble adults.

habitat.text: Pine and wiregrass flatwoods, longleaf pine-turkey oak hills, scrub, coastal hammocks and barrier islands, dry prairie and abandoned fields, particularly with abundant cover; large tracts are most suitable; rarely climbs.

behavior.text: Sit-and-wait ambush predator that coils in shade or underbrush; mostly diurnal but may be active at any time, with most activity early morning, evening and night per NatureServe.
Most activity April-October, though it visits the surface on warm winter days; hibernates singly; shelters in stump holes, burrows of gopher tortoises and other animals and brush piles.
Eats mainly rodents and rabbits (cottontails, marsh rabbits, cotton rats, squirrels); gives live birth in August-September to about 14 young.

resources.title: Hellbender
resources.description: Identify the hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis): Largest aquatic salamander in North America, 295-686 mm and 405-1010 g. Flat body with loose skin folds, very flat broad head with a short snout, no eyelids, small stubby limbs and webbed toes (four front, five hind); muscular tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central US: NatureServe lists New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi; not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes genomic evidence (Hime 2017) for five species-level lineages and proposals to split eastern (alleganiensis), Ozark (bishopi) and Ohio-drainage (horrida) populations, but keeps C. alleganiensis as the listed taxon.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central US: NatureServe lists New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi; not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Largest aquatic salamander in North America, 295-686 mm and 405-1010 g.
Flat body with loose skin folds, very flat broad head with a short snout, no eyelids, small stubby limbs and webbed toes (four front, five hind); muscular tail.
Deep brown or black, occasionally with dark orange spots above or below; belly lighter; sexes look alike; rare albino and red variants.
Larvae are 25-33 mm and limbless at hatching and have pale gill slits, lost at maturity.

habitat.text: Clear, rocky, fast-flowing creeks and rivers with large shelter rocks and steady oxygen and flow, usually where water stays below about 20 C; avoids wide, slow, muddy water.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and solitary; hides by day under large flat rocks at the stream bottom and hunts from dusk to dawn, with territory centred on the shelter rock (average about 113 m2) defended against other hellbenders.
Eats mainly crayfish, plus fish, tadpoles and insects, using suction feeding; peak nocturnal activity May-June in West Virginia.
Breeds late summer to fall; males guard eggs under large rocks or logs.

conservationStatus.text: Eastern Hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis), Missouri DPS: listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2021-04-07.
Ozark Hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis bishopi): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2011-11-07.

resources.title: Rough-tailed gecko
resources.description: Identify the rough-tailed gecko (Cyrtopodion scabrum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rough-tailed gecko (Cyrtopodion scabrum). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native from Egypt and the Middle East to western India; established through introduction in Texas (Galveston shipping docks), Arizona, California and Nevada (Center for North American Herpetology, citing SSAR); NatureServe lists Arizona and Texas as exotic.

taxonomicNotes.text: Reported in Texas literature under the name Cyrtodactylus scaber (NatureServe).

rangeSummary.value: Native from Egypt and the Middle East to western India; established through introduction in Texas (Galveston shipping docks), Arizona, California and Nevada (Center for North American Herpetology, citing SSAR); NatureServe lists Arizona and Texas as exotic.

habitat.text: Rock piles and escarpments in the native range; in Texas, the upper walls of dockside buildings, inside and out.

behavior.text: Active on warm nights (NatureServe).
A sample from Galveston, Texas in mid-September showed hatchlings, juveniles and adults present.

resources.title: Chicken turtle
resources.description: Identify the chicken turtle (Deirochelys reticularia), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Chicken turtle (Deirochelys reticularia): Identified by a very long, yellow-striped neck, about as long as the plastron and up to 80% of carapace length. Pear-shaped, olive to dark brown carapace with a reticulate network of yellow to orange lines; solid yellow plastron; yellow stripes on the legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern and south-central US coastal plain; NatureServe lists Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and ADW include three subspecies (chrysea, miaria, reticularia) within the species.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern and south-central US coastal plain; NatureServe lists Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Identified by a very long, yellow-striped neck, about as long as the plastron and up to 80% of carapace length.
Pear-shaped, olive to dark brown carapace with a reticulate network of yellow to orange lines; solid yellow plastron; yellow stripes on the legs.
Carapace 15.3-17.8 cm typically, to 25.4 cm; females about 1.5 times larger than males; males have thicker tails, longer front claws and a more compressed shell.

habitat.text: Shallow ponds and lakes with thick vegetation, cypress swamps, ditches and temporary pools, usually not flowing water; wanders overland, especially in spring.

behavior.text: Diurnal and often seen on land migrating between wetlands or seeking soil to burrow into; land activity in South Carolina peaks in March and April; basks, and is wary when basking.
Hibernates in mud and vegetation in the north of its range; Florida animals stay active all year; may aestivate on land when wetlands dry.
Eats crustaceans, aquatic insects, tadpoles, fish and plants, using suction feeding; nests August-September and February-March in South Carolina.

resources.title: Southern dusky salamander
resources.description: Identify the southern dusky salamander (Desmognathus auriculatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern dusky salamander (Desmognathus auriculatus): Brown to black salamander up to about 6.5 in, usually with one or two rows of white side spots. Belly gray-brown to black with small white speckles. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain: Virginia (to mid Mecklenburg County) and the North Carolina coastal plain per state agencies; NatureServe's narrower concept lists only Alabama and Florida. Not recorded for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe uses a narrower concept of D. auriculatus (Means et al. 2017; Pyron et al. 2022), splitting D. valentinei, D. pascagoula and D. valtos from it; Virginia and North Carolina agency pages use the broader concept.

rangeSummary.value: Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain: Virginia (to mid Mecklenburg County) and the North Carolina coastal plain per state agencies; NatureServe's narrower concept lists only Alabama and Florida. Not recorded for Canada.

identification.text: Brown to black salamander up to about 6.5 in, usually with one or two rows of white side spots.
Belly gray-brown to black with small white speckles.
Laterally compressed tail sharpening toward the tip; a light stripe runs from each eye back to the base of the jaw, as in all dusky salamanders.

habitat.text: Mucky areas near springs, swamps, cypress heads, mud-bottomed streams, floodplain pools and ravines with organic debris, usually in or near slow water; leaf-litter packs along slow mucky streams in Virginia.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; hides by day under leaves, logs or debris or in burrows.
Opportunistic feeder on arthropods, worms and other invertebrates; Virginia DWR notes cannibalism.
Breeds September-October, 9-20 eggs guarded by the female until fall hatching; larvae are aquatic with external gills and metamorphose the following spring.

resources.title: Spotted dusky salamander
resources.description: Identify the spotted dusky salamander (Desmognathus conanti), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spotted dusky salamander (Desmognathus conanti): Moderately stout body with a moderately keeled tail, 6.4-12.7 cm total length. Usually 6-8 pairs of golden spots on the back, which in adults may fuse into a light stripe with a dark, irregular border. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Lowland drainages east of the Mississippi River, from extreme southern Illinois and southwestern Kentucky to east-central Tennessee and northwest Georgia, south to the Florida Panhandle and west through Alabama and Louisiana. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Lowland drainages east of the Mississippi River, from extreme southern Illinois and southwestern Kentucky to east-central Tennessee and northwest Georgia, south to the Florida Panhandle and west through Alabama and Louisiana. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Moderately stout body with a moderately keeled tail, 6.4-12.7 cm total length.
Usually 6-8 pairs of golden spots on the back, which in adults may fuse into a light stripe with a dark, irregular border.
Belly light with dark flecks.
Wash of whitish or bluish speckling across sides and tail and no light-coloured 'portholes' on the flanks, separating it from several sympatric Desmognathus.
Nearly identical to northern dusky salamander; best told apart by range.
Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Very similar; best separated by range (northern dusky is the northeastern species).

habitat.text: Floodplains, sloughs and mucky sites along upland streams to about 900 m, usually near running or trickling water.
Abundant in and near cool streams and small rivers in the Piedmont and lower mountains of SC and GA.

behavior.text: Takes refuge under logs, rocks and leaf litter by day and moves on stream banks at night.
Feeds opportunistically on small invertebrates, mostly terrestrial insects; may be active by day in dark, wet weather.
Females brood up to 35 eggs under moss or rocks from mid-June through August.

resources.title: Northern dusky salamander
resources.description: Identify the northern dusky salamander (Desmognathus fuscus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern dusky salamander (Desmognathus fuscus): Small, robust salamander with 14 costal grooves and hind limbs larger than the front limbs. Keeled tail shorter than half the body length. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northeastern North America from southern New Brunswick and southern Quebec (and southeastern Ontario) south along the East Coast to North Carolina and west to Ohio, southern Indiana, Kentucky and Tennessee. Populations in southeastern Illinois and eastern Michigan are considered introduced.

rangeSummary.value: Northeastern North America from southern New Brunswick and southern Quebec (and southeastern Ontario) south along the East Coast to North Carolina and west to Ohio, southern Indiana, Kentucky and Tennessee. Populations in southeastern Illinois and eastern Michigan are considered introduced.

identification.text: Small, robust salamander with 14 costal grooves and hind limbs larger than the front limbs.
Keeled tail shorter than half the body length.
Upper body brown, reddish brown, gray or olive with slightly darker markings; tail base olive, yellow or bright chestnut.
Belly whitish with dark speckles.
Adults 6.4-14.2 cm; males typically longer than females.
Compared with the spotted dusky salamander: Near-identical; separated by range.

habitat.text: Rock-strewn wooded streams, seepages and springs, usually near running or trickling water, from sea level up the Appalachians.
Found under flat rocks or logs near rocky or hillside streams, or near waterfalls.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal; leaves cover under rocks or logs at night to forage along streams, and is active dusk to dawn on moist evenings.
Active year-round at spring-fed sites, otherwise often inactive in winter; burrows below the frost line in severe cold.
Generally solitary except during courtship and larval brooding; females guard 12-51 eggs under rocks, logs or moss near water.

resources.title: Seal salamander
resources.description: Identify the seal salamander (Desmognathus monticola), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Seal salamander (Desmognathus monticola): Fairly large: 3.0-6.0 in (7.6-15 cm). Light brown to grayish back with black or dark brown reticulated, irregular 'wormy' splotches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Endemic to the eastern United States: from southwestern Pennsylvania southwest in the uplands through West Virginia, western Maryland, Virginia, eastern Kentucky, western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, western South Carolina and northern Georgia. Not north or west of the Ohio River in the north. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats southern lineages formerly in D. monticola as the separate species D. cheaha.

rangeSummary.value: Endemic to the eastern United States: from southwestern Pennsylvania southwest in the uplands through West Virginia, western Maryland, Virginia, eastern Kentucky, western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, western South Carolina and northern Georgia. Not north or west of the Ohio River in the north. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Fairly large: 3.0-6.0 in (7.6-15 cm).
Light brown to grayish back with black or dark brown reticulated, irregular 'wormy' splotches.
Belly very pale, often white, contrasting sharply with the back.
Tail triangular in cross-section toward the end and moderately keeled.
Compared with the black-bellied salamander: Black belly and two rows of small white dots along the sides.
Compared with the shovel-nosed salamander: Different head shape and gray to dark belly.
Compared with the black mountain salamander: Belly less pale so back-to-belly contrast is gradual.

habitat.text: Mountain streams, small rocky spring-fed brooks in shaded ravines, seepages, and wet rock faces.
Prefers well-oxygenated, cool streams with moderate to steep gradient.

behavior.text: Sometimes perches on wet rocks; hides under rocks or moss and in burrows in mud banks.
Females with 15-40 eggs are seen June-October; eggs are laid on the undersides of rocks or leaves in water or seepages.
Occasionally eats small salamanders in addition to invertebrates.

resources.title: Allegheny dusky salamander
resources.description: Identify the allegheny dusky salamander (Desmognathus ochrophaeus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Allegheny dusky salamander (Desmognathus ochrophaeus): Adults 7-10 cm with long slender body, tapered tail and moderately long, well-developed legs. Straight light dorsal stripe running onto the tail (yellow, orange, olive, gray, brown or red), flanked by darker mottled pigment. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Ridge and Valley ridges of southwestern Virginia, the Cumberland Mountains and Plateau, and the Allegheny Mountains and Plateau from West Virginia north through Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York, including the Adirondacks, to southern Quebec and southern Ontario.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe names it Allegheny Mountain Dusky Salamander and treats D. ochrophaeus as a complex that has been split (D. carolinensis, D. ocoee, D. orestes); ADW calls it Mountain Dusky Salamander.

rangeSummary.value: Ridge and Valley ridges of southwestern Virginia, the Cumberland Mountains and Plateau, and the Allegheny Mountains and Plateau from West Virginia north through Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York, including the Adirondacks, to southern Quebec and southern Ontario.

identification.text: Adults 7-10 cm with long slender body, tapered tail and moderately long, well-developed legs.
Straight light dorsal stripe running onto the tail (yellow, orange, olive, gray, brown or red), flanked by darker mottled pigment.
Dorsal stripe may carry dark chevron-like spots; sides of tail black.
Light line from the eye to the bottom of the jaw in many individuals.
Juveniles are dorsally spotted with a yellow dorsal band.
Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Robust with no straight pale dorsal stripe; belly whitish with dark speckles.

habitat.text: Near seepages, springs and small streams at lower elevations and in winter; more terrestrial at higher elevations, especially on the floor of spruce-fir forest.
Often abundant on wet rock faces.

behavior.text: Active at all seasons in mild weather in the south; most active at night but diurnal activity is common.
Climbs trees and shrubs while foraging and ambushes prey by sight; eats worms, beetles and fly larvae.
Female stays with up to about 30 eggs laid in wet rock crevices or under rocks, logs or moss.

resources.title: Black Mountain salamander
resources.description: Identify the black mountain salamander (Desmognathus welteri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black Mountain salamander (Desmognathus welteri): Medium-sized, chubby: 3.0-5.0 in (7.6-12.7 cm). Light brown back with small dark brown spots or streaks. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern Kentucky, adjacent southwestern Virginia, southern West Virginia and eastern Tennessee (Cumberland Plateau and Mountains). Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern Kentucky, adjacent southwestern Virginia, southern West Virginia and eastern Tennessee (Cumberland Plateau and Mountains). Not in Canada.

identification.text: Medium-sized, chubby: 3.0-5.0 in (7.6-12.7 cm).
Light brown back with small dark brown spots or streaks.
Toe tips usually very dark.
Light line from just behind the eye to the angle of the jaw; weak whitish dots along the side between the legs.
Tail flattened at the base and strongly keeled; belly whitish with light brown to gray speckling and a gradual back-to-belly colour transition.
Compared with the seal salamander: Lighter belly giving a distinct back-to-belly contrast.
Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Formerly treated as the same species; welteri has darker toe tips and a strongly keeled tail.

habitat.text: Small to medium mountain streams with rocky substrate, spring runs and roadside puddles in wooded mountain terrain at 300-1220 m; may forage in surrounding forest on wet evenings.

behavior.text: Strongly aquatic; adults hide under rocks or logs in water or in splash-zone crevices, larvae and juveniles use smaller seeps.
Eats mostly worms, insects and crustaceans.
Females lay up to about 60 eggs (average 26) March-November and guard them; larvae metamorphose in about 2 years.

resources.title: Northern two-lined salamander
resources.description: Identify the northern two-lined salamander (Eurycea bislineata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern two-lined salamander (Eurycea bislineata): Adults 6.4-12.1 cm with a broad yellow to greenish-yellow or tan stripe from head to tail. Stripe bordered on each side by a narrow black line that may break into dashes toward the tail; may have a row of dark spots down the middle. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Quebec and eastern Ontario south to northern Virginia, eastern West Virginia and central Ohio, with isolated populations in southern Labrador.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Quebec and eastern Ontario south to northern Virginia, eastern West Virginia and central Ohio, with isolated populations in southern Labrador.

identification.text: Adults 6.4-12.1 cm with a broad yellow to greenish-yellow or tan stripe from head to tail.
Stripe bordered on each side by a narrow black line that may break into dashes toward the tail; may have a row of dark spots down the middle.
15-16 costal grooves; yellow belly.
Breeding males have whitish lower eyelid glands, a mental gland on the chin and cirri on the snout.
Larvae have short reddish-brown gills.
Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: 14 costal grooves rather than 15-16; ranges to the south.
Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Stocky with keeled tail and no dark-bordered dorsal stripe.

habitat.text: Rocky brooks, springs and seepages; adults hide under objects in or near water.

behavior.text: Sometimes active by day in shaded wet areas; apparently active throughout the year in most of its range.
Hides under objects in or near water and disperses into wooded uplands in wet, warm weather; aggregates in winter.
Feeds opportunistically on small invertebrates, mainly terrestrial insects; eggs are laid April-June on the undersides of submerged rocks, logs or plants.

resources.title: Two-lined salamander
resources.description: Identify the two-lined salamander (Eurycea cirrigera), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Two-lined salamander (Eurycea cirrigera): Small: about 6-12 cm total length, tail nearly half of total length. Yellow-orange to rusty body with two dark-brown stripes running its length that break into speckling toward the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Illinois, Indiana, southern Ohio, western West Virginia and central Virginia south to northern Florida, southern Alabama, southern Mississippi and southeastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe calls it Southern Two-lined Salamander; some authorities treat it as a subspecies of Eurycea bislineata.

rangeSummary.value: Illinois, Indiana, southern Ohio, western West Virginia and central Virginia south to northern Florida, southern Alabama, southern Mississippi and southeastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small: about 6-12 cm total length, tail nearly half of total length.
Yellow-orange to rusty body with two dark-brown stripes running its length that break into speckling toward the tail.
Back and often sides speckled with dark-brown spots.
14 costal grooves (northern two-lined has 15 or 16).
Breeding males grow two cirri, small antenna-like lobes hanging from the snout.
Compared with the northern two-lined salamander: 15-16 costal grooves; occurs to the north.
Compared with the dwarf salamander: Only four toes on each hind foot.

habitat.text: Rocky brooks, springs, seepages, river swamps and forested floodplains with stagnant pools; may disperse into wooded uplands in wet weather.

behavior.text: Cryptic; spends most time under logs or foliage and emerges to forage on the forest floor on damp nights; sometimes active by day in shaded wet areas.
Males may be territorial toward other males.
Often seen crossing roads in rainy weather during the breeding season; eggs are laid on or under submerged rocks, logs or plants, in winter in the south.

resources.title: Three-lined salamander
resources.description: Identify the three-lined salamander (Eurycea guttolineata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Three-lined salamander (Eurycea guttolineata): Mid-sized, slender: 4-6.25 in (10-15.9 cm). Tan to light yellow with three bold black longitudinal stripes from the eyes to the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Virginia and Tennessee south through the Carolinas, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the Gulf Coast, including eastern Louisiana and western Florida; absent from southern Georgia, most of peninsular Florida and high Appalachian elevations. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly treated as a subspecies of Eurycea longicauda (ADW still lists it as E. longicauda guttolineata).

rangeSummary.value: Virginia and Tennessee south through the Carolinas, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the Gulf Coast, including eastern Louisiana and western Florida; absent from southern Georgia, most of peninsular Florida and high Appalachian elevations. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Mid-sized, slender: 4-6.25 in (10-15.9 cm).
Tan to light yellow with three bold black longitudinal stripes from the eyes to the tail.
Tail about two-thirds of total length.
Underside boldly marbled black and white.
Compared with the longtail salamander: Yellow to orange with vertical black bars on the tail rather than three bold body stripes.

habitat.text: Forested floodplains, ditches, damp streamsides, seepage springs, bottomland hardwood streams and cypress swamp edges; sometimes disperses into woods in wet weather.

behavior.text: Mostly active at night, emerging to hunt insects and other small invertebrates.
Found under wood, rocks or other cover along streams and blackwater swamps.
Breeds in fall and winter; eggs are laid in underground crevices near springs and streams and attended by the female; larvae are aquatic.

resources.title: Longtail salamander
resources.description: Identify the longtail salamander (Eurycea longicauda), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Longtail salamander (Eurycea longicauda): Adults 10-15.9 cm (record 19.7 cm); tail about 60% of body length. Ground colour yellow to orange or even red. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern New York to Missouri, south to Arkansas, Tennessee, extreme northeastern Mississippi, northern Alabama, extreme northwestern Georgia, western North Carolina and northwestern Virginia. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southern New York to Missouri, south to Arkansas, Tennessee, extreme northeastern Mississippi, northern Alabama, extreme northwestern Georgia, western North Carolina and northwestern Virginia. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Adults 10-15.9 cm (record 19.7 cm); tail about 60% of body length.
Ground colour yellow to orange or even red.
Vertical black bars on the sides of the tail (herringbone or 'dumbbell' look), plus dark dashes or dots on the body.
13 or 14 costal grooves; belly light yellow to cream.
Large eyes, slender body and stout limbs.
Compared with the three-lined salamander: Three bold dark stripes along body and tail, not vertical tail bars.

habitat.text: Streamsides, spring runs, cave mouths and abandoned mines; sometimes ponds. Hides in rock crevices and under rocks, logs and debris.

behavior.text: Adults migrate uphill during heavy rain and into and out of caves and mine shafts; mainly nocturnal.
Eats a wide variety of small, mainly terrestrial invertebrates.
Active April-October in Indiana.

resources.title: Dwarf salamander
resources.description: Identify the dwarf salamander (Eurycea quadridigitata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Dwarf salamander (Eurycea quadridigitata): One of North America's smallest vertebrates; adults often under 2 in (5 cm) and under 1 g. Four toes on each hind foot, where all other Eurycea have five; the one sure diagnostic. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Lake Okeechobee, Florida, and west to eastern Texas. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe names it Southern Dwarf Salamander and notes the complex has been split (E. chamberlaini, E. paludicola, E. hillisi, E. sphagnicola), narrowing E. quadridigitata.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Lake Okeechobee, Florida, and west to eastern Texas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: One of North America's smallest vertebrates; adults often under 2 in (5 cm) and under 1 g.
Four toes on each hind foot, where all other Eurycea have five; the one sure diagnostic.
Superficially like a tiny southern two-lined salamander.
Bronze-brown in one species of the former complex, yellow in another.
Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: Five toes on each hind foot.

habitat.text: Low swampy areas, margins of pine savanna ponds and bottomland forests; edges of Carolina bays.

behavior.text: Migrates to the edges of Carolina bays to breed, in spring or fall depending on the bay.
Hides under logs or debris by day; terrestrial activity peaks with late-fall and early-winter rains (Alabama).
Females lay up to about 60 eggs in late fall to early winter and attend them; larvae metamorphose by spring or early summer.

resources.title: Mud snake
resources.description: Identify the mud snake (Farancia abacura), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mud snake (Farancia abacura): Non-venomous; adults 91-122 cm total length, females thicker-bodied, males longer-tailed. Shiny blue-gray to black back, often with a metallic sheen. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain from southeastern Virginia to southern Florida, west to eastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southern Illinois. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists it as Red-bellied Mudsnake.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain from southeastern Virginia to southern Florida, west to eastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southern Illinois. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Non-venomous; adults 91-122 cm total length, females thicker-bodied, males longer-tailed.
Shiny blue-gray to black back, often with a metallic sheen.
Sides with salmon, pink or red bars; belly checkered with alternating red and black bars.
Flat head, slightly constricted neck and small inconspicuous eyes; smooth scales in 19 rows at midbody.
Juveniles similar but with a needle-like tail that adults lack.

habitat.text: Marshes, swampy lake margins, river-edge wetlands, oxbows, beaver ponds, slow mud-bottomed streams, sloughs, floodplains, ditches and brackish tidal areas; burrows in soft soil and wet debris.

behavior.text: Semiaquatic and fossorial; prowls in the open at night, buried in mud much of the time on land.
Eats sirens, amphiumas, other salamanders, frogs, tadpoles and fish.
Active March-November in Texas; hibernates in the northern part of its range and is active year-round in the south.
Lays 6-104 eggs (usually under 50), mostly July to early August.

resources.title: Narrowmouth frog
resources.description: Identify the narrowmouth frog (Gastrophryne carolinensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Narrowmouth frog (Gastrophryne carolinensis): Small: up to 1.5 in (3.8 cm) snout-vent length. Gray, brown or reddish above, often with dark spots or mottling and sometimes a broad stripe on each side. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Maryland to southeastern Kansas and south to the Florida Keys, Gulf Coast and eastern Texas, with scattered disjunct northern and western populations. Introduced on the Bahamas and Grand Cayman. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe calls it Eastern Narrow-mouthed Toad.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Maryland to southeastern Kansas and south to the Florida Keys, Gulf Coast and eastern Texas, with scattered disjunct northern and western populations. Introduced on the Bahamas and Grand Cayman. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small: up to 1.5 in (3.8 cm) snout-vent length.
Gray, brown or reddish above, often with dark spots or mottling and sometimes a broad stripe on each side.
Smooth skin, short limbs, unwebbed toes, pointed snout and a fold of skin across the back of the head.
Males have a dark throat; females light.
Call is a nasal, sheep-like bleat with no trill.

habitat.text: Wide variety of habitats, usually with sandy or loamy soil, up to several hundred metres from water; breeds in ponds, ditches, swamps and rain puddles.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal, most active on wet nights in spring and summer.
Burrows or hides beneath objects by day and in cold or dry weather.
Eats mainly ants, termites and small beetles, feeding at anthill openings.
Breeds after heavy rains, mostly spring-summer (March-November); toxic skin secretions deter predators.

resources.title: Common map turtle
resources.description: Identify the common map turtle (Graptemys geographica), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Common map turtle (Graptemys geographica): Carapace olive or grayish brown with yellow-orange map-like lines bordered in dark; markings fade with age. Broad carapace with a moderately low keel and slightly scalloped rear edge. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Quebec, southern Ontario and northwestern Vermont to central Minnesota, south through the Mississippi drainage to Arkansas, northern Alabama and eastern Tennessee, west to eastern Kansas; Ohio River drainage; isolated populations in the Delaware, Susquehanna and Hudson drainages.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe names it Northern Map Turtle.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Quebec, southern Ontario and northwestern Vermont to central Minnesota, south through the Mississippi drainage to Arkansas, northern Alabama and eastern Tennessee, west to eastern Kansas; Ohio River drainage; isolated populations in the Delaware, Susquehanna and Hudson drainages.

identification.text: Carapace olive or grayish brown with yellow-orange map-like lines bordered in dark; markings fade with age.
Broad carapace with a moderately low keel and slightly scalloped rear edge.
Head, neck and limbs dark with thin yellow, green or orange stripes, usually with an oval spot behind the eye.
Females much larger (7-10.5 in) than males (3.5-6.5 in); males have narrower heads, longer front claws and thicker tails.
Plain yellowish plastron in adults.
Compared with the false map turtle: Lines form a web on the shell and a backward L behind the eye.
Compared with the ouachita map turtle: Large blotch below the eye and dark-ringed blotches on the scutes.

habitat.text: Slow rivers and lakes with mud bottoms, basking logs and abundant aquatic vegetation; also mill ponds and oxbows. Basks on logs and muskrat houses.

behavior.text: Avid baskers, often in groups, and very wary: slips into the water at the slightest alarm.
Dormant about November to early April, wedged under submerged logs, in bottom mud or in burrows.
Females eat mainly mollusks and crayfish; males more insectivorous.

resources.title: Pascagoula map turtle
resources.description: Identify the pascagoula map turtle (Graptemys gibbonsi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pascagoula map turtle (Graptemys gibbonsi): Large; females to 29.5 cm carapace, males to 12.4 cm. High-domed olive, brown or green carapace with a medial keel bearing spines on the second and third vertebrals. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Endemic to the Pascagoula River drainage in Mississippi (Pascagoula, Leaf and Chickasawhay rivers and tributaries). Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: ADW also calls it Gibbon's map turtle; G. pearlensis was split from it.

rangeSummary.value: Endemic to the Pascagoula River drainage in Mississippi (Pascagoula, Leaf and Chickasawhay rivers and tributaries). Not in Canada.

identification.text: Large; females to 29.5 cm carapace, males to 12.4 cm.
High-domed olive, brown or green carapace with a medial keel bearing spines on the second and third vertebrals.
Large greenish interorbital blotch joined to two postorbital blotches, with yellow paramedian neck stripes.
Yellow or orange vertical line on each marginal scute; nasal trident usually present.
Compared with the alabama map turtle: Low-domed shell with concentric yellow semicircles on the marginals and no nasal trident; Mobile Bay drainage.

habitat.text: Large to medium rivers with mollusks, sandy banks or bars, deep pools and logs; highest densities near deadwood. Nests in sandy banks or bars.

behavior.text: Forages and basks by day and spends nights underwater clinging to branches.
Adult females eat mainly mollusks; males and juveniles eat insects and other arthropods.
Competes for basking space by pushing; larger turtles win more often.

resources.title: Ouachita map turtle
resources.description: Identify the ouachita map turtle (Graptemys ouachitensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ouachita map turtle (Graptemys ouachitensis): Olive-green carapace with one to six black blotches on the rear of each scute, ringed yellow or orange; rings fade with age. Yellow or cream plastron with dark green swirls. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mississippi and St. Croix river basins from Minnesota and Wisconsin south through Louisiana, west to eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and eastern Texas, east into Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Sabine map turtle is sometimes treated as a subspecies and sometimes as a species.

rangeSummary.value: Mississippi and St. Croix river basins from Minnesota and Wisconsin south through Louisiana, west to eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and eastern Texas, east into Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Olive-green carapace with one to six black blotches on the rear of each scute, ringed yellow or orange; rings fade with age.
Yellow or cream plastron with dark green swirls.
Dark green head with yellow markings; a large blotch below each eye joins two narrow lines.
Keels prominent in juveniles and males, blunted in females.
Females 120-260 mm carapace, males 90-178 mm.
Compared with the false map turtle: Lines form a web over the shell; often a backward L behind the eye.
Compared with the common map turtle: Fine map-like lines over the shell and an oval spot behind the eye.

habitat.text: Mainly rivers (also impoundments) with submerged vegetation and basking logs or rocks; nests on sandbars and beaches within about 100 m of water.

behavior.text: Diurnal; basks in groups, then feeds from mid-morning, alternating feeding and basking.
Does not migrate; brumates near moderate current behind logs or rocks from late October to mid-April.
Eats vegetation, aquatic insects and some mollusks and carrion; females eat more vegetation.

resources.title: Mississippi map turtle
resources.description: Identify the mississippi map turtle (Graptemys pseudogeographica), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mississippi map turtle (Graptemys pseudogeographica): Olive, brown or black carapace with dark blotches ringed by yellow lines that may form a web over the shell; brighter in young. Serrate carapace margin with a vertebral keel most prominent in young. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mississippi and Missouri river basins from northern and central Wisconsin and Minnesota south through Louisiana and eastern Texas, west along the Missouri into North Dakota, east to western Tennessee, western Kentucky, Indiana and central Ohio. Introduced in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe calls it False Map Turtle; the 'Mississippi map turtle' is the subspecies G. p. kohnii, formerly a full species.

rangeSummary.value: Mississippi and Missouri river basins from northern and central Wisconsin and Minnesota south through Louisiana and eastern Texas, west along the Missouri into North Dakota, east to western Tennessee, western Kentucky, Indiana and central Ohio. Introduced in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Olive, brown or black carapace with dark blotches ringed by yellow lines that may form a web over the shell; brighter in young.
Serrate carapace margin with a vertebral keel most prominent in young.
Cream to yellow plastron; young have a dark pattern.
Yellow lines on legs, tail, chin and neck; some have a backward L behind each eye.
Males 9-15 cm, females 12-27 cm; males have elongated second and third front claws.
Compared with the ouachita map turtle: Large blotch below the eye and ringed blotches on the scutes.
Compared with the common map turtle: Map-like lines and an oval spot behind the eye.

habitat.text: Large rivers of the Mississippi basin with abundant vegetation, also lakes, ponds, reservoirs and sloughs; nests on sandbars and beaches.

behavior.text: Spends most of the day basking on lodges, logs, rocks, bars or stumps near shore; very wary.
Active roughly late March to mid-October; hibernates in bottom mud or behind rocks and logs.
Generalist omnivore eating insects, mollusks, fish carrion and aquatic plants.

resources.title: Alabama map turtle
resources.description: Identify the alabama map turtle (Graptemys pulchra), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Alabama map turtle (Graptemys pulchra): Females 273-292 mm carapace and up to about 1.9 kg; males 113-127 mm. Relatively low-domed shell with a black median keel and pale yellow outline; concentric yellow semicircles on each marginal scute. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mobile Bay drainage: eastern Mississippi, throughout Alabama and northwestern Georgia. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Mobile Bay drainage: eastern Mississippi, throughout Alabama and northwestern Georgia. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Females 273-292 mm carapace and up to about 1.9 kg; males 113-127 mm.
Relatively low-domed shell with a black median keel and pale yellow outline; concentric yellow semicircles on each marginal scute.
Head with a large light interorbital blotch connected to postorbital blotches; no nasal trident.
Females have larger heads, broader jaws and elongated front claws; males longer, thicker tails.
Compared with the pascagoula map turtle: Higher-domed shell with spines on the keel; nasal trident usually present.

habitat.text: Medium-sized rivers to large creeks with sand bars, sandy banks, logs, deep pools and abundant mollusks; nests in sand bars and banks.

behavior.text: Diurnal and active roughly March-November; bask on logs with limbs and neck stretched out.
Turtles feed or bask on logs May-October; daily torpor begins below about 19 C before hibernation.
Mainly molluscivorous; males and juveniles eat smaller bivalves and aquatic insects.

resources.title: Kentucky spring salamander
resources.description: Identify the kentucky spring salamander (Gyrinophilus porphyriticus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Kentucky spring salamander (Gyrinophilus porphyriticus): Large: 12-19 cm, females about 1 cm longer than males. Salmon-orange to yellowish skin with a brownish tint and dark blotchy spots and a reddish tint. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Quebec and southern Maine south through the Appalachians to northern Georgia, Alabama and northeastern Mississippi.

taxonomicNotes.text: 'Kentucky spring salamander' is a regional name; NatureServe and ADW treat the species as Spring Salamander (G. porphyriticus) and some authors lump related Gyrinophilus species into it.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Quebec and southern Maine south through the Appalachians to northern Georgia, Alabama and northeastern Mississippi.

identification.text: Large: 12-19 cm, females about 1 cm longer than males.
Salmon-orange to yellowish skin with a brownish tint and dark blotchy spots and a reddish tint.
Flat head with eyes on the sides and a broad snout.
Tail knife-edged, aiding swimming.
Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Much smaller and browner with a keeled tail and no salmon-orange colour.

habitat.text: Small clear upland streams, springs, caves and shaded seepages; often under rocks, logs, leaves or moss in or near water.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal; swims eel-like with legs held to the body and escapes by burrowing into mud or swimming.
Uses smell to locate prey in the dark; produces toxic skin secretions as defense.
Females stay with 20-60 (up to 100+) eggs about 3 months; larvae are aquatic for 2-4 years.

resources.title: Four-toed salamander
resources.description: Identify the four-toed salamander (Hemidactylium scutatum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Four-toed salamander (Hemidactylium scutatum): Small: 5-10.2 cm; rusty or gray-brown with grayish sides and black and bluish speckles. Four toes on each hind foot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Discontinuously from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, southern Quebec and southern Ontario through Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota south to southeastern Oklahoma, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, the Florida panhandle and Georgia; fairly continuous in the northeast, spotty in the southwest.

rangeSummary.value: Discontinuously from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, southern Quebec and southern Ontario through Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota south to southeastern Oklahoma, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, the Florida panhandle and Georgia; fairly continuous in the northeast, spotty in the southwest.

identification.text: Small: 5-10.2 cm; rusty or gray-brown with grayish sides and black and bluish speckles.
Four toes on each hind foot.
Constricted ring at the base of the tail.
13-14 costal grooves; tail about 57% of length.
Females have rounded snouts, breeding males squared snouts.
Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: Five toes on each hind foot and no tail constriction.

habitat.text: Swamps, boggy streams and wet wooded or open areas near quiet mossy or sedgy pools; Sphagnum moss is commonly abundant.

behavior.text: Relatively sedentary, moving short distances between breeding sites and nonbreeding habitat; mostly inactive in the coldest months.
If disturbed curls up with head under the tail, or may detach its tail.
Nests communally in moss or protected sites above or beside a pool, females guarding the eggs about 2 months.

resources.title: Eastern hognose snake
resources.description: Identify the eastern hognose snake (Heterodon platirhinos), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern hognose snake (Heterodon platirhinos): Thick body, wide head and a slightly upturned, pointed snout; adults 45-105 cm. Juveniles pinkish with alternating dark brown to black blotches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern New England and southern Ontario to Minnesota and South Dakota, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida.

taxonomicNotes.text: Species epithet formerly spelled 'platyrhinos'; NatureServe lists it as Eastern Hog-nosed Snake.

rangeSummary.value: Southern New England and southern Ontario to Minnesota and South Dakota, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida.

identification.text: Thick body, wide head and a slightly upturned, pointed snout; adults 45-105 cm.
Juveniles pinkish with alternating dark brown to black blotches.
Adults vary from tan, gray, red, yellowish or greenish to solid dark gray or black; lighter ones show dark blotches.
Belly white to light gray; 23-25 dorsal scale rows and a divided anal plate.

habitat.text: Open wooded hills, forest edges, fields, meadows, prairies, sand plains and river valleys with loose soil and amphibian prey.

behavior.text: Diurnal, most active around mid-day; active early April to October/November depending on temperature.
Eats mainly amphibians, especially toads.
Overwinters in burrows or under talus rocks; lays 4-61 eggs May-August.

resources.title: Bird-voiced treefrog
resources.description: Identify the bird-voiced treefrog (Hyla avivoca), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Bird-voiced treefrog (Hyla avivoca): Small: males 2.8-3.9 cm, females 3.2-5.2 cm snout-vent. Brown to gray mixed with green and black dorsal blotches; smooth skin. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Illinois and western Kentucky to the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, eastern Georgia and adjacent South Carolina, with disjunct populations in Louisiana, Arkansas and southeastern Oklahoma. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes avivoca.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Illinois and western Kentucky to the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, eastern Georgia and adjacent South Carolina, with disjunct populations in Louisiana, Arkansas and southeastern Oklahoma. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small: males 2.8-3.9 cm, females 3.2-5.2 cm snout-vent.
Brown to gray mixed with green and black dorsal blotches; smooth skin.
Small white spot below each eye.
Limbs with dark stripes; belly pale with dark spots in front.
Birdlike whistled call.
Compared with the cope's gray treefrog: Warty skin and orange-yellow hidden hindleg surfaces; trill rather than birdlike whistle.

habitat.text: Permanent wooded swamps (tupelo, cypress, birch, buttonbush, vine tangles) bordering rivers and streams; intolerant of impoundments that flood habitat.

behavior.text: Seldom observed outside the breeding period; males call from trees, shrubs and vines in or beside water.
Mostly solitary except for breeding; can climb high in trees.
Lays several hundred eggs in small clusters in spring or summer; larvae metamorphose in about a month.

resources.title: Cope's gray treefrog
resources.description: Identify the cope's gray treefrog (Hyla chrysoscelis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Cope's gray treefrog (Hyla chrysoscelis): 3.2-5.1 cm, up to 6 cm; warty skin, gray to green with black back blotches and a lichen-like pattern. Light spot under each eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central and southeastern US and areas west of the Great Lakes, from Manitoba, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, southern Ohio, West Virginia and Maryland south to eastern Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida; exact boundary with gray treefrog is not precisely known.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes chrysoscelis.

rangeSummary.value: South-central and southeastern US and areas west of the Great Lakes, from Manitoba, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, southern Ohio, West Virginia and Maryland south to eastern Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida; exact boundary with gray treefrog is not precisely known.

identification.text: 3.2-5.1 cm, up to 6 cm; warty skin, gray to green with black back blotches and a lichen-like pattern.
Light spot under each eye.
Orange-yellow concealed groin and hindleg surfaces with black mottling.
Large toe pads.
Physically indistinguishable from gray treefrog; identify by call: Cope's trill is faster and higher pitched.
Compared with the gray treefrog: Identical in appearance; slower, more musical trill.

habitat.text: Wooded areas and edges, often recently disturbed ground with shrubs and vines, within a few hundred metres of breeding water; rests in tree holes or under bark.

behavior.text: Mostly active at dusk and at night in summer; inactive in cold months.
Males call from water surface or nearby vegetation; calls are loud trills, often mistaken for a woodpecker.
Migrates up to several hundred metres between nonbreeding habitat and breeding pools; breeds spring to early summer.

resources.title: Green treefrog
resources.description: Identify the green treefrog (Hyla cinerea), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green treefrog (Hyla cinerea): Bright yellow-green back (sometimes yellowish, gray or reddish-brown), often with small golden spots. White or yellowish stripe along the jaw, side of the body and leg (may be reduced). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain from Delaware to southern Florida and west to south-central Texas; north to southeastern Oklahoma, southeastern Missouri, southern Illinois and Indiana, western Kentucky and Tennessee and northern Alabama. Introduced in south-central Missouri, northwestern Puerto Rico and Brownsville, Texas. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes cinereus.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain from Delaware to southern Florida and west to south-central Texas; north to southeastern Oklahoma, southeastern Missouri, southern Illinois and Indiana, western Kentucky and Tennessee and northern Alabama. Introduced in south-central Missouri, northwestern Puerto Rico and Brownsville, Texas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Bright yellow-green back (sometimes yellowish, gray or reddish-brown), often with small golden spots.
White or yellowish stripe along the jaw, side of the body and leg (may be reduced).
Smooth skin, long legs, large rounded toe tips; 34-64 mm, females larger.
Breeding male has gray or pinkish throat; call is a loud 'queenk' about 80 times a minute.
Compared with the squirrel treefrog: Smaller (about 3 cm), greenish to brown, often blotched, with a nasal 'rain' call.

habitat.text: Swamps, marshes and pond, lake and slow-stream margins with abundant floating and emergent vegetation.

behavior.text: Most active on warm, rainy nights; often inactive in colder months in the north.
Climbs vegetation to catch insects, sometimes near lights at night.
Hundreds may aggregate at breeding pools in April-August; males also give alarm and rain calls.

resources.title: Pine woods treefrog
resources.description: Identify the pine woods treefrog (Hyla femoralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pine woods treefrog (Hyla femoralis): About 4-4.5 cm; reddish brown to gray-green with dark blotches and sometimes a dark band through the eye and eardrum. Orange to silver spots or blotches on the rear of the thighs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains from southern Virginia to eastern Louisiana and south to southern Florida. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes femoralis.

rangeSummary.value: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains from southern Virginia to eastern Louisiana and south to southern Florida. Not in Canada.

identification.text: About 4-4.5 cm; reddish brown to gray-green with dark blotches and sometimes a dark band through the eye and eardrum.
Orange to silver spots or blotches on the rear of the thighs.
Expanded rounded toe pads.
Breeding male has a dark throat.
Call is a raspy staccato, like Morse code or a cicada.
Compared with the squirrel treefrog: Light stripe on the upper jaw and no orange spots on the thighs.

habitat.text: Longleaf pine-wiregrass flatwoods and savannas and pine-turkey oak sandhills near bogs or ponds; occasionally hardwood forests and swamps.

behavior.text: Mostly arboreal, perching from low shrubs to treetops; most active at night in spring through fall.
Calls from vegetation up to about 3 m above water, often as rain approaches.
Hides in or under rotting logs, stumps or snags in dry or cold weather; larvae metamorphose in 7-10 weeks.

resources.title: Barking treefrog
resources.description: Identify the barking treefrog (Hyla gratiosa), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Barking treefrog (Hyla gratiosa): Largest treefrog in the southeastern US: 5.1-7 cm, bulky. Very rough, granular skin. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain and some uplands from North Carolina to southern Florida and west to Louisiana, including northern Mississippi; disjunct populations in Delaware and Maryland, southwestern Kentucky and Tennessee and southeastern Virginia; introduced and probably extirpated in southern New Jersey. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes gratiosus.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain and some uplands from North Carolina to southern Florida and west to Louisiana, including northern Mississippi; disjunct populations in Delaware and Maryland, southwestern Kentucky and Tennessee and southeastern Virginia; introduced and probably extirpated in southern New Jersey. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Largest treefrog in the southeastern US: 5.1-7 cm, bulky.
Very rough, granular skin.
Colour varies from bright lime green to brown but almost always with darker back spots.
Lighter stripe from the upper jaw along the body; males have a light green or yellow throat.
Rounded pads on the digits; loud 'bark' call.
Compared with the green treefrog: Smooth skin and a bright white or yellowish side stripe; smaller.

habitat.text: Sandy pine savannas and low wet woods and swamps; breeds in shallow ponds, swamps and bayheads, preferring semi-permanent ponds without fish.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; rests high in trees by day and is mostly arboreal.
Burrows under roots, vegetation or soil in cold or dry seasons.
Breeds after heavy rains in spring or summer; clutches up to about 2,000 eggs; groups generally under 20-25 males.

resources.title: Squirrel treefrog
resources.description: Identify the squirrel treefrog (Hyla squirella), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Squirrel treefrog (Hyla squirella): Small: average about 30 mm snout-vent. Solid green to brown, sometimes with darker splotches; can change colour with temperature and time of day. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain and Mississippi Valley from southern Texas and southern Arkansas to southeastern Virginia and Florida; introduced on Grand Bahama. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes squirellus.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain and Mississippi Valley from southern Texas and southern Arkansas to southeastern Virginia and Florida; introduced on Grand Bahama. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small: average about 30 mm snout-vent.
Solid green to brown, sometimes with darker splotches; can change colour with temperature and time of day.
Light stripe (usually yellow, sometimes white or orange) along the upper jaw; stripe larger in males.
Breeding males have a prominent dark green or brown vocal sac.
Compared with the green treefrog: Larger with a white or yellowish side stripe running onto the leg.
Compared with the pine woods treefrog: Orange or silver spots on rear thighs; raspy Morse-like call.

habitat.text: Open woods, cities and towns and thick low vegetation near water; breeds in flooded ditches, flatwoods ponds, swamps and stock ponds.

behavior.text: Nocturnal, most active just after dusk and before dawn and in rain; in daylight enters torpor.
Gives a 'rain call' from trees and bushes when rain is impending.
Hides under loose bark, palm leaves and tree holes; lays up to about 1,000 eggs in spring or summer.

resources.title: Gray treefrog
resources.description: Identify the gray treefrog (Hyla versicolor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gray treefrog (Hyla versicolor): 3-5 cm (record 6 cm); warty skin, usually gray with black back blotches, or green, brown or pearl-gray; colour changes with background, season and humidity. Light spot beneath each eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Canada from southern Manitoba to New Brunswick, south through the northeastern and south-central US to North Carolina, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois, Tennessee, eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana, west to North Dakota, Minnesota, Iowa, eastern Kansas and eastern Oklahoma.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places North American treefrogs in Dryophytes (Duellman et al. 2016); ADW and the batch list use Hyla. NatureServe name: Dryophytes versicolor.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Canada from southern Manitoba to New Brunswick, south through the northeastern and south-central US to North Carolina, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois, Tennessee, eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana, west to North Dakota, Minnesota, Iowa, eastern Kansas and eastern Oklahoma.

identification.text: 3-5 cm (record 6 cm); warty skin, usually gray with black back blotches, or green, brown or pearl-gray; colour changes with background, season and humidity.
Light spot beneath each eye.
Orange to golden-yellow, black-speckled concealed hindleg surfaces; white belly.
Large toe pads.
Identical to Cope's gray treefrog; call is a slower, more musical trill.
Compared with the cope's gray treefrog: Indistinguishable by sight; faster, higher-pitched trill.

habitat.text: Wooded and forested habitats on the ground, shrubs or trees; rests in tree holes, under bark or in rotten logs; breeds in still shallow woodland ponds, marshes, puddles and swamps.

behavior.text: Most active at dusk and at night, especially in wet weather; inactive from fall through early spring.
Males are territorial when calling; adults may eat smaller gray treefrogs.
Migrates up to several hundred metres to breeding pools; breeds spring or summer (usually May in the north); larvae metamorphose within 2 months.

resources.title: Gulf Coast toad
resources.description: Identify the gulf coast toad (Incilius nebulifer), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gulf Coast toad (Incilius nebulifer). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Arkansas, southern Mississippi, Louisiana and central Texas in the United States, south to Veracruz, Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes I. nebulifer was formerly included in Bufo valliceps and separated from I. valliceps by mtDNA work (Mulcahy and Mendelson 2000); NatureServe uses Incilius rather than Bufo.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Arkansas, southern Mississippi, Louisiana and central Texas in the United States, south to Veracruz, Mexico.

habitat.text: Coastal prairies, barrier beaches, towns and a variety of other habitats; eggs and larvae develop in pools including roadside and irrigation ditches.

behavior.text: Migrates between breeding and nonbreeding habitats.
Lays eggs in spring or summer in pools, including roadside and irrigation ditches; in Texas, calling lasted 7-29 nights (mean 15.4) with choruses of 2-65 males.
Adults eat small terrestrial arthropods.

resources.title: Arizona mud turtle
resources.description: Identify the arizona mud turtle (Kinosternon arizonense), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Arizona mud turtle (Kinosternon arizonense): Dome-shaped carapace that lacks keels, brown, olive or yellow-brown; plastron and marginal rim yellow. Top of head grey; underside and sides of head cream to light yellow. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Arizona in the United States (NatureServe lists AZ only) and Sonora, Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the extant species as Kinosternon stejnegeri (McCord 2016; TTWG 2025), restricting the name K. arizonense to fossil material; it was formerly treated as a subspecies of K. flavescens.

rangeSummary.value: Arizona in the United States (NatureServe lists AZ only) and Sonora, Mexico.

identification.text: Dome-shaped carapace that lacks keels, brown, olive or yellow-brown; plastron and marginal rim yellow.
Top of head grey; underside and sides of head cream to light yellow.
No patterns on the limbs.

habitat.text: Prefers temporary ponds and puddles; found in Sonoran desert scrub and semidesert grassland.

behavior.text: Active by day, and also at night in the July-August monsoon; spends most of that period in water.
Hibernates in a burrow in winter; in drought can stay dormant underground for up to two years.
Eats frogs, tadpoles, toads, fish, aquatic invertebrates and carrion.

resources.title: Yellow mud turtle
resources.description: Identify the yellow mud turtle (Kinosternon flavescens), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Yellow mud turtle (Kinosternon flavescens): Small turtle, adults about 10-16 cm carapace length; smooth olive to brown carapace with no ornamentation. Yellow chin (throat too in most areas), yellowish cheeks; four pairs of barbels on the throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central United States from Nebraska to southeastern Arizona, with an isolated population in Illinois-Iowa-Missouri; also northern Mexico.

rangeSummary.value: South-central United States from Nebraska to southeastern Arizona, with an isolated population in Illinois-Iowa-Missouri; also northern Mexico.

identification.text: Small turtle, adults about 10-16 cm carapace length; smooth olive to brown carapace with no ornamentation.
Yellow chin (throat too in most areas), yellowish cheeks; four pairs of barbels on the throat.
Plastron black except where worn, with two well-developed transverse hinges; strongly webbed feet.
Male: slightly concave plastron, long thick spine-tipped tail; female: short stubby tail, flat plastron.
Emits a disagreeable musk odour when disturbed.

habitat.text: Quiet or slow water with soft mud or sand bottom in grassland and open woodland, often temporary water; in arid regions in cattle tanks and ditches.
Seeks shelter underground on land or burrows in mud underwater.

behavior.text: Diurnal in spring, crepuscular and nocturnal in summer; hibernates in winter and estivates in the hottest part of summer.
Seasonally aquatic then terrestrial: in the Illinois-Iowa-Missouri population turtles leave drying ponds in July-August and may be active under 100 days a year.
Often travels overland; adults wander about 190-220 m from water.
Omnivore: insects, mollusks, crustaceans, amphibian larvae, carrion and some vegetation.

resources.title: Sonora mud turtle
resources.description: Identify the sonora mud turtle (Kinosternon sonoriense), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Sonora mud turtle (Kinosternon sonoriense): Small, mostly aquatic turtle; olive-green to olive-brown shell mottled with dark spots; adult carapace 75-150 mm. Yellow plastron, greyish-black legs, usually a yellow line along the edge of the front legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
