keyFacts.value: Southern and central Arizona and southwestern New Mexico (Catron, Grant, Hidalgo counties), south into Sonora and Chihuahua, Mexico; considered extirpated from California.

rangeSummary.value: Southern and central Arizona and southwestern New Mexico (Catron, Grant, Hidalgo counties), south into Sonora and Chihuahua, Mexico; considered extirpated from California.

identification.text: Small, mostly aquatic turtle; olive-green to olive-brown shell mottled with dark spots; adult carapace 75-150 mm.
Yellow plastron, greyish-black legs, usually a yellow line along the edge of the front legs.
Green-grey head with dark side stripes and dark spots on chin and crown.
Plastron hinged front and rear, long chin barbels, webbed feet (as described for the Sonoyta subspecies).

habitat.text: Streams, springs, ponds and pools in intermittent streams, from desert to oak, pinyon-juniper and pine woodland; in southeastern Arizona about 90% of captures were in stock tanks.

behavior.text: Solitary outside breeding, with overlapping home ranges and very high local densities (over 3,000 per hectare recorded in New Mexico).
Most active in summer monsoon, least active in winter; may estivate on land 11-34 days and move overland up to 8 km.
Eats snails, fish, frogs, crayfish, aquatic insects and occasionally lizards and snakes.

conservationStatus.text: Sonoyta mud turtle (Kinosternon sonoriense longifemorale): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 2017-10-20.

resources.title: Eastern mud turtle
resources.description: Identify the eastern mud turtle (Kinosternon subrubrum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern mud turtle (Kinosternon subrubrum): Two plastral hinges under an oval carapace that is solid brown, olive with irregular yellow streaks, or solid black. Head has irregular, often jagged markings or stripes between eye and nostril; limbs smudged grey, brown or black. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States from Long Island, New York south to the Florida Panhandle, west along the Gulf Coast to eastern Texas and north to southern Illinois and Indiana; disjunct population in northwestern Indiana.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's primary common name is Common Mud Turtle and it keeps K. subrubrum (with subspecies) as one species; Reid et al. (2025) propose restoring the Mississippi mud turtle (K. hippocrepis) to species rank.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States from Long Island, New York south to the Florida Panhandle, west along the Gulf Coast to eastern Texas and north to southern Illinois and Indiana; disjunct population in northwestern Indiana.

identification.text: Two plastral hinges under an oval carapace that is solid brown, olive with irregular yellow streaks, or solid black.
Head has irregular, often jagged markings or stripes between eye and nostril; limbs smudged grey, brown or black.
Tail tipped with a spine; notch at the rear of the plastron.
Males: longer tail, larger head, patch of raised scales on the hind legs.
Striped mud turtle (K. baurii) has a pair of head stripes and carapace stripes; K. subrubrum has no carapace stripes.
Compared with the striped mud turtle: Striped mud turtle (Kinosternon baurii) has a pair of head stripes and usually carapace stripes; eastern mud turtle lacks carapace stripes.

habitat.text: Shallow, slow or nonflowing fresh or brackish water with soft bottom and abundant vegetation, and wet meadows; frequently travels overland.
Nests in soft soil in open areas not far from water.

behavior.text: Solitary and largely crepuscular in summer; active year-round in the south, hibernates about November-March in the north.
Seldom basks; bottom feeder on insects, mollusks, crustaceans, amphibian larvae, carrion and aquatic plants.
In South Carolina spent late summer through winter about 170 days in upland refugia up to 135 m from wetlands.

resources.title: Prairie kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the prairie kingsnake (Lampropeltis calligaster), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Prairie kingsnake (Lampropeltis calligaster): Tan, grey-brown or yellow-brown with reddish-brown dorsal blotches alternating with smaller lateral blotches; pale or yellowish belly. Older snakes lose the pattern with age; 19-27 rows of smooth scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Populations west of the Mississippi River across the plains states and east across the Mississippi embayment to Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, western Tennessee and northern Mississippi (NatureServe); the wider group reaches Maryland and Florida.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (McKelvy and Burbrink 2017) treats L. rhombomaculata (mole kingsnake) and L. occipitolineata as distinct species; Animal Diversity Web still lists them as subspecies of L. calligaster.

rangeSummary.value: Populations west of the Mississippi River across the plains states and east across the Mississippi embayment to Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, western Tennessee and northern Mississippi (NatureServe); the wider group reaches Maryland and Florida.

identification.text: Tan, grey-brown or yellow-brown with reddish-brown dorsal blotches alternating with smaller lateral blotches; pale or yellowish belly.
Older snakes lose the pattern with age; 19-27 rows of smooth scales.
Often mistaken for a copperhead: copperheads have brown hourglass crossbands, kingsnakes have blotches.
Compared with the copperhead: Copperheads have brown hourglass crossbands; prairie and mole kingsnakes have dorsal blotches.

habitat.text: Open habitats: fields, farmland, woodlots, rocky hillsides, favouring prairie and pasture on light soils.

behavior.text: Nocturnal and mostly solitary; active about April to mid-October and hibernates November-March in burrows or rock ledges.
Spends about 75% of radio-tracked time underground; can climb and swim.
Eats mice and voles, amphibians, snakes, lizards and birds and their eggs.

resources.title: Black kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the black kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Black kingsnake (Lampropeltis getula): Eastern kingsnake adults 61-153 cm: large, solid, glossy black with yellow (sometimes white) crossbars. Head solid black with yellow or white spots on head scales. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern West Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and southern New Jersey south through the southeastern United States to southern Alabama.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's L. getula is the eastern kingsnake (Krysko et al. 2017 split the former common kingsnake into several species); neither source read uses the name 'black kingsnake'. Animal Diversity Web treats L. getula broadly as the 'common kingsnake' with seven subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern West Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and southern New Jersey south through the southeastern United States to southern Alabama.

identification.text: Eastern kingsnake adults 61-153 cm: large, solid, glossy black with yellow (sometimes white) crossbars.
Head solid black with yellow or white spots on head scales.
Speckled kingsnake (L. g. holbrooki) is black with yellow specks on the scales, belly pale yellow to white.
Hatchlings 20-28 cm.

habitat.text: Wide range of habitats, often in or near woods and near water; cover includes wood, trash piles, barns and stone walls.

behavior.text: Diurnal; active late March-early April to October-early November and hibernates in crevices, burrows, hollow logs and stumps; in hot weather may be active at night.
Spends about 79% of time under cover; climbs and swims well.
Eats mainly other snakes, including venomous species, plus lizards, small turtles, reptile eggs, frogs, birds and small mammals.

resources.title: Madrean mountain kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the madrean mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis knoblochi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Madrean mountain kingsnake (Lampropeltis knoblochi): Coral-snake mimic with white crossbands where a coral snake has yellow. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Sierra Madre Occidental in eastern Sonora and western Chihuahua, north to the Madrean Sky Islands of southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (Burbrink et al. 2011) splits L. pyromelana into northern L. pyromelana and southern L. knoblochi; its habitat text is based mainly on L. pyromelana.

rangeSummary.value: Sierra Madre Occidental in eastern Sonora and western Chihuahua, north to the Madrean Sky Islands of southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico.

identification.text: Coral-snake mimic with white crossbands where a coral snake has yellow.

habitat.text: Rocky montane habitat often near streams or springs, and mesic canyons at lower elevation; pinyon-juniper, oak-juniper, pine-oak or pine-Douglas-fir woodland, or chaparral.
By day found among rocks, logs or dense vegetation.

behavior.text: Generally diurnal but may be most active late afternoon, evening and dusk.
Diet includes lizards and presumably snakes and small mammals.

resources.title: Scarlet kingsnake
resources.description: Identify the scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Scarlet kingsnake (Lampropeltis elapsoides): Bright red, black and yellow bands that extend across the belly. Snout nearly always red; red and black bands touch, red and yellow bands do not. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Virginia and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas south through Georgia to southern Florida and west to eastern Louisiana, Tennessee and Kentucky.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes L. elapsoides was long regarded as a subspecies of L. triangulum and is now treated as a distinct species.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Virginia and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas south through Georgia to southern Florida and west to eastern Louisiana, Tennessee and Kentucky.

identification.text: Bright red, black and yellow bands that extend across the belly.
Snout nearly always red; red and black bands touch, red and yellow bands do not.
A coral snake has a black snout and red bands touching yellow.
Compared with the eastern coral snake: Venomous coral snake has a black snout and red bands touching yellow; scarlet kingsnake has a red snout and red touching black.
Compared with the northern scarlet snake: Scarlet snake (Cemophora coccinea) has a plain white belly; scarlet kingsnake bands cross the belly.

habitat.text: Pine flatwoods and wet prairie hammocks; less often bottomland, mixed hardwood, upland pine, sandhills and maritime hammock.

behavior.text: Found in rotting logs and under bark in Coastal Plain pine forests; stumps and logs are common cover.
Constrictor that eats small snakes, lizards and mice.

resources.title: Milksnake
resources.description: Identify the milksnake (Lampropeltis triangulum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Milksnake (Lampropeltis triangulum): Gray or tan body with a light Y- or V-shaped patch on the neck. Black-bordered brown or rust-red blotches down back and sides. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Minnesota, Michigan, southern Ontario, southern Quebec and southern Maine south to North Carolina and northern Alabama and Georgia; also Mississippi and northeastern Louisiana.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (following SSAR 2025) restricts L. triangulum to the eastern populations and treats L. gentilis as separate; Chambers et al. (2023) argue for lumping, and Animal Diversity Web describes L. triangulum with 25 subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Minnesota, Michigan, southern Ontario, southern Quebec and southern Maine south to North Carolina and northern Alabama and Georgia; also Mississippi and northeastern Louisiana.

identification.text: Gray or tan body with a light Y- or V-shaped patch on the neck.
Black-bordered brown or rust-red blotches down back and sides.
Typically 60-130 cm in the United States; 19-23 rows of smooth scales and a single anal plate.
No colour difference between the sexes.

habitat.text: Forest edges, open woodland, prairies, rocky hillsides, small streams or marshes and farm or suburban areas; hibernates underground or in rock crevices.

behavior.text: Solitary and secretive; rarely seen in the open by day but often crosses roads at night; mostly nocturnal in hot weather.
Hides under rotting logs and damp trash; hunts rodents around barns and other buildings.
Groups only at hibernation, and may bask in groups just before and after; inactive about November-March in the north.
Eats voles, mice, rats, birds, eggs, lizards and other snakes.

resources.title: Three-lined boa
resources.description: Identify the three-lined boa (Lichanura trivirgata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Three-lined boa (Lichanura trivirgata): Relatively large, non-venomous snake, roughly 17-43 inches (San Diego museum figure for L. trivirgata, pre-split); rust or orange. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Extreme southern San Diego County (Tijuana and Otay watersheds), the Baja California peninsula and islands, Sonora, and isolated mountain ranges of western Arizona south of the Gila River (Maricopa, Pima, Pinal counties); sea level to 2,070 m.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe treats L. trivirgata as the southern species, split from L. orcutti (Wood et al. 2008); the San Diego atlas and Arizona's AWCS page list a single rosy boa / three-lined boa under L. trivirgata.

rangeSummary.value: Extreme southern San Diego County (Tijuana and Otay watersheds), the Baja California peninsula and islands, Sonora, and isolated mountain ranges of western Arizona south of the Gila River (Maricopa, Pima, Pinal counties); sea level to 2,070 m.

identification.text: Relatively large, non-venomous snake, roughly 17-43 inches (San Diego museum figure for L. trivirgata, pre-split); rust or orange.

habitat.text: Desert, arid scrub, brushland, sandy plains, rocky slopes and chaparral foothills, especially near springs, streams and canyon floors, but not dependent on permanent water; mainly terrestrial, sometimes climbs shrubs.

behavior.text: Inactive in cold temperatures and extreme heat; usually most active at night.
Movements tend to be limited; home ranges average under 2 ha.
Eats mainly small mammals and birds.

resources.title: Northern crawfish frog
resources.description: Identify the northern crawfish frog (Lithobates areolatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern crawfish frog (Lithobates areolatus): Stubby frog with dorsolateral ridges and dark rounded dorsal spots with light borders; throat and belly mostly unspotted. Usually 5.7-7.5 cm snout-vent (up to 9.2 cm per ADW); yellow on the groin and thigh; males may show yellow on the dorsolateral ridges. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Mississippi, northern Louisiana and eastern Texas north through Oklahoma, Arkansas, western Tennessee and Kentucky to eastern Kansas, southern Illinois and Indiana (formerly southern Iowa).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the species as Crawfish Frog (L. areolatus) without a northern/southern split; Animal Diversity Web recognises a northern subspecies (L. a. circulosa). NatureServe also notes competing generic arrangements for American ranids.

rangeSummary.value: Northern Mississippi, northern Louisiana and eastern Texas north through Oklahoma, Arkansas, western Tennessee and Kentucky to eastern Kansas, southern Illinois and Indiana (formerly southern Iowa).

identification.text: Stubby frog with dorsolateral ridges and dark rounded dorsal spots with light borders; throat and belly mostly unspotted.
Usually 5.7-7.5 cm snout-vent (up to 9.2 cm per ADW); yellow on the groin and thigh; males may show yellow on the dorsolateral ridges.
Call: low-pitched snore-like 'wurr-r-r-up' audible about 800 m away.
Compared with the gopher frog: Gopher frog (Rana capito) has a pigmented belly and lacks the light borders around the dark dorsal spots.

habitat.text: Moist meadows, pastures, flood plains and tall-grass prairie where crayfish burrows exist; breeds in flooded fields, ditches, farm ponds, usually fishless temporary water.

behavior.text: Lives in crayfish or rodent burrows; sits at the burrow mouth or on its platform to feed and retreats headfirst.
Migrates up to several hundred metres, occasionally a mile or more, between burrow and breeding pools; inactive in winter in the north.
Males call at night in choruses in warm weather; eats moths, ants, spiders, grasshoppers, beetles and crickets.

resources.title: Pig frog
resources.description: Identify the pig frog (Lithobates grylio), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pig frog (Lithobates grylio): Adults about 8.2-16.5 cm snout-vent; green, olive or brown with dark spots toward the hind end; white-grey belly; smooth skin. Resembles American bullfrog but the snout is much more pointed; hind feet almost fully webbed. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern South Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Texas; introduced in the Bahamas and northern Puerto Rico.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Dubois et al. (2021) place it in genus Aquarana; NatureServe keeps Lithobates and calls the generic arrangement of American ranids controversial.

rangeSummary.value: Southern South Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Texas; introduced in the Bahamas and northern Puerto Rico.

identification.text: Adults about 8.2-16.5 cm snout-vent; green, olive or brown with dark spots toward the hind end; white-grey belly; smooth skin.
Resembles American bullfrog but the snout is much more pointed; hind feet almost fully webbed.
Call: 1-13 short, loud pig-like grunts; choruses sound like a roar.
Compared with the american bullfrog: Pig frog has a much more pointed snout and is smaller than the bullfrog.

habitat.text: Permanent lakes, ponds, swamps, marshes and streams, especially with abundant emergent or floating vegetation; old rice fields.

behavior.text: Fully aquatic and confined to wetlands; males call floating in water and are territorial.
Feeds nocturnally, mostly on arthropods, especially crayfish (20-75% of diet).
Chorusing is typically nocturnal per NatureServe, while Animal Diversity Web says it typically calls by day.
Burrows into mud when wetlands dry or to hibernate (Nov-March) in colder regions.

resources.title: River frog
resources.description: Identify the river frog (Lithobates heckscheri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: River frog (Lithobates heckscheri): Large: 3.25-4.63 in snout-vent (record 6.13 in); greenish-black back. Light spots on the lips, larger on the lower jaw. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain from southern North Carolina (at least formerly) to northern Florida and west to southeastern Mississippi; most of the range is in northern Florida, southern Georgia and southern South Carolina.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes competing generic arrangements for American ranids (Lithobates used here).

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain from southern North Carolina (at least formerly) to northern Florida and west to southeastern Mississippi; most of the range is in northern Florida, southern Georgia and southern South Carolina.

identification.text: Large: 3.25-4.63 in snout-vent (record 6.13 in); greenish-black back.
Light spots on the lips, larger on the lower jaw.
Skin more rugose than most ranid frogs; no dorsolateral ridges.
Belly grey to almost black with light spots or short wavy lines; males often have yellowish throat.
Webbing on hind feet reaches the last phalanx of the longest toe.

habitat.text: Swamps along streams and edges of shallow ponds and impoundments, including beaver ponds; open, thinly vegetated shorelines.

behavior.text: Highly aquatic and approachable; sits in shallow open water and on logs.
Eats insects and other invertebrates, occasionally small vertebrates including other ranid frogs.

resources.title: Pickerel frog
resources.description: Identify the pickerel frog (Lithobates palustris), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pickerel frog (Lithobates palustris): Tan back with two parallel rows of roughly rectangular dark spots (about seven pairs) plus a snout spot. Groin and base of hind legs yellow or orange (faint or absent in juveniles). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Gaspe Peninsula of Quebec and New Brunswick/Nova Scotia west to Wisconsin and Missouri, south to South Carolina, northern Georgia, southern Mississippi and southeastern Texas; largely absent from Florida and southern Georgia.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes competing generic arrangements for American ranids (Lithobates used here).

rangeSummary.value: Gaspe Peninsula of Quebec and New Brunswick/Nova Scotia west to Wisconsin and Missouri, south to South Carolina, northern Georgia, southern Mississippi and southeastern Texas; largely absent from Florida and southern Georgia.

identification.text: Tan back with two parallel rows of roughly rectangular dark spots (about seven pairs) plus a snout spot.
Groin and base of hind legs yellow or orange (faint or absent in juveniles).
Light stripe along upper jaw; glandular ridge down each side; hind toes extensively webbed.
Maximum about 8.7 cm snout-vent; call a low snore lasting 1-2 seconds.
Compared with the northern leopard frog: Pickerel frog has squarish, parallel dorsal spots and a yellow-orange groin; Animal Diversity Web calls the two visually similar.

habitat.text: Freshwater and wetland habitats in wooded regions, from cool clear streams and ponds in the north to warm, turbid swamps in the south; in the south and midwest often tied to limestone caves for overwintering.

behavior.text: Gathers at water after hibernation; in summer commonly ranges into fields and woods away from water.
Most active at night in the breeding season; hibernates in pond bottoms, caves or mines, later than the northern leopard frog.
Skin secretions are distasteful; some predators reject it.
Eats terrestrial insects and arachnids.

resources.title: Wood frog
resources.description: Identify the wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus): Dark mask running from each eye over the tympanum to the forelimb, with a white line along the upper lip. Dorsolateral folds; webbed hind toes; smooth skin; a light mid-dorsal stripe may or may not be present; up to about 83 mm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Alaska across boreal Canada to Labrador and south to New Jersey, northern Georgia and northern Idaho, with spotty distribution south to northern Colorado and disjunct populations in Arkansas-Missouri; extends farther north than any other North American amphibian.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Dubois et al. (2021) place it in its own genus Boreorana; NatureServe keeps Lithobates sylvaticus.

rangeSummary.value: Northern Alaska across boreal Canada to Labrador and south to New Jersey, northern Georgia and northern Idaho, with spotty distribution south to northern Colorado and disjunct populations in Arkansas-Missouri; extends farther north than any other North American amphibian.

identification.text: Dark mask running from each eye over the tympanum to the forelimb, with a white line along the upper lip.
Dorsolateral folds; webbed hind toes; smooth skin; a light mid-dorsal stripe may or may not be present; up to about 83 mm.
Colour ranges brown, tan, rust to green or grey; females larger; males have swollen thumb bases.
Call: rapid series of 1-8 (usually 3-5) rough clacking notes, like softly quacking ducks.

habitat.text: Wooded habitats including pond and stream edges, willow thickets and bogs; shelters in logs, humus and leaf litter; breeds in vernal pools and other fish-free ponds.

behavior.text: Winters on land and can freeze and thaw without harm.
Migrates to fish-free breeding pools in late winter or early spring and shows strong pond fidelity; mostly solitary otherwise.
Mostly diurnal, though breeding can occur at night; most active in summer in damp conditions.
Eats terrestrial invertebrates such as spiders, beetles, moth larvae, slugs and snails.

resources.title: Alligator snapping turtle
resources.description: Identify the alligator snapping turtle (Macrochelys temminckii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Alligator snapping turtle (Macrochelys temminckii): Very large: adult carapace usually 38-66 cm (to 80 cm), 16-68 kg; huge head with strongly hooked jaws. Three pronounced keels on the carapace plus an extra row of scutes along each side of the shell. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Mississippi and Mobile drainage basins and the Gulf Coast from eastern Texas to the Florida panhandle, north to southeastern Kansas, southeastern Iowa, Illinois and southern Indiana; very rare in Kentucky and possibly extirpated in Indiana and Iowa.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's concept includes M. apalachicolae and excludes M. suwanniensis (Taggart and Carr 2025; TTWG 2025); Thomas et al. (2014) had split it into three species.

rangeSummary.value: Mississippi and Mobile drainage basins and the Gulf Coast from eastern Texas to the Florida panhandle, north to southeastern Kansas, southeastern Iowa, Illinois and southern Indiana; very rare in Kentucky and possibly extirpated in Indiana and Iowa.

identification.text: Very large: adult carapace usually 38-66 cm (to 80 cm), 16-68 kg; huge head with strongly hooked jaws.
Three pronounced keels on the carapace plus an extra row of scutes along each side of the shell.
Long tail without a saw-toothed mid-dorsal ridge; eyes set more to the sides.
Pink worm-like lure on the tongue.
Compared with the common snapping turtle: Alligator snapping turtle has a larger head, an extra row of scutes on each side of the shell and lacks the saw-toothed mid-dorsal tail ridge.

habitat.text: Slow, deep water of rivers, sloughs, oxbows, canals and river-connected lakes, also swamps, bayous and ponds; under logjams, undercut banks and in deep holes.

behavior.text: Highly aquatic and secretive; leaves water only to nest and occasionally bask; mostly nocturnal or crepuscular.
Lies motionless on the bottom, sometimes algae-covered, and lures fish with its tongue; stays submerged 40-50 minutes.
Eats fish, mollusks, other turtles and other aquatic animals plus carrion.

resources.title: Diamond-backed terrapin
resources.description: Identify the diamond-backed terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Diamond-backed terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin): Keeled grey-to-black carapace with deep concentric growth rings; plastron unhinged, yellowish to greenish with dark flecks. Grey head and neck with conspicuous black spots; consistently white upper lip. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Texas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe spells the common name Diamond-backed Terrapin and says subspecies are poorly defined and possibly clinal.

rangeSummary.value: Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Texas.

identification.text: Keeled grey-to-black carapace with deep concentric growth rings; plastron unhinged, yellowish to greenish with dark flecks.
Grey head and neck with conspicuous black spots; consistently white upper lip.
Carapace 10-14 cm in males, 15-24 cm in females.
Unlike snapping turtles it lacks a long saw-toothed tail; unlike mud turtles it has no hinged plastron; unlike wood turtle no orange on neck and limbs.
Compared with the common snapping turtle: Terrapin has black-spotted head and neck and lacks a long saw-toothed tail.
Compared with the eastern mud turtle: Mud turtles have a hinged plastron; terrapins do not.
Compared with the wood turtle: Wood turtle has orange on the neck and limbs; terrapin does not.

habitat.text: Coastal marshes, tidal flats, coves, estuaries and lagoons behind barrier beaches; brackish water, intolerant of long-term fresh or full-strength salt water.

behavior.text: Wary and quick to flee; basks on oyster beds and mudflats.
Burrows into mud when inactive; may hibernate in moist sand; ventures into grassy lowlands at high tide.
Eats marine clams, snails, worms and crabs, and scavenges.

resources.title: Eastern coral snake
resources.description: Identify the eastern coral snake (Micrurus fulvius), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern coral snake (Micrurus fulvius): Venomous. Red, yellow and black bands with red and yellow bands touching; red bands may be speckled with black. Black snout followed by a broad yellow band across the head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern North Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Louisiana, disjunctly north to central Alabama.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's primary name is Harlequin Coralsnake and M. tener (Texas coral snake), formerly a subspecies, is treated as a distinct species.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern North Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Louisiana, disjunctly north to central Alabama.

identification.text: Venomous. Red, yellow and black bands with red and yellow bands touching; red bands may be speckled with black.
Black snout followed by a broad yellow band across the head.
Slender, smooth scales in 15 rows; adults usually 51-76 cm.
Nonvenomous mimics (scarlet kingsnake, scarlet snake) have a red snout and red bands touching black.
Compared with the scarlet kingsnake: Scarlet kingsnake has a red snout and red bands touching black; coral snake has a black snout and red touching yellow.
Compared with the northern scarlet snake: Scarlet snake has a red snout and a plain white belly.

habitat.text: Hardwood forest, pine-oak woodland, pine flatwoods and scrub, often on sandy soil; sometimes marsh edges and residential areas.

behavior.text: Secretive: mostly underground, under leaf litter, logs or stumps; solitary outside breeding.
Mainly diurnal in the north (morning and late afternoon); active all year in Florida, least in winter; males most active March-May.
Eats mainly snakes and limbless lizards, sometimes frogs and rodents.

resources.title: Gulf Coast waterdog
resources.description: Identify the gulf coast waterdog (Necturus beyeri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gulf Coast waterdog (Necturus beyeri): Aquatic salamander 6.25-8.75 in long; dark brown ground colour with tan spots joining into a net-like pattern. Some have a dark stripe through the eye; juveniles lighter with small dull yellow spots. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Gulf Coast drainages: western lineage from west-central Louisiana to northeastern and eastern Texas; other lineages from southeastern Louisiana to northeastern Mississippi and Alabama (Mobile Bay drainage).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe follows Guyer et al. (2020), who redescribed N. beyeri and described the Apalachicola (N. moleri) and Escambia (N. mounti) lineages as new species; older sources (e.g. Outdoor Alabama) give a broader range to Georgia and Florida.

rangeSummary.value: Gulf Coast drainages: western lineage from west-central Louisiana to northeastern and eastern Texas; other lineages from southeastern Louisiana to northeastern Mississippi and Alabama (Mobile Bay drainage).

identification.text: Aquatic salamander 6.25-8.75 in long; dark brown ground colour with tan spots joining into a net-like pattern.
Some have a dark stripe through the eye; juveniles lighter with small dull yellow spots.
Four toes on all four feet.

habitat.text: Sandy, spring-fed streams, also large rivers and standing backwater.

behavior.text: Opportunistic feeder on fish, eggs, crayfish, mollusks and worms.
Courtship in fall and winter in other parts of the range; eggs laid April-June under debris on the bottom.

resources.title: Red River waterdog
resources.description: Identify the red river waterdog (Necturus louisianensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red River waterdog (Necturus louisianensis): Smaller than the mudpuppy, maximum about 12 inches; lighter grey-brown or red-brown ground colour. Dark spots on the upper body more distinct and more numerous than on the mudpuppy. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern Louisiana north to Arkansas, eastern Oklahoma, southern Missouri and southeastern Kansas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's primary name is Red River Mudpuppy; some authorities treat it as a subspecies of N. maculosus, and NatureServe says its status needs further research.

rangeSummary.value: Northern Louisiana north to Arkansas, eastern Oklahoma, southern Missouri and southeastern Kansas.

identification.text: Smaller than the mudpuppy, maximum about 12 inches; lighter grey-brown or red-brown ground colour.
Dark spots on the upper body more distinct and more numerous than on the mudpuppy.
Belly has a wide, light, unspotted central area, light grey with pale pink edges.
Compared with the mudpuppy: Common mudpuppy is larger (to about 19 in); Red River mudpuppy has a lighter ground colour, more numerous spots and a wide pale unspotted belly strip.

habitat.text: Missouri's mudpuppy account says mudpuppies are permanently aquatic in large creeks, rivers and reservoirs, hiding by day under logs, rocks and debris; the Red River mudpuppy replaces the common mudpuppy in the southernmost quarter of the state.

resources.title: Mudpuppy
resources.description: Identify the mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus): Permanently aquatic salamander, 20-33 cm (MDC: usually 8-13 in, up to about 19 in) with large maroon external gills kept for life. Grey, rusty brown to nearly black with black or blue-black spots or blotches; belly whitish to grey, sometimes spotted. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern Manitoba east to southern Quebec, south to Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, northern Kentucky, southern Illinois, central Missouri and south-central Kansas.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes N. louisianensis is treated as a distinct species by some authors and as a subspecies by others; a Hiwassee drainage population may be two species.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern Manitoba east to southern Quebec, south to Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, northern Kentucky, southern Illinois, central Missouri and south-central Kansas.

identification.text: Permanently aquatic salamander, 20-33 cm (MDC: usually 8-13 in, up to about 19 in) with large maroon external gills kept for life.
Grey, rusty brown to nearly black with black or blue-black spots or blotches; belly whitish to grey, sometimes spotted.
Hellbenders lose external gills by 4-5 inches; mudpuppies keep them.
Compared with the red river mudpuppy: Red River mudpuppy is smaller (max about 12 in) with more distinct spots and a pale unspotted central belly strip.
Compared with the hellbender: Hellbenders lose external gills once 4-5 inches long.

habitat.text: Rivers, weedy ponds, large lakes and perennial streams with shelter; hides under logs, rocks or weeds by day; recorded to 30 m depth.

behavior.text: Fully aquatic and usually nocturnal, though it may be active by day in murky or weedy water.
Solitary; active all year and does not hibernate; moves deeper in winter and summer, shallower in spring and fall; breeds in fall.
Eats crayfish, insect larvae, small fish, fish eggs, worms, snails and carrion, and is often caught on baited lines or traps.

resources.title: Gulf salt marsh snake
resources.description: Identify the gulf salt marsh snake (Nerodia clarkii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gulf salt marsh snake (Nerodia clarkii): Keeled scales in 21 (occasionally 23) rows and a divided anal scale; 38-76 cm, up to 91 cm. Gulf form typically shows four dark stripes along the back on a lighter body; other forms vary from plain to blotched or banded. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Brackish coasts of the northern Gulf of Mexico from near Corpus Christi, Texas to Florida (including the Keys) and the Atlantic coast of northern Florida to Volusia County; also northern Cuba.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's name is Saltmarsh Snake (N. clarkii); Rautsaw et al. (2021) question the three subspecies, and Lawson et al. (1991) proposed N. clarkii and N. fasciata as distinct species. The Gulf salt marsh snake is subspecies clarkii.

rangeSummary.value: Brackish coasts of the northern Gulf of Mexico from near Corpus Christi, Texas to Florida (including the Keys) and the Atlantic coast of northern Florida to Volusia County; also northern Cuba.

identification.text: Keeled scales in 21 (occasionally 23) rows and a divided anal scale; 38-76 cm, up to 91 cm.
Gulf form typically shows four dark stripes along the back on a lighter body; other forms vary from plain to blotched or banded.
Proportionally smaller head and laterally compressed tail base compared with the banded water snake (N. fasciata, 23 rows).
Compared with the banded water snake: Saltmarsh snake typically has 21 dorsal scale rows, a smaller head and a laterally compressed tail base; banded water snake has 23 rows.
Compared with the queen snake: Queen and Graham's crayfish snakes have 19 or fewer dorsal scale rows; saltmarsh snake has more than 19.
Compared with the garter snakes: Garter snakes have a single anal scale; saltmarsh snake has a divided one.

habitat.text: Estuarine brackish and salt marshes with Spartina, Juncus and Salicornia, mangrove swamps, and less often inland freshwater marshes.

behavior.text: Lures small fish by flicking its tongue; eats small fish and fiddler crabs.
Needs fresh water to rehydrate and shifts between saltier and fresher water.
Uses crayfish, fiddler-crab or muskrat burrows, and sometimes shelters under rocks and logs.

conservationStatus.text: Atlantic salt marsh snake (Nerodia clarkii taeniata): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1977-12-29.

resources.title: Green water snake
resources.description: Identify the green water snake (Nerodia cyclopion), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green water snake (Nerodia cyclopion): Medium-sized, heavy-bodied, dark semiaquatic snake, averaging 30-45 in. Back greenish brown with obscure olive-brown or dark markings and dim black crossbars; belly dark grey or brown with yellow half-moon markings. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain from extreme western Florida and southern Alabama to southeastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southeastern Missouri and southern Illinois.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe places Nerodia in Colubridae; Illinois DNR lists the species under Natricidae. NatureServe notes N. floridana (Florida green watersnake) was formerly included in N. cyclopion.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain from extreme western Florida and southern Alabama to southeastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southeastern Missouri and southern Illinois.

identification.text: Medium-sized, heavy-bodied, dark semiaquatic snake, averaging 30-45 in.
Back greenish brown with obscure olive-brown or dark markings and dim black crossbars; belly dark grey or brown with yellow half-moon markings.
A short row of small subocular scales between the eye and the upper-lip scales separates it from other Missouri watersnakes.
Keeled scales; females larger than males.
Compared with the northern cottonmouth: Cottonmouth is heavier-bodied with a chunky head, a facial pit between nostril and eye, and a light line from eye to mouth corner.
Compared with the plain-bellied water snake: Other Bootheel watersnakes have prominent bands, a plain yellow belly or a yellow belly with black patches.

habitat.text: Cypress swamps, river sloughs, marshes, bayous, ditches, shallow lakes, oxbows and tree-lined sluggish streams, sometimes brackish Gulf Coast marshes.

behavior.text: Basks on logs, brush and banks, seldom far from water; flattens body and releases foul musk when disturbed.
Primarily diurnal in Illinois, almost exclusively nocturnal in Texas; hunts late evening.
Eats fish, frogs, salamanders, tadpoles, small turtles and invertebrates; live-bearing, young born August-September.

resources.title: Plainbelly water snake
resources.description: Identify the plainbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Plainbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster): Large, typically solid-coloured water snake: dorsum black, grey, olive-grey, brown or pink, sometimes with faint crossbars. Near-uniform colour on back, belly and underside of tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Delaware and southeastern Maryland to northern Florida, west through Georgia and Alabama to southeastern New Mexico and western Texas, north to northeastern Kansas, western Missouri, central Illinois and southern Indiana; disjunct populations in Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Iowa and Illinois.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe retains two U.S. subspecies (N. e. erythrogaster and N. e. transversa; Nicholson 2025) although Makowsky et al. (2010) recognised none; Animal Diversity Web describes more subspecies. NatureServe's name is Plain-bellied Watersnake.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Delaware and southeastern Maryland to northern Florida, west through Georgia and Alabama to southeastern New Mexico and western Texas, north to northeastern Kansas, western Missouri, central Illinois and southern Indiana; disjunct populations in Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Iowa and Illinois.

identification.text: Large, typically solid-coloured water snake: dorsum black, grey, olive-grey, brown or pink, sometimes with faint crossbars.
Near-uniform colour on back, belly and underside of tail.
N. e. erythrogaster: uniform brown back, orange to pink belly; N. e. flavigaster: grey to olive-grey back, orange-yellow to pale yellow or white belly.
Compared with the mississippi green watersnake: Green watersnake has small subocular scales between eye and lip scales and a dark belly with yellow half-moons; plain-bellied has a near-uniform belly.

habitat.text: Wide range of wetlands with permanent or semipermanent water: swamps, marshes, pond and lake edges, ditches and slow streams; basks in water-edge vegetation.

behavior.text: Basks by day, forages in evening and at night (NatureServe); Animal Diversity Web calls it diurnal.
Active March to October in the north, all year in the south except in cold weather; wanders far from water in warm wet weather.
Hibernates underground, in rock piles and crayfish burrows.
Eats mainly fish and frogs; also tadpoles, salamanders and crayfish.

conservationStatus.text: Copperbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta), Indiana north of 40 degrees north latitude, Michigan, Ohio: listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1997-01-29.

resources.title: Banded watersnake
resources.description: Identify the banded watersnake (Nerodia fasciata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Banded watersnake (Nerodia fasciata): Dark stripe from the eye to the angle of the jaw. Base colour gray, tan, dark olive or black, with dorsal cross bands along the entire body; belly off-white or white. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States: eastern Texas, southeastern Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, southeastern Missouri, western Tennessee, Mississippi, southern Alabama and Georgia, Florida and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and Animal Diversity Web call this species Southern Watersnake (Nerodia fasciata); 'banded' is used for the nominate subspecies group, and salt-marsh populations formerly included are now N. clarkii.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States: eastern Texas, southeastern Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, southeastern Missouri, western Tennessee, Mississippi, southern Alabama and Georgia, Florida and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Dark stripe from the eye to the angle of the jaw.
Base colour gray, tan, dark olive or black, with dorsal cross bands along the entire body; belly off-white or white.

Nerodia f. fasciata has square dark ventral markings; N. f. confluens has wide bands (11-17 along the body) and reddish-brown rectangular belly-side spots; N. f. pictiventris has wavy reddish transverse lines on the belly.
Adults 61-106.7 cm; neonates about 24 cm and more vividly patterned than adults; females longer and heavier.

habitat.text: Vegetated freshwater ponds, lakes, marshes, wet prairies, sluggish streams and rivers, ditches and swamps; shelters in bank-side burrows or under debris.
Tolerates slightly brackish water (under about 1 ppt) but does not survive in saltwater.

behavior.text: Active day and night; basks on banks and in edge vegetation, and is most active at night after summer rains.
Eats frogs, toads, salamanders, tadpoles, fishes and aquatic invertebrates; juveniles eat mostly fish, adults mainly frogs or large fish.
Hibernates beneath logs or rocks or in burrows; may leave an area in severe drought.

resources.title: Diamondback water snake
resources.description: Identify the diamondback water snake (Nerodia rhombifer), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Diamondback water snake (Nerodia rhombifer): Large, heavy-bodied watersnake; adults usually 3-5 ft (Missouri: 30-48 in, occasionally to 69 in). Dark brown blotches along the back usually connect into a chainlike pattern, with light diamond-shaped areas between; dark bars on the sides alternate to form diamonds. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Concentrated in the Mississippi River drainage, north to southern Illinois and Indiana, west to Texas and Oklahoma (and Mexico), east into Alabama. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Brandley et al. (2010) found multiple lineages within N. rhombifer (east and west of the Mississippi River, plus Mexico); treated here as one species.

rangeSummary.value: Concentrated in the Mississippi River drainage, north to southern Illinois and Indiana, west to Texas and Oklahoma (and Mexico), east into Alabama. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Large, heavy-bodied watersnake; adults usually 3-5 ft (Missouri: 30-48 in, occasionally to 69 in).
Dark brown blotches along the back usually connect into a chainlike pattern, with light diamond-shaped areas between; dark bars on the sides alternate to form diamonds.
Belly yellow with irregular rows of dark spots or half-moon marks.
Scales keeled, so the snake feels rough.
Compared with the northern cottonmouth: Cottonmouth has a distinctly triangular head, a sensory pit between nostril and eye, a light line from eye to mouth corner, and no chainlike dark back pattern.

habitat.text: Margins and shallows of lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, swamps, marshes, canals and ditches; most common in swamps, sloughs, oxbows and drainage ditches in Missouri.

behavior.text: Diurnal in spring and fall and nocturnal in summer; bask on branches, logs and banks except in the hottest weather.
Eats mainly fishes and frogs, also salamanders, carrion and small turtles; feeds by day.
Overwinters underground below the frost line, including in crayfish burrows; bites hard and musks when handled.

resources.title: Northern water snake
resources.description: Identify the northern water snake (Nerodia sipedon), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Northern water snake (Nerodia sipedon): Brownish, tan or gray; back and sides have square blotches alternating and often merging into bands toward the front; large adults can look solid brown or black, especially when dry. Belly white, yellowish or orangish, with dark half-moon marks and often red or orange blotches. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Ontario and the northeastern United States, from Nebraska and Kansas east to the Atlantic coast and south to North Carolina and southern Missouri.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the primary common name as Common Watersnake (Nerodia sipedon); same scientific name.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Ontario and the northeastern United States, from Nebraska and Kansas east to the Atlantic coast and south to North Carolina and southern Missouri.

identification.text: Brownish, tan or gray; back and sides have square blotches alternating and often merging into bands toward the front; large adults can look solid brown or black, especially when dry.
Belly white, yellowish or orangish, with dark half-moon marks and often red or orange blotches.
Juveniles have reddish-brown saddles on a tan, brown or gray ground colour.
Scales keeled, anal plate divided, 21-25 scales at midbody; adults 61-140 cm, males smaller than females; mature males have knobbed keels near the vent.
Compared with the northern cottonmouth (water moccasin): Commonly mistaken for it; the northern water snake is non-venomous (Animal Diversity Web gives no further field mark).

habitat.text: Creeks, rivers, canals, lakes, ponds, marshes, bogs and swamps; favours sunny spots with debris, logs or rocks at the water's edge.
Hibernates in burrows, rock crevices or uplands near water.

behavior.text: Active day and night but mainly by day; basks on overhanging branches, beaver lodges, logs and shallow margins; social at basking sites in spring and fall, otherwise solitary.
Eats amphibians, fish (live or dead), crayfish, insects, leeches, small mammals; swallows prey alive and is not a constrictor.
Inactive in cold months in the north (activity mainly March-April through October); bites and discharges musk when handled.

resources.title: Eastern newt
resources.description: Identify the eastern newt (Notophthalmus viridescens), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern newt (Notophthalmus viridescens): Adult: olive-green, brown or yellowish-brown above with small black-bordered red spots in most of the range; yellow belly with small black spots; rough, not slimy, skin; 7-12.4 cm. Red eft (terrestrial juvenile, 2-7 years): bright orange or orange-red, usually under 3.5 in, dry rough skin; efts commonly walk in the open by day. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Most of eastern North America, from the Canadian Maritime Provinces west to the Great Lakes and south to Texas, Alabama, Georgia and Florida.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Frost (2025) treats all subspecies as synonyms, while Crother (2017) and others recognize four; treated here as one species.

rangeSummary.value: Most of eastern North America, from the Canadian Maritime Provinces west to the Great Lakes and south to Texas, Alabama, Georgia and Florida.

identification.text: Adult: olive-green, brown or yellowish-brown above with small black-bordered red spots in most of the range; yellow belly with small black spots; rough, not slimy, skin; 7-12.4 cm.
Red eft (terrestrial juvenile, 2-7 years): bright orange or orange-red, usually under 3.5 in, dry rough skin; efts commonly walk in the open by day.
Breeding males: tall tail fin, swollen vent, blackish horny patches on inner thighs and toe tips.
Larvae have feathery gills and a dark stripe through each eye; Carolina Coastal Plain adults have a broken black-bordered red stripe on each side.
Compared with the red salamander: Red salamander has about 16 costal grooves, a black chin and a yellow iris; the newt has rough skin without prominent grooves on the sides.

habitat.text: Lakes, ponds, swamps and quiet stream pools, especially without predatory fishes; efts live in adjacent wooded areas.

behavior.text: Adults migrate between terrestrial habitat and breeding ponds, mostly on rainy nights; aquatic stages can stay active all year, even under ice.
Skin secretions are highly toxic, the red eft most of all; efts curl and show bright colours when attacked.
Adults and larvae eat small aquatic animals including amphibian eggs; efts eat small invertebrates, often snails.

resources.title: Rough green snake
resources.description: Identify the rough green snake (Opheodrys aestivus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rough green snake (Opheodrys aestivus): Small, thin snake, uniform green above; underside, chin and lip scales yellowish-green to cream. Juveniles resemble smaller adults but are lighter in colour. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States, north to southern New Jersey, through Florida to the Keys, west to central Oklahoma and Texas and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Rittmeyer et al. (2021) suggested peninsular Florida populations be elevated to a separate species, O. carinatus.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States, north to southern New Jersey, through Florida to the Keys, west to central Oklahoma and Texas and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, thin snake, uniform green above; underside, chin and lip scales yellowish-green to cream.
Juveniles resemble smaller adults but are lighter in colour.
Females longer and heavier; males have a longer tail; average lengths about 947 mm (females) and 892 mm (males).

habitat.text: Dense vegetation (vines, shrubs, trees) near water, at forest edges and in fairly open forests, overgrown pasture, thickets and marsh edges.

behavior.text: Diurnal and largely arboreal; sleeps coiled on branch ends near shorelines, less arboreal in spring and fall.
Insectivore hunting by sight: crickets, grasshoppers, caterpillars and spiders.
Flees into dense vegetation rather than biting; active roughly April-November in the north, hibernates in winter; may nest communally.

resources.title: Slender glass lizard
resources.description: Identify the slender glass lizard (Ophisaurus attenuatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Slender glass lizard (Ophisaurus attenuatus): Legless with movable eyelids, external ear openings and a lateral groove; tail more than half of length; adults 57-107 cm. Narrow dark stripes below the lateral groove and under the tail; young and medium-sized animals have a dark middorsal stripe or dashes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central United States, from the southern end of Lake Michigan and Wisconsin south through Texas and eastward to the Atlantic coast; Wisconsin populations are disjunct. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes subspecies longicaudus has been proposed as a distinct species (Collins 1991) but most authors keep it as a subspecies.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central United States, from the southern end of Lake Michigan and Wisconsin south through Texas and eastward to the Atlantic coast; Wisconsin populations are disjunct. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Legless with movable eyelids, external ear openings and a lateral groove; tail more than half of length; adults 57-107 cm.
Narrow dark stripes below the lateral groove and under the tail; young and medium-sized animals have a dark middorsal stripe or dashes.
Old adults may be brown with irregular dark-bordered crossbands; males become flecked whitish and can look salt-and-pepper.
Compared with the eastern glass lizard: Eastern glass lizard has no stripe on the middle of the back and no stripes below the lateral groove.
Compared with the snakes (legless look-alikes): Glass lizards have eyelids and ear openings, rigid bodies and very long tails; snakes have fixed eye coverings and no ear openings.

habitat.text: Open grassland, prairie, woodland edge, oak savanna, longleaf pine flatwoods and fallow fields, often on sandy soil.

behavior.text: Mostly diurnal, occasionally crepuscular or nocturnal; surface activity is triggered by warm summer rains; often seen on roads in spring.
Eats grasshoppers, crickets, katydids, beetles, spiders, snails and occasionally eggs and small vertebrates; forages on and under the ground.
Tail breaks off readily (almost 80% of adults in one study had a regrown tail); overwinters in burrows below the frost line.

resources.title: Mimic glass lizard
resources.description: Identify the mimic glass lizard (Ophisaurus mimicus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mimic glass lizard (Ophisaurus mimicus): Legless with movable eyelids, external ear openings, a lateral fold and a tail up to three-quarters of total length; 38-66 cm. Dark middorsal stripe (sometimes faint) bordered by tan and another dark stripe; 3-4 narrow dark stripes above the lateral fold continuing onto the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, including Florida, coastal South Carolina and coastal and southern Georgia; rare and poorly documented. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, including Florida, coastal South Carolina and coastal and southern Georgia; rare and poorly documented. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Legless with movable eyelids, external ear openings, a lateral fold and a tail up to three-quarters of total length; 38-66 cm.
Dark middorsal stripe (sometimes faint) bordered by tan and another dark stripe; 3-4 narrow dark stripes above the lateral fold continuing onto the tail.
Below the lateral fold, marking is reduced to freckles, spots or dashes; 95 or fewer scales along the lateral fold.
Smallest of the four Florida glass lizards; lateral striping poorly developed in juveniles.
Compared with the snakes (legless look-alikes): Snakes have wide belly scales, fixed eye coverings, no ear openings, short tails and more flexible bodies.
Compared with the slender glass lizard: Mimic has a low lateral-fold scale count (95 or fewer); the species are separated by colour pattern and scalation.

habitat.text: Longleaf (occasionally slash) pine uplands with grassy groundcover, especially mesic to wet flatwoods; occasionally hillside seepage bogs, dome swamp edges and wet prairies next to pine uplands.

behavior.text: Surface records run 27 March to 16 November, peaking April-June; less active in winter, possibly underground.
Eats crickets and other insects.
Forages actively by day in open habitat and shelters under boards and debris; tail breaks off when seized.

resources.title: Eastern glass lizard
resources.description: Identify the eastern glass lizard (Ophisaurus ventralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern glass lizard (Ophisaurus ventralis): Legless, with eyelids, external ear openings and lateral grooves; tail usually over twice the snout-vent length; 45-108 cm, the longest lizard in North America. Adults dark green above with many black lines running from head to tail, yellow below, usually with white marks on the neck and back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains: Florida, most of Georgia and South Carolina, coastal North Carolina and southeastern Virginia, west along the Gulf coast to eastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains: Florida, most of Georgia and South Carolina, coastal North Carolina and southeastern Virginia, west along the Gulf coast to eastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Legless, with eyelids, external ear openings and lateral grooves; tail usually over twice the snout-vent length; 45-108 cm, the longest lizard in North America.
Adults dark green above with many black lines running from head to tail, yellow below, usually with white marks on the neck and back.
No stripe on the middle of the back and none below the lateral grooves; juveniles tan.
Females greener; males yellowish-green with broader stripes and gold or brown speckles.
Compared with the slender glass lizard: Slender glass lizard has a dark middorsal stripe or dashes and stripes below the lateral groove; eastern has neither.
Compared with the snakes (legless look-alikes): Glass lizards have eyelids and ear openings; snakes do not.

habitat.text: Moist and dry areas, especially damp grassy areas, pine flatwoods, maritime forest and sandy friable soils near ponds, marshes and estuaries.

behavior.text: Crepuscular; hunts at dawn, dusk or after rain, mostly burrowing through loose soil; may bask mid-morning or early evening on roads or open ground.
Eats insects (grasshoppers mainly), spiders, worms, slugs and snails, and sometimes bird eggs, snakes and lizards.
Brumates in burrows below the frost line; mostly solitary.

resources.title: Central ratsnake
resources.description: Identify the central ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Central ratsnake (Pantherophis alleghaniensis). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: East of the Mississippi River to the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line in Virginia, north to Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Massachusetts, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists P. alleghaniensis as Eastern Ratsnake, while New York DEC (2025) calls it the central ratsnake and treats yellow ratsnake P. quadrivittatus as a separate eastern-clade species; Burbrink et al. and the NY assessment note hybridization and unresolved boundaries.

rangeSummary.value: East of the Mississippi River to the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line in Virginia, north to Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Massachusetts, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

habitat.text: Mix of open and wooded land: hardwood forest, old fields, farmland near woods, barnyards and rural buildings; hibernates in deep crevices or underground.

behavior.text: Diurnal in spring and fall and nocturnal in summer; active late April to October in the north.
Proficient climber and swimmer; eats birds and eggs, small mammals, lizards, frogs; adults eat mainly endotherms, young mainly ectotherms.
Emerges from hibernacula mid-April to early June; overwinters communally in rocky talus, ledges, basements, cisterns and wells, and may migrate between hibernaculum and summer range.

resources.title: Corn snake
resources.description: Identify the corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus): Large spots down the back, brown and red-orange body (gray and yellow variants occur), belly with a black-and-white checkerboard. Hatchlings paler and duller, 20-35 cm; adults average 70-120 cm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States from southern New Jersey to Florida and west through Mississippi to Louisiana; related Great Plains rat snake reaches Illinois, Texas and New Mexico. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (Burbrink 2002) restricts P. guttatus to east of the Mississippi River and treats the Great Plains rat snake as P. emoryi and western Louisiana/eastern Texas populations as P. slowinskii; Animal Diversity Web still lists P. g. emoryi as a subspecies and covers it in this species' range.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States from southern New Jersey to Florida and west through Mississippi to Louisiana; related Great Plains rat snake reaches Illinois, Texas and New Mexico. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Large spots down the back, brown and red-orange body (gray and yellow variants occur), belly with a black-and-white checkerboard.
Hatchlings paler and duller, 20-35 cm; adults average 70-120 cm.
Head narrower than a copperhead's, colour lighter, and spots square-shaped.
Compared with the southern copperhead: Corn snake has a narrower head, lighter coloration and square spots.

habitat.text: Pine woodlands, brushy fields, open hardwood forests, rocky areas with crevices and logs, fields, barnyards and abandoned buildings; up to about 1800 m.

behavior.text: Mostly diurnal, crepuscular in warm weather; climbs trees and shrubs, basks on rocks, enters rodent burrows; constricts prey.
Over half the diet is rodents (hispid cotton rats, white-footed mice) plus moles, bird eggs, and lizards and frogs in Florida.
Hibernates in crevices, logs or caves from about October to April in most of the range, briefly or not at all in the south.

resources.title: Gray rat snake
resources.description: Identify the gray rat snake (Pantherophis obsoletus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Gray rat snake (Pantherophis obsoletus): Glossy black dorsal scales often speckled with brown, orange or yellow; creamy white belly; distinct checkerboard pattern. Slender body with a rounded head and weakly keeled scales; adult snout-vent length 96-154 cm, males larger; one of the longest snakes in North America. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central United States, north to southern Minnesota, south along the Mississippi River to the Gulf Coast; west to southern Nebraska and the eastern halves of Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (Burbrink 2000, 2001) splits the former P. obsoletus complex into P. obsoletus (Western Ratsnake), P. alleghaniensis and P. spiloides, and lists P. obsoletus as Western Ratsnake; 'gray rat snake' is the batch's common name, and Animal Diversity Web's page title for P. obsoletus is 'Eastern Rat Snake' while its text says western rat snake.

rangeSummary.value: Central United States, north to southern Minnesota, south along the Mississippi River to the Gulf Coast; west to southern Nebraska and the eastern halves of Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Glossy black dorsal scales often speckled with brown, orange or yellow; creamy white belly; distinct checkerboard pattern.
Slender body with a rounded head and weakly keeled scales; adult snout-vent length 96-154 cm, males larger; one of the longest snakes in North America.
Juveniles grayish with tan blotches, darkening with age.
Compared with the central (eastern) ratsnake: Western ratsnake has a distinct checkerboard pattern; both have weakly keeled scales (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Rocky hillsides and canyons, scrub fields, prairie farmland, deciduous forest, swamps, woodland edges, grasslands and rural structures.

behavior.text: Diurnal especially in cool spring, more active at night in summer; partly arboreal and climbs to raid tree-hollow nests; swims.
Adults eat mainly mammals (66% in one study), plus birds and eggs, lizards, other snakes and amphibians.
When cornered coils, opens mouth and may vibrate the tail against leaves like a rattlesnake; brumates October-February in hollow trees, burrows, caves or stumps.

resources.title: Florida pine snake
resources.description: Identify the florida pine snake (Pituophis melanoleucus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Florida pine snake (Pituophis melanoleucus): Large, stout snake 91-254 cm with a small head, sharply pointed snout and enlarged rostral scale. Florida pine snake (mugitus): tan to gray-brown or rusty-brown with faded, indistinct blotches and a pale belly; northern pine snake is white to cream with black blotches; black pine snake is nearly uniform black or dark brown with reddish snout. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States; the Florida subspecies occurs in Florida, Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina and southwestern South Carolina. Not in Canada as this subspecies (Animal Diversity Web places the bullsnake subspecies in parts of Canada).

taxonomicNotes.text: The batch name 'Florida pine snake' is the subspecies P. m. mugitus; NatureServe and Animal Diversity Web treat Pituophis melanoleucus as the species (Eastern Pinesnake), with Animal Diversity Web listing five subspecies including bullsnakes, and NatureServe cautions that Pituophis may be revised.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States; the Florida subspecies occurs in Florida, Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina and southwestern South Carolina. Not in Canada as this subspecies (Animal Diversity Web places the bullsnake subspecies in parts of Canada).

identification.text: Large, stout snake 91-254 cm with a small head, sharply pointed snout and enlarged rostral scale.

Florida pine snake (mugitus): tan to gray-brown or rusty-brown with faded, indistinct blotches and a pale belly; northern pine snake is white to cream with black blotches; black pine snake is nearly uniform black or dark brown with reddish snout.
Keeled scales, 4 prefrontals and an undivided anal scale; dark bars from the eye to the lips.
Juveniles dull at emergence, brightening after first shed.
Compared with the rat snakes (pantherophis) and kingsnakes: They have only 2 prefrontal scales, and rat snakes have a divided anal scale.
Compared with the racers, whipsnakes and indigo snakes: These have smooth body scales; pine snakes have keeled scales.

habitat.text: Xeric pine or pine-oak woodland with open understory on sandy soils, longleaf pine sandhills, dry rocky ridges and old fields; needs level, well-drained sandy forest openings for nesting and hibernation.

behavior.text: Mostly diurnal, active about April-October in the north; hibernates underground and may aestivate in summer.
Eats small mammals mainly, plus birds and eggs, lizards, small snakes and insects (juveniles take more lizards and insects); forages underground.
Hisses loudly using a cartilaginous keel in front of the glottis and vibrates its tail like a rattlesnake; digs with its snout.

conservationStatus.text: Black pinesnake (Pituophis melanoleucus lodingi): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 2015-11-05.

resources.title: Coal skink
resources.description: Identify the coal skink (Plestiodon anthracinus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Coal skink (Plestiodon anthracinus): Medium lizard, 5-7 in, with smooth shiny scales and short legs; back olive-gray to brown. Wide dark brown or black lateral stripe from head onto tail, edged above and below by a thin light line; belly gray or bluish-gray. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Only the Tennessee range was sourced: a southern coal skink subspecies along the Tennessee River in the west and a northern one in Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

rangeSummary.value: Only the Tennessee range was sourced: a southern coal skink subspecies along the Tennessee River in the west and a northern one in Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

identification.text: Medium lizard, 5-7 in, with smooth shiny scales and short legs; back olive-gray to brown.
Wide dark brown or black lateral stripe from head onto tail, edged above and below by a thin light line; belly gray or bluish-gray.
No stripe down the centre of the back (the common and southeastern five-lined skinks have one).
Breeding males have an orange or reddish tint on the sides of the head; females slightly larger.
Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has a stripe down the centre of the back; coal skink does not.
Compared with the southeastern five-lined skink: Southeastern five-lined skink has a stripe down the centre of the back; coal skink does not.

habitat.text: Open, moist forests near streams, rivers or sloughs, also rocky hillsides and near springs; humid wooded areas with leaf litter and loose rocks, sometimes clearcuts and rights-of-way.

behavior.text: Courtship and breeding in spring (late winter in Georgia); females lay 4-9 eggs in rotten logs or moist soil and guard them.
Eats small insects and spiders.
Sheds its tail if grasped; active March-September in Kansas and all year in Georgia; often shelters under logs and rocks near water and may take refuge in water.

resources.title: Five-lined skink
resources.description: Identify the five-lined skink (Plestiodon fasciatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Five-lined skink (Plestiodon fasciatus): Five yellow to cream stripes of equal width from snout to tail on a dark background; scales smooth and shiny; adults 12.7-21.6 cm. Hatchlings black with bright blue tails; adult females keep stripes and a gray tail; adult males fade to brown or olive, jaws orange-red in breeding season. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southern Ontario and the eastern and central United States: from lower Michigan and eastern New York south to northern Florida, west to Wisconsin, Missouri and eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, with isolated populations in Iowa and Minnesota.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the primary name as Common Five-lined Skink and notes Howes et al. (2006) and Richmond (2006) found substantial phylogeographic structure suggesting possible cryptic species; Animal Diversity Web text uses the older name Eumeces fasciatus.

rangeSummary.value: Southern Ontario and the eastern and central United States: from lower Michigan and eastern New York south to northern Florida, west to Wisconsin, Missouri and eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, with isolated populations in Iowa and Minnesota.

identification.text: Five yellow to cream stripes of equal width from snout to tail on a dark background; scales smooth and shiny; adults 12.7-21.6 cm.
Hatchlings black with bright blue tails; adult females keep stripes and a gray tail; adult males fade to brown or olive, jaws orange-red in breeding season.
Enlarged row of scales under the middle of the tail.
Compared with the southeastern five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has an enlarged row of scales under the tail and prefers moister habitats.
Compared with the broadhead skink: Five-lined skink has four labial scales around the mouth; broadhead skink has five.

habitat.text: Moist but not wet, wooded or partly wooded areas with abundant cover and basking sites, including forest edges, cleared and burned areas and Great Lakes driftwood beaches.

behavior.text: Active April-October in the north; spends much time under cover (rotting wood, rock crevices, sawdust piles, foundations) and basks on logs and rocky outcrops.
Eats spiders, millipedes, crickets, termites, grasshoppers, caterpillars, beetles, snails and sometimes small vertebrates.
Males defend territories against other males; females guard eggs in logs or under rocks; tail detaches readily.

resources.title: Southeastern five-lined skink
resources.description: Identify the southeastern five-lined skink (Plestiodon inexpectatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southeastern five-lined skink (Plestiodon inexpectatus): 5-8.5 in (12.5-21.5 cm); gray, brown or black with five white or yellowish stripes (two per side, one down the back). Young have a bright blue tail; adult male stripes may fade and a reddish or orange colour may develop on the head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Throughout South Carolina and all but extreme northern Georgia (SREL); the wider range was not sourced in detail. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Throughout South Carolina and all but extreme northern Georgia (SREL); the wider range was not sourced in detail. Not in Canada.

identification.text: 5-8.5 in (12.5-21.5 cm); gray, brown or black with five white or yellowish stripes (two per side, one down the back).
Young have a bright blue tail; adult male stripes may fade and a reddish or orange colour may develop on the head.
No enlarged row of scales under the tail, unlike five-lined and broadhead skinks.
