Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has an enlarged row of scales under the tail and usually uses moister habitat.
Compared with the broadhead skink: Broadhead skinks are usually larger and more arboreal, and have an enlarged row of scales under the tail.

habitat.text: Dry wooded habitats with abundant fallen trees and stumps, especially dry pine forests and coastal areas; also wet pine flatwoods, sandhills and abandoned buildings.

behavior.text: Found on the ground or in trees, but less arboreal than broadhead skinks; most often beneath logs or under bark and runs for the nearest tree or log when pursued.
Eats a wide variety of insects, spiders and other invertebrates.
Females lay several eggs in moist soil or rotten logs in summer and attend them; tail breaks off when restrained.

resources.title: Broadhead skink
resources.description: Identify the broadhead skink (Plestiodon laticeps), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Broadhead skink (Plestiodon laticeps): Second-largest skink in the account, up to 324 mm; males become uniform brown and lose their stripes. Breeding-season males have a greatly enlarged orange to red head. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central and eastern United States, from Pennsylvania to Florida and Indiana to Texas. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Central and eastern United States, from Pennsylvania to Florida and Indiana to Texas. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Second-largest skink in the account, up to 324 mm; males become uniform brown and lose their stripes.
Breeding-season males have a greatly enlarged orange to red head.
Juveniles brown to black with five to seven white to light-orange stripes and a bright blue tail; adult females keep some striping but lose the blue tail.
Five labial scales around the mouth (five-lined skinks have four).
Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has four labial scales around the mouth; broadhead skink has five.

habitat.text: Open forests and woodland edges, hammocks and cypress heads in Florida, swamps and barrier islands; uses tree hollows and old woodpecker holes, and large live oaks on coastal islands.

behavior.text: Diurnal and solitary; mainly arboreal but often hunts and nests on the ground; sun themselves on snags and stumps.
Eats insects, arachnids, mollusks, isopods, rodents and smaller reptiles including juveniles of its own species, hunting by sight and tongue-flicking.
Hibernates October-March in northern parts of range; males are territorial in the breeding season; females guard eggs in rotting stumps or dead trees.

resources.title: Mississippi slimy salamander
resources.description: Identify the mississippi slimy salamander (Plethodon mississippi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mississippi slimy salamander (Plethodon mississippi): Medium to large terrestrial salamander, about 4-6.5 in. Black to bluish-black with numerous white, yellow or brassy spots on back, tail and sides; heavy white lateral flecking in some; white spotting on chin and throat; plain belly. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern Kentucky, western Tennessee, western Alabama, most of Mississippi and a small part of southeastern Louisiana, west of the Tennessee River on the Coastal Plain. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes P. ainsworthi was tentatively removed from synonymy of P. mississippi by Pierson et al. (2020); the species was formerly part of P. glutinosus.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern Kentucky, western Tennessee, western Alabama, most of Mississippi and a small part of southeastern Louisiana, west of the Tennessee River on the Coastal Plain. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Medium to large terrestrial salamander, about 4-6.5 in.
Black to bluish-black with numerous white, yellow or brassy spots on back, tail and sides; heavy white lateral flecking in some; white spotting on chin and throat; plain belly.
Cannot be told from other members of the slimy salamander complex by appearance alone.
Compared with the other slimy salamanders (plethodon glutinosus complex): Identification based on appearance is impossible; range and genetics separate them.

habitat.text: Forested areas: maritime and river-bottom hardwoods and pine forests; under rotting logs, branches, rocks, leaf litter, in rock crevices, caves and rubbish piles.

behavior.text: Forages on the surface at night or in rain but typically stays near its burrow; adults defend small territories.
Terrestrial breeder with no aquatic larval stage; females guard 1-33 eggs from a cavity roof through 2-3 months of development.
Sticky tail secretion deters predators; goes underground in dry or freezing weather.

resources.title: Southern zigzag salamander
resources.description: Identify the southern zigzag salamander (Plethodon ventralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern zigzag salamander (Plethodon ventralis): Small, 2.5-3.5 in; sides brown to dark gray with a yellowish or orange stripe down the back that may be straight, wavy or lobed. Brownish-gray unstriped morph occurs; small white flecks on back and sides give a metallic look. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Illinois and Indiana south to north and central Alabama, mainly in the Southwestern Appalachians and Interior Plateau uplands. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Until 1997 Alabama populations were called northern zigzag salamander (P. dorsalis); NatureServe notes Highton (1997) recognized P. ventralis as distinct from P. dorsalis and P. angusticlavius.

rangeSummary.value: Illinois and Indiana south to north and central Alabama, mainly in the Southwestern Appalachians and Interior Plateau uplands. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, 2.5-3.5 in; sides brown to dark gray with a yellowish or orange stripe down the back that may be straight, wavy or lobed.
Brownish-gray unstriped morph occurs; small white flecks on back and sides give a metallic look.
Belly gray or black, mottled or speckled with orange or red; most Alabama specimens have 18 costal grooves.

Compared with the webster's salamander: Basically identical in appearance; separated by geographic range and genetics, and in P. websteri the stripe tends to be wavy only on the front half of the body.

habitat.text: Upland rocky hardwood woodlands, ravines, seepages, rubble and cave mouths; often under rotten logs and rocks.

behavior.text: Forages on the forest floor for small invertebrates.
Completely terrestrial with no aquatic larval stage; nests presumably in subterranean cavities in summer.
Found under rocks, logs or leaves by day.

resources.title: Webster's salamander
resources.description: Identify the webster's salamander (Plethodon websteri), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Webster's salamander (Plethodon websteri): Small woodland salamander, 2.75-3.2 in (7.0-8.2 cm); striped form has a wavy yellowish-brown to orange-red stripe head to tail; unstriped form may have scattered red pigment. Tiny silvery-white spots and brassy flecks give a frosted look. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Small, scattered populations in the southeastern Piedmont and adjacent areas: western South Carolina, west Georgia, central and east-central Alabama, south-central Mississippi and Louisiana. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Feist et al. (2019) suggested mtDNA evidence for two lineages within P. websteri; formerly confused with the P. dorsalis group.

rangeSummary.value: Small, scattered populations in the southeastern Piedmont and adjacent areas: western South Carolina, west Georgia, central and east-central Alabama, south-central Mississippi and Louisiana. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small woodland salamander, 2.75-3.2 in (7.0-8.2 cm); striped form has a wavy yellowish-brown to orange-red stripe head to tail; unstriped form may have scattered red pigment.
Tiny silvery-white spots and brassy flecks give a frosted look.
Belly mottled orange or reddish; males have a swollen cloaca.
Compared with the southern zigzag salamander: Nearly identical; best separated by geographic distribution and genetics.
Compared with the southern redback salamander (plethodon serratus): Where ranges overlap in western Georgia, redback has a straighter stripe with serrated edges; Webster's stripe is more jagged.

habitat.text: Hardwood or mixed pine-hardwood forested hillsides, often bordering rocky feeder streams; under rocks, logs, bark and leaf litter.

behavior.text: Active in forest litter roughly October-May and apparently inactive underground in other months.
Terrestrial breeder: courtship January-March, eggs laid June-July, hatching August-September.
Some populations move to rocky outcrops in spring and leave them in fall.

resources.title: Mountain chorus frog
resources.description: Identify the mountain chorus frog (Pseudacris brachyphona), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mountain chorus frog (Pseudacris brachyphona): Small frog; adult males 26-30 mm, females 28-34 mm. Mostly light brown with stripes or spots of varying shades of brown along the back; a stripe from the snout across the eye. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Appalachian Mountains from northwestern Pennsylvania to central Alabama, generally at elevations of about 365-1066 m. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Ospina et al. (2020) split the Southern clade as P. collinsorum, restricting P. brachyphona to the Northern clade; Animal Diversity Web treats P. brachyphona as a single Appalachian species.

rangeSummary.value: Appalachian Mountains from northwestern Pennsylvania to central Alabama, generally at elevations of about 365-1066 m. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small frog; adult males 26-30 mm, females 28-34 mm.
Mostly light brown with stripes or spots of varying shades of brown along the back; a stripe from the snout across the eye.
Legs usually yellow; throat yellow to black in males and white in females.

habitat.text: Wooded, hilly areas with deciduous trees; breeds in spring pools, flooded ditches, stream pools and woodland ponds.

behavior.text: Primarily nocturnal, also diurnal when breeding; breeding February-June, eggs in small clusters attached to vegetation.
Relatively solitary outside breeding; males defend breeding spots in vernal ponds.
Eats beetles (about 45% of diet), spiders, bugs, ants and other small invertebrates; migrates between breeding pools and upland habitat.

resources.title: Spring peeper
resources.description: Identify the spring peeper (Pseudacris crucifer), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Spring peeper (Pseudacris crucifer): Small frog, about 20-25 mm (to 3.7 cm); gray, pink, brown, olive or yellowish above. Dark X-shaped cross on the back (may be broken), a dark stripe from snout to eardrum and a dark bar between the eyes; dark bands on legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern North America from southeastern Manitoba east to the Atlantic, south to eastern Texas and mainland Florida (not the Florida Peninsula, per Animal Diversity Web). Introduced in Cuba.

taxonomicNotes.text: Formerly Hyla crucifer; some authors place western Pseudacris species in Hyliola but NatureServe notes this has not gained traction, and P. crucifer is unaffected.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern North America from southeastern Manitoba east to the Atlantic, south to eastern Texas and mainland Florida (not the Florida Peninsula, per Animal Diversity Web). Introduced in Cuba.

identification.text: Small frog, about 20-25 mm (to 3.7 cm); gray, pink, brown, olive or yellowish above.
Dark X-shaped cross on the back (may be broken), a dark stripe from snout to eardrum and a dark bar between the eyes; dark bands on legs.
Toe tips enlarged into disks, hind toes only moderately webbed; belly cream or white.
Call is a single high piping whistle rising slightly, repeated about once a second; a chorus sounds like sleigh bells.

habitat.text: Moist wooded areas near ponds, marshes, ditches and swamps, preferring fishless, often temporary pools with standing plants and debris.

behavior.text: Mostly active at dusk and night but also by day in wet weather; males call from vegetation beside water or low in woody plants.
Eats small terrestrial invertebrates such as ants, beetles, flies and spiders; larvae eat algae and debris.
Calls from uplands in autumn, far from water; hibernates under logs and in tree holes; breeds early spring in the north.

resources.title: Southeastern chorus frog
resources.description: Identify the southeastern chorus frog (Pseudacris feriarum), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southeastern chorus frog (Pseudacris feriarum): Small; females 25-33 mm, males 23-31 mm; brown, tan or gray. Three stripes (sometimes broken into spots) down the back, often a dark triangle between the eyes (absent in some South Carolina populations). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States: southeastern Missouri, northeastern Arkansas and eastern Mississippi east to coastal Virginia and the Carolinas, north to central and southern Pennsylvania, south to northern Florida. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and Animal Diversity Web use the name Upland Chorus Frog for Pseudacris feriarum (NatureServe lists synonym Pseudacris triseriata feriarum); 'southeastern chorus frog' is the batch's name.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States: southeastern Missouri, northeastern Arkansas and eastern Mississippi east to coastal Virginia and the Carolinas, north to central and southern Pennsylvania, south to northern Florida. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small; females 25-33 mm, males 23-31 mm; brown, tan or gray.
Three stripes (sometimes broken into spots) down the back, often a dark triangle between the eyes (absent in some South Carolina populations).
Belly light tan to white; breeding males have brownish-yellow throats; calls a trill.

habitat.text: Meadows, moist forests, bottomland swamps and areas near ponds and bogs; mainly upland in the north and lowland in the south; uses ditches, flooded pastures and rain pools.

behavior.text: Breeds in temporary pools, not permanent water; choruses can be heard by day and night in the breeding season.
Does not wander more than about 200 m from breeding sites after breeding and is found in leaf litter; southern populations may stay active all year.
Insectivore eating ants, beetles, flies, caterpillars, springtails, mites and snails; sit-and-wait feeder.

resources.title: Southern chorus frog
resources.description: Identify the southern chorus frog (Pseudacris nigrita), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southern chorus frog (Pseudacris nigrita): Small; males 21-30 mm, females 22-33 mm snout-vent; light gray to tan, brown or black with blackish stripes or spots in three rows. White line along the pointed snout and upper lip, dark band through the eye; skin with small warts. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern coast of the United States: Florida, southern Georgia, eastern South Carolina and North Carolina (north to the Tar and Pamlico Rivers), west to southern Alabama and Mississippi, with a disjunct population in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern coast of the United States: Florida, southern Georgia, eastern South Carolina and North Carolina (north to the Tar and Pamlico Rivers), west to southern Alabama and Mississippi, with a disjunct population in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small; males 21-30 mm, females 22-33 mm snout-vent; light gray to tan, brown or black with blackish stripes or spots in three rows.
White line along the pointed snout and upper lip, dark band through the eye; skin with small warts.
No stripe on the rear of the thighs; rear toes weakly webbed.
Breeding males have a dark (olive or rusty orange) throat.

habitat.text: Pine flatwoods, pine-oak forests, sandhills and disturbed areas; breeds in flooded grassy depressions, roadside ditches, pond margins and temporary pools.

behavior.text: Mostly nocturnal, though males may call by day around dusk; breeds from fall to early spring (winter peak) in the north and in any month in Florida, often after heavy rain.
Seldom found outside the breeding season; burrows or hides when conditions are poor; sexually mature at 1 year and few live longer.
Opportunistic insectivore; moves between wetlands and upland pine forest.

resources.title: Ornate chorus frog
resources.description: Identify the ornate chorus frog (Pseudacris ornata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ornate chorus frog (Pseudacris ornata): Small, 2.5-3.9 cm; gray, green, reddish-brown, sometimes blackish or silvery white. Black mask-like stripe through each eye, often extending along the side of the body. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, absent from southern peninsular Florida. Not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, absent from southern peninsular Florida. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, 2.5-3.9 cm; gray, green, reddish-brown, sometimes blackish or silvery white.
Black mask-like stripe through each eye, often extending along the side of the body.
Light-bordered black spots on sides and groin; yellow groin and inner thighs.
Call is a sharp metallic 'tink' or high peeps about 1-1.5 per second; breeding males have a dark throat.

habitat.text: Sandhills, pine flatwoods and upland pine forests; breeds in small fishless wetlands such as Carolina bays, flooded meadows, ditches and cypress ponds.

behavior.text: Secretive and nocturnal, rarely seen outside the winter breeding season (November-March).
Burrows into the ground among roots when inactive; migrates between breeding pools and upland habitat.
Females lay 10-100 eggs in clusters attached to vegetation; eats small terrestrial invertebrates.

resources.title: River cooter
resources.description: Identify the river cooter (Pseudemys concinna), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: River cooter (Pseudemys concinna): Shell up to about 43.7 cm, flattened, elongated and oval with light and dark brown markings plus green, yellow, brown and black patterns. Hatchlings 27-39 mm and bright green with light markings; markings darken with age. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central United States: northern Ohio south to northern Florida, eastern Virginia west to eastern Texas, with disjunct populations in the New River (VA/WV) and Tennessee River. Introduced in Europe (Spain) through the pet trade. Not native to Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe follows the Turtle Taxonomy Working Group (2021) in recognizing two subspecies and treating P. floridensis as a distinct species, while Crother (2017) recognizes P. suwanniensis as a separate species; Animal Diversity Web lists the species as Eastern River Cooter.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central United States: northern Ohio south to northern Florida, eastern Virginia west to eastern Texas, with disjunct populations in the New River (VA/WV) and Tennessee River. Introduced in Europe (Spain) through the pet trade. Not native to Canada.

identification.text: Shell up to about 43.7 cm, flattened, elongated and oval with light and dark brown markings plus green, yellow, brown and black patterns.
Hatchlings 27-39 mm and bright green with light markings; markings darken with age.
Females larger (mean carapace about 287 mm) than males (about 223 mm); males have flatter shells and elongated foreclaws.

habitat.text: Permanent rivers and lakes with current, aquatic vegetation, basking sites and rocky bottoms; occasionally ponds, springs, swamps and brackish tidal marshes.

behavior.text: Active about April-October across most of the range; hibernates in mud at the bottom of rivers, lakes and ponds in colder areas.
Mostly herbivorous, eating aquatic vegetation, algae and pondweeds; juveniles take more crayfish and animal prey.
Basks by day and nests on land within about 30 m of water; males court females by stroking their faces with long claws.

resources.title: Mud salamander
resources.description: Identify the mud salamander (Pseudotriton montanus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Mud salamander (Pseudotriton montanus): Stocky, coral pink, bright red, rusty or brownish-salmon with a short tail; 7-17 cm. Dorsal black spots distinct or obscure; older individuals darker; belly reddish or yellowish; eyes brown. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States from southern New York to northern Florida and from the Atlantic coast west to Kentucky and Tennessee. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Fouquette and Dubois (2014) moved this species to Gyrinophilus (not adopted by Crother 2017) and that P. m. diastictus was elevated to species by Collins (1991) but is retained as a subspecies by Crother (2017).

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States from southern New York to northern Florida and from the Atlantic coast west to Kentucky and Tennessee. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Stocky, coral pink, bright red, rusty or brownish-salmon with a short tail; 7-17 cm.
Dorsal black spots distinct or obscure; older individuals darker; belly reddish or yellowish; eyes brown.
16-18 costal grooves; red salamander has a yellow iris and longer snout.
Compared with the red salamander: Red salamander has a yellow iris and a longer snout; mud salamander has brown eyes.

habitat.text: Muddy springs, slow floodplain streams, swamps, bogs and beaver-pond backwaters; under logs and rocks, in decaying vegetation, muddy bank burrows and crayfish holes.

behavior.text: Secretive and difficult to find; retreats into burrows, stays at the burrow entrance, and builds underground passages and underwater tunnels.
Not migratory; eats earthworms, insects, arthropods and possibly other salamanders.
Females lay 65-200 eggs in late fall to early winter, apparently every other year; larvae take 14-32 months to metamorphose.

resources.title: Red salamander
resources.description: Identify the red salamander (Pseudotriton ruber), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Red salamander (Pseudotriton ruber): Bright orange-red to red above with scattered black spots; black chin; short tail; about 16 body grooves; 11-18 cm. Older adults fade to purplish-brown with larger spots. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States from New York south along the Appalachians to the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, Alabama and the western Florida panhandle; absent from the Coastal Plain of Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. NatureServe lists a Canadian national record (CA), but no Canadian range was sourced.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe recognizes four subspecies (ruber, nitidus, schencki, vioscai) that Folt et al. (2016) found are not monophyletic lineages.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States from New York south along the Appalachians to the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, Alabama and the western Florida panhandle; absent from the Coastal Plain of Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. NatureServe lists a Canadian national record (CA), but no Canadian range was sourced.

identification.text: Bright orange-red to red above with scattered black spots; black chin; short tail; about 16 body grooves; 11-18 cm.
Older adults fade to purplish-brown with larger spots.
Larvae purplish-brown above with a yellowish underside and black spots.
Yellow iris and longer snout than the mud salamander.
Compared with the mud salamander: Mud salamander has brown eyes and a shorter snout; red salamander has a yellow iris.
Compared with the eastern newt: Newt skin is rough and lacks prominent grooves; red salamander has about 16 grooves and a black chin.

habitat.text: Cold, clear, rocky streams and springs in wooded or open areas; adults in leaf litter, under rocks and in crevices and burrows near water, sometimes in caves.

behavior.text: Mainly nocturnal; adults move from streams to terrestrial shelter in spring and return in late summer or fall to breed.
Eats aquatic and terrestrial insects, earthworms, snails, slugs, spiders and small salamanders; larvae eat aquatic flies and crustaceans.
Larval stage lasts 18-33 months; females lay 50-100 eggs in fall under rocks in water; aposematic coloration resembles the toxic eastern newt.

resources.title: Graham's crayfish snake
resources.description: Identify the graham's crayfish snake (Regina grahamii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Graham's crayfish snake (Regina grahamii): Medium-sized, dull semiaquatic snake; brown to yellowish-brown above with a broad yellowish-tan stripe along each lower side, sometimes edged by a thin dark line. May show a faint tan stripe down the middle of the back. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central United States only, per NatureServe: Arkansas, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas; not listed for Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and the Missouri Department of Conservation spell the common name 'Graham's crawfish snake'; NatureServe notes the genus Regina is polyphyletic and awaits further study.

rangeSummary.value: Central United States only, per NatureServe: Arkansas, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas; not listed for Canada.

identification.text: Medium-sized, dull semiaquatic snake; brown to yellowish-brown above with a broad yellowish-tan stripe along each lower side, sometimes edged by a thin dark line.
May show a faint tan stripe down the middle of the back.
Chin and throat cream to yellow; belly cream or light yellow with a faint central row of gray or light-brown dots and a dark zigzag along both edges.
Adults 18-28 in (occasionally to 47 in).

Compared with the northern cottonmouth: The venomous cottonmouth is heavier-bodied with a large chunky head, a facial pit between nostril and eye, a darker body and a light line from eye to mouth corner (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Sluggish streams, river-bottom sloughs, bayous, pond and lake margins, marshes, swamps, rice fields and roadside ditches, often in water-edge vegetation or crayfish burrows.
In Missouri it favours the grassy edges of marshes and prairie streams and is absent from the Ozarks.

behavior.text: Feeds mainly, sometimes only, on molting or freshly molted crayfish; also frogs, snails, shrimp, small fish and salamanders.
Active spring to early November in Missouri with peaks in April-May and October; nocturnal in hot summer weather, otherwise diurnal or crepuscular.
Basks on branches over water in spring and early summer; shelters under rocks or logs and in crayfish burrows, including in winter.
Gives birth to live young (litters of 6-39) in July-September.

resources.title: Glossy crayfish snake
resources.description: Identify the glossy crayfish snake (Regina rigida), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Glossy crayfish snake (Regina rigida): Small, heavy-bodied snake, usually 14-24 in; glossy brown to olive-brown, sometimes with a faint dark stripe down the back and each side. Yellow lip scales contrast sharply with the olive-brown head; lower sides yellowish-tan. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States, per NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia; in Florida from Osceola County northwest into the Panhandle.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and the Florida Museum treat this snake as Liodytes rigida (Glossy Swampsnake), with Regina rigida as a synonym; Animal Diversity Web still files it as Regina rigida.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States, per NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia; in Florida from Osceola County northwest into the Panhandle.

identification.text: Small, heavy-bodied snake, usually 14-24 in; glossy brown to olive-brown, sometimes with a faint dark stripe down the back and each side.
Yellow lip scales contrast sharply with the olive-brown head; lower sides yellowish-tan.
Belly yellow or cream with two rows of small black half-moon markings.
Keeled scales in 19 rows at midbody; relatively large eyes with round pupils.
Compared with the striped swampsnake (striped crayfish snake): Unpatterned belly and smooth body scales, versus keeled scales and a half-moon-marked belly in the glossy swampsnake (Florida Museum).
Compared with the black swampsnake: Glossy black with a bright red belly (Florida Museum).

habitat.text: Slow-moving lowland waters: cypress swamps, marshes, bogs, ponds, lakes, ditches, rice fields, streams and floodplains.
Usually secluded in crayfish or muskrat burrows, under wet vegetation or debris at the water's edge, or among aquatic plants; rarely far from water.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; feeds mainly on crayfish, also small fishes, salamanders and small frogs.
Adults eat mainly crayfish; the young take small aquatic invertebrates such as dragonfly larvae.
Flees into water and dives to the bottom when approached; a captured snake may flatten its head and release musk.
Gives birth to live young (6-16) in summer; active March to early November in Texas.

resources.title: Queen snake
resources.description: Identify the queen snake (Regina septemvittata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Queen snake (Regina septemvittata): Slender semiaquatic snake, 34-92 cm; brownish or olive above with a yellow stripe along each side extending onto the lip scales. Belly bright yellow with four brownish lengthwise stripes converging toward the tail. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States from the southern Great Lakes to the Florida panhandle and east to the Carolinas, north to Pennsylvania and New York; in Canada only southern Ontario (Georgian Bay, Bois Blanc Island), ranked N2 and listed Endangered under SARA.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes that one study nests Regina septemvittata within Nerodia and another relates it to Tropidoclonion; Crother (2017) retained Regina pending further study.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States from the southern Great Lakes to the Florida panhandle and east to the Carolinas, north to Pennsylvania and New York; in Canada only southern Ontario (Georgian Bay, Bois Blanc Island), ranked N2 and listed Endangered under SARA.

identification.text: Slender semiaquatic snake, 34-92 cm; brownish or olive above with a yellow stripe along each side extending onto the lip scales.
Belly bright yellow with four brownish lengthwise stripes converging toward the tail.
Keeled scales (19 rows at midbody), round pupils, divided anal plate; no light stripe down the back, unlike garter snakes.
Young show dark horizontal bands on the back.
Compared with the garter snakes: Garter snakes have a light dorsal stripe and an undivided anal plate; queen snakes lack a dorsal stripe and have a divided anal plate (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Occurs only where crayfish are abundant, generally in moderate to fast-flowing streams with rocky or sandy bottoms, cover and sun exposure.
Sometimes uses ditches, canals, marsh or pond edges, but is usually scarce there.

behavior.text: Eats almost exclusively crayfish, preferring freshly molted ones; occasionally small fish and amphibian larvae.
Diurnal and solitary outside breeding; basks on rocks, logs and branches overhanging the water.
Active May-September in the north, and year-round in warm climates; hibernates in crayfish or mammal burrows in the north.
Live-bearing; 5-31 young born July to early September.

resources.title: Pine woods snake
resources.description: Identify the pine woods snake (Rhadinaea flavilata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pine woods snake (Rhadinaea flavilata): Slender, smooth-scaled snake, usually 25-33 cm (to about 40 cm); yellowish-brown to reddish-brown, paler on the lower sides. Dark line from the snout through the eye to the jaw corner; lips plain white or yellowish in Florida but often dark-speckled in the north and west of the range. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern coastal plain of the United States only: Alabama, Florida (most of the peninsula south to near Lake Okeechobee plus the central panhandle), Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard name is 'Pine Woods Littersnake'; 'Pine Woods Snake' is given as an alternate name.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern coastal plain of the United States only: Alabama, Florida (most of the peninsula south to near Lake Okeechobee plus the central panhandle), Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina.

identification.text: Slender, smooth-scaled snake, usually 25-33 cm (to about 40 cm); yellowish-brown to reddish-brown, paler on the lower sides.
Dark line from the snout through the eye to the jaw corner; lips plain white or yellowish in Florida but often dark-speckled in the north and west of the range.
Belly white, cream or yellowish; 17 scale rows behind the neck, divided anal plate, round pupils.
Often a faint dark stripe down the middle of the back and another on each side.

habitat.text: Damp pine flatwoods, slash and longleaf pine woodland maintained by periodic fire; also hardwood hammocks near flatwoods, sandhills near water and wooded wet-prairie edges.

behavior.text: Secretive and fossorial; found under loose bark, in or under rotting logs and stumps, leaf litter or buried in sandy soil.
Active on the surface chiefly at night; most active in spring and may be active year-round.
Eats small amphibians and reptiles (lizards, frogs, salamanders); rear teeth deliver a mild venom to immobilise prey and it does not bite when handled.
Lays 2-4 eggs, usually in rotting wood, from late April or May through August.

resources.title: Couch's spadefoot
resources.description: Identify the couch's spadefoot (Scaphiopus couchii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Couch's spadefoot (Scaphiopus couchii): Stout toad-like amphibian, 5.6-8.8 cm; bright green-yellow to brown-yellow with dark green, brown or black mottling (more extensive in females), white belly. Vertically elliptical pupil in bright light and a single hard, black, sickle-shaped spade on each hind foot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern United States (Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas) into northern Mexico and Baja California; not found in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern United States (Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas) into northern Mexico and Baja California; not found in Canada.

identification.text: Stout toad-like amphibian, 5.6-8.8 cm; bright green-yellow to brown-yellow with dark green, brown or black mottling (more extensive in females), white belly.
Vertically elliptical pupil in bright light and a single hard, black, sickle-shaped spade on each hind foot.
Parotoid glands present but indistinct; skin with many small warts.
Breeding male has dark patches on the inner three digits and a large, rounded vocal sac; call is a harsh lamb- or goat-like bleat lasting 0.5-1 s.

habitat.text: Arid and semi-arid shrublands, shortgrass plains, mesquite savanna, creosote-bush desert, thornforest and cultivated areas; eggs are attached to vegetation in shallow rain pools.

behavior.text: Nocturnal; spends most of its time underground in burrows dug backwards with the hind spades, and surfaces after heavy rains.
Breeds explosively after heavy spring or summer rains, often in a single night, in temporary pools; eggs hatch within about 36 hours and metamorphosis takes about 1-2 weeks if pools persist.
Eats mostly insects and other small terrestrial arthropods; can go about ten months without feeding while dormant.

resources.title: Eastern spadefoot
resources.description: Identify the eastern spadefoot (Scaphiopus holbrookii), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern spadefoot (Scaphiopus holbrookii): Stout toadlike amphibian to about 7 cm; light to dark brown, olive or blackish above, mottled with dark brown, with a yellow lyre-shaped pair of lines down the back. Large protruding eyes with vertically elliptical pupils; no raised boss between the eyes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and southeastern United States from Massachusetts to Florida and west to the Mississippi River basin; absent from higher Appalachian elevations; not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and southeastern United States from Massachusetts to Florida and west to the Mississippi River basin; absent from higher Appalachian elevations; not in Canada.

identification.text: Stout toadlike amphibian to about 7 cm; light to dark brown, olive or blackish above, mottled with dark brown, with a yellow lyre-shaped pair of lines down the back.
Large protruding eyes with vertically elliptical pupils; no raised boss between the eyes.
Single sickle-shaped black spade on the inner side of each hind foot; skin with small warts and small parotoid glands.
Male call is a coarse nasal 'wank' or 'quonk' repeated every few seconds.
Compared with the plains spadefoot: Has a raised boss between the eyes and a wedge-shaped spade at the base of each hind foot (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Sandy, gravelly or loose soils in wooded or open terrain, including sand prairies, pastures, farmland and suburbs; uses temporary rain-filled pools for breeding.

behavior.text: Nocturnal burrower that spends most of the time underground, becoming active on warm, damp or rainy nights.
Breeds whenever heavy rains fill temporary pools and temperatures exceed about 45 F; breeding groups may number dozens to hundreds; larvae can metamorphose in as little as 2 weeks.
Eats ants, beetles, flies, grasshoppers, crickets, termites and worms; skin secretions can irritate people, so wash hands after handling.

resources.title: Southwestern fence lizard
resources.description: Identify the southwestern fence lizard (Sceloporus cowlesi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southwestern fence lizard (Sceloporus cowlesi): Small lizard (to about 76 mm snout-vent), gray-brown to golden-brown with pointed, keeled, overlapping scales and two light stripes on the back. Males have two large bright-blue belly patches usually edged dark gray or black, and two blue blotches on the throat; belly patches faint or absent in females. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southwestern United States: southern and eastern Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (NatureServe also lists Navajo Nation) into northern Chihuahua; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web lists cowlesi only as a subspecies of Sceloporus undulatus; NatureServe and the Arizona field guide treat it as a full species.

rangeSummary.value: Southwestern United States: southern and eastern Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (NatureServe also lists Navajo Nation) into northern Chihuahua; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small lizard (to about 76 mm snout-vent), gray-brown to golden-brown with pointed, keeled, overlapping scales and two light stripes on the back.
Males have two large bright-blue belly patches usually edged dark gray or black, and two blue blotches on the throat; belly patches faint or absent in females.
Gravid females often have an orange or yellow tint on the back.
Paired throat blotches separate it from the common sagebrush lizard; lack of side blotches separates it from the side-blotched lizard.

Compared with the plateau lizard (striped plateau lizard): Nearly identical in appearance to the southwestern fence lizard but genetically distinct, and its boundary with cowlesi is poorly known; the striped plateau lizard has a plain belly (Reptiles of Arizona).

habitat.text: Usually open, sunlit areas with basking sites such as rock piles and logs, from Chihuahuan desertscrub and grassland to woodland and montane conifer forest.

behavior.text: Diurnal; most active mid-morning and late afternoon in summer and all day in spring and fall.
Sit-and-wait forager that takes the ground but climbs rocks, trees, fence posts and wood piles to bask.
Eats termites, ants, beetles, grasshoppers, flies, spiders, snails and small lizards; females lay eggs from mid-May to mid-August (7-9 eggs in New Mexico).

resources.title: Eastern fence lizard
resources.description: Identify the eastern fence lizard (Sceloporus undulatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern fence lizard (Sceloporus undulatus): Gray, brown or rusty lizard, 9-19 cm total length, with keeled scales. Males have a blue patch on the belly and throat; colour varies geographically. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia); Animal Diversity Web gives the broader concept as mid New York to mid Florida and west to Colorado; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes Leache and Reeder (2002) proposed splitting S. undulatus into several species (east of Mobile Bay keeps the name); Animal Diversity Web still treats S. undulatus broadly, including subspecies now proposed as S. cowlesi, S. tristichus and S. consobrinus.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia); Animal Diversity Web gives the broader concept as mid New York to mid Florida and west to Colorado; not in Canada.

identification.text: Gray, brown or rusty lizard, 9-19 cm total length, with keeled scales.
Males have a blue patch on the belly and throat; colour varies geographically.
Northern populations (New York to Maryland) are generally smaller than southern ones.

habitat.text: Mostly arboreal in wooded landscapes in open, sunny situations; also grasslands, shrublands and the edges of pine or hardwood forests.

behavior.text: Diurnal, active roughly 0600-2000 h; basks on fences, logs, rocks, wood piles and tree trunks, using trunks and branches more in summer.
Males head-bob, do push-ups and flash the blue belly patches to signal territory; territories are roughly 47-61 square metres.
Eats mostly insects, spiders, centipedes and occasionally snails; inactive in cold periods and the hottest part of summer days.

resources.title: Ground skink
resources.description: Identify the ground skink (Scincella lateralis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ground skink (Scincella lateralis): Tiny skink with smooth, shiny scales, cylindrical body, conical head and short legs; light tan to golden-brown above. Dark brown to black stripe along each side extending onto the tail; belly white or yellow. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central-eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia) and northern Mexico; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard common name is 'Little Brown Skink'; 'Ground Skink' is listed as an alternate name.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central-eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia) and northern Mexico; not in Canada.

identification.text: Tiny skink with smooth, shiny scales, cylindrical body, conical head and short legs; light tan to golden-brown above.
Dark brown to black stripe along each side extending onto the tail; belly white or yellow.
Total length averages about 146 mm (75-146 mm range); females have larger heads, males longer tails.
Juveniles are bronze with black specks; adults can drop and regrow the tail.

habitat.text: Humid deciduous forest, dry upland woodland, stream and pond edges, and vacant lots or building edges in suburbs, always where ground cover (leaf litter, logs, rocks) is present.

behavior.text: Diurnal and ground-dwelling, basking and moving through leaf litter; generally does not climb.
Active March-October in the north and all year in Florida; goes underground in cold weather.
Eats termites, millipedes, roaches, ants, beetle larvae, caterpillars and other small arthropods, finding prey by sight and smell.

resources.title: Green ratsnake
resources.description: Identify the green ratsnake (Senticolis triaspis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Green ratsnake (Senticolis triaspis): Long, slender snake (to about 1.8 m); adults over about 800 mm are uniform gray-green, green or yellowish-green above. Belly white to yellowish and unmarked; head elongated and broader than the neck, tail long (23-37% of total length), anal plate divided. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Northern edge of a largely tropical range: southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico in the United States (state rank S1, state-threatened in New Mexico), south to Costa Rica; not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Northern edge of a largely tropical range: southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico in the United States (state rank S1, state-threatened in New Mexico), south to Costa Rica; not in Canada.

identification.text: Long, slender snake (to about 1.8 m); adults over about 800 mm are uniform gray-green, green or yellowish-green above.
Belly white to yellowish and unmarked; head elongated and broader than the neck, tail long (23-37% of total length), anal plate divided.
Hatchlings and juveniles are tan or gray with dark blotches that fade with age.
Compared with the glossy snake: Juvenile green ratsnakes resemble glossy snakes, but glossy snakes lack the elongated head and have an undivided anal plate (Tucson Herpetological Society).
Compared with the coachwhip: Young coachwhips have 17 scale rows at midbody and no elongated head distinct from the neck (Tucson Herpetological Society).

habitat.text: Montane woodland and chaparral, in Arizona mostly oak woodland and savanna and adjoining semidesert grassland, often on rocky canyons with water.

behavior.text: Active mostly mid-March to late November in Arizona; diurnal and crepuscular.
Both terrestrial and arboreal; uses rock crevices or burrows for shelter.
Eats mainly rodents, also other small mammals, birds and lizards, killed by constriction.

resources.title: Lesser siren
resources.description: Identify the lesser siren (Siren intermedia), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Lesser siren (Siren intermedia): Eel-like, permanently aquatic salamander with external gills and forelimbs only (four toes each), no hind limbs. Gray to brown to nearly black with a lighter belly; 31-38 costal grooves; adults 18-69 cm. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States; NatureServe lists Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia under the current name, while Animal Diversity Web's older concept runs from Virginia to Florida and west to eastern Texas and up the Mississippi drainage; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (citing Fedler et al. 2023) splits the former S. intermedia complex, elevating S. i. nettingi to a species and describing a new species, so its current S. intermedia range is narrower than the older concept used by Animal Diversity Web; NatureServe lists the name 'Intermediate Siren'.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States; NatureServe lists Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia under the current name, while Animal Diversity Web's older concept runs from Virginia to Florida and west to eastern Texas and up the Mississippi drainage; not in Canada.

identification.text: Eel-like, permanently aquatic salamander with external gills and forelimbs only (four toes each), no hind limbs.
Gray to brown to nearly black with a lighter belly; 31-38 costal grooves; adults 18-69 cm.
Hatchlings have a red or yellow band across the snout and sides of the head and bold longitudinal stripes that fade with growth.

habitat.text: Shallow, warm, quiet, sometimes turbid water with abundant vegetation: swamps, sloughs, ponds, lakes, ditches and, less often, streams.

behavior.text: Nocturnal bottom forager that hides among plants and debris by day; clicks and yelps are its sounds.
Survives drought by burrowing into mud and forming a mucous cocoon; can aestivate for weeks to over a year.
Eats aquatic invertebrates (crayfish, worms, mollusks), amphibian eggs and larvae, and some plant material; most active in fall and winter in a Louisiana pond.

resources.title: Pygmy rattlesnake
resources.description: Identify the pygmy rattlesnake (Sistrurus miliarius), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Pygmy rattlesnake (Sistrurus miliarius): Small rattlesnake, usually 38-64 cm; grey, tan, brown or reddish with alternating dark mid-dorsal and lateral blotches and an orange-brown dorsal stripe in some. Dark stripe from the eye to the corner of the mouth, heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril, keeled scales, single anal plate. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes that some authors place Sistrurus within Crotalus because Crotalus is paraphyletic without it; the genus name Sistrurus is still in standard use.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small rattlesnake, usually 38-64 cm; grey, tan, brown or reddish with alternating dark mid-dorsal and lateral blotches and an orange-brown dorsal stripe in some.
Dark stripe from the eye to the corner of the mouth, heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril, keeled scales, single anal plate.
Tiny rattle with a faint buzz like a grasshopper, audible only about a yard away; juveniles have a bright yellow tail tip that darkens with age.
Compared with the timber rattlesnake: Adults are 3-5 ft long with a large rattle, versus a tiny rattle on the pygmy rattlesnake (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Mainly moist or wet lowlands: wet prairies and savannas, pine flatwoods, swamps, floodplains, sandhills and pond or canal edges; in Missouri, south-facing rocky partly wooded hillsides.

behavior.text: Solitary, reclusive and sedentary, sheltering under logs, brush, stumps or in small-mammal burrows; will flee but may strike if cornered.
Ambush predator that eats lizards, snakes, frogs, insects, centipedes, nestling birds and small mammals; juveniles lure prey with the tail tip.
In Florida seen most often July-November; in the north activity peaks June-September.

resources.title: Razorback musk turtle
resources.description: Identify the razorback musk turtle (Sternotherus carinatus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Razorback musk turtle (Sternotherus carinatus): Small turtle, carapace about 10-12 cm; high, triangular, domed shell with a prominent medial keel; scutes light brown to orange with dark streaks that fade with age. Yellowish plastron that is reduced and weakly hinged, with ten rather than eleven scutes (no gular scute). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: South-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Texas (Brazos River in Texas to the Pascagoula River in Mississippi); not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard name is 'Razor-backed Musk Turtle' with 'Keeled Musk Turtle' and 'Razorback Musk Turtle' as alternates.

rangeSummary.value: South-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Texas (Brazos River in Texas to the Pascagoula River in Mississippi); not in Canada.

identification.text: Small turtle, carapace about 10-12 cm; high, triangular, domed shell with a prominent medial keel; scutes light brown to orange with dark streaks that fade with age.
Yellowish plastron that is reduced and weakly hinged, with ten rather than eleven scutes (no gular scute).
Skin gray to pink to light brown with small dark spots; slightly hooked jaws with dark streaks, pair of chin barbels and a tubular snout.
Males have longer, thicker tails and rough scale patches on the thighs.

habitat.text: Medium to large flowing streams and rivers, also swamps and lakes, with soft or sandy/rocky bottoms, aquatic vegetation and basking deadwood.

behavior.text: Diurnal, active mornings and late afternoons; spends more time basking high on deadwood than other musk turtles.
Hibernates underwater; active roughly March-November in Oklahoma and largely crepuscular in summer.
Omnivorous bottom feeder on insects, crustaceans, mollusks (including invasive Asian clams), amphibian larvae, carrion and aquatic plants.

resources.title: Loggerhead musk turtle
resources.description: Identify the loggerhead musk turtle (Sternotherus minor), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Loggerhead musk turtle (Sternotherus minor): Small musk turtle, carapace roughly 7.5-14.5 cm; dark brown to orange shell with a darker border. Brown or gray skin with spots, bolder in juveniles; webbed feet. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States; NatureServe restricts the species to river drainages in Alabama, Georgia and Florida (Athens, Georgia south to near Orlando), while the broader older concept reaches central Florida north to Virginia and west to Louisiana; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe (following Scott et al. 2018 and SSAR 2025) restricts S. minor to the Atlantic/Gulf drainages of Alabama, Georgia and Florida, elevating S. m. peltifer and recognising S. intermedius; Animal Diversity Web still covers S. m. minor and S. m. peltifer under one species.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States; NatureServe restricts the species to river drainages in Alabama, Georgia and Florida (Athens, Georgia south to near Orlando), while the broader older concept reaches central Florida north to Virginia and west to Louisiana; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small musk turtle, carapace roughly 7.5-14.5 cm; dark brown to orange shell with a darker border.
Brown or gray skin with spots, bolder in juveniles; webbed feet.
Males have thicker, longer tails and older males have enlarged heads; the stripe-necked form (S. m. peltifer) has yellow stripes on the neck.

habitat.text: Permanent freshwater including springs, sinkhole ponds, rivers, swamps and oxbow lakes with rock or sand bottoms and often dense vegetation; shelters in crayfish burrows, under submerged logs and in rock crevices.

behavior.text: Aquatic, diurnal and nocturnal with morning activity; basks on limbs and females leave water to nest.
Hibernates in rock crevices or bottom mud in cooler waters; can stay submerged for long periods.
Adults shift to a mollusc diet (snails and clams) while juveniles eat small insects; often forages at night.

resources.title: Stinkpot
resources.description: Identify the stinkpot (Sternotherus odoratus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Stinkpot (Sternotherus odoratus): Small turtle, adults 100-127 mm; narrow, elongated brown domed carapace with black streaks or spots, often algae-covered. Two light (pale yellow) stripes on each side of the head, one above and one below the eye, distinguish it from other Sternotherus. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central United States from southern Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin to Florida and east Texas (absent from higher elevations); in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N3; federally Special Concern).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard name is 'Eastern Musk Turtle'; 'Stinkpot' and 'Common Musk Turtle' are alternates.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central United States from southern Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin to Florida and east Texas (absent from higher elevations); in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N3; federally Special Concern).

identification.text: Small turtle, adults 100-127 mm; narrow, elongated brown domed carapace with black streaks or spots, often algae-covered.
Two light (pale yellow) stripes on each side of the head, one above and one below the eye, distinguish it from other Sternotherus.
Elongated pointed snout with barbels on the chin and neck; small yellow plastron with a single non-functional hinge and skin showing between the plastral scutes.
Males have larger heads and longer tails than females.
Compared with the striped mud turtle: Mud turtles have two plastral hinges and unkeeled carapaces, and lack skin visible between plastral scutes (Animal Diversity Web).
Compared with the eastern mud turtle: Two hinges on the plastron and a never-keeled carapace; stinkpots show skin between plastron scutes (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Virtually any permanent freshwater with slow current and soft bottom and plenty of aquatic plants: ponds, lakes, impoundments, streams, rivers and swamps.

behavior.text: Mostly aquatic and crepuscular (more nocturnal in the south); bottom walker that basks on branches up to 2 m above the water and may drop into passing boats.
Brumates buried about 30 cm in mud when water is below about 10 C; active April-October in the north.
Threatened animals release a foul-smelling orange musk from glands under the shell.
Omnivorous: algae, seeds, insects, mollusks, crayfish, carrion and fish.

resources.title: Brown snake
resources.description: Identify the brown snake (Storeria dekayi), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Brown snake (Storeria dekayi): Small, stout snake rarely over about 13-15 in; grayish-brown to reddish-brown with a lighter stripe down the back bordered by two rows of small dark spots. Dark spot under each eye and on each side of the neck; heavily keeled scales (17 rows) and divided anal plate; belly cream, yellow or pink. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States (east of the Rockies) and northern Mexico; in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N5).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard name is 'Dekay's Brownsnake' and notes some authors treat Storeria victa as a separate species; Missouri Department of Conservation says former subspecies are no longer recognised.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States (east of the Rockies) and northern Mexico; in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N5).

identification.text: Small, stout snake rarely over about 13-15 in; grayish-brown to reddish-brown with a lighter stripe down the back bordered by two rows of small dark spots.
Dark spot under each eye and on each side of the neck; heavily keeled scales (17 rows) and divided anal plate; belly cream, yellow or pink.
Young are black or dark gray with a light neck ring but keeled scales separate them from ring-necked snakes.
Compared with the ring-necked snake: Young brown snakes have a pale neck ring but keeled scales, which ring-necked snakes lack (Animal Diversity Web).

Compared with the red-bellied snake: Close relative with a tan back stripe bordered by two rows of small dark spots and a cream, yellow or pink belly, versus the red-bellied snake's red, orange or pink belly and three light nape spots (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Nearly all terrestrial and wetland habitat types including cities: moist forests, woodland edges along ravines and creeks, and grasslands near wetlands; hibernates underground or beneath buildings, often communally.

behavior.text: Secretive, hides under stones, boards and debris; most active late March to early November; often seen crossing roads in spring and fall.
Eats earthworms, slugs and snails (one study 75% slugs); specialised teeth help pull snails from their shells.
When threatened flattens its body and releases musk; gives birth to 3-41 young from mid-July to September.

resources.title: Redbelly snake
resources.description: Identify the redbelly snake (Storeria occipitomaculata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Redbelly snake (Storeria occipitomaculata): Very small snake, 20-41 cm; gray, brown or reddish-brown, often with four faint dark stripes and/or a pale or red-orange mid-dorsal stripe. Belly usually bright red, orange or pink (rarely yellow, gray or black). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern North America: United States from eastern North Dakota and Wyoming (Black Hills) to the Atlantic and Gulf; in Canada Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island (NatureServe also shows Newfoundland as an exotic record).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe gives 'Red-bellied Snake' as its standard name and questions the validity of the subspecies pahasapae; Missouri Department of Conservation says subspecies are no longer recognised.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern North America: United States from eastern North Dakota and Wyoming (Black Hills) to the Atlantic and Gulf; in Canada Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island (NatureServe also shows Newfoundland as an exotic record).

identification.text: Very small snake, 20-41 cm; gray, brown or reddish-brown, often with four faint dark stripes and/or a pale or red-orange mid-dorsal stripe.
Belly usually bright red, orange or pink (rarely yellow, gray or black).
Three light spots around the neck (top and each side) sometimes fuse into a collar; white chin and throat, keeled scales (15 rows), divided anal plate.
Compared with the copperhead (young): Copperheads are stout-bodied with hourglass markings, vertical pupils and a pit between nostril and eye (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Compared with the dekay's brownsnake: Brownsnake has a tan back stripe flanked by two rows of small dark spots and a cream, yellow or pink belly, whereas the red-bellied snake typically has a red or orange belly and three light nape spots (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Mostly moist deciduous and mixed forests, bog and swamp edges and adjacent meadows with abundant ground cover; often near buildings.

behavior.text: Secretive, hiding under bark, logs, rocks and leaf litter; diurnal but nocturnal in hot or dry weather, more active after rain.
Specialist feeder on slugs and snails, also earthworms and insect larvae; hibernates in ant mounds, foundations and animal burrows.
Active April to October/November in the north and year-round in the south; migrates between floodplain and hillside overwintering sites.

resources.title: Southeastern crowned snake
resources.description: Identify the southeastern crowned snake (Tantilla coronata), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Southeastern crowned snake (Tantilla coronata): Very small, slender snake, about 8-10 in (Louisiana reports 6-13 in) with smooth scales in 15 rows. Black or dark-brown head, a light collar, then a black neck band; body light brown, tan or reddish-brown, unpatterned. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern United States from North Carolina west to Louisiana, with an isolated population in Kentucky (Indiana also records it); generally absent from southern Georgia and peninsular Florida; not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern United States from North Carolina west to Louisiana, with an isolated population in Kentucky (Indiana also records it); generally absent from southern Georgia and peninsular Florida; not in Canada.

identification.text: Very small, slender snake, about 8-10 in (Louisiana reports 6-13 in) with smooth scales in 15 rows.
Black or dark-brown head, a light collar, then a black neck band; body light brown, tan or reddish-brown, unpatterned.
Belly white, pink or yellowish; young resemble adults; tiny eyes.
Compared with the midland brownsnake: Lacks the black neck band and has keeled scales (Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency).
Compared with the red-bellied snake: Lacks the black neck band and has keeled scales (Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency).
Compared with the ring-necked snake: Has a bright yellow belly (Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency).

habitat.text: Dry, well-drained wooded ridges and hillsides, pine and oak woodland, sandy pine flatwoods and sandhills, always with cover such as rocks, logs and stumps.

behavior.text: Highly fossorial; burrows under rocks, woody debris, leaf litter and in rotting logs or stumps and is rarely seen except when cover is turned.
Eats centipedes, insect larvae, earthworms, spiders, termites and snails; small rear fangs do not threaten people.
Active March to October in the north; lays 1-3 eggs under cover in summer.

resources.title: Ringed wall gecko
resources.description: Identify the ringed wall gecko (Tarentola annularis), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Ringed wall gecko (Tarentola annularis): Large, stocky gecko, up to about 15 cm total length (USGS notes about 108 mm snout-vent). Gray to tan back covered with rows of large rough tubercular scales; a distinctive group of four white spots on the shoulders. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to northern and Saharan/sub-Saharan Africa. Introduced in the United States: Florida (known since the 1990s from scattered sites including Lee and Miami-Dade counties) and California (Redlands, San Bernardino County, since the early 2000s; San Juan Capistrano, Orange County, 2020); NatureServe lists it as non-native. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: USGS and GeckoWeb call the species the white-spotted wall gecko; NatureServe and the batch use 'ringed wall gecko'.

rangeSummary.value: Native to northern and Saharan/sub-Saharan Africa. Introduced in the United States: Florida (known since the 1990s from scattered sites including Lee and Miami-Dade counties) and California (Redlands, San Bernardino County, since the early 2000s; San Juan Capistrano, Orange County, 2020); NatureServe lists it as non-native. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Large, stocky gecko, up to about 15 cm total length (USGS notes about 108 mm snout-vent).
Gray to tan back covered with rows of large rough tubercular scales; a distinctive group of four white spots on the shoulders.
White belly with shingle-like round, slightly overlapping scales; large bulging eyes with fixed transparent covering.
Undivided toepads (house geckos have divided pads).
Compared with the common (moorish) wall gecko: Lacks the two pairs of white shoulder spots (GeckoWeb).
Compared with the bibron's thick-toed gecko: Lacks the pairs of white shoulder spots (GeckoWeb).

habitat.text: Introduced populations are associated with buildings and urban environs; in its native North African range habitat is desert.

behavior.text: In Florida lives on the walls of buildings; pugnacious, bites and squeaks when grabbed.
Preys on insects and smaller lizards, including house geckos; native-range clutches are 1-2 eggs, several per year.

resources.title: Eastern box turtle
resources.description: Identify the eastern box turtle (Terrapene carolina), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern box turtle (Terrapene carolina): Hinged plastron lets adults close the domed, keeled shell almost completely; upper jaw slightly hooked. Carapace colour highly variable: brown with yellow or orange markings in eastern box turtle (about 15 cm, four hind toes). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern United States from southern Maine to Florida and west to Michigan, Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. In Canada NatureServe treats Ontario as an exotic record and SARA lists the species as Extirpated.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe's standard name is 'American Box Turtle' (Terrapene carolina) and records disagreement over whether bauri and triunguis are subspecies or separate species; Crother (2017) recognised only carolina and triunguis.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern United States from southern Maine to Florida and west to Michigan, Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. In Canada NatureServe treats Ontario as an exotic record and SARA lists the species as Extirpated.

identification.text: Hinged plastron lets adults close the domed, keeled shell almost completely; upper jaw slightly hooked.
Carapace colour highly variable: brown with yellow or orange markings in eastern box turtle (about 15 cm, four hind toes).
Mature males often have red irises and a concave rear plastron; females have a flat plastron and vent at or inside the rear shell edge.
Three-toed box turtle (T. c. triunguis) has a tan or olive shell and three hind toes; males' heads may be entirely red.

habitat.text: Forests, fields, forest-brush and forest-field edges; open woodlands, pastures and marshy meadows, often near streams and ponds.

behavior.text: Diurnal; in summer activity is mostly morning and after rain; hibernates in October/November to March-May burrowed in loose soil, mud or stump holes.
Omnivore: snails, insects, berries, fungi, worms, carrion; young are mainly invertebrate eaters.
Home ranges are usually 2 ha or less and overlap; individuals often return to the same hibernation area.

resources.title: Western ribbon snake
resources.description: Identify the western ribbon snake (Thamnophis proximus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Western ribbon snake (Thamnophis proximus): Slender garter-snake relative, typically about 3 ft (max recorded snout-vent 1250 mm); dark brown or black back with lighter side stripes. Underside pale, usually light yellow or green; tail about 30% of body length and relatively long muzzle. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Central United States (NatureServe: Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin); Animal Diversity Web adds the range south through Mexico into Central America; not in Canada.

rangeSummary.value: Central United States (NatureServe: Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin); Animal Diversity Web adds the range south through Mexico into Central America; not in Canada.

identification.text: Slender garter-snake relative, typically about 3 ft (max recorded snout-vent 1250 mm); dark brown or black back with lighter side stripes.
Underside pale, usually light yellow or green; tail about 30% of body length and relatively long muzzle.
Large paired parietal spots; reduced or absent broad brown ventrolateral stripe that the very similar eastern ribbon snake shows.
Compared with the eastern ribbon snake: Eastern has a broad brown ventrolateral stripe; western has paired large parietal spots, a longer muzzle and longer tail (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Brushy habitats near streams, ponds, lakes, sloughs, ditches, swamps and marshes, often in water-edge vegetation; hibernation sites may be upland away from water.

behavior.text: Semi-aquatic and fast; dives into water or vanishes into brush or crevices when disturbed; active by day in warm periods.
Forages for frogs by making closed-mouth head thrusts in sets of three to flush them; amphibians make up an estimated 80-92% of the diet, with fish, snails and eggs also taken.
Active March to October in the north; hibernates in rocky outcrops or crevices, sometimes with other snakes and may migrate between winter and summer habitats.

resources.title: Eastern ribbon snake
resources.description: Identify the eastern ribbon snake (Thamnophis sauritus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Eastern ribbon snake (Thamnophis sauritus): Slim, long-tailed striped snake, 46-86 cm, with three white, yellow or greenish stripes on a black or dark-brown ground colour. Head wider than the neck with large eyes and a light bar in front of each; upper lip scales bright white or yellow without the dark borders of garter snakes. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern North America east of the Mississippi River from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Louisiana; in Canada Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia (NatureServe rank N4).

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe and Crother (2017) spell the species name 'saurita' (spelling corrected by Kraus and Cameron 2016); Animal Diversity Web and the batch use 'sauritus'. NatureServe also lists Great Lakes and Atlantic populations separately.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern North America east of the Mississippi River from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Louisiana; in Canada Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia (NatureServe rank N4).

identification.text: Slim, long-tailed striped snake, 46-86 cm, with three white, yellow or greenish stripes on a black or dark-brown ground colour.
Head wider than the neck with large eyes and a light bar in front of each; upper lip scales bright white or yellow without the dark borders of garter snakes.
Belly white, yellow or green and unblotched; scales keeled; females slightly larger than males.
Compared with the western ribbon snake: Western lacks the broad brown ventrolateral stripe and has large paired parietal spots and a longer muzzle and tail (Animal Diversity Web).
Compared with the garter snakes: Garter snakes have dark borders on the upper lip scales, whereas ribbon snake lip scales are plain white or yellow (Animal Diversity Web).

habitat.text: Wet meadows, marshes, seasonally flooded prairies, bogs, pond and lake shores and swamps, in or near sun-exposed vegetation along water's edge; climbs low vegetation.

behavior.text: Fast-moving and diurnal; usually at the edge of water but also in moist meadows; basks on logs and rocks and in bushes.
Active April-October, hibernating in abandoned rodent or crayfish burrows or anthills, sometimes with other snakes.
Eats mainly frogs, salamanders and their larvae plus small fish, taken by stalking or chasing; live-bearing with young 16-24 cm.

resources.title: Nile monitor
resources.description: Identify the nile monitor (Varanus niloticus), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Nile monitor (Varanus niloticus): Very large lizard: typical adults about 5 ft (up to about 2.4 m) with a neck longer than the narrow head and a laterally compressed, rudder-like tail about 1.5 times body length. Olive-green to black or brownish with cream or yellow stripes on the jaw and head and rows of yellowish V-shaped stripes from the neck that become bands or spots on the back.
