This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile valley. Non-native in the United States: established in Lee (Cape Coral) and Palm Beach counties, Florida; USGS NAS also records sightings in Georgia, Texas, Arizona, California and Virginia. Not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: Animal Diversity Web notes a former subspecies, now Varanus ornatus, is recognised as a separate species.

rangeSummary.value: Native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile valley. Non-native in the United States: established in Lee (Cape Coral) and Palm Beach counties, Florida; USGS NAS also records sightings in Georgia, Texas, Arizona, California and Virginia. Not in Canada.

identification.text: Very large lizard: typical adults about 5 ft (up to about 2.4 m) with a neck longer than the narrow head and a laterally compressed, rudder-like tail about 1.5 times body length.
Olive-green to black or brownish with cream or yellow stripes on the jaw and head and rows of yellowish V-shaped stripes from the neck that become bands or spots on the back.
Forked blue-black tongue and long sharp claws; juveniles are black with bold yellow cross-bars and spots.
Nothing native to the U.S. reaches this size with these features (USGS).

habitat.text: In Florida, favoured habitat is along canal systems and water edges, including coastal mangroves and salt marshes; native habitat is woodland, savanna, scrub, swamp and mangrove near water.

behavior.text: Semi-aquatic, mostly diurnal, basking on rocks and branches and often near water; strong swimmer that can stay under for 12-15 minutes.
Skilled climber; sleeps on branches or submerged in warm weather or in burrows when cooler; lays 12-60 eggs in burrows.
Generalist predator of crabs, crayfish, mollusks, fish, frogs, reptiles, birds, eggs and small mammals.

resources.title: Rough earth snake
resources.description: Identify the rough earth snake (Virginia striatula), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Rough earth snake (Virginia striatula): Small, plain, secretive snake, 7-10 in, uniform gray, brown or reddish-brown with an unmarked cream or light-gray belly. Strongly keeled back scales (feels rough), 5 upper-lip scales, a single scale between the nostrils and one postocular scale touching the eye; anal plate usually divided. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri (Ozarks), Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe lists the species as Haldea striatula (genus resurrected by McVay and Carstens 2013); the Missouri Department of Conservation lists it as Virginia striatula, 'formerly Haldea striatula', so the source genus disagrees in direction.

rangeSummary.value: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri (Ozarks), Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small, plain, secretive snake, 7-10 in, uniform gray, brown or reddish-brown with an unmarked cream or light-gray belly.
Strongly keeled back scales (feels rough), 5 upper-lip scales, a single scale between the nostrils and one postocular scale touching the eye; anal plate usually divided.
Differs from the smooth earth snake by five supralabials, usually one preocular and keeled dorsal scales.
Compared with the smooth earth snake: Nearly smooth scales, 6 upper-lip scales, 2 scales between the nostrils and 2 postoculars (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Rocky hillsides of dry open woods, cedar glades, woodland edges, pastures, wooded bottomlands, hammocks, pine flatwoods, gardens and vacant urban lots, where moisture and cover occur.

behavior.text: Semifossorial and seldom above ground; hides under logs, flat rocks and leaf litter and may be active at night in warm, damp weather.
Eats mainly earthworms, occasionally slugs, snails, small frogs and lizards.
Active March-October (late March to early November in Missouri); young 2-13 per litter are born live in late July-September.

resources.title: Smooth earth snake
resources.description: Identify the smooth earth snake (Virginia valeriae), tell it from its lookalikes, and see its habitat, behaviour and North American range.
resources.quickAnswer: Smooth earth snake (Virginia valeriae): Small snake 6-13 in; gray, tan, brown or red-brown above with tiny black dots on the head and a faint pale line down the back in some. Pale yellow to white below; scales smooth or weakly keeled in 17 rows. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Range
keyFacts.value: Eastern and central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia; not in Canada.

taxonomicNotes.text: NatureServe notes that Virginia is polyphyletic (Haldea resurrected for V. striatula) and that V. valeriae is close to Tropidoclonion lineatum; no source read renames V. valeriae itself.

rangeSummary.value: Eastern and central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia; not in Canada.

identification.text: Small snake 6-13 in; gray, tan, brown or red-brown above with tiny black dots on the head and a faint pale line down the back in some.
Pale yellow to white below; scales smooth or weakly keeled in 17 rows.
Compared with the rough earth snake it has 6 upper-lip scales, 2 scales between the nostrils and 2 postoculars, and an always-divided anal plate (Missouri Department of Conservation comparison).
Compared with the rough earth snake: Strongly keeled back scales, 5 upper-lip scales, 1 scale between the nostrils and 1 postocular (Missouri Department of Conservation).

habitat.text: Deciduous and pine woods, rocky wooded slopes, moist floodplain woodland, forest edges, old fields and wooded residential areas.

behavior.text: Secretive; hides in leaf litter, pulpy logs or under logs and trash; may aggregate in hibernation.
Eats mainly earthworms, also slugs and small soft-bodied invertebrates; gives birth to 3-8 young.
Active April to October/November in the north; surface activity peaks after heavy rains.

content.plainText: Confirm a american alligator before you act. Compared with the american crocodile: Narrower snout and a fourth lower tooth that protrudes upward near the snout tip.
Confirm a burmese python before you act. Compared with the northern african python: Less vivid back pattern and black-and-white belly scales; Burmese python belly scales are white.
Confirm a red-eared slider before you act. Compared with the painted turtle: Two yellow patches behind each eye instead of the slider's single red streak (per Animal Diversity Web).
Confirm a timber rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the milk snake: Slender with smooth glossy skin, no rattle and no facial pit.
Confirm a eastern copperhead before you act. Compared with the water snakes and cottonmouth: Animal Diversity Web notes they resemble copperheads but differ in pattern and behaviour.

Confirm a prairie rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the western rattlesnake: Formerly grouped with C. viridis; ranges from southern British Columbia to Baja California and east to the Rockies.
Confirm a western rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the prairie rattlesnake: Former parent species; occupies the plains east of the Rockies from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Confirm a american bullfrog before you act. Compared with the green frog: Has a ridge along each side of the back and a banjo-string call; bullfrogs have no such ridges.
Confirm a green frog before you act. Compared with the american bullfrog: Lacks the dorsolateral ridges.
Confirm a northern leopard frog before you act. Compared with the pickerel frog: Squarish spots and yellow or orange on the hidden hind-limb and groin surfaces.
Confirm a plains leopard frog before you act. Compared with the northern leopard frog: Can be green, usually lacks the pale eardrum spot, ridges not inset at the rear.

Confirm a western tiger salamander before you act. Compared with the eastern tiger salamander: Ranges meet and meld in the Great Plains, so the two cannot be separated by appearance alone; locality is the practical guide.
Confirm a eastern tiger salamander before you act. Compared with the western tiger salamander: Ranges meld in the Great Plains; distribution is the practical guide.
Confirm a western toad before you act. Compared with the woodhouse's toad: Woodhouse's toad has L-shaped cranial crests and parotoid glands longer than the eye; the western toad has neither.

Confirm a great plains toad before you act. Compared with the woodhouse's toad: Woodhouse's toad has an L-shaped cranial crest and a white back stripe rather than a raised snout shield with V-shaped ridges and large white-edged blotches.

Confirm a woodhouse's toad before you act. Compared with the western toad: Western toad lacks cranial crests and has short oval parotoid glands; Woodhouse's has L-shaped crests and elongate glands longer than the eye.

Confirm a black salamander before you act. Compared with the clouded salamander: Clouded salamander has squared toe tips and brassy specks on a brown, often lighter back; black salamander toe tips are not squared and adults are slate to black.

Confirm a wandering salamander before you act. Compared with the clouded salamander: Formerly treated as the same species (A. ferreus); the sources read give no simple field mark, so locality and expert identification are the guides.
Confirm a tiger whiptail before you act. Compared with the new mexico whiptail: Female-only species, smaller than the western whiptail, with a blue tint on the underbelly and tail end.

Confirm a southern california slender salamander before you act. Compared with the black-bellied slender salamander: Black-bellied has a thinner body and may have a lighter dorsal stripe; the garden slender salamander has a slightly wider body and lighter grey belly.
Confirm a forest sharp-tailed snake before you act. Compared with the common sharp-tailed snake: Shorter tail with fewer subcaudal scales (24-42 versus 43-58).

Confirm a common sharp-tailed snake before you act. Compared with the forest sharp-tailed snake: Forest sharp-tailed snake has a longer tail with more subcaudal scales (43-58 versus 24-42 in this species).

Confirm a western diamond-backed rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the mohave rattlesnake: Often slightly greenish, with thick white and narrower black tail bands, where the diamondback's tail bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro).

Confirm a mohave rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the western diamond-backed rattlesnake: Tail bands are more uniform in width and the body lacks the Mohave's greenish tinge (NPS Saguaro; NPS Parashant).
Confirm a great basin collared lizard before you act. Compared with the eastern collared lizard: Eastern collared lizard has a black-lined mouth; Great Basin lacks oral melanin (NatureServe; CPW).

Confirm a eastern collared lizard before you act. Compared with the great basin collared lizard: Great Basin lacks the black mouth lining and males have a compressed tail with a pale dorsal stripe (NatureServe).

Confirm a baja california collared lizard before you act. Compared with the great basin collared lizard: Great Basin lacks the widely separated posterior collars and slender white dorsal bars (NatureServe); listed as similar species by theNAT.

Confirm a coastal giant salamander before you act. Compared with the cope's giant salamander: Pacific giant is larger with a wider head and longer legs; when legs are pressed against the body the toes touch or cross (WDFW).

Confirm a northern alligator lizard before you act. Compared with the southern alligator lizard: Larger (up to 5.5 in snout-vent), yellow or gold eyes, and no dark pigment on the lateral edges of the belly scales (WDFW).

Confirm a southern alligator lizard before you act. Compared with the northern alligator lizard: Smaller (under 3.9 in snout-vent), brown eyes, dark pigment on the lateral edges of the belly scales (WDFW).
Confirm a mediterranean gecko before you act. Compared with the western banded gecko: Native western banded gecko lacks the Mediterranean gecko's raised tubercles on bumpy skin (NDOW).
Confirm a desert nightsnake before you act. Compared with the chihuahuan nightsnake: Lacks the extra scale in front of the eye, behind the nostril (CPW).
Confirm a coast nightsnake before you act. Compared with the desert nightsnake: Listed by theNAT as a similar species; no distinguishing marks were published on the pages read.

Confirm a california kingsnake before you act. Compared with the california mountain kingsnake: Red, black and white ringed pattern with red bands bordered by black (WDFW); listed as a similar species by theNAT.

Confirm a western milk snake before you act. Compared with the coral snakes: Coral snakes have red and black bands of about equal width separated by thin yellow or white bands; the milksnake's red is widest (CPW).

Confirm a arizona mountain kingsnake before you act. Compared with the coral snakes: US coral snakes have the pattern red-yellow or white-black-yellow or white-red with thin pale bands, with red and black about equal in width (CPW).
Confirm a california mountain kingsnake before you act. Compared with the coral snakes: Harmless and superficially resembles a coral snake; its red bands are bordered by black (WDFW).
Confirm a smooth green snake before you act. Compared with the rough green snake: Has keeled rather than smooth dorsal scales.
Confirm a great plains ratsnake before you act. Compared with the bullsnake: Scales have more distinct keels (Animal Diversity Web).
Confirm a pygmy short-horned lizard before you act. Compared with the greater short-horned lizard: Larger; wide notch between the head horns gives a heart-shaped head, horns project horizontally.
Confirm a greater short-horned lizard before you act. Compared with the pygmy short-horned lizard: Much smaller as an adult, lacks the wide notch between head horns, horns project almost vertically.
Confirm a desert horned lizard before you act. Compared with the greater short-horned lizard: Short head spines and high-elevation habitat, versus long head spines at low elevation.
Confirm a gophersnake before you act. Compared with the rattlesnakes (crotalus spp.): Have a rattle; the gophersnake lacks one (Animal Diversity Web).
Confirm a gilbert's skink before you act. Compared with the western skink: Western skink has a conspicuous white or beige stripe down each side; confirm against a field guide.
Confirm a western skink before you act. Compared with the western fence lizard: Keeled, prickly scales and never a blue tail.
Confirm a dunn's salamander before you act. Compared with the western red-backed salamander: Lacks blotches and flecks of the stripe colour on the sides of the body.

Confirm a california treefrog before you act. Compared with the baja california treefrog: Usually has a dark eye stripe, more often green, smaller toe pads; tadpoles have eyes at the margin of the head.
Confirm a baja california treefrog before you act. Compared with the california treefrog: Larger toe pads and usually no dark eye stripe.

Confirm a boreal chorus frog before you act. Compared with the sierran treefrog: Adults of other Montana frogs and toads are much larger with webbed hind feet; only the Sierran treefrog is similarly small, and its range does not overlap.
Confirm a pacific treefrog before you act. Compared with the sierran treefrog: Not separable by appearance; genetics and range distinguish them (Montana Field Guide).
Confirm a sierran treefrog before you act. Compared with the pacific treefrog: Distinguishable only by genetics (Montana Field Guide).
Confirm a western patch-nosed snake before you act. Compared with the striped whipsnake: Slender, black to brown back with four narrow stripes (Zion NPS key).
Confirm a common chuckwalla before you act. Compared with the gila monster: Dorsal scales are large and beadlike and lack femoral pores; chuckwalla has small granular scales and femoral pores.
Confirm a prairie lizard before you act. Compared with the eastern fence lizard: Can be impossible to tell apart by pattern in Missouri; DNA testing needed (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Confirm a common sagebrush lizard before you act. Compared with the western fence lizard: Larger, prickly scales with longer spines, yellow or orange on the rear of the thighs, and a checkered or V-shaped pattern.
Confirm a desert spiny lizard before you act. Compared with the clark's spiny lizard: Found at higher elevation, often in trees; black and white stripes on the forelimbs (Tuzigoot NPS page).
Confirm a western fence lizard before you act. Compared with the common sagebrush lizard: Smaller scales with shorter spines and pale dorsolateral stripes; no yellow on the thighs.
Confirm a granite spiny lizard before you act. Compared with the desert spiny lizard: Listed as a similar species by the San Diego Natural History Museum atlas (no distinguishing marks given).

Confirm a plateau fence lizard before you act. Compared with the prairie lizard (sceloporus consobrinus): Near-identical in the hand; Colorado Parks and Wildlife says the plateau fence lizard looks slightly spinier, and they are separated mainly by range.

Confirm a yellow-backed spiny lizard before you act. Compared with the desert spiny lizard (sceloporus magister): Treated as a subspecies of S. magister until recently; the sources read give no field character, so separate mainly by range and the black neck collar with yellow dorsal pattern described here.

Confirm a plains spadefoot before you act. Compared with the mexican spadefoot (spea multiplicata): Lacks the hard boss between the eyes, has red-tipped tubercles, and reportedly smells of peanuts when handled; its call is a longer, stuttering snore.

Confirm a great basin spadefoot before you act. Compared with the plains spadefoot (spea bombifrons): Separated mainly by range; plains spadefoot has a hard boss between the eyes, a four-line hourglass marking and a brief snore call.

Confirm a mexican spadefoot before you act. Compared with the plains spadefoot (spea bombifrons): Has a hard bony boss between the eyes and does not smell of peanuts; its call is a brief snore, faster than the Mexican spadefoot's long stuttering snore.

Confirm a smith's black-headed snake before you act. Compared with the western black-headed snake (tantilla planiceps): Visually similar; separated mainly by range, as T. planiceps is now the California and Baja California species while populations east of California belong to T. hobartsmithi.

Confirm a western black-headed snake before you act. Compared with the smith's black-headed snake (tantilla hobartsmithi): Visually similar; Smith's has a cream collar and a reddish belly stripe and occurs east of California, whereas the western black-headed snake is the California/Baja species.

Confirm a aquatic gartersnake before you act. Compared with the sierra gartersnake (thamnophis couchii): Distinguished mainly by range: Sierra gartersnake is the Sierra Nevada species, aquatic gartersnake the Coast Ranges species; both were once lumped as T. couchii.

Confirm a sierra gartersnake before you act. Compared with the aquatic gartersnake (thamnophis atratus): Distinguished mainly by range; aquatic gartersnake occupies the Coast Ranges west of the Central Valley.

Confirm a black-necked gartersnake before you act. Compared with the checkered gartersnake (thamnophis marcianus): Checkered gartersnake has 21 rows of keeled dorsal scales, a pale-yellow crescent behind the head and a single thick black neck line, versus 19 rows and two black neck blotches in the black-necked.

Confirm a terrestrial gartersnake before you act. Compared with the common gartersnake (thamnophis sirtalis): Common gartersnake has 7 upper labials, 19 scale rows at midbody and a uniformly dark head; terrestrial usually has 8 upper labials and 21 rows.

Confirm a checkered gartersnake before you act. Compared with the black-necked gartersnake (thamnophis cyrtopsis): Black-necked has 19 dorsal scale rows and two black blotches on the neck sides, versus 21 rows and a single black neck line in the checkered.

Confirm a plains gartersnake before you act. Compared with the common gartersnake (thamnophis sirtalis): Plains gartersnake's lateral stripe sits on scale rows 3 and 4; the common gartersnake's is on rows 2 and 3.

Confirm a common gartersnake before you act. Compared with the ribbon snakes (thamnophis sauritus, t. butleri): Close relatives of similar appearance; Animal Diversity Web lists them as the species commonly confused with the common gartersnake.

Confirm a sonoran lyresnake before you act. Compared with the california lyresnake (trimorphodon lyrophanes): Occurs west of the Salton Trough in southern California and Baja California; specimens from contact zones in southeastern California or southern Nevada may be hard to identify.

Confirm a california lyresnake before you act. Compared with the sonoran lyresnake (trimorphodon lambda): Sonoran lyresnake occurs east of the Salton Trough; specimens from contact zones in southeastern California or southern Nevada may be difficult to identify.

Confirm a long-tailed brush lizard before you act. Compared with the ornate tree lizard (urosaurus ornatus): Tail under twice the body length and a series of smaller scales down the middle of the enlarged dorsal band.

Confirm a baja california brush lizard before you act. Compared with the long-tailed brush lizard (urosaurus graciosus): Tail more than twice the body length and relatively large dorsal scales that change abruptly to granular side scales.

Confirm a ornate tree lizard before you act. Compared with the long-tailed brush lizard (urosaurus graciosus): Tail more than twice the body length and no row of smaller scales down the middle of the enlarged dorsal band.

Confirm a desert night lizard before you act. Compared with the arizona night lizard (xantusia arizonae): Granite-adapted rather than yucca-dwelling; Arizona populations formerly called X. vigilis are now split among X. arizonae, X. bezyi and X. wigginsi.

Confirm a northern cricket frog before you act. Compared with the southern cricket frog: Southern is smaller and more slender, with a more pointed snout, longer legs, less toe webbing, and a dark longitudinal stripe on the rear of the thigh.
Confirm a southern cricket frog before you act. Compared with the northern cricket frog: Northern is larger and stockier with a blunter snout, shorter legs, more webbing and more prominent warts.

Confirm a two-toed amphiuma before you act. Compared with the three-toed amphiuma: Three-toed has three toes on each foot (two-toed has two), and the two species overlap in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.
Confirm a three-toed amphiuma before you act. Compared with the two-toed amphiuma: Two-toed has two toes on each foot (three-toed has three); both occur in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama.
Confirm a american toad before you act. Compared with the southern toad: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which American lacks.
Confirm a fowler's toad before you act. Compared with the american toad: American has only one or two warts per dark back spot.

Confirm a oak toad before you act. Compared with the southern toad: Adult oak toads are often mistaken for half-grown southern toads; the oak toad is only 1.9-3.3 cm with a long pale dorsal stripe and teardrop-shaped parotoid glands.

Confirm a southern toad before you act. Compared with the american toad: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which helps separate it from the American toad.

Confirm a worm snake before you act. Compared with the northern red-bellied snake: Connecticut DEEP notes the worm snake is sometimes confused with it; the worm snake is uniform brown above with a pink belly, a tiny head and a spined tail tip.
Confirm a scarlet snake before you act. Compared with the scarlet kingsnake: Its bands encircle the whole body including the belly; scarlet snake has a plain white belly.

Confirm a southern painted turtle before you act. Compared with the painted turtle: The painted turtle (western painted in Missouri) usually lacks the broad lengthwise stripe on the carapace; Tennessee WRA notes genetics are required to separate them with certainty.
Confirm a spotted dusky salamander before you act. Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Very similar; best separated by range (northern dusky is the northeastern species).
Confirm a northern dusky salamander before you act. Compared with the spotted dusky salamander: Near-identical; separated by range.
Confirm a seal salamander before you act. Compared with the black-bellied salamander: Black belly and two rows of small white dots along the sides.
Confirm a allegheny dusky salamander before you act. Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Robust with no straight pale dorsal stripe; belly whitish with dark speckles.
Confirm a black mountain salamander before you act. Compared with the seal salamander: Lighter belly giving a distinct back-to-belly contrast.
Confirm a northern two-lined salamander before you act. Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: 14 costal grooves rather than 15-16; ranges to the south.
Confirm a two-lined salamander before you act. Compared with the northern two-lined salamander: 15-16 costal grooves; occurs to the north.
Confirm a three-lined salamander before you act. Compared with the longtail salamander: Yellow to orange with vertical black bars on the tail rather than three bold body stripes.
Confirm a longtail salamander before you act. Compared with the three-lined salamander: Three bold dark stripes along body and tail, not vertical tail bars.
Confirm a dwarf salamander before you act. Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: Five toes on each hind foot.
Confirm a common map turtle before you act. Compared with the false map turtle: Lines form a web on the shell and a backward L behind the eye.
Confirm a pascagoula map turtle before you act. Compared with the alabama map turtle: Low-domed shell with concentric yellow semicircles on the marginals and no nasal trident; Mobile Bay drainage.
Confirm a ouachita map turtle before you act. Compared with the false map turtle: Lines form a web over the shell; often a backward L behind the eye.
Confirm a mississippi map turtle before you act. Compared with the ouachita map turtle: Large blotch below the eye and ringed blotches on the scutes.
Confirm a alabama map turtle before you act. Compared with the pascagoula map turtle: Higher-domed shell with spines on the keel; nasal trident usually present.
Confirm a kentucky spring salamander before you act. Compared with the northern dusky salamander: Much smaller and browner with a keeled tail and no salmon-orange colour.
Confirm a four-toed salamander before you act. Compared with the southern two-lined salamander: Five toes on each hind foot and no tail constriction.
Confirm a bird-voiced treefrog before you act. Compared with the cope's gray treefrog: Warty skin and orange-yellow hidden hindleg surfaces; trill rather than birdlike whistle.
Confirm a cope's gray treefrog before you act. Compared with the gray treefrog: Identical in appearance; slower, more musical trill.
Confirm a green treefrog before you act. Compared with the squirrel treefrog: Smaller (about 3 cm), greenish to brown, often blotched, with a nasal 'rain' call.
Confirm a pine woods treefrog before you act. Compared with the squirrel treefrog: Light stripe on the upper jaw and no orange spots on the thighs.
Confirm a barking treefrog before you act. Compared with the green treefrog: Smooth skin and a bright white or yellowish side stripe; smaller.
Confirm a squirrel treefrog before you act. Compared with the green treefrog: Larger with a white or yellowish side stripe running onto the leg.
Confirm a gray treefrog before you act. Compared with the cope's gray treefrog: Indistinguishable by sight; faster, higher-pitched trill.

Confirm a eastern mud turtle before you act. Compared with the striped mud turtle: Striped mud turtle (Kinosternon baurii) has a pair of head stripes and usually carapace stripes; eastern mud turtle lacks carapace stripes.
Confirm a prairie kingsnake before you act. Compared with the copperhead: Copperheads have brown hourglass crossbands; prairie and mole kingsnakes have dorsal blotches.

Confirm a scarlet kingsnake before you act. Compared with the eastern coral snake: Venomous coral snake has a black snout and red bands touching yellow; scarlet kingsnake has a red snout and red touching black.
Confirm a northern crawfish frog before you act. Compared with the gopher frog: Gopher frog (Rana capito) has a pigmented belly and lacks the light borders around the dark dorsal spots.
Confirm a pig frog before you act. Compared with the american bullfrog: Pig frog has a much more pointed snout and is smaller than the bullfrog.

Confirm a pickerel frog before you act. Compared with the northern leopard frog: Pickerel frog has squarish, parallel dorsal spots and a yellow-orange groin; Animal Diversity Web calls the two visually similar.

Confirm a alligator snapping turtle before you act. Compared with the common snapping turtle: Alligator snapping turtle has a larger head, an extra row of scutes on each side of the shell and lacks the saw-toothed mid-dorsal tail ridge.
Confirm a diamond-backed terrapin before you act. Compared with the common snapping turtle: Terrapin has black-spotted head and neck and lacks a long saw-toothed tail.

Confirm a eastern coral snake before you act. Compared with the scarlet kingsnake: Scarlet kingsnake has a red snout and red bands touching black; coral snake has a black snout and red touching yellow.

Confirm a red river waterdog before you act. Compared with the mudpuppy: Common mudpuppy is larger (to about 19 in); Red River mudpuppy has a lighter ground colour, more numerous spots and a wide pale unspotted belly strip.
Confirm a mudpuppy before you act. Compared with the red river mudpuppy: Red River mudpuppy is smaller (max about 12 in) with more distinct spots and a pale unspotted central belly strip.

Confirm a gulf salt marsh snake before you act. Compared with the banded water snake: Saltmarsh snake typically has 21 dorsal scale rows, a smaller head and a laterally compressed tail base; banded water snake has 23 rows.

Confirm a green water snake before you act. Compared with the northern cottonmouth: Cottonmouth is heavier-bodied with a chunky head, a facial pit between nostril and eye, and a light line from eye to mouth corner.

Confirm a plainbelly water snake before you act. Compared with the mississippi green watersnake: Green watersnake has small subocular scales between eye and lip scales and a dark belly with yellow half-moons; plain-bellied has a near-uniform belly.

Confirm a diamondback water snake before you act. Compared with the northern cottonmouth: Cottonmouth has a distinctly triangular head, a sensory pit between nostril and eye, a light line from eye to mouth corner, and no chainlike dark back pattern.

Confirm a northern water snake before you act. Compared with the northern cottonmouth (water moccasin): Commonly mistaken for it; the northern water snake is non-venomous (Animal Diversity Web gives no further field mark).

Confirm a eastern newt before you act. Compared with the red salamander: Red salamander has about 16 costal grooves, a black chin and a yellow iris; the newt has rough skin without prominent grooves on the sides.
Confirm a slender glass lizard before you act. Compared with the eastern glass lizard: Eastern glass lizard has no stripe on the middle of the back and no stripes below the lateral groove.
Confirm a mimic glass lizard before you act. Compared with the snakes (legless look-alikes): Snakes have wide belly scales, fixed eye coverings, no ear openings, short tails and more flexible bodies.

Confirm a eastern glass lizard before you act. Compared with the slender glass lizard: Slender glass lizard has a dark middorsal stripe or dashes and stripes below the lateral groove; eastern has neither.
Confirm a corn snake before you act. Compared with the southern copperhead: Corn snake has a narrower head, lighter coloration and square spots.
Confirm a gray rat snake before you act. Compared with the central (eastern) ratsnake: Western ratsnake has a distinct checkerboard pattern; both have weakly keeled scales (Animal Diversity Web).
Confirm a florida pine snake before you act. Compared with the rat snakes (pantherophis) and kingsnakes: They have only 2 prefrontal scales, and rat snakes have a divided anal scale.
Confirm a coal skink before you act. Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has a stripe down the centre of the back; coal skink does not.
Confirm a five-lined skink before you act. Compared with the southeastern five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has an enlarged row of scales under the tail and prefers moister habitats.
Confirm a southeastern five-lined skink before you act. Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has an enlarged row of scales under the tail and usually uses moister habitat.
Confirm a broadhead skink before you act. Compared with the common five-lined skink: Five-lined skink has four labial scales around the mouth; broadhead skink has five.

Confirm a mississippi slimy salamander before you act. Compared with the other slimy salamanders (plethodon glutinosus complex): Identification based on appearance is impossible; range and genetics separate them.

Confirm a southern zigzag salamander before you act. Compared with the webster's salamander: Basically identical in appearance; separated by geographic range and genetics, and in P. websteri the stripe tends to be wavy only on the front half of the body.
Confirm a webster's salamander before you act. Compared with the southern zigzag salamander: Nearly identical; best separated by geographic distribution and genetics.
Confirm a mud salamander before you act. Compared with the red salamander: Red salamander has a yellow iris and a longer snout; mud salamander has brown eyes.
Confirm a red salamander before you act. Compared with the mud salamander: Mud salamander has brown eyes and a shorter snout; red salamander has a yellow iris.

Confirm a graham's crayfish snake before you act. Compared with the northern cottonmouth: The venomous cottonmouth is heavier-bodied with a large chunky head, a facial pit between nostril and eye, a darker body and a light line from eye to mouth corner (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Confirm a glossy crayfish snake before you act. Compared with the striped swampsnake (striped crayfish snake): Unpatterned belly and smooth body scales, versus keeled scales and a half-moon-marked belly in the glossy swampsnake (Florida Museum).

Confirm a queen snake before you act. Compared with the garter snakes: Garter snakes have a light dorsal stripe and an undivided anal plate; queen snakes lack a dorsal stripe and have a divided anal plate (Animal Diversity Web).

Confirm a eastern spadefoot before you act. Compared with the plains spadefoot: Has a raised boss between the eyes and a wedge-shaped spade at the base of each hind foot (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Confirm a southwestern fence lizard before you act. Compared with the plateau lizard (striped plateau lizard): Nearly identical in appearance to the southwestern fence lizard but genetically distinct, and its boundary with cowlesi is poorly known; the striped plateau lizard has a plain belly (Reptiles of Arizona).

Confirm a green ratsnake before you act. Compared with the glossy snake: Juvenile green ratsnakes resemble glossy snakes, but glossy snakes lack the elongated head and have an undivided anal plate (Tucson Herpetological Society).

Confirm a pygmy rattlesnake before you act. Compared with the timber rattlesnake: Adults are 3-5 ft long with a large rattle, versus a tiny rattle on the pygmy rattlesnake (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Confirm a stinkpot before you act. Compared with the striped mud turtle: Mud turtles have two plastral hinges and unkeeled carapaces, and lack skin visible between plastral scutes (Animal Diversity Web).
Confirm a brown snake before you act. Compared with the ring-necked snake: Young brown snakes have a pale neck ring but keeled scales, which ring-necked snakes lack (Animal Diversity Web).

Confirm a redbelly snake before you act. Compared with the copperhead (young): Copperheads are stout-bodied with hourglass markings, vertical pupils and a pit between nostril and eye (Missouri Department of Conservation).
Confirm a southeastern crowned snake before you act. Compared with the midland brownsnake: Lacks the black neck band and has keeled scales (Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency).
Confirm a ringed wall gecko before you act. Compared with the common (moorish) wall gecko: Lacks the two pairs of white shoulder spots (GeckoWeb).

Confirm a western ribbon snake before you act. Compared with the eastern ribbon snake: Eastern has a broad brown ventrolateral stripe; western has paired large parietal spots, a longer muzzle and longer tail (Animal Diversity Web).

Confirm a eastern ribbon snake before you act. Compared with the western ribbon snake: Western lacks the broad brown ventrolateral stripe and has large paired parietal spots and a longer muzzle and tail (Animal Diversity Web).

Confirm a rough earth snake before you act. Compared with the smooth earth snake: Nearly smooth scales, 6 upper-lip scales, 2 scales between the nostrils and 2 postoculars (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Confirm a smooth earth snake before you act. Compared with the rough earth snake: Strongly keeled back scales, 5 upper-lip scales, 1 scale between the nostrils and 1 postocular (Missouri Department of Conservation).
